Method: The paper distinguishes generated context from governed state; separates five conflated objects (true state, observations, evidence, belief, simulated state); defines a tiered governance standard; decomposes accountability into four information requirements; and proposes a six-level maturity framework.

Result: Provides conceptual framework converting "accountable clinical AI" from a slogan into an audit instrument, locating current LLM-centric practice at high capability but low maturity. No empirical results claimed - this is a conceptual/analytic contribution.

Conclusion: Longitudinal clinical reasoning should be treated as a state-estimation problem requiring governed patient state representations. The framework establishes conceptual hygiene for accountable clinical AI and poses research questions for developing Clinical World Models.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the dominant interface of clinical artificial intelligence, yet the interface they expose (text in, text out, one context window at a time) maintains no explicit, persistent, governed representation of what is currently true about a patient. This paper argues that longitudinal clinical reasoning is a state-estimation problem under partial observability, and that the axis on which clinical AI succeeds or fails is not the fluency of the model reading the record but the governance of the patient state it reasons over. We distinguish generated context from governed state; separate five objects that clinical AI habitually conflates (true state, observations, evidence, belief, and simulated state); define a tiered governance standard against which any clinical AI system can be audited; and show that an operational definition of accountability decomposes into four information requirements: an immutable evidence ledger with awareness-time versioning, a belief state distinct from accumulated evidence, an observation-process model, and claim-level causal typing. We are explicit that this decomposition is analytic rather than a necessity theorem, and that its value is conceptual hygiene: it converts "accountable clinical AI" from a slogan into an audit instrument. A six-level maturity framework separates what a system makes governable from what it can compute, locating current LLM-centric practice at high capability but low maturity. The paper is fully self-contained: the four research questions the framework poses are stated in the introduction, and the conclusion records what the paper establishes toward each; future work develops the buildable core of the architecture and the research program toward full Clinical World Models. No empirical result is claimed here.

</details>


### [50] [Do LLMs Know What to Ask and When? Evaluating Multi-Turn Information Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14808)
*Yepeng Huang,Jiawen Zhang,Michelle Dai,Xiaorui Su,Shanghua Gao,Zi Wang,Marinka Zitnik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes multi-turn information seeking as solving k-underspecified constraint satisfaction problems, creates MT-InfoSeek benchmark, and shows models struggle with recognizing missing information, making sufficient queries, and proper query ordering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current models fail to adequately handle underspecified user questions - they don't properly recognize when context is insufficient, identify missing information, ask for it appropriately, and wait to respond only when information determines a unique answer.

Method: Formalizes multi-turn information seeking as solving k-underspecified constraint satisfaction problems (k measures degree of missing information). Creates MT-InfoSeek evaluation suite with 5,251 problems and 9,006 instances across multiple domains. Evaluates models along three axes: what they ask, when they ask, and how information affects final answers.

Result: Models degrade as underspecification increases; recognize need for more info but underestimate how much (under-predict missing info 4x more than over-predict in k=2 logical problems). Fail to identify minimal sufficient query sets, improve only marginally when given true k, often stop early. Incorrect query order reduces accuracy. New "final sufficiency" metric reveals differences that final accuracy alone doesn't capture.

Conclusion: Multi-turn information seeking ability is distinct from answer generation and not measured by current LLM evaluations. Models need significant improvement in recognizing underspecification, determining needed information quantity, making minimal sufficient queries, and managing query ordering.

Abstract: When a user question is underspecified, a capable model should recognize that its context is insufficient, identify the missing information, ask for it, and respond only once that information determines a unique answer. We formalize multi-turn information seeking as solving a k-underspecified constraint satisfaction problem, where k is the number of variables jointly required to determine the target and therefore measures the degree of missing information. We instantiate the formulation in MT-InfoSeek, a controlled evaluation suite of 5,251 problems and 9,006 task instances spanning mathematics, logic, biology, medicine, and general knowledge. We evaluate models along three axes: what they ask, when they ask it, and how the acquired information affects the final answer. Performance degrades across models and domains as underspecification increases. Models recognize that additional information is needed but underestimate how much, and in logical problems at k = 2 they under-predict the degree of missing information about four times as often as they over-predict it. They also fail to identify a minimal sufficient set of queries, improve only marginally when given the true k, and often stop before acquiring sufficient information. In tasks with ordered dependencies, an incorrect query order reduces final accuracy even when the model eventually acquires all necessary information. We measure information seeking directly through final sufficiency, which records whether the acquired information determines the target independent of answer generation. This separation shows differences between models that final accuracy alone does not capture, and indicates that the ability to seek information over multiple turns is distinct from the ability to generate answers and is not measured by current LLM evaluations.

</details>


### [51] [MINT: Min-Selection Preference Distillation for Balanced Multi-Objective Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14828)
*Tony Tu,Sayan Chakraborty,Ruomeng Xu,Tony Qin,Austin Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Mint (MIN-selection preference distillation), a simple modification to preference distillation that selects candidates based on their weakest objective rather than additive reward sums, which prevents optimization collapse and achieves better-balanced multi-objective alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current preference-based training for language agents fails when aligning to multiple objectives simultaneously. When objectives are combined additively, optimization collapses onto whichever objective is cheapest to improve, sacrificing others. For example, a support agent might learn to sound warm while providing no real help. The root problem is that additive rewards have no notion of balance between objectives.

Method: The paper proposes Mint (MIN-selection preference disTillation), which makes a one-line change to preference distillation: instead of ranking sampled candidates by a weighted sum of rewards, it ranks them by their weakest objective. This selects the best-balanced candidate over the most lopsided one while keeping the DPO objective unchanged. This approach represents the p → -∞ limit of a generalized-mean family that spans from additive to worst-case selection.

Result: Across cooperative emotional support and adversarial negotiation tasks, min-selection improves both objectives while sharply reducing their imbalance. On emotional support, it raises the weaker axis from 0.37 to 0.64 (p < 10^-40), surpassing human experts and persisting across full multi-turn rollouts. A turn-by-turn analysis shows that min-selection corrects imbalance proportionally to how imbalanced the reference policy is, and its benefit endures throughout interactions as long as that imbalance persists.

Conclusion: Min-selection provides an effective solution to the multi-objective alignment problem in language agents by focusing on balanced performance across objectives rather than additive optimization. The approach successfully prevents the common failure mode where agents optimize for the easiest objective at the expense of others, leading to more robust and genuinely helpful agents.

Abstract: Aligning a language agent to several objectives at once is a persistent failure mode of preference-based training: when objectives are combined additively, optimization collapses onto whichever is cheapest to improve and sacrifices the rest, so a support agent learns to sound warm while giving no real help. The root issue is that an additive reward has no notion of balance. We introduce Mint (MIN-selection preference disTillation), a one-line change to preference distillation: rather than ranking sampled candidates by a weighted sum of rewards, we rank them by their weakest objective, distilling the best-balanced candidate over the most lopsided one with an unchanged DPO objective. This is the p -> negative infinity limit of a generalized-mean family spanning additive to worst-case selection. Across cooperative emotional support and adversarial negotiation, min-selection lifts both objectives while sharply cutting their imbalance; on emotional support it raises the weaker axis from 0.37 to 0.64 (p < 10^-40), surpassing human experts and persisting across full multi-turn rollouts. A turn-by-turn analysis yields our central finding: min-selection corrects imbalance in proportion to how imbalanced the reference policy is, and its benefit endures over an interaction precisely as long as that imbalance does.

</details>


### [52] [What the Reranker Sees: Multi-Aspect Page Annotation for Long-Document Multimodal Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14841)
*Guanchen Wu,Jiayuan Ding,Subhabrata Mukherjee,Carl Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trident improves long-document VQA by using structured annotation for better evidence selection and multi-lens prompting for synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current retrieve-then-read pipelines for long-document VQA suffer from poor evidence selection - even with good retrieval recall, rerankers miss visual evidence like tables, charts, and layout information when only seeing raw text snippets.

Method: Trident has two components: 1) Trident-R - a retriever-agnostic LLM reranker that converts candidates into structured semantic records (visual caption, section path, entity tags, concept hits, text snippet) and performs adaptive-K reranking; 2) Trident-S - a generation module that prompts VLM with topical, entity, and structural lenses before synthesis.

Result: Trident substantially improves retrieval F1 across five heterogeneous pools, with every reranked pool exceeding strongest baseline PageIndex. Trident-S adds up to 6.6 points in generation accuracy on open-ended synthesis questions. Best Trident configuration is strongest downstream QA pipeline with high inter-judge agreement (kappa = 0.913).

Conclusion: Structured annotation is crucial for effective evidence selection in long-document VQA, and multi-lens prompting improves open-ended question answering. The Trident framework provides a comprehensive solution for handling diverse document elements in lengthy documents.

Abstract: Long-document visual question answering (VQA) over documents of tens to hundreds of pages mixing text, tables, charts, and figures typically follows retrieve-then-read pipelines. In our setting, the bottleneck shifts from retrieval recall to reranker-side evidence selection: on MMLongBench-Doc, BGE-M3 reaches Recall@20 = 0.86 but only F1@5 = 0.254, and even the visual retriever ColPali reaches only F1@5 = 0.332; a text-only rerank LLM seeing only raw snippets misses table, chart, and layout evidence even when the upstream retriever encoded images. We propose Trident, with two complementary components: Trident-R, a retriever-agnostic LLM reranker that converts each candidate into an LLM-readable semantic record, including a visual caption, section path, entity tags, multi-axis concept hits, and a text snippet, then performs a single adaptive-K rerank call; and Trident-S, a generation-side module that prompts the VLM under topical, entity, and structural lenses before synthesis. On two long-document datasets, the annotation+rerank protocol substantially improves retrieval F1 across five heterogeneous pools, with every reranked pool exceeding the strongest adaptive-K baseline PageIndex. An LLM rerank without the annotation barely changes first-hit ranking, indicating the lift comes from the structured annotation. Trident-S targets open-ended synthesis questions by design, adding up to 6.6 points in generation accuracy on these questions. The best Trident configuration is the strongest downstream QA pipeline in our evaluation, with rankings consistent across two LLM judges (kappa = 0.913).

</details>


### [53] [Discovering High-Quality Chess Puzzles with Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14851)
*Allen Nie,Anirudhan Badrinath,Nicholas Tomlin,Timothy Dai,Carissa Yip,Rose E Wang,Emma Brunskill,Chris Piech*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using offline reinforcement learning on 1.5 billion chess puzzle-solving histories, researchers developed a system to automatically select pedagogically valuable puzzles for beginners, showing significant impact on stagnant learners and validating discoveries with expert chess players.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional chess puzzle generation by human experts is time-consuming and requires high domain expertise, while automated puzzle generation on platforms like Chess.com and Lichess often produces puzzles with low pedagogical value. Existing heuristics for puzzle recommendation are suboptimal, and there's a need for data-driven approaches to understand the pedagogical value of practice items and provide better learning support.

Method: Used offline reinforcement learning on a massive dataset of 1.5 billion puzzle-solving histories collected over one year from chess platforms. Applied offline policy evaluation to learn the pedagogical value of puzzles and develop an automated system for selecting optimal puzzle sets for chess learners, particularly beginners.

Result: The trained policy showed significant impact on beginners with puzzle-solving Elo ratings of 100-1000, especially for learners whose growth had been stagnant. Qualitative analysis with expert chess player annotations validated the pedagogical value of puzzles discovered by the model, confirming better teaching quality than existing automated approaches.

Conclusion: The pipeline successfully demonstrates that user interaction data can be leveraged to understand pedagogical values of practice items, promising future applications for data-driven educational systems across domains. The approach bridges the gap between automated content generation and pedagogical quality.

Abstract: Learning and skill mastery require extensive and deliberate practice. In many learning settings, producing high-quality pedagogical materials can require a high level of domain expertise and be very time-consuming. Pedagogical materials often need to train students to engage in different thinking patterns. In some domains, such as chess, puzzles are used to help students practice their skills in calculating the next moves and recognizing known patterns on a board. Giving students a practice set of puzzles to help them learn different modes of thinking is challenging because the teacher needs to carefully balance between different motifs and how many look-ahead steps a student needs to perform. Popular online platforms like Chess.com and Lichess offer players millions of puzzles. Unlike chess tactics puzzles procured by human experts, where chess beginners can learn valuable insights, these puzzles are automatically generated and often regarded as having low pedagogical value. These platforms also rely on a heuristic to recommend puzzles to users for practice. Using the user history data over an entire year, a total of 1.5 billion puzzle-solving histories, we learn the pedagogical value of a puzzle and how to automatically choose a set of puzzles to better support chess learners using insights from offline reinforcement learning. We show that using offline policy evaluation, our trained policy has significant impact on beginners with puzzle-solving Elo range of 100--1000, particularly for the group of beginners whose learning growth was stagnant. We also performed a qualitative analysis of the puzzles discovered by our model by collecting annotation ratings from expert chess players. The success of our pipeline shows promise for a future where we can understand the pedagogical values of practice items given general user interaction data.

</details>


### [54] [JarvisBench: Always-on Intelligence Between Humans and Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14870)
*Chen Chen,Zhehuai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Jarvis is an always-on attention-coordination layer that mediates human-agent interaction, with JarvisBench evaluating both user-initiated questions and agent-initiated judgment requests across diverse agentic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a mismatch between long-horizon agents that execute continuously and human attention that remains intermittent and scarce, creating a bidirectional coordination problem where users need immediate access while agents may need user judgment during unattended execution.

Method: Proposed Jarvis as an attention-coordination layer that mediates human-agent interface, and introduced JarvisBench with 45 agentic task instances (20 single-agent tasks, 25 multi-agent workstreams) across 19 domains, designed to integrate with arbitrary agent runtimes without modifying execution loops.

Result: JarvisBench provides a stable evaluation framework for assessing two key coordination dimensions: whether intermediaries can accurately answer user-initiated questions about ongoing work, and whether they can recognize when agents need user judgment, solicit it appropriately, and route it back to improve task outcomes.

Conclusion: By separating agent execution from attention coordination, JarvisBench offers a practical solution to human-agent coordination challenges and provides a stable evaluation target as agent capabilities evolve, with a reference implementation featuring full-duplex speech interface for natural user interaction.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents can execute continuously, but human attention remains intermittent and scarce. This creates a bidirectional coordination problem: users may need immediate access to an agent while work continues in the background, whereas agents may encounter consequential decisions that require user judgment after the user has stopped monitoring execution. We posit an always-on attention-coordination layer---\textit{Jarvis}\footnote{Named after the fictional AI assistant in \textit{Iron Man}.}---that mediates this interface and allocates human attention across one or more working agents. We introduce \textit{JarvisBench} to evaluate both directions of this coordination: whether an intermediary can accurately and promptly answer user-initiated questions about ongoing work, and whether it can recognize when an agent requires user judgment, solicit that judgment at the right moment, and route it back to improve task outcomes. JarvisBench contains 45 agentic task instances: 20 single-agent tasks and 25 workstreams organized into 10 multi-agent projects. The tasks span 19 domains and were selected and adapted from more than 2,000 public candidates. Crucially, the need for user attention arises naturally during execution rather than from an obvious omission in the initial prompt. JarvisBench is designed to integrate with arbitrary agent runtimes without modifying their underlying execution loops. Our reference implementation further provides a full-duplex speech interface, allowing users to reach Jarvis naturally while timely attention coordination supports agents working in the background. By separating agent execution from attention coordination, JarvisBench provides a stable evaluation target as agent capabilities continue to improve.

</details>


### [55] [Personalized Auto-Research: Towards a True AI Co-Scientist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14881)
*Bo Ni,Franck Dernoncourt,Hongjie Chen,Yu Wang,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Zhengzhong Tu,Tyler Derr,Ryan A. Rossi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces personalized auto-research, arguing that AI research assistants must be customized to individual researchers' backgrounds and contexts rather than being generic, researcher-agnostic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI co-scientists optimize for generic metrics like novelty or reviewer scores while ignoring individual researchers' unique contexts - their prior work, methodological repertoire, collaborators, and communities. This overlooks that research value is inherently personal and contextual.

Method: Proposes a framework with three components: (1) graph-grounded researcher representations, (2) personalization across the full research pipeline (retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, review), and (3) evaluation grounded in individual researchers rather than generic metrics.

Result: Introduces the problem of personalized auto-research as fundamental to creating genuine AI co-scientists. Identifies the "one-size-fits-all failure mode" where identical inputs produce identical outputs across different researchers, erasing the tacit knowledge essential for novel ideas.

Conclusion: Personalization is not just a convenience layer but the fundamental property that allows AI systems to serve as genuine co-scientists rather than generic instruments. The paper outlines a framework for personalized auto-research and discusses open challenges in this new paradigm.

Abstract: AI co-scientists that generate hypotheses, retrieve related work, design experiments, execute code, and draft full papers are beginning to change how research is carried out. Despite this rapid progress, state-of-the-art systems remain researcher-agnostic: given a research goal, they optimize novelty, validity, or reviewer score while ignoring the individual scientist who will use the output. This overlooks a fundamental fact about research, namely, that what counts as novel, valuable, or feasible depends on the researcher, including their prior work, methodological repertoire, and the collaborators and communities in which they are embedded. In this work, we introduce the problem of personalized auto-research, which conditions every stage of the research process on a representation of the individual researcher. We argue that personalization is not a convenience layer, but rather the fundamental property that allows an AI system to serve as a genuine co-scientist rather than a generic instrument. To address this problem, we propose a general and flexible framework that threads a graph-grounded researcher context through retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, and review. The framework consists of three fundamental components: (i) graph-grounded researcher representations, (ii) personalization across the full research pipeline, and (iii) evaluation grounded in the individual. Notably, we highlight a one-size-fits-all failure mode where distinct researchers issuing the same goal receive essentially the same research, erasing the tacit knowledge through which novel ideas arise. Finally, we discuss fundamental open problems and challenges.

</details>


### [56] [Frontier AI Forecasting Has a Measurement Problem: An Audit of Progress Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14903)
*Fabricio F Costa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits whether current AI forecasting methods using trends in benchmark scores, compute, or timelines are supported by actual measurement data, finding significant gaps in available data and methodological issues that challenge reliable frontier AI forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI forecasting often connects trends in benchmarks, compute, or timelines to dated capability targets, but it's unclear whether these connections are supported by actual measurement data rather than just fitted trends.

Method: Constructed a frozen event-centric record through August 2026 with 62 systems, 12 benchmarks, 7 criteria, 144 graded events, 27 source records, and 408 typed relations as an audit sample to examine available measurements.

Result: Critical data gaps exist: only 7 systems have both training compute and METR 50% task horizon data; training compute missing for 19/27 closed systems; no open-weight systems have METR horizon data. Benchmark succession creates measurement breaks. Most quantitative events (73.2%) come from one program, with 76.1% from lab releases.

Conclusion: Defensible AI forecasting requires explicit measurement systems with proper joins, protocols, links, and documented source dependencies—not just fitted curves. The paper identifies 16 complementary measurement directions but notes no single scalar metric replacement exists.

Abstract: Quantitative forecasts of frontier artificial intelligence often connect dated targets to trends in benchmark scores, training compute, release time, or expert belief. This paper audits whether the public measurement record supports those connections before another trend is fitted. I construct a frozen, event-centric record through 12 August 2026 with 62 selected systems, 12 versioned benchmarks, seven capability or impact criteria, 144 graded events, 27 source records, and 408 typed relations. The record is an audit sample, not a census. Only seven systems jointly observe estimated training compute and a METR 50 percent task horizon. Training compute is absent for 19 of 27 closed systems, including every selected closed release from 2026, while none of the 35 open-weight systems has a METR horizon observation. Benchmark succession creates a second break: a seven-system link from METR Time Horizon 1.0 to 1.1 has a log-scale slope of 1.206 (95 percent CI 1.021 to 1.390), whereas a six-system MMLU to MMLU-Pro comparison appears shift-like under logit and probit links but not under linear or logarithmic links. The observed bridges have about 80 percent power only for slope departures near 25 percent. Provenance is concentrated: 52 of 71 substantive quantitative events, or 73.2 percent, come from one measurement programme, and 76.1 percent are laboratory releases. A review of 56 methodological and empirical sources identifies 16 complementary measurement directions spanning resources, inference budgets, reliability, agentic work, safety, human preference, field outcomes, and forecast backtesting. No direction supplies a replacement scalar. The result is not that frontier AI forecasting is impossible, but that a defensible dated forecast is a claim about a versioned measurement system with explicit joins, protocols, links, and source dependence, not merely a fitted curve or calendar date.

</details>


### [57] [LLMs Can Predict Failure Risk, But Struggle to Predict Which Collaboration Protocol Pays Off: Cost-Aware Protocol Routing Across Reasoning Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14927)
*Chih-Hsuan Yang,Jingyan Jiang,Cheng-Hau Yang,Vikram Vasudevan,Huihuo Zheng,Venkatram Vishwanath,Rajeev Thakur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-agent LLM collaboration improves reasoning but adds computational cost; researchers evaluate different collaboration protocols and routing strategies to determine when extra collaboration is worth it, finding confidence-based gating effective but protocol-specific routing remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems can enhance reasoning through collaboration, but deployment requires cost-benefit analysis: deciding when additional computational expense of collaboration is justified by improved performance. Current approaches lack systematic understanding of optimal collaboration strategies across different problem types and protocols.

Method: Evaluated four collaboration protocols on competition-level math problems: direct solving (Baseline), iterative self-correction (Single), planner-executor-reviewer collaboration (PER), and multi-agent deliberation (Broadcast). Used large dataset (4,181 problems) with robustness checks across multiple domains. Tested fixed policies, trained routers, and frozen LLM routers, plus confidence-based gating strategies. Analyzed predictive power of pre-collaboration probes and self-confidence metrics.

Result: Pre-collaboration gpt-4o-2024-08-27 probe accurately predicts Baseline failures (0.8847 AUROC) and whether any collaboration helps (0.7683 AUPRC), but poorly identifies protocol-specific benefits. Confidence-based gating achieved 78.0% solve rate at 45K tokens vs. 73.8% at 71.3K tokens for frozen router. Oracle analysis shows retrospective coverage improvements of 23.2-58.3 points over Baseline, but protocol effectiveness varies by task type. Frozen routers often over-escalate while conservative policies under-escalate.

Conclusion: Confidence-based gating provides effective initial escalation decision, but optimal protocol-specific routing remains an open problem. Collaboration benefits are significant but protocol effectiveness varies substantially across tasks, making cost-aware protocol selection challenging despite good overall failure prediction.

Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can improve reasoning by spending more computation, but deployment requires deciding when extra collaboration is worth its cost. We isolate this decision by running every problem under four protocols while holding the solver fixed within each setting: direct solving (Baseline), iterative self-correction (Single), planner-executor-reviewer collaboration (PER), and multi-agent deliberation (Broadcast). The primary benchmark comprises 4,181 competition-level math problems; paired robustness checks cover four benchmarks spanning competition math, biology, and broader science with two solver families. Across fixed policies, trained routers, and frozen LLM routers, conservative policies under-escalate, whereas higher-solve frozen routers often over-escalate. A post-answer, pre-collaboration gpt-oss-120b probe ranks Baseline failures with 0.8847 AUROC (4,151 parseable cases; 95% CI [0.8732, 0.8955]). The same score remains informative for predicting whether any collaboration helps (0.7683 AUPRC), but is much weaker for identifying PER- or Broadcast-specific value (0.1674 and 0.1041 AUPRC). Separately, the pre-answer self-confidence gate reaches 78.0% solve at 45K tokens, compared with 73.8% at 71.3K for a frozen gpt-oss-120b router and 92.4% for a retrospective fixed-order oracle. Across 10 paired model-condition settings, the oracle adds 23.2-58.3 points of retrospective coverage over Baseline, but protocol profiles vary by task. In the six settings with held-out router evaluations, oracle gaps remain 18.5-28.9 points. Confidence can therefore support initial escalation, while protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved.

</details>


### [58] [Small Models Scout Bottleneck Order for Large-Model Data Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14936)
*Seungmin Choi,Jiwon Sung,Muhammad Umer,Abhiram Rao Gorle,Guijin Son,Youngjae Yu,John M. Cioffi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LogFloor algorithm uses small proxy models to identify optimal training order for skill bottlenecks, reducing token cost by 30-56% when transferring curriculum to larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small proxy models are commonly used to identify data mixtures for larger-scale training, but the paper asks whether their training trajectories can reveal another transferable structure: the optimal order in which larger models should resolve skill bottlenecks.

Method: Introduces LogFloor, a closed-loop controller that directs each training round toward current bottlenecks, producing phase-ordered resolution trajectories. The approach formulates "first-passage skill training" where each monitored skill has a target floor and the objective is to minimize tokens required to reach all floors.

Result: Across five bAbI skill slices on Qwen2.5-1.5B, LogFloor reduces token cost by 56.2% on average. In 70M-to-12B transfer, three-round replay of a 70M scout path reaches every floor in all eight target runs, saving 30.9% by pair mean, 39.4% in pooled training tokens, and 37.6% under source-cost accounting. On MMLU-control, a frozen scout path succeeds across all eight 12B runs.

Conclusion: Phase-ordered bottleneck resolution is identified as a transferable curriculum structure for monitored skill-targeted training, with collapsing paths to static mixtures or reversing phase order removing most benefits, while bottleneck labels alone remain partially useful.

Abstract: Small proxy models are commonly used to identify data mixtures for larger-scale training. We ask whether their training trajectories reveal another transferable structure: the order in which larger models should resolve skill bottlenecks. We formulate first-passage skill training, where each monitored skill has a target floor and the objective is to minimize the tokens required to reach all floors. We introduce LogFloor, a closed-loop controller that directs each round toward current bottlenecks, producing phase-ordered resolution trajectories. Across five bAbI skill slices on Qwen2.5-1.5B, LogFloor reduces token cost by 56.2% on average. In 70M-to-12B transfer, three-round replay of a 70M scout path reaches every floor in all eight target runs, saving 30.9% by pair mean, 39.4% in pooled training tokens, and 37.6% under source-cost accounting. On MMLU-control, a frozen scout path succeeds across all eight 12B runs. Collapsing a path to its static marginal mixture or reversing its phase order removes most benefits, while bottleneck labels alone remain partially useful. These results identify phase-ordered bottleneck resolution as a transferable curriculum structure for monitored skill-targeted training.

</details>


### [59] [When Is an Agent Evaluation Over? Outcome Finality and Cross-Unit Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14940)
*Avyay M. Casheekar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper argues that current agent evaluations incorrectly treat endpoint states as final results, failing to account for delayed operations and shared state between runs, leading to inaccurate scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent evaluation methods score models based on the state visible at the end of a stopped run (endpoint), but this doesn't ensure outcome finality or proper separation between different runs/trials. The endpoint doesn't guarantee that all operations have completed or that there's no state carryover between runs, potentially leading to inaccurate evaluation scores.

Method: The authors develop a "completion argument" framework specifying evidence needed for reliable evaluation decisions. They conduct: 1) controlled replay experiments with fixed agent actions to demonstrate how delayed operations affect scoring, 2) review of ten public evaluation protocols to assess documentation practices, and 3) propose an "open-effects record" system to track operations/resources that remain relevant after endpoints.

Result: 1) In controlled replay, endpoint and terminal labels differ for every delayed operation; delayed writes affect next run's score when state persists between runs but not after isolation or reset. 2) Protocol review shows all protocols document when runs stop and what's scored, but consistently lack documentation about unfinished operations and evidence for treating runs as separate trials. 3) The open-effects record proposal helps track post-endpoint relevant factors.

Conclusion: Agent evaluations should not treat endpoint states as final results without verifying outcome finality and run separation. Proper evaluation requires documenting both when operations finish and evidence for trial independence. The proposed open-effects record provides a systematic way to track potential post-endpoint influences on scoring accuracy.

Abstract: Current agent evaluations score models on the state visible at the end of a stopped run which they count as one trial. However, interpreting the score as a final result would require two conditions that the endpoint does not itself necessarily establish: outcome finality and cross-unit separation. These conditions are independent, since reconciling a delayed outcome can settle the label while runs still share state and isolating runs can prevent carryover while the scored outcome remains unfinished. We develop a completion argument that specifies the evidence needed for each decision and argue that a final label is justified only when anything that could still change the claimed outcome is resolved, bounded, or retained as uncertainty. First, in a controlled replay to demonstrate the mechanism where an agent's actions were held fixed, we find that the endpoint and terminal labels differ for every delayed operation, while a delayed write changes the next run's score when service state persists between runs but not after isolation or verified reset. Second, in a review of ten public protocols, we find that all protocols identify when a run stops and what is scored, while unfinished operations and the evidence for treating runs as separate trials are documented less consistently. Finally, we propose an open-effects record that lists operations or resources that may remain relevant after the endpoint, their current status, and whether they could change the scored outcome or affect another run.

</details>


### [60] [Skill Blocks: How Should an Agent Load Its Skill? A Caching-Correct Comparison of Pre-load, On-Demand Tool-Loading, Progressive Disclosure, and Hybrid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14943)
*Hironobu Nakasuji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Comparing four content-preserving skill loading methods shows no universal winner, but Hybrid reduces input tokens by 27.4-39.8% on some benchmarks, with even larger reductions (52.8-73.0%) on large multi-turn skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills are often injected in full on every request, which increases token costs unnecessarily. There's a need for more efficient skill loading methods to reduce computational overhead.

Method: The paper compares four content-preserving skill loading methods: Full (baseline), Skill Block, Reference, and Hybrid. Evaluation uses five benchmarks (SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, SynthProc) measuring token usage with raw input for single-turn tasks and cache-correct effective input for multi-turn tasks, plus paired outcome tests for quality assessment.

Result: No universal winner across all benchmarks. Hybrid reduces input by 27.4% on SearchQA and 39.8% on SpreadsheetBench. For large multi-turn skills, Skill Block and Hybrid achieve substantial reductions: 62.5% and 52.8% on ScienceWorld, 73.0% and 66.6% on SynthProc. ALFWorld shows smaller gains due to short, repeatedly needed procedures. Paired outcome tests show no quality differences but don't establish equivalence.

Conclusion: Conditional loading of agent skills is most beneficial when large portions of a skill are not needed on every turn. Different methods work best for different scenarios, with Hybrid and Skill Block providing substantial token savings in multi-turn tasks with large skills.

Abstract: Agent skills are often injected in full on every request, increasing token cost. We compare four content-preserving loading methods: Full, Skill Block, Reference, and Hybrid. Across SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SynthProc, we measure token usage using raw input for single-turn tasks and cache-correct effective input for multi-turn tasks. Results show no universal winner. Hybrid reduces input by 27.4% on SearchQA and 39.8% on SpreadsheetBench. On large multi-turn skills, Skill Block and Hybrid achieve substantial reductions, reaching 62.5% and 52.8% on ScienceWorld and 73.0% and 66.6% on SynthProc. ALFWorld shows smaller gains because procedures are short and repeatedly needed. Paired outcome tests detect no quality differences, though they do not establish equivalence. Overall, conditional loading is most beneficial when large portions of a skill are not needed on every turn.

</details>


### [61] [Trust Is Not Enough: Influence Calibration for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14945)
*Qizhen Lan,Xi Xiao,Xiangchen Guan,Mengchen Fan,Moule Lin,Jung Im Choi,Lijing Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICSD improves on-policy self-distillation for language agents by calibrating token-level supervision allocation based on influence on policy objectives rather than just teacher trust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation methods allocate supervision based primarily on teacher trust, but trust doesn't reveal whether emphasizing a token actually supports the current policy objective, creating a trust-utility mismatch.

Method: ICSD measures first-order response of importance-weighted RL surrogate contribution to teacher-directed output perturbations for each supervised token. Batch-adaptive calibration converts this non-stationary signal into bounded allocation weights while preserving auxiliary-loss mass within each action turn.

Result: ICSD improves all matched aggregate metrics over trust-only allocation across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, achieving 96.1% ALFWorld success and 93.1 WebShop score at 7B parameters. It reduces teacher-supported mass assigned to objective-opposed tokens from 60.1% to 37.8% and raises cosine compatibility with RL gradient by 0.192.

Conclusion: Influence calibration effectively addresses the trust-utility mismatch in on-policy self-distillation, providing better alignment between token supervision and policy objectives, leading to improved agent performance across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) gives language agents dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher on the policy's own trajectories. Existing methods allocate this supervision mainly by teacher trust, but trust does not reveal whether emphasizing a token supports the current policy objective. We call this the trust-utility mismatch and introduce Influence Calibration for Self-Distillation (ICSD). For each supervised token, ICSD measures the first-order response of its importance-weighted RL surrogate contribution to a teacher-directed output perturbation. Batch-adaptive calibration converts this non-stationary signal into a bounded allocation weight while preserving the original auxiliary-loss mass within each action turn. These detached weights affect only the distillation loss and require no additional model pass. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, ICSD improves all matched aggregate metrics over trust-only allocation under Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO), across two model families spanning 1.5B to 7B. At 7B, it reaches 96.1% ALFWorld success and a WebShop score of 93.1. Frozen-batch analyses show that ICSD reduces teacher-supported mass assigned to objective-opposed tokens from 60.1% to 37.8% and raises cosine compatibility with the RL gradient by 0.192. A companion repository is avail- able at https://github.com/lanqz7766/Influence-Calibration-for-On-Policy-Self-Distillation-in-Agentic-RL.

</details>


### [62] [RETRACE: Resilience-Guided Trait-Conditioned Craving Estimation from Wearable Physiology in Opioid Use Disorder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14947)
*Yi Xiao,Harshit Sharma,Dessa Bergen-Cico,Asif Salekin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RETRACE is a resilience-guided framework that improves subject-independent opioid craving detection from wearable physiological signals by incorporating subject-level resilience traits rather than assuming uniform physiological interpretations across individuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Opioid craving detection from wearable signals is challenging due to craving's subjective and heterogeneous nature, especially under subject-independent evaluation. Craving signals are weak, sparse, and physiologically entangled with stress responses, which are stronger and more reproducible. Current approaches fail to account for how individual differences in psychological resilience affect stress regulation and craving vulnerability.

Method: RETRACE introduces a dual-encoder framework: 1) A frozen stress-pretrained encoder captures generalizable stress physiology, and 2) A resilience-conditioned craving encoder interprets stress physiology in subject-specific context. The method uses feature-level gating and representation-level fusion for lightweight personalization without requiring target-user craving labels or per-user retraining. It leverages reusable subject-level proxies like post-stress heart-rate recovery and autobiographical memory recall to capture resilience traits.

Result: RETRACE achieves up to 7% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline in subject-independent evaluation (leave-one-subject-out setup) on a novel multimodal OUD dataset containing wearable physiology, stress/craving annotations, and autobiographical narratives.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that reframing craving detection as trait-conditioned physiological interpretation, guided by resilience-related subject context, significantly improves subject-independent performance. This approach enables more accurate, personalized craving estimation without requiring labeled craving data from target users, supporting proactive interventions for opioid use disorder.

Abstract: Detecting opioid craving from wearable physiological signals is critical yet difficult, with the potential to support proactive interventions for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). This challenge is especially pronounced under subject-independent evaluation because craving is subjective, heterogeneous, and often physiologically entangled with stress. Our empirical analysis shows that stress elicits strong and reproducible autonomic responses, while craving-related signals are weaker, sparse, and largely embedded within stress-related physiology. We further show that psychological resilience, which shapes stress regulation and craving vulnerability, is not reliably observable from short-term wearable windows, but can be captured through reusable subject-level proxies, including post-stress heart-rate recovery and autobiographical memory recall.Motivated by these findings, we introduce RETRACE, a resilience-guided trait-conditioned framework for subject-independent craving estimation from wearable physiology. RETRACE reframes craving detection as trait-conditioned physiological interpretation: rather than assuming the same physiological pattern has the same meaning across individuals, it uses resilience-related subject context to guide inference. Technically, RETRACE introduces a novel dual-encoder design that separates generalizable stress physiology from subject-specific craving interpretation. It combines a frozen stress-pretrained encoder with a resilience-conditioned craving encoder, using feature-level gating and representation-level fusion to enable lightweight personalization without target-user craving labels or per-user retraining. We evaluate RETRACE on a novel multimodal OUD dataset containing wearable physiology, stress and craving annotations, and autobiographical narratives. Under LOSO setup, RETRACE achieves up to 7% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline

</details>


### [63] [T-LLM Compiler: Trusted LLM-based Code Optimization and Verification Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14953)
*Zahra Fazel,Sunanda Gamage,Shayan Shirahmad Gale Bagi,Amir H. Ashouri,Tomasz S. Czajkowski,Bryan Chan,Reza Azimi,Yaoqing Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: T-LLM Compiler combines LLMs with traditional compilers and verification tools to improve code optimization accuracy and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs struggle with complex code optimization tasks due to code complexity and inability to independently verify transformation correctness, despite recent advances making this a fundamental LLM task.

Method: Proposes T-LLM Compiler that uses a collaborative approach: high-level LLM code transformations, traditional compilers, and verification tools, with iterative optimization and verification strategies enabling corrective actions.

Result: Achieves up to 83.3% code optimization accuracy and up to 16.1% speedup on PolyBench/C benchmarks, with transformed code reaching average 26.7% speedup compared to standard baselines.

Conclusion: The T-LLM Compiler demonstrates an effective integration of LLMs with traditional compilation and verification approaches for code optimization, improving both correctness and performance while being released as open source.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened opportunities to apply high-level code transformations to the field of code optimization, and it has since emerged as one of the most fundamental tasks for LLMs to perform; however, at present, LLMs struggle to apply wide-ranging code optimization tasks due to both the complexity of the code and the inability to independently verify the correctness of the transformations. In this paper, we present the Trusted LLM (T-LLM) Compiler, which proposes an advancement in compiler technology through a collaborative effort involving high-level LLM code transformations, traditional compilers, and verification tools. Experimental results reveal that it can significantly improve code correctness when tested on a set of PolyBench/C benchmarks. Our approach facilitates iterative code optimization efforts with verification strategies that enable corrective actions. Through this approach, T-LLM Compiler achieves code optimization accuracy of up to 83.3% and a speedup of up to 16.1\% on the PolyBench/C benchmarks, with the transformed code reaching an average of 26.7% speedup wrt standard baselines. Additionally, we release the project's source code to the open-source community.

</details>


### [64] [Demand-Driven Vertiport Siting and Discrete-Event Fleet Simulation for On-Demand Urban Air Mobility Network Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14974)
*Hossein Z. Saghazadeh,Yonas Ayalew,Reza Ahmari,Parham Kebria,Abdollah Homaifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A demand-driven framework for designing on-demand Urban Air Mobility networks that links vertiport siting, fleet simulation, and travel-time feasibility, showing UAM works best for longer or congestion-heavy trips.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to design effective on-demand Urban Air Mobility (UAM) networks that can provide door-to-door travel feasibility while addressing operational challenges like spatial demand imbalance and resource allocation.

Method: Demand estimation from commuter/passenger data converted to spatial trip points, K-means clustering for candidate vertiport locations, network screening with range/constraints, discrete-event simulation modeling multi-vehicle dispatch, deadhead relocation, battery swaps, and flight performance using point-mass eVTOL performance model.

Result: In Greater Los Angeles case study, optimal design expands from 4 stations/4 eVTOLs at low demand to 16 stations/12 eVTOLs at high demand; larger fleets improve completion time and regularity but don't eliminate deadhead flights; UAM most defensible for longer or congestion-heavy trips where significant non-flight time remains.

Conclusion: The framework successfully integrates vertiport siting with operational simulation to design scalable UAM networks; spatial demand imbalance remains a persistent operational challenge requiring deadhead flights; UAM offers greatest travel-time savings for longer or congested trips where ground transportation inefficiencies can be bypassed.

Abstract: This paper presents a demand-driven framework for on-demand Urban Air Mobility (UAM) network design that links vertiport siting, fleet simulation, and door-to-door travel-time feasibility. Demand is estimated from commuter and passenger activity data, converted into spatial trip-end points, and clustered using K-means to generate candidate vertiport locations. Candidate networks are screened using range and minimum station-spacing constraints, then evaluated with a discrete-event simulation that models multi-vehicle dispatch, deadhead relocation, battery swaps, and service regularity. Flight time and energy consumption are computed using a point-mass eVTOL performance model. In a Greater Los Angeles case study, the preferred design expands from four stations and four eVTOLs at low demand to sixteen stations and twelve eVTOLs at the highest tested demand level. Results show that larger fleets improve completion time and vehicle-arrival regularity but do not eliminate deadhead flights, indicating that spatial demand imbalance remains an operational burden. The travel-time savings analysis further suggests that UAM is most defensible for longer or congestion-heavy trips where sufficient non-flight time remains after accounting for flight time.

</details>


### [65] [Does a Tool Result Carry More Authority Than Plain Text? Three Prospective Studies of False-Claim Adoption in a Synthetic Assignment Task with Claude Opus 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14992)
*Justin Bronder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs can adopt false information they previously wrote themselves when that information appears in tool-result formats rather than as plain assertions, showing context formatting influences information acceptance in self-referential reading tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models increasingly read from stores they also write to, there's concern about circular validation where models might accept their own earlier writings as verified facts. The research examines how different formats of presenting information affect whether models accept unsupported claims.

Method: The study used Claude Opus 5 in a synthetic lookup task where it selected color codes or abstained. A four-arm experimental design tested different formats: no target claim, prior assistant assertion, tool-result record, and tool-result with metadata wrapper. Subsequent preregistered studies included replication attempts and live text controls comparing tool-result vs inline JSON formats.

Result: False-code adoption rates varied significantly: 0% with no target or assistant assertions, 58% with tool-result records, and 63% with wrapped tool results. Tool results were accepted even in unsupported trials, ruling out fixed output bias. Replication showed tool-result superiority over assertions but rates dropped over time. Inline text alone produced 100% adoption, showing tool results not strictly necessary.

Conclusion: Formatting context significantly influences LLM information acceptance, with tool-result formats promoting adoption of unsupported claims. However, inline text is sufficient for false information adoption, and the effect is not exclusive to tool results. The findings highlight model sensitivity to presentation formats in self-referential information systems.

Abstract: Language-model systems increasingly read from stores they also write to, so a claim that was merely written earlier can return looking retrieved. We tested whether the message package carrying an unsupported assignment changes which answer a model gives in a synthetic lookup task. Claude Opus 5 selected a color code for a named item or abstained. In an exploratory four-arm study, false-code adoption was 0/24 with no target claim, 0/22 scorable trials when a prior assistant assertion named the target, 14/24 when a tool-result record named it, and 15/24 when that result used a ten-field metadata wrapper that marked it unchecked. The tool-result arm selected the record's code in 11/12 supported trials and 14/24 unsupported trials, ruling out a fixed output-token bias while leaving substantial planted-token heterogeneity. A document-preregistered replication reproduced the tool-result versus assistant-assertion gap, 7/24 against 0/24, one-sided Fisher exact p = 0.0047. The tool-result rate nevertheless fell from 14/24 to 7/24 across runs made four days apart. A second preregistered study gave the earlier comparison a live text control: both records were announced in advance and placed in the same final user turn, then target binding was swapped between the linked tool result and later inline JSON. Inline text was sufficient for false-code adoption in 60/60 trials; the tool-result condition produced 57/60, so the registered result-first superiority criterion failed, p = 1. The result does not show that tool results have no effect. It shows that native tool-result placement was not necessary and that this experiment did not find greater behavioral weight for the result package than for announced inline text. The findings concern a single model on one synthetic task template, accessed through one API.

</details>


### [66] [S2-MoE: Enabling Efficient Self-Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts on Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15018)
*Haochen Huang,Shengxuan Qiu,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: S2-MoE is an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for Mixture-of-Experts models on edge devices that combines routing-aware adaptive speculative expansion, reuse-aware expert gating, and shared context to achieve up to 5.3x speedup over standard autoregressive decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying large language models on edge devices faces severe memory and bandwidth constraints. While speculative decoding and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) individually help with inference efficiency, naive combination of these techniques leads to excessive verification overhead and poor expert reuse, limiting effectiveness in memory-bound edge settings.

Method: S2-MoE proposes three key techniques: 1) Routing-aware adaptive speculative expansion to reduce redundant verification, 2) Reuse-aware expert gating to improve verification efficiency, and 3) Shared context alignment between draft and target execution. The framework is implemented in llama.cpp for edge device deployment.

Result: S2-MoE achieves up to 5.3x speedup (approximately 2.0x on average) over standard autoregressive decoding across diverse MoE models and datasets on edge devices.

Conclusion: S2-MoE successfully addresses the challenges of combining speculative decoding with MoE architectures for edge deployment, demonstrating significant performance improvements through its intelligent routing and reuse optimization techniques while being implemented in practical edge-focused frameworks like llama.cpp.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) for inference on edge devices is challenging due to severe memory and bandwidth constraints. While speculative decoding and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have been proposed to improve inference efficiency, naively combining them often incurs excessive verification overhead and poor expert reuse, limiting their effectiveness in memory-bound edge settings. In this work, we propose S2-MoE, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for MoE inference on edge devices. S2-MoE reduces redundant verification through routing-aware adaptive speculative expansion, improves verification efficiency with reuse-aware expert gating, and aligns draft and target execution via shared context. Implemented in llama.cpp, S2-MoE achieves up to 5.3x speedup (about 2.0x on average) over standard autoregressive de?coding across diverse MoE models and datasets on edge devices.Code is available at https://github.com/angerybob/S2-MoE.

</details>


### [67] [Gathered, Not Admitted: How Attention Brings a Latent Variable into Verbalizable Form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15022)
*Parsa Mazaheri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers find that in language models, internal representations become more readable/accessible when the task requires flexible reuse of information, with this effect occurring in specific mid-depth layers rather than through a gating mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates how language models store and access latent information. The motivation is to understand what causes representations to become accessible/readable - specifically whether there's a "gating" mechanism controlling workspace access, or if accessibility emerges from task demands for flexible information reuse.

Method: Used Jacobian lenses on open-weight models across a benchmark with five arms sharing identical context. The study separates patch depth from readout depth to examine attention-mediated gathering. Tested different models (including 64-layer hybrid and 62-layer dense models) and analyzed where variables are installed and read versus transported.

Result: Found no evidence of a gating mechanism as predicted. Task demand increases concept visibility (+0.050 percentile rank). Variables are decoded from all arms via a shared linear map (6.4-9.0x above selection-corrected floor). The readable form emerges in a specific mid-depth window (17x above shallower depths) through attention-mediated gathering, not MLP outputs. This window appears at similar fractional depths across different model architectures.

Conclusion: The readable form of latent quantities emerges in specific mid-depth layers when task demands require flexible information reuse, not through a gating mechanism. However, readability doesn't directly correspond to functional use (components can differ 7.4x in what they contribute to the answer while appearing similar in readout metrics).

Abstract: Language models hold latent quantities in a form they can report on, and more of a quantity is present in that form when the task requires reusing it flexibly. What causes a representation to enter that form is open, and the word workspace invites an admission story: a gate that decides what gets in. Testing it on open-weight models with Jacobian lenses, over a benchmark whose five arms share an identical context, we find no gate where it predicts one. Demand raises a concept's lens visibility beyond what applying an operator to a supplied value produces: +0.050 [+0.045, +0.057] in percentile rank on our primary checkpoint, positive on all four we measure, though that arm answers at ceiling and the accuracymatched contrast is stronger under that readout. At the same time one shared linear map decodes the variable from every arm, the control included, at 6.4-9.0x its selection-corrected floor. What produces the later readable form at the queried position is attention-mediated gathering inside a mid-depth window: separating patch depth from readout depth puts transport there at least 17x above anywhere shallower under non-saturating readouts, with no tested MLP output contributing positively inside it. Under the saturating percentile rank the same grid does not localise the window, which is a fact about that measure. An arm that needs the variable for nothing concentrates sevenfold less, so the window is demand-specific. That window has two measured edges, a survival failure below and destruction above, and it falls at the same fractional depth in a 64-layer hybrid and a 62-layer dense model from another family. We localise where the variable is installed and read, not the route from the passage, which transports nothing. But the readout is not a calibrated measure of use: three components move it to within 12% of one another and differ 7.4x in what they do to the answer.

</details>


### [68] [LLM-Based Hierarchical Coordinated Control with Continuation-Aware Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15041)
*Changhong He,Jinda Gao,Xinkuan Liu,Le Zhang,Xizi Luo,Yu Mei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based hierarchical framework for complex system coordination that uses heterogeneous context reasoning, task-specific controllers, and continuation-aware policy learning to outperform traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordinating multiple interacting units in complex engineering systems is challenging due to difficult-to-model interactions, heterogeneous operational information, and strict action constraints that must be satisfied.

Method: Proposes an LLM-based hierarchical framework where the LLM coordinates units based on heterogeneous context while task-specific controllers generate constraint-aware actions. Introduces Continuation-Aware GRPO to evaluate coordination decisions over subsequent control intervals, assessing both immediate outcomes and future system evolution under current policy.

Result: Validated on multi-ramp traffic control and virtual power plant energy management, the method consistently outperforms direct task-specific control/optimization, end-to-end RL, rule-based/RL hierarchical coordination, and prompting-only LLM coordinators.

Conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates value in heterogeneous-context reasoning, hierarchical execution, and continuation-aware policy learning for complex system coordination, showing superior performance across multiple real-world applications.

Abstract: Coordinating multiple interacting units in complex engineering systems is challenging when system interactions are difficult to model, operational information is heterogeneous, and low-level actions must satisfy strict constraints. We propose an LLM-based hierarchical framework in which the LLM coordinates interacting units based on heterogeneous operational context, while task-specific controllers or optimizers generate executable and constraint-aware actions. We further introduce Continuation-Aware GRPO to capture the consequences of coordination decisions over subsequent control intervals. Rather than judging a decision only by its immediate outcome, the method also evaluates how the system evolves afterward under the current policy. We validate the framework on multi-ramp traffic control and virtual power plant (VPP) energy management, using simplified system models for training and more realistic simulators for evaluation. Across both tasks, the proposed method consistently outperforms direct task-specific control and optimization, end-to-end reinforcement learning, rule-based and RL-based hierarchical coordination, and prompting-only LLM coordinators, demonstrating the value of heterogeneous-context reasoning, hierarchical execution, and continuation-aware policy learning.

</details>


### [69] [SCOPE: Score-Isolated Agentic Optimization for Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15043)
*Yuhua Jiang,Jiaming Wang,Qingbin Liu,Feifei Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is a framework for auditable inference-time adaptation of frozen video world models that uses typed state updates with development evidence, preventing contamination of held-out evaluation while improving performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a problem with evaluating inference-time improvements to video world models: when prompts, samplers, verifiers, and selectors evolve together during development, it becomes difficult to attribute performance gains and prevent held-out feedback from influencing the final policy, compromising reliable evaluation.

Method: SCOPE represents external controls as typed state, updates this state only through bounded changes supported by development evidence, and freezes the resulting policy before held-out evaluation, ensuring auditable inference-time adaptation.

Result: On Physics-IQ benchmark, SCOPE improves over the exact frozen base by +14.24 (95% CI [+8.10,+21.23]). Ablations show gains from scene specification, sampling, and learned selection, though margin over strongest agentic baseline remains unresolved. Cross-backbone evaluations reveal inference-time updates exist but benefits don't transfer uniformly across models.

Conclusion: Reliable inference-time adaptation requires not only better proposals but also a principled mechanism for deciding which updates should become part of the deployed system, and SCOPE provides such a framework for auditable adaptation.

Abstract: Video world models are increasingly used as simulators for planning and embodied decision making, yet improving them at inference time introduces a subtle evaluation problem: prompts, samplers, verifiers, and selectors may evolve together, making it difficult to attribute gains or prevent held-out feedback from shaping the final policy. We introduce \scope (\emph{\scopefullname}), a framework for auditable inference-time adaptation of frozen video world models. \scope represents external controls as a typed state, updates this state only through bounded changes supported by development evidence, and freezes the resulting policy before held-out evaluation. On Physics-IQ benchmark, \scope improves over the exact frozen base by $+14.24$ (95\% CI $[+8.10,+21.23]$). Controlled ablations further identify gains from scene specification, sampling, and learned selection, while the margin over the strongest matched agentic baseline remains unresolved. Cross-backbone and prospective evaluations reveal a complementary result: useful inference-time updates exist, but their benefits do not transfer uniformly across models and settings. Together, these findings suggest that reliable inference-time adaptation requires not only better proposals, but also a principled mechanism for deciding which updates should become part of the deployed system. Code is available at https://github.com/YuhuaJiang2002/SCOPE.

</details>


### [70] [Andy: A Mathematical Agent for Rigorous Proof and Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15052)
*Zi'an Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Andy is an autonomous mathematical research agent that can solve problems, formulate new research questions, and construct rigorous proofs. The paper demonstrates Andy's capabilities by having it learn from a published result on self-triggered impulsive consensus and then formulate and solve a more complex synchronization problem for delayed heterogeneous networks with switching topologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to demonstrate and validate the capabilities of Andy as an autonomous mathematical research agent. The paper aims to show that Andy can not only solve given problems but also learn from existing research, formulate meaningful new research problems, and develop rigorous proofs autonomously.

Method: Andy separates proof generation from correctness evaluation and supports knowledge acquisition, targeted revision, and multistage verification. For the specific problem demonstrated, the method involves formulating a global exponential leader-follower synchronization problem for delayed heterogeneous networks with switching communication topologies. The proposed hybrid control combines self-triggered impulses with execution delay and recovery-phase continuous feedback that cancels the delayed error channel during recovery windows.

Result: The paper establishes sufficient conditions for global exponential synchronization and excludes Zeno behavior for both sampling and impulse sequences. A numerical example confirms the theoretical result. The case demonstrates Andy's successful autonomous research capabilities including learning from existing results, problem formulation, and proof development/verification.

Conclusion: The paper successfully demonstrates Andy's capabilities as an autonomous mathematical research agent. It shows that Andy can learn from existing literature, formulate meaningful research problems that extend previous work, develop rigorous proofs with sufficient conditions, and verify results through numerical examples. This represents a significant step toward autonomous mathematical research systems.

Abstract: Andy is an autonomous mathematical research agent that solves and verifies submitted problems, formulates new research problems, and constructs rigorous proofs. It separates proof generation from correctness evaluation and supports knowledge acquisition, targeted revision, and multistage verification. This paper illustrates the workflow using a published result on self-triggered impulsive consensus as a starting point. Andy formulates a global exponential leader-follower synchronization problem for delayed heterogeneous networks with switching communication topologies. The proposed hybrid control combines self-triggered impulses with execution delay and recovery-phase continuous feedback. After each delayed impulse, this feedback cancels the delayed error channel during a recovery window. Sufficient conditions for global exponential synchronization are established, and Zeno behavior is excluded for both the sampling and impulse sequences. A numerical example confirms the result. This case demonstrates Andy's ability to learn from existing results, formulate meaningful research problems, and develop and verify rigorous proofs.

</details>


### [71] [TAHB: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Text-Attributed Hypergraph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15055)
*David Yoon Suk Kang,JungHyun Kim,Juhyun Jeon,Sang-Wook Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TAHB is the first public benchmark for text-attributed hypergraphs, combining hypergraph structures with textual attributes across 10 real-world datasets to enable systematic evaluation of language model-enhanced hypergraph learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a research gap in combining language models with hypergraph learning due to the lack of public text-attributed hypergraph benchmarks, limiting progress in this intersection area.

Method: Created TAHB benchmark with 10 real-world datasets from four domains (e-commerce, academia, movies, politics), preserving key structural properties of real hypergraphs. Evaluated under both LLM-as-Enhancer (using LLMs to improve textual semantics) and LLM-as-Predictor (using LLMs for prediction tasks) settings.

Result: TAHB consistently reproduces performance tendencies from existing benchmarks and demonstrates that: 1) LLM-enhanced textual semantics improve hypergraph learning performance, and 2) structural and textual information jointly provide the best setting for LLM-based prediction.

Conclusion: TAHB provides a foundational benchmark for future research at the intersection of hypergraph learning and language models, enabling systematic evaluation of text-aware hypergraph representation learning methods.

Abstract: Hypergraphs effectively model higher-order groupwise relationships beyond pairwise interactions, while pretrained language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs) provide rich semantic understanding from textual attributes. However, research on combining language models with hypergraph learning remains limited due to the lack of public text-attributed hypergraph benchmarks. To address this limitation, we present TAHB (Text-Attributed Hypergraph Benchmark), the first public benchmark integrating hypergraph structures and raw textual attributes. TAHB contains 10 real-world datasets from four domains - e-commerce, academia, movies, and politics networks - enabling systematic evaluation of text-aware hypergraph representation learning. Experimental results show that TAHB preserves key structural properties of real-world hypergraphs and consistently reproduces performance tendencies observed in existing benchmarks. Furthermore, experiments under both LLM-as-Enhancer and LLM-as-Predictor settings demonstrate that LLM-enhanced textual semantics improve hypergraph learning performance, while structural and textual information jointly provide the best setting for LLM-based prediction. Our benchmark provides a foundation for future research at the intersection of hypergraph learning and language models.

</details>


### [72] [GraphLoom: Reliability-Calibrated Graph Evidence Routing for Multimodal KG-RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15056)
*Zafar Ali,Asad Khan,Aalia Malik,Pavlos Kefalas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GraphLoom is a reliability-calibrated multimodal knowledge-graph RAG framework that uses compact graph-based evidence routing instead of long unstructured contexts to improve faithfulness and reduce noise in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal RAG systems face challenges with noisy evidence, weakened multi-hop reasoning, and unsupported generation when using long unstructured contexts or aggressively expanded evidence graphs. These approaches introduce inefficiencies and reduce reliability in complex reasoning tasks.

Method: GraphLoom constructs instance-level multimodal knowledge graphs from grounded scene descriptions, relational triples, and commonsense knowledge. It performs reliability-aware subgraph retrieval with bounded expansion and routes high-utility evidence through hierarchical graph memory slots and joint graph-sequence attention in frozen language models. It also features interleaved retrieval with budgeted corrective retrieval for adaptive multi-hop evidence refinement.

Result: GraphLoom shows consistent gains in answer quality and evidence faithfulness over strong multimodal RAG, graph-retrieval, and vision-language baselines on ScienceQA, MultiModalQA, and OK-VQA datasets. It improves retrieval quality on MultiModalQA and maintains stable performance under noisy evidence pools. Additional verification and latency analyses confirm its effectiveness.

Conclusion: Reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing provides an effective alternative to long-context multimodal evidence injection, offering more compact and faithful evidence routing for multimodal RAG systems while maintaining robustness under noisy retrieval conditions.

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often rely on long unstructured contexts or aggressively expanded evidence graphs, which can introduce noisy evidence, weaken multi-hop reasoning, and increase unsupported generation. We present GraphLoom, a reliability-calibrated multimodal knowledge-graph RAG framework for compact and faithful evidence routing. Given a question and its associated multimodal input, GraphLoom constructs an instance-level multimodal knowledge graph from grounded scene descriptions, extracted relational triples, and external commonsense knowledge.
