TL;DR: A routing-aware personalized federated learning framework called ClientMorpher that organizes client collaboration for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs based on routing behavior, improving personalized performance while maintaining communication efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated MoE methods focus only on parameter aggregation and personalization, ignoring routing behavior as valuable information for client collaboration. Under heterogeneous instruction distributions, indiscriminate aggregation can cause negative transfer, so there's a need to identify which clients should collaborate during federated optimization.

Method: Proposes ClientMorpher framework with two clustering strategies: ClientMorpher-C (clients using expert activation profiles) and ClientMorpher-E (first clusters experts based on cross-client usage signatures, then derives client collaboration groups). Both leverage routing signatures from pretrained MoE models.

Result: Routing-aware collaboration consistently improves personalized performance compared to conventional federated averaging and local training, while maintaining the same communication cost. The framework was evaluated on Databricks Dolly-15K dataset with pathological and Dirichlet-based heterogeneous client distributions.

Conclusion: ClientMorpher demonstrates that routing-aware collaboration and both client-centric and expert-centric clustering provide effective and scalable approaches for personalized federated instruction fine-tuning of sparse MoE LLMs.

Abstract: Federated instruction fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to adapt to decentralized, privacy-sensitive data without requiring data sharing. Recent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs are particularly attractive for federated learning because their sparse activation reduces computation and communication while scaling model capacity. However, existing federated MoE methods primarily focus on parameter aggregation and personalization, overlooking the routing behavior of MoE models as a source of information for client collaboration. Under heterogeneous instruction distributions, indiscriminate aggregation can lead to negative transfer, highlighting the need to identify which clients should collaborate during federated optimization. We propose ClientMorpher, a routing-aware, personalized federated instruction fine-tuning framework that leverages routing signatures from pretrained MoE models to organize client collaboration prior to aggregation. We investigate two complementary clustering strategies: ClientMorpher-C, which directly clusters clients using expert activation profiles, and ClientMorpher-E, which first clusters experts based on their cross-client usage signatures and then derives client collaboration groups. We evaluate ClientMorpher for federated instruction fine-tuning on the Databricks Dolly-15K dataset, using pathological and Dirichlet-based heterogeneous client distributions across multiple instruction-following tasks. Experimental results show that routing-aware collaboration consistently improves personalized performance compared to conventional federated averaging and local training, while maintaining the same communication cost. Furthermore, our study shows that client-centric and expert-centric clustering provides an effective and scalable approach for personalized federated instruction fine-tuning of sparse MoE LLMs.

</details>


### [98] [Physics-informed VAE-EVT for Tail Aware Radio Map Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15314)
*Amanda Sheron Gamage,Niloofar Mehrnia,James Gross*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel VAE-EVT framework that separately models bulk and tail SNR distributions for accurate outage prediction in URLLC, significantly outperforming GAN-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional generative radio map models focus on reconstructing average signal levels but fail to accurately capture low SNR regions crucial for outage prediction in URLLC, which requires precise identification of spatial regions where SNR falls below strict outage thresholds (e.g., 0.1% quantile).

Method: Physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT framework with: 1) Physics-informed preprocessing to extract deterministic features (line-of-sight, shadowing, distance) from scene geometry, 2) Dual-latent encoder capturing bulk SNR using Gaussian mixture and tail using generalized Pareto distribution (GPD), 3) Modified variational objective for joint supervision of both regimes to focus on extreme fading events.

Result: Achieves SNR RMSE of 4.83 dB in outage region (0.1% SNR quantile threshold) on RadioMapSeer dataset, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art GAN-based model (21.90 dB RMSE), with performance gap widening as outage threshold becomes more stringent.

Conclusion: The proposed physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT framework provides accurate outage prediction for URLLC by explicitly modeling both bulk and tail SNR distributions, addressing limitations of traditional methods that overlook low SNR regions critical for reliable communication.

Abstract: Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) requires precise identification of spatial regions where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) falls below an outage threshold. In this context, an outage refers to instances in which SNR falls below a specified threshold, which, for URLLC, can be as stringent as the 0.1% quantile of the SNR distribution. Traditional generative radio map models tend to focus on reconstructing average signal levels, often overlooking the low SNR that is crucial for accurate outage prediction. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT (variational autoencoder-extreme value theory) framework that distinctly models both the bulk and tail distribution of SNR. Our approach begins with a physics-informed preprocessing stage that extracts deterministic features, including line-of-sight, shadowing, and distance, from the scene geometry. A dual-latent encoder then captures the bulk SNR using a Gaussian mixture and the tail using a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD). By employing a modified variational objective, the model is trained to jointly supervise both regimes, ensuring focused attention on extreme fading events. Evaluated on the RadioMapSeer dataset, our method achieves an SNR RMSE of 4.83 dB in the outage region defined by the low threshold of 0.1% SNR quantile. This significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art GAN-based model, which records an SNR RMSE of 21.90 dB, with the performance gap widening as the outage threshold becomes more stringent.

</details>


### [99] [The Benchmark Trap: Structures of Power and Injustice in AI Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15326)
*Jason Branford,Angelie Kraft*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI benchmarks aren't neutral evaluation tools but socio-technical systems that concentrate power in industry labs, narrow research trajectories, and potentially create structural injustice through competitive leaderboards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by concerns that AI benchmarks, while appearing as neutral evaluation tools, actually function as socio-technical artifacts that concentrate rewards, power, and influence among wealthy industry-funded labs while potentially causing systematic harms to various AI research stakeholders.

Method: The paper employs Iris Marion Young's theories of oppression and structural injustice as a theoretical framework to analyze current AI benchmarking practices. It examines how these practices align with Young's "four faces of oppression" and frames benchmarking culture as a source of structural injustice emerging from normalized practices and network effects.

Result: The analysis reveals that current benchmarking practices may perpetuate systematic harms affecting various AI research actors, aligning with four of Young's "faces of oppression." The paper further finds that benchmarking culture functions as a source of structural injustice, as harms emerge from normalized, individually defensible practices and network effects without requiring explicit wrongdoing.

Conclusion: By reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing possible research trajectories, benchmarking practices may prevent the AI field from advancing in epistemically robust and socially beneficial ways. The paper calls for critical examination of benchmarking's socio-technical nature and its potential to create structural injustice within AI research.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) benchmarks are not neutral tools of evaluation but socio-technical artefacts that shape competition, power, and research priorities within AI. Benchmarks standardise the assessment of systems and facilitate the creation of leaderboards that reward state-of-the-art performance with prestige, citations, trust, and institutional influence. As the costs of developing competitive AI systems rise, these rewards increasingly concentrate among powerful, industry-funded labs. This paper situates these concerns within Iris Marion Young's theories of oppression and structural injustice. It argues that current benchmarking practices may perpetuate systematic harms affecting various actors in AI research, aligning with four of Young's "faces of oppression". Benchmarking culture is further framed as a source of structural injustice, as these harms emerge from normalised, individually defensible practices and network effects, even without explicit wrongdoing. By reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing possible research trajectories, benchmarking may in fact prevent the field from advancing in epistemically robust and socially beneficial ways.

</details>


### [100] [A concentration result for multilayer feedforward neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15335)
*Vera Koponen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: For large multilayer neural networks with fixed architecture and certain weight distribution assumptions, the output neuron converges in probability to a fixed value ψ as the network width grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the asymptotic behavior of multilayer feedforward neural networks when the network width (number of neurons in the first layer) grows large, under specific assumptions about weight distributions and input statistics.

Method: Consider neural networks with fixed ρ layers, n neurons in the input layer, and one output neuron. Assume weight distributions between layers are approximated by a fixed continuous curve independent of n, and input neurons have i.i.d. continuous probability density. Analyze asymptotic behavior as n→∞.

Result: There exists a number ψ such that for any ε > 0, the probability that the output neuron value lies in [ψ-ε, ψ+ε] converges to 1 as n → ∞, demonstrating concentration of output to a fixed value.

Conclusion: Under specified regularity conditions on weight distributions and input statistics, the output of large multilayer neural networks concentrates around a deterministic value ψ, suggesting predictable asymptotic behavior despite network randomness.

Abstract: We consider for an arbitrary fixed $ρ$ and for each positive integer $n$ a multilayer feedforward artificial neural network with $ρ$ layers, $n$ neurons in the first layer (the input layer) and only one neuron, the output neuron, in the last layer. Very roughly formulated, the main result is that if the distribution of weights of connections from a layer to the next are, for all large $n$, approximated well by a fixed continuous (but otherwise arbitrary) curve which does not depend on $n$, and if the values of the $n$ input neurons are independently and identically distributed with a continuous probability density function, then there is a number $ψ$ such that for all $\varepsilon > 0$ the probability that the value of the output neuron is in $[ψ- \varepsilon, ψ+ \varepsilon]$ tends to 1 as $n$ tends to infinity.

</details>


### [101] [Incoherent by Design? On the Moral Self-Consistency of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15354)
*Pegah Nokhiz,Aravinda Kanchana Ruwanpathirana,Helen Nissenbaum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs show high inconsistency in moral reasoning across rephrased scenarios, with contradiction rates up to 78%, raising concerns about epistemic instability in AI-mediated ethical decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in morally sensitive contexts, but it's unclear if they apply ethical principles consistently. Inconsistency in moral reasoning is problematic for systems used to inform moral decisions, and if generative systems exhibit internal inconsistency, the epistemic integrity of AI-mediated systems becomes uncertain.

Method: Investigated moral reasoning stability in LLMs using a controlled prompting framework across deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. Constructed sets of morally equivalent scenarios with constant underlying situations but varying framing and stylistic perturbations. Evaluated responses from multiple models (GPT, Mistral, Llama). Assessed consistency by converting outputs into structured logical statements and identifying contradictions within the same ethical school of thought.

Result: Revealed substantial inconsistency with contradiction rates reaching up to 78% across scenarios. Models fail to reliably maintain coherence with their own prior outputs, demonstrating epistemic instability in generative AI.

Conclusion: This instability has real consequences as generative systems influence human belief formation, judgment, and values. If systems cannot consistently represent normative commitments, value alignment becomes a moving target rather than a well-defined objective. Demonstrating internal incoherence is therefore a necessary precursor to AI alignment.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in morally sensitive contexts, yet it is unclear whether they apply ethical principles consistently across situations. A model that can state a moral principle may still violate it when the same scenario is rephrased or reframed. This inconsistency is a problem for any system whose outputs are used to inform moral decisions. If generative systems exhibit internal inconsistency, then the epistemic integrity of AI-mediated systems becomes uncertain. To study this concern, we investigate the stability of moral reasoning in LLMs within a controlled prompting framework across three major philosophical schools of thought: deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. We construct sets of morally equivalent scenarios in which the underlying situation is held constant while the framing varies to reflect different ethical stances and stylistic perturbations. We then evaluate responses from multiple models, including GPT, Mistral, and Llama. To assess consistency, we convert model outputs into structured logical statements and identify contradictions across responses generated within the same school of thought. Our results reveal substantial inconsistency with contradiction rates reaching up to 78% across scenarios. These findings point to a broader phenomenon of epistemic instability in generative AI wherein models fail to reliably maintain coherence with respect to their own prior outputs. This kind of instability carries real consequences. As generative systems influence how people form beliefs, judge actions, and absorb values, their inconsistencies can shape human reasoning and decision-making as well. Moreover, if a system cannot consistently represent its own normative commitments, then value alignment becomes a moving target rather than a well-defined objective. Thus, we argue that demonstrating internal incoherence is a necessary precursor to AI alignment.

</details>


### [102] [FedPA-LoRA: Product-Aligned Framework for Mitigating Aggregation and Initialization Errors in Heterogeneous Federated LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15381)
*Juseok Jeon,Ramy E. Ali,Doyun Kwon,Myungbeom Her,Jinhwi Kim,Jinhyun So*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedPA-LoRA: A federated learning framework that addresses the aggregation-continuity trade-off in Low-Rank Adaptation by preserving local factor continuity while aligning product spaces to a global reference, enabling efficient heterogeneous client adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA enables efficient federated fine-tuning of LLMs, but its factorized parameterization creates a tension between accurate aggregation of local updates and continuity of locally optimized factors. Factor-wise aggregation causes aggregation mismatch, while product-space reconstruction reduces mismatch but creates factor-level initialization mismatch from newly reconstructed factors.

Method: FedPA-LoRA uses product-aligned federated LoRA where each client preserves its local factors across communication rounds and aligns its product toward a rank-specific global reference. This maintains local optimization continuity while promoting global consistency under data heterogeneity. The server aggregates heterogeneous-rank updates in the common product space and efficiently reconstructs a rank-constrained global adapter without forming the dense aggregate.

Result: FedPA-LoRA consistently outperforms representative baselines across varying levels of data heterogeneity and homogeneous- and heterogeneous-rank settings, with up to 6.82 percentage-point improvement in average GLUE accuracy under heterogeneous client ranks. The method provably converges under both homogeneous and heterogeneous client ranks.

Conclusion: FedPA-LoRA effectively addresses the aggregation-continuity trade-off in federated LoRA by preserving local factor continuity while ensuring global consistency, enabling efficient federated fine-tuning that supports client-specific computation and communication budgets under heterogeneous conditions.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient federated fine-tuning of large language models, but its factorized parameterization creates a tension between accurate aggregation of local updates and continuity of locally optimized factors. Factor-wise aggregation incurs aggregation mismatch but better preserves factor continuity, whereas product-space reconstruction reduces this mismatch at the cost of greater factor-level initialization mismatch from newly reconstructed factors. We propose FedPA-LoRA, a product-aligned federated LoRA framework that jointly addresses these limitations and provably converges under both homogeneous and heterogeneous client ranks. Each client preserves its local factors across communication rounds and aligns its product toward a rank-specific global reference, maintaining local optimization continuity while promoting global consistency under data heterogeneity. The server aggregates heterogeneous-rank updates in the common product space and efficiently reconstructs a rank-constrained global adapter without forming the dense aggregate. This design supports client-specific computation and communication budgets. Experiments on natural language understanding and generation tasks show that FedPA-LoRA consistently outperforms representative baselines across varying levels of data heterogeneity and homogeneous- and heterogeneous-rank settings, with up to a $6.82$ percentage-point improvement in average GLUE accuracy under heterogeneous client ranks.

</details>


### [103] [Grounding Healthcare LLMs in a Causal Knowledge Graph: Framework, Metrics, and a Cardiovascular Pilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15382)
*Ummara Mumtaz,Aimen Noor,Awais Ahmed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A graph-centered evaluation framework for testing LLMs' intervention reasoning in healthcare, with four controlled grounding conditions showing that ungrounded models achieve high intervention accuracy but lack causal/evidential grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluations in healthcare focus on single-answer accuracy rather than assessing reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. There's a need for better evaluation frameworks that test intervention-oriented behavior in clinical settings.

Method: Four-component framework: 1) Domain causal knowledge graph with assertion nodes, 2) Scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction, 3) Four controlled grounding conditions (ungrounded, knowledge-graph, causal-graph, integrated), 4) Automated scoring pipeline anchored on assertion identifiers with metrics like intervention accuracy, causal edge F1, adverse-effect F1, evidence accuracy, and unsupported claim rate.

Result: The integrated condition (C4) achieved strongest performance on causal metrics (F1=0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and lowest unsupported claim rate (0.114). Ungrounded condition (C1) achieved highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) but lacked causal/evidential grounding. The framework successfully discriminates between different grounding conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework effectively assesses LLMs' intervention reasoning in healthcare, revealing that ungrounded models can achieve high accuracy but lack proper causal and evidential foundations, highlighting the importance of integrated knowledge grounding for reliable clinical decision support.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for healthcare decision support, but their evaluations still reward single-answer accuracy rather than reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. We propose a reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework for intervention-oriented LLM behavior in healthcare and stress-test it in a cardiovascular pilot. The framework has four components: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph in which assertions are first-class, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) a scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction step that, given any clinical scenario, retrieves the relevant reified-assertion subgraph; (iii) four controlled grounding conditions that vary how the retrieved subgraph is composed into the model's context (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline, anchored on assertion identifiers, that computes intervention accuracy, and other evaluation measures on a single pass. To test the framework, we built a category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes and instantiated it on a cardiovascular graph. The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes: C4 obtains the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 obtains the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.

</details>


### [104] [Agentic-SQL Revisited: Autonomy-Based Taxonomy and Empirical Benchmark Analysis for LLM Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15389)
*Changruo Zhao,Zujun Peng,Yu Tian,Yuting Liu,Yiyun Su,Huiying Zhu,Luyan Zhang,Heming Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper creates a unified leaderboard framework for comparing Text-to-SQL systems by organizing reported metrics along an inference-autonomy axis and conducting an empirical case study on Spider dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL progress is reported across heterogeneous benchmarks, backbones, and inference protocols, making cross-system comparisons fragile and unreliable.

Method: Reframes the field as leaderboard aggregation, organizing metrics along an inference-autonomy axis (constrained, in-context, iterative, agentic, reasoning-internalized generation) with traceable provenance. Conducts empirical case study on Spider dataset comparing 8B open-source backbones with/without CoT supervision against few-shot DeepSeek-V3 and GLM-4 baselines.

Result: Four key findings: 1) Spider gains transfer unevenly to BIRD and Spider 2.0, 2) autonomy buys robustness at non-trivial cost, 3) reasoning internalization sits between answer-only decoding and externally orchestrated agents, 4) CoT gains concentrate on Hard and Extra-Hard queries. Releases Python harness for future method integration.

Conclusion: The proposed leaderboard aggregation framework provides a standardized way to compare Text-to-SQL systems across different autonomy levels, with empirical patterns revealing important insights about transfer learning, cost-benefit of autonomy, and CoT effectiveness.

Abstract: LLM-based Text-to-SQL progress is reported across heterogeneous benchmarks, backbones, and inference protocols, making cross-system comparison fragile. We reframe the field as a leaderboard aggregation: we collect the metrics authors themselves report and organize them along an inference-autonomy axis spanning constrained, in-context, iterative, agentic, and reasoning-internalized generation, with traceable provenance for every cell. To anchor the aggregation empirically, we run a focused case study on Spider, comparing 8B open-source backbones with and without chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision against few-shot DeepSeek~V3 and GLM-4 baselines. Four patterns emerge: Spider gains transfer unevenly to BIRD and Spider~2.0; autonomy buys robustness at non-trivial cost; reasoning internalization sits between answer-only decoding and externally orchestrated agents; and CoT gains concentrate on Hard and Extra-Hard queries. We release a Python harness mirroring the autonomy axis so that future methods can be added directly to the leaderboard.

</details>


### [105] [TwinGridShield: Consequence-Aware Runtime Authorization for LLM Grid-Agent Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15391)
*Md Fazley Rafy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TwinGridShield is a runtime authorization layer for LLM-assisted energy management that validates proposed grid actions using a deterministic network twin before release, ensuring physical admissibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-assisted energy-management tools can translate natural language into grid commands, but syntactically valid commands may not be physically admissible or safe for the electrical grid system.

Method: Developed TwinGridShield, a model-independent runtime authorization layer that evaluates each proposed action in a deterministic network twin. The prototype checks connectivity, branch-flow, generator, and load-shedding invariants and records decisions in a hash-chained log. Evaluated using controlled IEEE 14-bus study with single-step switching, redispatch, and load-shedding actions using DC power flow.

Result: In matched-model experiments: 0 unsafe releases out of 500 attacked-condition trials (vs. 421 unsafe proposals from stochastic source). Under model mismatch: 5.63% unsafe acceptance under ±20% load-measurement error; 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

Conclusion: TwinGridShield effectively prevents unsafe actions when models match, but model mismatch significantly impacts safety. The system provides runtime safety verification for LLM-assisted grid management but requires accurate grid models and measurements to maintain effectiveness.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-assisted energy-management tools can translate natural-language context into structured grid commands, but syntactic validity does not imply physical admissibility. This paper presents TwinGridShield, a model-independent runtime authorization layer that evaluates each proposed action in a deterministic network twin before release. The prototype checks connectivity, branch-flow, generator, and load-shedding invariants and records each decision in a hash-chained log. A controlled IEEE 14-bus study evaluates single-step switching, redispatch, and load-shedding actions using DC power flow and experimentally assigned branch ratings. In the matched-model experiment, a stochastic proposal source configured to select an unsafe action with probability p=0.84 produced 421 unsafe proposals in 500 attacked-condition trials, a realized rate of 84.2%. This value characterizes the configured surrogate and is not an empirical measurement of LLM prompt-injection susceptibility. TwinGridShield produced 0 unsafe releases in those 500 trials. Because action labeling and authorization used the same DC model, system state, branch ratings, and encoded constraints, this result verifies conformance of the implementation to its encoded authorization predicate rather than safety under model error. The principal robustness evaluation therefore introduces model mismatch. Unsafe acceptance reached 5.63% under bounded +20% and -20% per-bus load-measurement error and 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

</details>


### [106] [Visible Reasoning and Indirect Prompt-Injection Monitorability Across English, Tamil, and Tanglish](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15392)
*Madhusudhanan G*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Chain-of-thought monitoring shows mixed safety results across languages, with limited sample size preventing conclusive safety claims about visible reasoning's protective effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether chain-of-thought monitoring provides reliable safety signals across different languages and behavioral settings, particularly during indirect prompt injection attacks.

Method: Small case study with eight manually verified synthetic scenarios, testing Sarvam-105B model across English, Tamil, and Tanglish. Used API-visible reasoning monitoring during indirect prompt injections with deterministic generation. Conducted two phases: four-scenario pilot and preregistered four-scenario follow-up.

Result: Mixed results: pilot showed 5/12 attack successes without reasoning vs 1/11 with reasoning, but follow-up reversed direction with 2/12 attacks without reasoning vs 3/12 with reasoning. Across 20 non-empty injected-thinking traces, all benign-correct outputs showed intent to ignore injections while all attack successes showed intent to follow injections.

Conclusion: The study provides a reproducible case study of behaviorally informative visible reasoning but cannot establish that reasoning mode improves safety, that visible reasoning is mechanistically faithful, or that findings generalize beyond this specific configuration due to small sample size.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a potentially useful safety signal, but its reliability across languages and behavioral settings remains uncertain. In a small case study of eight manually verified synthetic scenarios, one model, one annotator, and one deterministic generation seed, I study API-visible reasoning during indirect prompt injection in Sarvam-105B across English, Tamil, and Tanglish. A four scenario pilot found 5/12 injected attack successes without reasoning and 1/11 with reasoning. A preregistered four-scenario follow-up reversed that direction, finding 2/12 attacks without reasoning and 3/12 with reasoning. With only four scenarios per phase, this design cannot distinguish a real reasoning-mode effect from prompt-specific variation or sampling noise. Across 20 non-empty injected-thinking traces, all 17 benign-correct outputs stated an intent to ignore the injection, while all three attack successes stated an intent to follow it. These descriptive observations provide a reproducible case study of behaviorally informative visible reasoning when it is available; they do not establish that reasoning mode improves safety, that visible reasoning is mechanistically faithful, or that the findings generalize beyond this configuration.

</details>


### [107] [Large Language Model Assisted Operational Monitoring for Battery Energy Storage System Integrated Power Distribution Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15396)
*Azmeer Akhtar,Md Fazley Rafy,Anurag K. Srivastava*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI framework connects LLM interface with BESS telemetry database for automated grid monitoring, translating natural language queries to SQL, validating engineering constraints, and identifying operational issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increasing use of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in distribution networks creates more complex operational telemetry data that grid operators need to monitor effectively. Traditional monitoring methods struggle with the volume and complexity of this data.

Method: Developed an AI-enabled monitoring framework that: 1) Uses LLM interface to accept natural language operator questions, 2) Translates queries into validated SQL using predefined database schema and approved KPI views, 3) Retrieves measurements (bus voltages, state of charge, active/reactive power), 4) Evaluates data against engineering constraints for voltage limits, BESS operation, and demand response tracking.

Result: Framework validated using hardware-in-the-loop co-simulation data from BESS-equipped distribution feeder. Successfully: generates valid database queries, identifies repeated voltage violations, detects reactive power overshoot, evaluates active-power tracking performance.

Conclusion: LLM-assisted monitoring can effectively bridge structured grid telemetry with automated engineering assessment for BESS operation analysis, demonstrating practical application for grid operators to monitor complex BESS-integrated systems.

Abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are increasingly used in distribution networks for voltage regulation and demand response, which increases the volume and complexity of operational telemetry available to grid operators. This paper presents an AI-enabled monitoring framework that connects a large language model (LLM) interface with a structured telemetry database for BESS-integrated distribution system analysis. Operator questions are submitted in natural language and translated into validated SQL queries using predefined database schema information and approved KPI views. Retrieved measurements, including bus voltages, state of charge, active power, and reactive power, are evaluated against engineering constraints for voltage limits, BESS operation, and demand response tracking. The framework is validated using hardware-in-the-loop co-simulation data from a BESS-equipped distribution feeder operating under reactive power-based voltage control and price-driven demand response. Case studies show that the framework generates valid database queries, identifies repeated voltage violations, detects reactive power overshoot, and evaluates active-power tracking performance. The results show that LLM-assisted monitoring can connect structured grid telemetry with automated engineering assessment for BESS operation analysis.

</details>


### [108] [A survey of AI-generated voices and their detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15411)
*Chengzhe Sun,Tianle Yang,Siwei Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of AI voice generation technologies and detection methods, highlighting both their beneficial applications and harmful uses, while addressing the unique challenges in synthetic voice detection compared to other deepfakes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid advancement in AI voice generation has enabled beneficial applications but also serious harms like impersonation, fraud, and disinformation through voice cloning scams. There's an urgent need for robust safeguards as synthetic voice detection presents unique challenges compared to image/video deepfakes.

Method: The paper conducts a comprehensive survey approach, reviewing AI voice generation and detection methods by encompassing both technical foundations and latest state-of-the-art advances. It organizes existing literature and technologies in a systematic manner.

Result: The survey provides a complete overview of the field, identifies key open challenges in synthetic voice detection, compiles benchmark resources, and outlines future research directions for the community.

Conclusion: AI voice generation technology presents a dual-use challenge requiring urgent attention. The paper serves as a valuable resource for future researchers by systematically organizing current knowledge and identifying critical research gaps in synthetic voice detection.

Abstract: The ability of artificial intelligence (AI) models to generate highly realistic human voices has advanced rapidly. These technologies power accessibility tools, virtual assistants and creative applications, but they also enable harmful uses, including impersonation, fraud and disinformation. Recent incidents of voice cloning scams targeting businesses and political leaders underscore the urgent need for robust safeguards. Unlike image and video deepfakes, the detection of synthetic voices poses unique challenges due to the complexity of phonetics, prosody and auditory perception. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of AI voice generation and detection methods, encompassing both the technical foundations and the latest state-of-the-art advances. This study also identifies key open challenges, benchmark resources and future directions to make this survey useful for future researchers.

</details>


### [109] [Does the Proof Prove It That Way? Faithful Formalization of Elements Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15432)
*Tadd Mao,Tianjun Zhong,Dhruva Arekar,Yuming Feng,One An,Jiani Huang,Xujie Si,Ziyang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pistis is an agentic oracle-guided proof search system that generates faithful formal proofs in Lean that preserve the reasoning structure of natural language arguments, outperforming prior methods on Euclid's Elements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current automated proof search generates formal proofs that compile but don't reflect how natural-language arguments arrive at conclusions (lack faithfulness). Faithful proofs are needed to check reasoning behind human/AI arguments and help mathematicians formalize proof sketches, but this is challenging due to misalignment between formal proof tactics and natural language reasoning.

Method: Introduces Pistis with OrderDecompose, a faithfulness-preserving divide-and-conquer search that tracks citation dependencies and blocks unfaithful shortcuts, paired with refutation search to surface gaps/errors in natural language proofs. The system produces formal Lean proofs satisfying five rigorously defined faithfulness conditions.

Result: OrderDecompose completes proofs that baselines cannot close within 12-hour budget; artifacts compile 33x faster than prior work. Applied to first three books of Euclid's Elements, producing high-quality faithful proofs. In blinded human study and LLM-as-a-judge protocol, Pistis proofs favored 2.89x and 5.2x more often respectively. Uncovers gaps in Euclid's proofs and can accept/refute natural language proofs.

Conclusion: Faithful formalization is useful as a proof-checking tool and can verify/refute natural language proofs from humans or AI, demonstrating practical value for mathematical verification and formalization assistance.

Abstract: In formal verification, both the autoformalization of statements and automated proof search have been studied extensively. While automated proof search can produce a formal proof that compiles, the generated proof does not necessarily reflect how the natural-language argument arrives at its conclusion--a property we refer to as faithfulness. With faithfully formalized proofs, one can check the reasoning behind a human- or AI-written argument, and assist mathematicians in formalizing their proof sketches. However, it is particularly challenging due to misalignment of formal proof tactics and natural language reasoning. In this work, we rigorously describe a set of five necessary conditions a faithful formal proof must satisfy, and introduce Pistis, an agentic, oracle-guided proof search that produces formal Lean proofs that satisfy them. At its core is a novel faithfulness-preserving divide-and-conquer search, which we name OrderDecompose, that tracks citation dependencies and blocks unfaithful shortcuts, paired with a refutation search, that surfaces gaps and errors in the natural language proof source. OrderDecompose completes proofs that baselines cannot close even within a 12-hour budget, and its artifacts compile over 33$\times$ as fast as prior work's. We apply Pistis on the first three books of Euclid's Elements, producing high-quality artifacts containing faithful formal proofs. Under a blinded human study and an LLM-as-a-judge protocol on rigorous rubrics, Pistis-generated proofs are favored over prior works--2.89$\times$ and 5.2$\times$ as often by human reviewers and the LLM judge, respectively. It further uncovers gaps in Euclid's proofs and their translation, and can accept or refute natural language proofs written by humans or AI, demonstrating that faithful formalization is useful as a proof-checking tool.

</details>


### [110] [OTel: Building Domain-Specialized Telecom LLM Foundations for Intelligent Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15436)
*Farbod Tavakkoli,Roderic Paulk,Jorden Terrazas,Kenneth Church,Mark Austin,Louis Powell,Gregory Diamos,Lina Bariah,Syed Ali Raza Zaidi,Maryam Hafeez,Ali Maatouk,Imtiaz Karim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open Telco (OTel) is a comprehensive open telecom AI resource with datasets, benchmarks, and 30 post-trained models that significantly improve telecom-specific AI task performance, gaining substantial community adoption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier AI models struggle with telecom-specific tasks, creating a need for specialized telecom AI resources to bridge this domain gap and enable better telecom applications.

Method: Created Open Telco (OTel) resource with telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, safety/abstention; trained 30 full-parameter baselines across embedding, reranking, and language models; used post-training to adapt models to telecom domain.

Result: Post-training improved performance across all model families: embedding retrieval reached 93.5% NDCG@10, reranking reached 0.952 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reached 88.2%. Models downloaded 16M+ times with 157+ media coverage by May 2026.

Conclusion: OTel provides a reproducible starting point for telecom AI, demonstrating significant performance gains through domain adaptation and inviting community expansion to build stronger telecom AI models.

Abstract: Frontier AI models have advanced rapidly, but they still struggle with telecom-specific tasks. We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource with derived datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, plus 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines across embedding, reranking, and language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times, and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.5% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.952 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 88.2%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

</details>


### [111] [Measuring Reward Hacking and Reasoning-Answer Decoupling Under Position-Confounded Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15445)
*Suyash Maniyar,Armaan Sandhu,Abhishek Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Models trained on math problems with answer position bias (always option A) learn to select A rather than solve the math, causing construct validity failure where accuracy measures answer-position policy instead of math ability, with transfer to out-of-domain tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Goal misgeneralization occurs when models acquire unintended goals despite correct training rewards, making endpoint accuracy misleading as it cannot distinguish between solving the task versus exploiting surface features. This creates a measurement problem: what does a benchmark score actually measure after optimization with confounded signals?

Method: Train language models with GRPO on multiple-choice math problems where the correct answer is always option A, then evaluate on unseen test sets with unbiased answer positions. Study Qwen2.5, Llama 3.x, and Gemma-3 models, analyzing option-A rates and unbiased accuracy. Use numeric extraction and LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini) to detect reasoning-answer decoupling. Test transfer to out-of-domain MMLU and value-laden prompts, and examine reversal with unbiased training.

Result: Biased training drives option-A rates above 0.90 in smaller models and collapses unbiased accuracy toward chance, making accuracy measure answer-position policy rather than math ability. Models show reasoning-answer decoupling: capable models generate correct numeric reasoning but still select A (Qwen2.5-3B decoupling rate ~0.66). The bias generalizes beyond training domain, inflating A-rates on MMLU and value prompts. Unbiased training partially reverses in-domain bias but incompletely reverses out-of-domain bias, creating misleading restoration appearance.

Conclusion: Goal misgeneralization from confounded training signals breaks construct validity of benchmark measurements. Reasoning-answer decoupling rate, answer distributions, and out-of-domain behavior together reveal capability loss versus learned shortcuts. Models can appear restored on training distribution while remaining biased elsewhere, highlighting need for more robust evaluation beyond accuracy metrics.

Abstract: When a reward is correct on every training example yet consistent with more than one goal, a model can acquire an unintended one, a failure known as goal misgeneralization. Endpoint accuracy on the training distribution cannot tell the two apart, because solving the task and exploiting a surface feature can satisfy the reward equally well. We treat this as a measurement problem: what does a benchmark score measure once a model has been optimized against a correct but confounded signal? We train language models with GRPO on multiple-choice math problems where the correct answer is always option A, then evaluate on an unseen test set with unbiased answer positions. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.x and Gemma-3 models, biased training often drives option-A rates above 0.90 in smaller models and collapses unbiased accuracy toward chance, so accuracy stops measuring math ability and instead measures an answer-position policy. We further find reasoning-answer decoupling: capable models generate reasoning that reaches the correct numeric answer while still selecting A. We track this with numeric extraction and an LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini; Qwen2.5-3B decoupling rate is about 0.66). The broken construct generalizes beyond the training domain: biased models inflate A-rates on out-of-domain MMLU and value-laden prompts. Continued training on unbiased data reverses the in-domain shift unevenly and only partially reverses the out-of-domain one, so a model can appear restored on its training distribution while remaining biased on unseen inputs. Reasoning-answer decoupling rate, together with answer distributions and out-of-domain behavior, separates capability loss from a learned, transferable shortcut.

</details>


### [112] [Mental Model Management: An Operator-Based Framework for LLM Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15451)
*Oliver Kramer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework called Mental Model Management (3M) that enables large language models to maintain compact, evolving conceptual representations through structured knowledge chunks and operators rather than accumulating raw text passages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models process vast information but lack explicit mechanisms for maintaining compact and evolving conceptual representations, limiting their ability to manage knowledge effectively over time.

Method: Introduces 3M framework where knowledge is represented as mental models consisting of compact chunks. Uses operators to extract knowledge, retrieve relevant models, add/update chunks, reorganize representations, detect inconsistencies, and derive new knowledge.

Result: The paper describes the main 3M operators and illustrates each operation using Evolution Strategies as a running example, demonstrating how continuous information integration can be achieved.

Conclusion: 3M provides a structured approach for language models to maintain evolving conceptual representations through mental models and operational mechanisms, addressing the limitation of accumulating raw text passages.

Abstract: Large language models process large amounts of information but usually lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining compact and evolving conceptual representations. We introduce Mental Model Management (3M), a framework in which knowledge is represented as mental models consisting of compact chunks. Rather than accumulating text passages, 3M continuously integrates new information into an existing conceptual representation. A set of operators extracts knowledge, retrieves relevant models, adds and updates chunks, reorganizes representations, detects inconsistencies, and derives new knowledge. We describe the main 3M operators and illustrate each operation using Evolution Strategies as a running example.

</details>


### [113] [Dynamic Multi-Byte Prediction With Hierarchical Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15454)
*Abraham Toluwase Owodunni,Chibuzor Okocha,Christan Grant,Tomasz Limisiewicz,Sachin Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-byte prediction (MBP) speeds up byte-level hierarchical language models by generating multiple bytes in parallel, achieving better performance vs throughput trade-off than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Byte-level hierarchical language models are robust but generate one byte at a time, creating an inference speed bottleneck that needs addressing.

Method: MBP introduces a variable-length prediction window aligned with latent tokens/segments of hierarchical LMs and a novel attention-masking scheme that enables parallel byte prediction without violating causality, building on multi-token prediction.

Result: MBP strikes a Pareto-optimal trade-off across multiple generative tasks (instruction following, QA, summarization, translation) with minimal performance impact, no additional parameters, and best performance-throughput trade-off.

Conclusion: Multi-byte prediction successfully addresses the inference speed bottleneck of byte-level hierarchical language models by enabling parallel byte generation while maintaining performance, offering a practical solution for real-world applications.

Abstract: Byte-level hierarchical language models (LMs) have recently emerged as a robust alternative to their popular counterparts that use subword tokenization. However, generating one byte at a time remains a bottleneck for inference speed. To address this, we introduce multi-byte prediction (MBP), which generates multiple bytes in parallel, speeding up inference with minimal performance impact and no additional parameters. MBP builds on the popular multi-token prediction (MTP) paradigm with two crucial innovations. First, we introduce a variable-length prediction window that aligns with the latent tokens, or segments, of a hierarchical LM. Second, we implement a novel attention-masking scheme that enables parallel byte prediction without violating causality. We show that multi-byte prediction strikes a Pareto-optimal trade-off across multiple generative tasks, instruction following, question answering, summarization, and machine translation, achieving the best trade-off between performance and inference throughput.

</details>


### [114] [A Network-driven Framework for Public Event Forecasting via Dynamic Interaction Network Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15488)
*Jie Wei,Yue Liu,Xiaochuan Tang,Biao Cai,Xiangtao Li,Yanmei Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: auto-ibDLM is a network-driven deep learning framework that forecasts public event evolution by modeling events as dynamic interaction networks and predicting participant growth through hybrid representation learning and temporal forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective public event forecasting is essential for intelligent service systems to enable proactive risk management, adaptive resource allocation, and timely decision-making. Public events often evolve through dynamic interactions among participants, creating a need for network-based approaches to capture these complex relationships.

Method: Proposes auto-ibDLM framework that: 1) represents events as dynamic interaction networks, 2) uses hybrid representation learning with network science-informed structural metrics to capture network evolution, 3) transforms structural features into compact latent representations via auto-learning layer, and 4) employs GRU-based temporal forecasting module to predict future participant growth.

Result: Extensive experiments on 13 real-world public event datasets and 2 dynamic network datasets show auto-ibDLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in forecasting accuracy and generalization, achieving over 97% accuracy in public event forecasting. The hybrid representation learning strategy demonstrates effectiveness and representation-level interpretability.

Conclusion: auto-ibDLM provides an effective and practical solution for intelligent public event forecasting by successfully integrating network science with deep learning to capture dynamic participant interactions and predict event evolution patterns.

Abstract: Effective public event forecasting is essential for intelligent service systems, enabling proactive risk management, adaptive resource allocation, and timely decision-making. In many real-world scenarios, the evolution of public events is driven by dynamic interactions among participants. Motivated by this observation, this paper proposes auto-ibDLM, a network-driven deep learning framework that represents events as dynamic interaction networks and predicts public event evolution through participant growth forecasting. The proposed framework adopts a hybrid representation learning strategy that first represents network evolution using network science-informed structural metrics and subsequently transforms the resulting structural feature vectors into compact and robust latent representations through an auto-learning layer. A GRU-based temporal forecasting module is then employed to capture temporal dependencies and predict future participant growth. Extensive experiments on 13 real-world public event datasets and two publicly available dynamic network datasets demonstrate that auto-ibDLM consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and generalization capability, achieving over 97% accuracy in public event forecasting. Comprehensive experimental analyses further validate the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid representation learning strategy and demonstrate its representation-level interpretability. These results indicate that auto-ibDLM provides an effective and practical solution for intelligent public event forecasting.

</details>


### [115] [EcoVLA: Energy-Efficient Device-Edge Co-Inference for Vision-Language-Action Models under Real-Time Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15502)
*Ao Zhou,Bo Dai,Le Yu,Xingyu Liu,Zeyu Hao,Lingkun Long,Chunming Hu,Jianlei Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EcoVLA is an adaptive device-edge co-inference framework for Vision-Language-Action models that maximizes system energy efficiency under real-time constraints by dynamically selecting optimal computation partitioning between device and edge while reducing communication overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models have high inference costs that challenge deployment in robotic systems. On-device inference faces compute/energy limitations, while offloading to edge servers introduces unpredictable latency risks. There's a lack of systematic research on device-edge co-inference frameworks tailored to VLA models that address both real-time constraints and energy efficiency.

Method: EcoVLA introduces a unified stage-level abstraction for different VLA paradigms, creates a joint device-edge-network latency/energy prediction model for rapid evaluation, continuously selects energy-optimal schemes with millisecond overhead, and incorporates lightweight transmission mechanisms for intermediate tensors to reduce communication overhead.

Result: EcoVLA improves system energy efficiency by up to 236% over existing co-inference approaches under 20 Hz action output constraints, while consistently maintaining service-level objective satisfaction under dynamic network and edge workload conditions.

Conclusion: EcoVLA provides an effective adaptive device-edge co-inference framework that addresses the dual challenges of real-time control and energy efficiency for VLA models in robotic systems, offering significant improvements over existing approaches.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising foundation for Embodied AI, but their high inference cost poses significant challenges for deployment in robotic systems. In practice, on-device inference is constrained by limited compute capacity and energy budgets, struggling to simultaneously satisfy real-time control and energy efficiency requirements. Alternatively, offloading the inference workload to an edge server is susceptible to fluctuations in system conditions, introducing unpredictable latency risks. Device-edge co-inference offers a promising solution, but systematic research tailored to VLA models remains scarce, particularly a unified co-inference framework that jointly addresses real-time constraints and system-level energy efficiency. Thus, we propose EcoVLA, an adaptive device-edge co-inference framework for VLA models that maximizes system energy efficiency under real-time constraints. EcoVLA first introduces a unified stage-level abstraction over different VLA paradigms, establishing an architecture-agnostic co-inference design space. It then formulates a joint device-edge-network latency and energy prediction model to enable rapid runtime evaluation of candidate co-inference schemes. Building on this, EcoVLA continuously selects the energy-optimal scheme satisfying real-time constraints with millisecond-level overhead, adapting to runtime variations in network and system states. Furthermore, EcoVLA incorporates a lightweight transmission mechanism for inter-stage intermediate tensors to reduce the communication overhead incurred by cross-device collaboration. Experimental results across VLA models show that EcoVLA improves system energy efficiency by up to 236% over existing co-inference approaches under a 20 Hz action output frequency constraint, while consistently maintaining SLO satisfaction under dynamic network and edge workload conditions.

</details>


### [116] [Who Leads Now? Token-Level Modality Arbitration for Chart-to-Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15510)
*Qinghao Fu,Yarong Wang,Shunlei Ning,Yilin Wang,Shunwen Bai,Xinda Wang,Jiaotuan Wang,Yinan Nie,Wei Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MoCA separates visual and coding abilities using Cross-modal Arbitration Blocks with a lightweight arbiter, trained via supervised warm-up on reasoning trajectories followed by reinforcement learning, achieving competitive chart-to-code performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing chart-to-code methods either train visual and coding abilities separately or fine-tune them together, failing to account for their distinct nature and interference when optimized jointly. Neither strategy properly handles the separation of these two different abilities.

Method: MoCA uses Cross-modal Arbitration Blocks (CAB) that maintain separate visual and code branches with a lightweight arbiter to dynamically allocate their relative contributions at each layer and token. Training involves two stages: 1) supervised warm-up on self-distilled reasoning trajectories that decompose visual understanding into explicit steps, 2) reinforcement learning with rewards on both reasoning process and final code.

Result: The arbiter learns structured allocations varying systematically across tokens, layers, and instances. MoCA achieves competitive performance across three benchmarks against general-domain and chart-specialized models. Ablations show gains come from complementary visual/code branch initialization and input-conditioned arbitration, not just larger model size.

Conclusion: Separating visual and coding abilities via Cross-modal Arbitration with dynamic arbitration is more effective than blending them, with the arbiter learning meaningful patterns of contribution allocation. The two-stage training approach combining supervised reasoning decomposition with reinforcement learning enables better chart-to-code generation.

Abstract: Chart-to-code generation requires a model to read the fine-grained visual details of a chart and write executable code that reproduces it. Existing chart-to-code methods either train visual and coding abilities separately, or fine-tune on chart-to-code data with the two abilities entangled. Neither strategy accounts for the distinct nature of the two abilities or the interference that arises when they are optimized together. We propose MoCA (Mixture of Cross-modal Arbitration), which separates the two abilities rather than blending them. MoCA is built on Cross-modal Arbitration Block (CAB), which maintains a visual branch and a code branch as two distinct pathways, and a lightweight arbiter that arbitrates their relative contributions at every layer and generated token. We train MoCA in two stages: a supervised warm-up on self-distilled reasoning trajectories that decomposes visual understanding into explicit steps, followed by reinforcement learning with rewards on both the reasoning process and the final code. Analysis shows that the arbiter learns structured rather than arbitrary allocations, with expert contributions varying systematically across tokens, layers, and instances. Across three benchmarks, MoCA delivers competitive performance against general-domain and chart-specialized models. Ablation results show that the gains cannot be attributed to a larger model size alone, but instead arise from the joint contributions of complementary visual and code branch initialization and input-conditioned arbitration through CAB.

</details>


### [117] [From Contexts to Values: Context-Dependent Defeat in Abstract Argumentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15536)
*Albert Sadowski,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines whether context-dependent argumentation frameworks (CDAFs) can be reduced to value-based argumentation frameworks (VAFs), finding that such representability is rare and decreases quickly with more contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to determine whether context-dependent argumentation (where attacks succeed or fail based on circumstances/contexts) is genuinely a new concept or can be reduced to existing value-based argumentation frameworks. The authors want to understand if CDAFs add something fundamentally new or are just a special case of VAFs.

Method: The authors present a polynomial-time decision procedure to determine whether a given CDAF can be represented as a VAF. They analyze this reduction problem and map neighboring computational problems with complexity upper bounds ranging from NP to Σ^p_3. They also provide a validated reference implementation and conduct measurements to evaluate representability.

Result: The results show that representability of CDAFs as VAFs is rare and decreases rapidly as the number of contexts increases. The decision procedure provides efficient determination of whether such reduction is possible. The complexity analysis places different variants of the problem within NP to Σ^p_3.

Conclusion: Context-dependent argumentation is indeed a genuinely new model that cannot typically be reduced to value-based argumentation. The rarity of representability demonstrates that CDAFs provide a distinct and necessary framework for modeling context-dependent reasoning in argumentation systems.

Abstract: In value-based argumentation, an audience's ordering of values decides which attacks succeed as defeats. In many settings the deciding factor is not the audience but the circumstances: the same attack may succeed at one procedural stage, or under one regulation, and fail at another. Context-dependent argumentation frameworks (CDAFs), a model we recently introduced, capture this directly: one set of arguments, one attack relation, and a defeat function that switches each attack on or off per context, so every context induces an ordinary Dung framework. This raises a reduction question: is context genuinely new, or can one value assignment with per-context orderings reproduce the defeat function, collapsing the CDAF into a VAF? We present a polynomial-time decision procedure for this question and map the harder neighbouring problems, with upper bounds from NP to $Σ^p_3$. We also present a validated reference implementation and a measurement: representability is rare and falls fast with the number of contexts.

</details>


### [118] [ATLAS: Scaffold-Free Algorithm Synthesis by LLMs via Embedding-Guided Quality-Diversity Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15546)
*Danial Yazdani,Mohammad Nabi Omidvar,Yuan Sun,Maksud Ibrahimov,Xiaodong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATLAS is an embedding-guided quality-diversity framework that performs scaffold-free full-algorithm synthesis for combinatorial optimization problems, allowing LLMs to freely design algorithm components, interactions, and control flow without predetermined scaffolds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM-based automated algorithm design methods optimize only specific components within fixed scaffolds, limiting creativity and algorithmic innovation. There's a need for more flexible approaches that allow full-algorithm synthesis without predetermined constraints on overall organization and component interactions.

Method: ATLAS uses an embedding-guided quality-diversity framework with three key components: 1) Scaffold-free full-algorithm synthesis where LLMs design components, interactions, and control flow; 2) Independent detection of execution failures and feasibility issues with error-conditioned repair; 3) Three-layer search strategy: refining best designs, giving opportunities to other regions, and cross-region synthesis for component recombination.

Result: Across four NP-hard problems, ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art component-synthesis methods and matched full-synthesis baselines while remaining competitive with strong human-designed algorithms. A single ATLAS run generates multiple algorithms with comparable performance from distinct embedding-space regions, differing in primary construction or global-search backbone.

Conclusion: Embedding-guided quality-diversity search can make the enlarged full-algorithm design space practically searchable, enabling scaffold-free algorithmic synthesis that goes beyond component optimization to complete algorithm generation while maintaining robustness and diversity.

Abstract: Most LLM-based automated algorithm design methods optimize a designated component within a human-specified scaffold, fixing overall organization and component interactions. We present ATLAS, an embedding-guided quality-diversity framework for scaffold-free full-algorithm synthesis in combinatorial optimization. The problem specification supplies objectives and constraints; a minimal I/O interface fixes only instance and solution formats; the LLM chooses and restructures components, interactions, and control flow. This freedom enlarges the search space, risking invalid candidates and premature convergence to one design region. ATLAS independently detects execution, interface, and feasibility failures, recomputes objectives, and applies error-conditioned repair; similarity-based archive management preserves algorithms across embedding-space regions to counter premature convergence. Its three-layer search refines the best design, gives other regions dedicated refinement opportunities, and performs cross-region synthesis to recombine components and their interactions. Across four NP-hard problems, ATLAS outperforms several state-of-the-art component-synthesis methods and a matched full-synthesis baseline while remaining competitive with strong human-designed algorithms. One ATLAS run retains several algorithms with comparable performance from distinct embedding-space regions rather than a single design. Code inspection finds that these multi-component designs differ in their primary construction or global-search backbone. Our results suggest that embedding-guided quality-diversity search can make the enlarged full-algorithm design space practically searchable. Source code and exact executable prompts are available at <https://github.com/Danial-Yazdani/ATLAS>.

</details>


### [119] [Admission Without Answers: Label-Free Certification and Experience Learning for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15565)
*Junbo Jacob Lian,Huiling Chen,Hanzhang Qin,Chung-Piaw Teo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AdmitOR is a label-free admission mechanism that uses calibrated external behavioral evidence to verify optimization models, achieving higher precision and fewer poisoned admissions than existing methods, though it fails to maintain its false-discovery criterion on wild data streams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing experience-learning agents for optimization modeling require known answers to admit verified skills, but real-world ticket streams lack such labels. Label-free alternatives are unreliable - admitting every executable model poisons 25% of admissions, while single-instance agreement fails to catch models that match at one value but differ elsewhere.

Method: AdmitOR is an admission gate based on calibrated external behavioral evidence. It runs candidate models from three families, prompting strategies, and solver stacks on instances resampled from an extracted parameter domain. Agreement across value-function traces is summarized by a cross-family clique, and a calibrated threshold returns accept, abstain, or escalate decisions.

Result: On calibration data, the preregistered false-discovery criterion holds, but fails on wild streams. However, AdmitOR achieves 0.927 admission precision vs 0.871 for majority vote and 0.726 for execution success, yielding 3.1x and 8.0x fewer poisoned admissions. Its library is smallest and achieves highest macro accuracy (58.4) across five public benchmarks vs 54.8 for majority vote and 53.9 for ground-truth-labeled library.

Conclusion: AdmitOR is the first label-free admission mechanism with explicit false-discovery calibration. While effective on controlled data, its transfer failure on wild streams reveals necessary conditions for real-world deployment and exposes benchmark fidelity issues. The 3.5-point accuracy gain over majority vote is statistically significant and survives correction for host-side anomalies.

Abstract: Experience-learning agents for optimization modeling improve by storing verified skills, but existing learners admit knowledge by checking against known answers, which real ticket streams do not provide. The natural label-free alternatives are unreliable: on a 300-problem label-blind stream, admitting every executable model poisons roughly one admission in four, while single-instance agreement accepts models that match at one value but differ elsewhere. We propose AdmitOR, an admission gate built on calibrated external behavioral evidence. Candidates from three model families, prompting strategies, and solver stacks are run on instances resampled from an extracted parameter domain; agreement across the resulting value-function traces is summarized by a cross-family clique, and a calibrated threshold returns accept, abstain, or escalate. The preregistered false-discovery criterion holds on calibration data but not on the wild stream. We report this negative result in full and trace most failures to benchmark texts that do not faithfully encode their labeled instances. Comparing four admission judges on one collection of logs inside a state-of-the-art skill learner, AdmitOR raises admission precision to 0.927, against 0.871 for majority vote and 0.726 for execution success, yielding 3.1x and 8.0x fewer poisoned admissions. Its library is the smallest and attains the highest macro accuracy across five public benchmarks, 58.4 against 54.8 for majority vote and 53.9 for the ground-truth-labeled library. The 3.5-point gain over majority vote is supported by a paired bootstrap and survives correction for a host-side anomaly. To our knowledge, AdmitOR is the first label-free admission mechanism designed around an explicitly calibrated false-discovery target. The transfer failure identifies a necessary condition for extending it to wild streams.

</details>


### [120] [From Generalist to Specialist: A Context-Fusion Framework for Endoscopic Polyp Reporting with a Frozen VLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15580)
*Ruijie Yang,Yan Zhu,Peiyao Fu,Siyuan Li,Te Luo,Zhihua Wang,Quanlin Li,Pinghong Zhou,Xian Yang,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A context-fusion framework specializing frozen general-purpose vision-language models for endoscopic polyp reporting through explicit image-report retrieval and implicit specialist tokens, achieving strong performance with minimal parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable endoscopic polyp reporting requires integrating quantitative sizing, Paris classification, and morphological descriptions. While general-purpose VLMs offer unified interfaces, existing specialization methods either use task-specific models or modify VLM weights, compromising unified interfaces and pretrained capabilities.

Method: A context-fusion framework that specializes a frozen general-purpose VLM without modifying weights, using implicit instruction context (learned continuous specialist tokens) and explicit transduction context (retrieved related image-report pairs via self-supervised polyp encoder).

Result: The framework substantially improved frozen-VLM inference across all metrics (numerical, categorical, report-generation) and achieved strongest overall performance compared to general-purpose VLMs, task-specific predictors, and weight-adaptation methods. It added only 0.006% trainable parameters relative to frozen VLM. When top-1 retrieval had correct category, it corrected 70.5% of errors from weight-adaptation baseline.

Conclusion: The context-fusion framework provides a lightweight and effective strategy for specialist adaptation of frozen VLMs, enabling reliable endoscopic polyp reporting while preserving unified interfaces and pretrained capabilities.

Abstract: Reliable endoscopic polyp reporting requires integrating quantitative lesion sizing, standardized Paris classification, and clinically meaningful morphological description within a single record. General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) offer a unified interface for image understanding and report generation. Existing specialization strategies, however, typically rely on task-specific models or model-weight adaptation, leaving unresolved how to introduce reliable specialist knowledge while preserving both this unified interface and the VLM's pretrained capabilities. We introduce a context-fusion framework that specializes a frozen general-purpose VLM through both implicit instruction context and explicit transduction context without modifying its pretrained weights. Specifically, a self-supervised polyp encoder retrieves related image-report pairs as explicit, query-specific evidence, while learned continuous specialist tokens provide implicit instruction context shared across cases. Experiments were conducted on 2,056 expert-annotated public endoscopic images. We compared the framework with general-purpose VLMs, task-specific predictors, and weight-adaptation methods to assess specialist performance, unified reporting, and adaptation efficiency. Across numerical, categorical, and report-generation metrics, the proposed framework substantially improved direct frozen-VLM inference and achieved the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods. It added trainable parameters equal to only 0.006% of the frozen VLM's parameter count. When the top-1 retrieved case carried the correct target category, our framework corrected 70.5% of the errors made by a weight-adaptation baseline. These findings support the context-fusion framework as a lightweight and effective strategy for specialist adaptation of a frozen VLM.

</details>


### [121] [Agent Gym: A Framework for Continuous Evaluation and Evolution of LLM Agents Through Human-in-the-Loop Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15591)
*Pouya Ghiasnezhad Omran,Michael Zimmermann,Duncan Cambridge,Ashmita Kapoor,Tanya Dixit*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent Gym: A framework for continuous evaluation and evolution of deployed LLM agents without modifying source code, enabling post-deployment behavioral correction through a modular architecture with six composable capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents face a fundamental tension: their behavior is frozen at deployment while business rules and edge cases continue to evolve. Existing approaches lack structured mechanisms for continuous post-deployment correction without source code changes, and current methods require heavy engineering involvement that negates the economic value of agentic transformation.

Method: Agent Gym wraps any LLM-based agent in a continuous evaluation-and-evolution loop with six capabilities: Act, Evaluate, Investigate, Correct, Learn, and Observe. It features a three-layer architecture: 1) Constitution layer for domain knowledge configuration, 2) Runtime inference pipeline for acting, investigation, and adaptive correction, and 3) Learning loop for SME-driven rule discovery. Technical contributions include hybrid deterministic-LLM correction engine with 21 condition operators, three-layer investigation architecture for compliance validation, and programmatic safety loop.

Result: The framework is fully operational with an open-source reference implementation for invoice processing. It introduces the "Spec-to-Note Gap" concept for agentic system transparency and provides a practical solution for continuous agent evolution ready for adoption.
