Conclusion: Agent Gym addresses the critical need for continuous post-deployment correction of LLM agents, enabling businesses to evolve agent behavior as requirements change without heavy engineering overhead, thereby preserving the economic value of agentic transformation.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents deployed in production environments face a fundamental tension: the agent's behavior is frozen at deployment time, while the business rules and edge cases it must handle continue to evolve. Existing approaches address agent construction and one-time evaluation but provide no structured mechanism for continuous post-deployment behavioral correction without modifying the agent's source code. Most of the approaches offered in the market, require intense collection of logs and traces, and re-examining the agent design by the engineering team, a process which is heavy, long and negates the economical value of agentic transformation. We introduce Agent Gym, a modular, domain-agnostic framework that wraps any existing LLM-based agent in a continuous evaluation-and-evolution loop. The framework provides six composable capabilities --- Act, Evaluate, Investigate, Correct, Learn, and Observe --- organized across three architectural zones: a constitution layer that codifies domain knowledge in configuration artifacts, a runtime inference pipeline that chains acting, investigation, and adaptive correction, and a learning loop that enables subject matter experts to discover and validate new correction rules through natural language interaction. The key technical contributions include a hybrid deterministic-LLM correction engine with 21 condition operators and three-tier actions, a three-layer investigation architecture for ground-truth-free compliance validation, and a programmatic safety loop that guarantees rule correctness before human approval. We further introduce the Spec-to-Note Gap, an autoencoder-inspired view of agentic system transparency. An open-source reference implementation for invoice processing demonstrates that the framework is fully operational and ready for adoption.

</details>


### [122] [When Entropy Is Not Enough: Reclaiming Lost Semantics in LLM Output Length Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15592)
*Feiyang Ren,Shengtao Wen,Lingbing Guo,Yu Tian,Yuanning Cui,Xiang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ESTP (Entropy-and-Semantic Token Pooling) is a lightweight framework that improves LLM serving efficiency by combining entropy with attention-based importance scores to better predict output lengths, enabling length-aware scheduling that reduces padding overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM serving suffers from inefficient padding to fixed maximum lengths, wasting compute and degrading throughput. Existing approaches like entropy-guided token pooling fail to consider semantic importance differences across tokens, causing important tokens to be underweighted and uninformative tokens to be overemphasized, which hurts length prediction reliability.

Method: ESTP combines entropy measurements with attention-based importance scores derived from self-attention weights computed during the LLM prefill phase. This allows the framework to capture both uncertainty (via entropy) and semantic importance (via attention weights) with minimal additional computation. The approach reuses prefill activations, adding almost no extra memory overhead and introducing minimal latency.

Result: On the ForeLen benchmark, ESTP outperforms baseline methods, achieving better prediction accuracy and lower error rates in most scenarios. When integrated with a length-aware scheduler in end-to-end system tests, it further improves overall throughput and reduces padding ratio.

Conclusion: ESTP offers a practical and effective building block for length-aware LLM serving systems, particularly benefiting long-context reasoning and reinforcement learning applications where efficient length prediction is crucial for reducing computational waste and improving throughput.

Abstract: Efficient LLM serving is often bottlenecked by the need to pad sequences to a fixed maximum length, and this wastes compute and degrades throughput. Predicting output lengths in advance makes it possible to adopt length-aware scheduling, and this reduces the overhead. This advantage is especially pronounced in long-context reasoning and reinforcement learning applications. Existing approaches, such as entropy-guided token pooling, use token-wise entropy as their primary signal, but they tend to ignore differences in semantic content across tokens. So, important tokens are often underweighted, and tokens carrying little information receive disproportionate emphasis. This hurts the reliability of length prediction. We introduce ESTP (Entropy-and-Semantic Token Pooling), a lightweight framework that addresses this issue by combining entropy with attention-based importance scores. These scores are derived directly from the self-attention weights computed during the LLM prefill phase, and this allows ESTP to capture both uncertainty and semantic importance with minimal additional computation. Since the framework reuses prefill activations, it adds almost no extra memory overhead and introduces only minimal latency. On the ForeLen benchmark, ESTP outperforms baseline methods, achieves better prediction accuracy and lower error rates in most scenarios. When integrated with a length-aware scheduler in end-to-end system tests, it further helps improve overall throughput and reduce the padding ratio. Our results offer a practical and effective building block for length-aware LLM serving systems.

</details>


### [123] [TRACE: Trajectory Aware Reasoning for Multi-Turn Adversarial Conversation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15594)
*Md Messal Monem Miah,Adrita Anika,Zhiyuan Yu,Ruihong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trace is a multi-turn defense system for LLMs that uses trajectory-aware structured reasoning to detect manipulation patterns across conversations, balancing safety against jailbreak attacks while maintaining helpfulness on legitimate requests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a critical safety threat by distributing harmful objectives across multiple seemingly benign turns to bypass existing LLM guardrails. Current defenses lack reasoning capacity to identify evolving manipulation patterns and often over-refuse legitimate requests related to sensitive topics, trading helpfulness for safety.

Method: Trace employs trajectory-aware structured reasoning where before generating each response, the model: 1) identifies manipulation cues from the conversation trajectory, 2) evaluates both benign and adversarial interpretations of user intent, 3) assigns a jailbreak score, and 4) commits to an action (Allow, Caution, or Decline). The authors train Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO using a multi-component reward function that jointly optimizes helpfulness on benign prompts and robustness against jailbreak attempts.

Result: Across seven multi-turn attack benchmarks, Trace achieves an average attack success rate of 14.5% compared to 31.4% for the strongest baseline and 74.9% for the undefended target. The system significantly increases attacker effort required per successful jailbreak while maintaining 93.3% average compliance on over-refusal benchmarks, showing effective balance between usability and safety.

Conclusion: Trace provides an effective multi-turn defense against jailbreak attacks through structured reasoning that tracks manipulation patterns across conversation trajectories, successfully balancing safety and helpfulness while reducing attack success rates substantially below current state-of-the-art defenses.

Abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks have emerged as a critical safety threat to LLMs, as harmful objectives are decomposed across a sequence of apparently benign turns to bypass guardrails. Existing defenses lack the reasoning capacity to identify evolving manipulation patterns, often trading helpfulness for safety by over-refusing benign requests related to sensitive topics. We introduce Trace, a multi-turn defense with trajectory-aware structured reasoning. Before generating each response, the model identifies manipulation cues from the trajectory, evaluates both the benign and adversarial interpretations of user intent, assigns a jailbreak score, and commits to an action: Allow, Caution, or Decline. We curate 4k multi-turn adversarial conversations from five attack frameworks, pair them with 2.4k benign dialogs, and 600 sensitive-but-benign conversations. We train Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with SFT and GRPO under a multi-component reward that jointly optimizes helpfulness on benign prompts and robustness against jailbreak attempts. Across seven multi-turn attack benchmarks, Trace attains an average attack success rate (ASR) of 14.5% against 31.4% for the strongest baseline and 74.9% for the undefended target, while significantly raising the attacker effort required per successful jailbreak. Trace also balances usability and safety, achieving a 93.3% average compliance on over-refusal benchmarks.

</details>


### [124] [VARM-Bench: Benchmarking Verifiable Structured Reasoning in Chinese Abusive Speech Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15600)
*Mingyu Yuan,Shengtao Wen,Lingbing Guo,Zhen Bi,Xiang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VARM-Bench is a new Chinese benchmark for abusive-speech moderation that provides field-anchored chain-of-thought rationales to verify moderation decisions, moving beyond simple label classification to complete, auditable moderation records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Chinese moderation benchmarks focus on label classification, fine-grained categorization, and target extraction but lack a unified representation for verifying the specific basis of moderation decisions, making it hard to audit why content was flagged or ensure consistent rationale generation.

Method: Created VARM-Bench with instances containing natural-language rationales explicitly anchored to six moderation fields: target, target type, target explicitness, author stance, harmfulness label, and fine-grained category. Developed a deterministic evaluation protocol assessing field correctness, target alignment, output validity, complete-record agreement, and hidden errors, without relying on LLM judges. Evaluated multiple language model families using zero-shot prompting, taxonomy guidance, and structured CoT supervision.

Result: Evaluation revealed that strong performance at label-level classification can mask substantial errors in complete moderation records. The benchmark successfully identifies various error types including field-level inaccuracies and demonstrates the limitations of current moderation approaches that don't capture full rationales.

Conclusion: VARM-Bench provides an auditable, reproducible benchmark for evaluating verifiable moderation rationales in Chinese abusive speech, addressing the critical need for transparent moderation systems that can explain their decisions beyond simple labeling.

Abstract: The widespread circulation of abusive online content has increased the need for reliable moderation of Chinese social-media text. Existing Chinese benchmarks support label classification, fine-grained toxicity categorization, and target-aware extraction, but do not provide a unified representation for deterministically verifying the stated basis of a moderation decision. We introduce VARM-Bench, a benchmark for field-anchored chain-of-thought rationales in Chinese abusive-speech moderation. Each instance contains a concise natural-language rationale with explicit anchors for six decisions: target, target type, target explicitness, author stance, harmfulness label, and fine-grained category. Our deterministic protocol evaluates field correctness, target alignment, output validity, complete-record agreement, and hidden record errors conditioned on correct final decisions, without relying on an LLM judge. Under a common structured-output protocol, we evaluate language models across multiple model families using zero-shot prompting, taxonomy guidance, and structured CoT supervision, and analyze lexical-cue sensitivity and field-level errors. Results show that strong label-level performance can conceal substantial errors in complete moderation records. VARM-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible benchmark for evaluating verifiable moderation rationales in Chinese abusive-speech moderation.

</details>


### [125] [Bias-Corrected Ceilings of Emotion Predictability from Human Label Variation Based on Instance-Level Fano Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15619)
*Keito Inoshita*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BACE framework estimates bias-corrected accuracy ceilings for emotion recognition, showing irreducible error exists and saturation claims need disciplined evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emotion recognition accuracy keeps improving on benchmarks, but it's unclear whether an accuracy ceiling has been reached; current approaches lack discipline in claiming saturation, and need to account for annotation limitations, estimator choice, and evaluation protocol dependencies.

Method: Proposes Bias-corrected Affective Ceiling Estimation (BACE) framework with: anchored Dirichlet-mixture empirical Bayes estimator (bracketed between plug-in and NSB) to recover human-consensus distribution; annotator split, noise deconvolution, and fixed claim gate to attribute error without circularity.

Result: Unconstrained point estimates show reachability ranges from 0.38 to 1.03, making saturation claims based on any single estimator unreliable; Only assertion passing the claim gate: at least ~33% of a representative classifier's error on GoEmotions is irreducible; Same pattern found on offensiveness and irony tasks.

Conclusion: Saturation claims in emotion recognition require disciplined statistical frameworks like BACE; irreducible error exists (at least 33% on GoEmotions), and arbitrary estimator choices produce widely varying ceiling estimates; Future work should use similar discipline when making claims about model performance limits.

Abstract: Emotion recognition from text keeps improving on benchmarks, yet whether an accuracy ceiling has been reached is seldom asked with discipline. Our aim is not to pin this ceiling to a single number, but to quantify how far it depends on finite annotation, estimator choice, annotation noise, and the evaluation protocol, and thereby to discipline how confidently saturation can be claimed. We propose Bias-corrected Affective Ceiling Estimation (BACE), an analysis framework that estimates a bias-corrected ceiling, separates irreducible from reducible error, and disciplines the resulting claims. An anchored Dirichlet-mixture empirical Bayes estimator, bracketed between plug-in and NSB, recovers the human-consensus distribution; an annotator split, a noise deconvolution, and a fixed claim gate then attribute error without circularity. Methodologically, unconstrained point estimates place reachability anywhere from 0.38 to 1.03, so saturation cannot be decided by any single estimator. Substantively, the only assertion passing the claim gate is that at least about 33% of a representative classifier's error on GoEmotions is irreducible, with the same pattern recurring on offensiveness and irony.

</details>


### [126] [Rotation-Invariant Multi-IMU Activity Recognition under Independent Per-Location Orientation Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15621)
*Seungyeol Baek,Yoonbyung Chai,Yonghyeon Lee,Sungjoon Choi,Sungho Suh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRI-HAR is a novel framework that achieves truly rotation-invariant human activity recognition by structurally handling independent per-IMU orientation offsets without needing data augmentation or calibration pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-IMU HAR applications like at-home rehabilitation, users must reattach sensors across sessions, causing independent orientation offsets at different body locations. Existing methods rely on rotational augmentation (which has limited robustness) or complex calibration pipelines, lacking structural handling of this deployment shift.

Method: The TRI-HAR framework: 1) Reshapes accelerometer and gyroscope streams into triaxial vectors, 2) Applies a shared SO(3)-equivariant backbone and invariant projection to each IMU location separately, 3) Fuses the resulting invariant features for activity classification.

Result: Across four multi-IMU benchmarks, TRI-HAR preserves macro-F1 under fixed independent per-location SO(3) rotations and outperforms rotation-augmented baselines under this target shift without requiring rotational augmentation.

Conclusion: TRI-HAR provides a structural solution to the orientation offset problem in multi-IMU HAR by making rotation invariance a fundamental model property, eliminating the need for data augmentation or calibration procedures.

Abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) with self-administered wearables, such as at-home rehabilitation and exercise monitoring, often requires reattaching inertial measurement units (IMUs) across sessions. In multi-IMU settings, this can induce independent orientation offsets across body locations, a deployment shift that conventional scalar HAR models do not structurally handle. Existing remedies rely on rotation augmentation, whose robustness depends on sampled transformations, or calibration and orientationnormalization pipelines requiring additional reference-frame assumptions or explicit procedures. We present Truly Rotation-Invariant HAR (TRI-HAR), a rotation-invariant framework that makes robustness to independent per-location IMU orientation offsets a structural model property. TRI-HAR reshapes accelerometer and gyroscope streams into triaxial vectors, applies a shared SO(3)-equivariant backbone and invariant projection to each IMU location, and fuses the resulting invariant features for activity classification. Across four multi-IMU benchmarks, TRI-HAR preserves macro-F1 under fixed independent per-location SO(3) rotations and outperforms rotation-augmented baselines under this target shift without requiring rotational augmentation.

</details>


### [127] [Argumentation for Common Ground: Finding Zones of Possible Agreement between Individuals in Conflict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15634)
*Elisa Cavatorta,Antonio Rago*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Computational argumentation approach identifies mutually acceptable peace agreements by modeling conflicting sides' subjective reasoning about agreement clauses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing peace negotiation approaches often fail because they don't account for citizens' subjective reasoning shaped by contested narratives. Need methods to identify common ground in polarized conflicts like Palestinian-Israeli conflict where public acceptability matters.

Method: Introduces quantitative bipolar argumentation framework to represent each side's reasoning about peace agreements. Merges these frameworks to identify mutually acceptable agreements (ZOPA - Zone of Possible Agreement). Evaluates using Palestinian-Israeli conflict case study with survey data from existing work and LLM-generated data.

Result: Framework successfully identifies potential ZOPAs through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments. Demonstrates how argumentation can help negotiators map feasible agreements grounded in citizens' reasoning.

Conclusion: Computational argumentation provides a novel approach to conflict resolution by formally modeling subjective reasoning, enabling identification of mutually acceptable agreements in polarized conflicts where narrative acceptability matters.

Abstract: How can common ground between societies in conflict be identified when citizens' acceptability of peace agreements is shaped by contested narratives? Such acceptability is mediated not only by the clauses that agreements include or exclude, but crucially by citizens' subjective reasoning concerning agreements' clauses. In this paper, we leverage computational argumentation to introduce a novel approach to identifying mutually acceptable agreements among individuals in conflict, i.e. a Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA). First, we introduce a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework tailored to represent each side's reasoning about peace agreements. We then show how merging these frameworks can enable negotiators to identify peace agreements that are mutually acceptable. To evaluate our approach under conditions of real-world relevance, we focus on the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, where long-standing policy, practitioner and public interest underscores the demand for methods capable of analysing polarised public reasoning. We show how our framework identifies a ZOPA through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments using survey data from both existing work and retrieved by a large language model. The results illustrate how argumentation can empower negotiators and conflict-resolution teams in mapping feasible ZOPAs grounded in citizens' reasoning.

</details>


### [128] [A Responsible Artificial Intelligence Framework for Groundwater Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15657)
*Chong Chen,Yulu Zhang,Qingxi Guo,Yihan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes six Responsible AI principles for groundwater prediction in China's Heihe River Basin, comparing LSTM and Transformer models on these ethical dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While AI has raised important ethical discussions in many fields, its application in groundwater management remains limited with scarce research on responsible AI. The paper aims to address this gap by applying responsible AI principles to groundwater prediction.

Method: Six Responsible AI principles are proposed (transparency, technical robustness, privacy governance, fairness, accountability, sustainability). LSTM and Transformer time-series models are developed using multi-source hydrometeorological data, validated through post-hoc interpretability, Monte Carlo simulation, and scenario analysis in the Heihe River Basin.

Result: Transformer outperforms LSTM in accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. The study demonstrates the operability and practical value of Responsible AI principles in groundwater prediction for sustainable water management under climate change and human activities.

Conclusion: The application of Responsible AI principles to groundwater prediction is both feasible and valuable. The proposed framework can support sustainable water management in the face of climate change and human impacts, with Transformer models showing particular promise for ethical AI implementation.

Abstract: The rapid development and widespread application of artificial intelligence (AI) have sparked intense discussions on how to deploy responsible AI systems in a manner aligned with human values and ethical standards. Compared to fields like healthcare, energy, or finance, the application of AI in groundwater is relatively limited, and research on responsible AI is even more scarce. Taking the middle reaches of the Heihe River Basin as the study area, this paper proposes six Responsible AI principles: transparency, technical robustness, privacy governance, fairness, accountability, and sustainability. LSTM and Transformer time-series models are developed using multi-source hydrometeorological data, and validated via post-hoc interpretability, Monte Carlo simulation, and scenario analysis. The results show that Transformer outperforms LSTM in accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, demonstrating the operability and practical value of Responsible AI principles in groundwater prediction to support sustainable water management under climate change and human activities.

</details>


### [129] [THESIS-MoE: Trainable Hierarchical Extraction and SteerIng of Sycophancy in Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15687)
*Kareem Hassani,Chaymaa Abbas,Lama Mawlawi,Mariette Awad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Conditional activation steering for sycophancy reduction in MoE models, using contrastive signals to target specific computational subcircuits rather than applying uniform interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods apply unconditional interventions that trade knowledge retention for behavioral correction. In MoE models, sycophantic behavior is encoded within expert computations, making precise steering challenging. Need for conditional interventions that target only where sycophancy is present to maintain knowledge retention.

Method: Introduce shared contrastive signal from matched prompts with/without stated beliefs to identify sycophancy locations across MoE hierarchy. Formulate localization as causal search over granularity ladder (MoE blocks, experts, attention blocks, heads). Compare unconditional subtraction against two conditional alternatives: analytic projection-based subtraction and learned per-token gate to steer away from sycophancy while keeping weights frozen.

Result: Conditional interventions removed up to 90% of belief-induced sycophancy while maintaining favorable removal-retention trade-off. Sycophancy resides in identifiable computational subcircuits that can be selectively steered. Evaluated on three MoE models across sycophancy, general knowledge, and reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Syco-phancy can be effectively reduced through conditional activation steering that targets specific computational subcircuits in MoE models, preserving knowledge retention while correcting undesirable behavior. This demonstrates the viability of precise behavioral intervention in complex model architectures.

Abstract: Sycophancy, the tendency of a language model to change its answer to match a user's stated belief, is a common alignment failure. Existing activation steering methods typically apply a single contrastive direction uniformly throughout the model, which is an unconditional intervention that alters activations even when no sycophantic behavior is present, trading knowledge retention for behavioral correction. In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, prior work further suggests that behavior is encoded within expert computations rather than routing decisions alone, making precise behavioral steering particularly challenging. In this work, we introduce a shared contrastive signal, built from matched prompts with and without a stated belief, that identifies where sycophancy lives across the MoE hierarchy and drives interventions that act only where the behavior is present. We formulate localization as a causal search over a granularity ladder of MoE blocks, experts, attention blocks, and heads, and compare unconditional subtraction against two conditional alternatives: an analytic projection-based subtraction and a learned per-token gate that steers the model away from sycophancy while keeping its weights frozen. We evaluate on three MoE models measuring sycophancy alongside general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks. Our conditional interventions removed up to 90\% of the belief-induced sycophancy. Our results demonstrate that sycophancy resides in identifiable computational subcircuits and can be selectively steered while maintaining a favorable removal-retention trade-off.

</details>


### [130] [Large Models for Small Devices: Recent Advances and Empirical Analysis of Edge AI Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15693)
*Subhransu Das,Jiaming Cheng,Arnav Kumar,Sadia Afrose,Mingzhe Han,Michael Silagy,Shreya Palande,Brijesh Soni,Rajiv Ramnath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Practical deployment guidelines for AI model compression on edge devices show no single technique wins across tasks - quantization works best for language tasks while pruning excels for vision tasks, with important tradeoffs in hardware compatibility and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running large AI models on resource-constrained edge devices requires model compression, but what compresses well doesn't necessarily deploy well. The paper aims to extract practical deployment guidelines from recent works that report compression results on real hardware.

Method: Surveyed dozens of recent works reporting compression results on real hardware, deployed compact language and image models on GPU, CPU, and Raspberry Pi platforms across question answering and image segmentation tasks. Used neural-flow graph analysis and prefill-decode-level latency decomposition to explain effects.

Result: For question answering, Qwen3.5 0.8B reached 93.85 SQuAD F1 with Q5_K_M GGUF quantization, while structured pruning cost 16 F1 at 1% ratio. For segmentation, pruning cut model size by nearly 80% at near-constant mIoU, while quantization left parameters unchanged. Pruning could inflate artifacts by 21-49% due to k-quant super-block alignment issues, raising Raspberry Pi latency up to 3.4x. LoRA-recovered variants showed surface competence while having biased predictions.

Conclusion: The right compression technique depends on task, model, and hardware - no single approach wins across all scenarios. The paper provides task-specific deployment research directions and open-sources experiment code, emphasizing practical deployment considerations over just compression metrics.

Abstract: Running large AI models on resource-constrained edge devices requires model compression to reduce model size and computation. What compresses well, however, need not deploy well. We survey dozens of recent works that report compression results on real hardware and extract practical deployment guidelines from them. Following these guidelines, we deploy compact language and image models on GPU, CPU, and Raspberry Pi platforms across question answering and image segmentation. No single technique wins across tasks. For question answering, Qwen3.5 0.8B reaches 93.85 SQuAD F1 and 92 EM under Q5_K_M GGUF quantization, while structured pruning at the same precision costs 16 F1 at a 1% ratio. For segmentation, the ranking reverses: default quantization leaves parameters and MACs unchanged, whereas pruning cuts model size by nearly 80% at near-constant mIoU. Pruning can even inflate the deployed artifact by 21-49% by breaking k-quant super-block alignment; combined with longer, less format-compliant outputs, this raises Raspberry Pi latency up to 3.4x. Compression can also manufacture the appearance of competence rather than destroy it visibly: one LoRA-recovered variant stays fully parseable and holds 71% strict BoolQ accuracy while sending 97 of 100 predictions to a single class, at 52.6% balanced accuracy. We explain these effects through neural-flow graph analysis and prefill-decode-level latency decomposition, and condense them into task-specific deployment research directions. The right technique depends on the task, the model, and the hardware. Our experiment code and artifacts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Arnavvvkumar/deployment

</details>


### [131] [Adaptive Mixing of Policies from Searching and Policies from Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15700)
*Gavin B. Rens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Flexer: Adaptive search depth for policy learning by mixing neural network and MCTS policies based on network error and model variance


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search/planning for distillation targets in reinforcement learning can be very slow when using fixed search depth. The authors aim to reduce search time by adapting search depth based on policy network quality instead of using fixed-depth searches.

Method: Flexer architecture dynamically mixes neural network policy and Monte Carlo Tree Search policy at each step. The mixing factor favors MCTS policy when: 1) policy imitation error of the network is high, and 2) environment models' variance is high.

Result: Flexer outperforms AlphaZero (and DQN and ADP) in experiments on three toy symbolic problems, showing improved performance with adaptive search depth.

Conclusion: Adaptively adjusting search depth based on policy network quality and model uncertainty improves efficiency and performance in reinforcement learning compared to fixed-depth search approaches.

Abstract: Background: Distillation of training targets generated thru search/planning has proven useful in reinforcement learning, but search can take exceedingly long. Objectives: Rather than perform search to the same depth every time (typically at a fixed period of steps), reduce the search depth proportionally to the quality of the policy network priors. Methods: We describe Flexer, an architecture that, for each step, mixes the policy from a neural network and the policy from Monte Carlo tree search. The mixing factor favors the MCTS policy as the policy imitation error of the network and the environment models' variance increases. Results: Flexer outperforms a version of AlphaZero (and DQN and ADP) for some experiments on three toy symbolic problems.

</details>


### [132] [HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703)
*XinQi Wang,Jinwei Xiao,Sijia Cui,Hongming Zhang,Yanna Wang,Qingyang Zhang,Bo Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyMem is a hierarchical framework that separates LLM agent context into functional layers to reduce clutter and improve performance on complex, long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents perform poorly on complex, long-horizon tasks due to context clutter from accumulating execution traces and intermediate outputs. Existing compression/retrieval methods applied to flat context don't separate different context types, leading to degraded reasoning.

Method: HyMem organizes context hierarchically by function: separates high-level planning from execution/complex analysis. Has an isolated reasoning module for complex subtasks (without adding reasoning traces to planning context) and a memory management module that preserves task progress via structured summaries across context refreshes.

Result: Experiments on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus show HyMem with DeepSeek-V4 achieves average Pass@1 scores of 66.7% and 61.3%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points respectively. Effectively controls reasoning context growth, maintaining focus and accuracy.

Conclusion: HyMem's hierarchical approach to context management successfully reduces redundant context accumulation, retains task-critical information, and supports coherent long-horizon reasoning within limited context windows.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often perform poorly on complex, long-horizon tasks because their context becomes increasingly cluttered over time. As interactions accumulate, detailed execution traces and intermediate outputs dominate the context, making it difficult for the model to retain and use high-level planning information. Most existing methods address this issue through compression or retrieval applied to a single, flat context, which does not clearly separate different types of context information and often leads to degraded reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose HyMem, a hierarchical framework that explicitly separates the agent's context into distinct functional layers. HyMem organizes context by function to separate high-level planning from execution and complex analysis. Its isolated reasoning module handles complex subtasks without adding intermediate reasoning traces to the persistent planning context, while its memory management module preserves task progress across context refreshes through structured summaries. These components reduce redundant context accumulation, retain task-critical information, and support coherent long-horizon reasoning within a limited context window. Experiments on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus show that, with DeepSeek-V4, HyMem achieves average Pass@1 scores of 66.7% and 61.3%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis indicates that HyMem effectively controls the growth of the reasoning context, allowing the model to maintain focus and accuracy across complex, long-horizon tasks.

</details>


### [133] [PLeDO: Pain Level Detection for Osteoarthritis from EMR Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15719)
*Yuhao Chen,Jiahao Cai,Nafiz Sadman,Farhana Zulkernine,John Queenan,David Barber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers develop two tools (SPaDe and PLeDO) to detect osteoarthritis pain severity from electronic medical records using NLP and machine learning to categorize patients as having mild or moderate-to-severe pain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Osteoarthritis is a chronic joint disease where damaged tissues don't repair normally. Current pain assessment from EMRs is challenging due to subjective expressions in chart notes influenced by cultural background and demographics. There's a need to better understand pain severity to improve diagnosis and treatment methods in primary care settings.

Method: 1) SPaDe: A synonym-based pain level detection tool that analyzes only pain-related expressions in unstructured chart notes. 2) PLeDO: An integrated tool that combines SPaDe with medication information from structured EMR data and pain scale information from chart notes. Both use information extraction, natural language processing, and machine learning techniques with human-labeled gold standard data for validation.

Result: Both SPaDe and PLeDO successfully demonstrated the ability to detect mild and moderate-to-severe pain from EMR data. The tools can categorize patients into these pain severity groups for analysis of diagnosis and treatment methods in primary care settings.

Conclusion: The developed tools show promise for analyzing pain severity in osteoarthritis patients from EMR data, which could potentially improve quality of care in primary care settings by enabling better understanding of diagnosis and treatment methods based on pain levels.

Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive chronic joint disease resulting in a breakdown of articular cartilage and bone when damaged joint tissues are not able to normally repair themselves. The aim of this pilot research study is to understand the pain severity for OA from patients' primary care Electronic Medical Records (EMR), both from the structured medical data and the unstructured chart note data using information extraction, natural language processing and machine learning techniques. We propose SPaDe, a Synonym-based Pain level Detection tool to categorize patients into having mild or moderate-to-severe pain to understand diagnosis and treatment methods based on only the pain related expressions in the unstructured chart note. Expressions are subjective, objective, and influenced by cultural background and demography which poses a difficult challenge. Therefore, we improve the model by incorporating the medication information from the structured EMR data and pain scale related information from the chart note to propose an integrated pain level detection tool for OA called PLeDO. With the help of human labeled gold standard data, we demonstrate that both SPaDe and PLeDO can detect mild and moderate-to-severe pain from the EMR data to analyze and potentially improve the quality of care in primary care setting.

</details>


### [134] [Toward AI-Friendly Cartography: Understanding How Color Design Influences Foundation Model Spatial Reasoning on Sequential Choropleth Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15736)
*Yonghe Sun,Zhenjia Liu,Hua Liao,Wenjia Xu,Nai Yang,Weihua Dong,Zhiwei Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sequential choropleth map design principles (color ordering and contrast) significantly affect foundation models' spatial reasoning performance, with traditional human-centric design guidelines remaining relevant for machine map understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As foundation models increasingly handle multimodal and geospatial reasoning, there's uncertainty about whether cartographic principles designed for human perception are equally effective for machines, particularly for sequential choropleth maps.

Method: Created a controlled benchmark of 5,760 maps and 28,800 questions across five spatial reasoning tasks. Evaluated 21 open-source and proprietary multimodal FMs, examining effects of hue palette, color ordering, and lightness contrast. Conducted additional factorial experiments and LoRA fine-tuning.

Result: Hue choice had limited/inconsistent effects. Disrupting sequential color ordering substantially reduced performance, especially for comparison/ranking tasks. Reduced lightness contrast consistently impaired reasoning, while excessive contrast provided marginal gains. LoRA fine-tuning improved overall accuracy but preserved sensitivity patterns.

Conclusion: Conventional sequential ordering and sufficient contrast remain important for machine map understanding. The research provides empirical guidance for AI-friendly cartographic design, showing errors arise from color-legend decoding, spatial reasoning, and attribute-spatial structure integration challenges.

Abstract: Foundation models (FMs) increasingly support multimodal and geospatial reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether cartographic principles designed for human perception are equally effective for machines. Focusing on sequential choropleth maps, we examine how hue palette, color ordering, and lightness contrast influence FM spatial reasoning. We construct a controlled benchmark of 5,760 maps and 28,800 questions spanning Attribute Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, and Pattern Delineate, and evaluate 21 open-source and proprietary multimodal FMs. Results show that hue choice has limited and inconsistent effects, whereas disrupting sequential color ordering substantially reduces performance, especially for comparison and ranking. Reduced lightness contrast also consistently impairs reasoning, while increasing contrast beyond sufficient separability provides only marginal gains. LoRA fine-tuning improves overall accuracy but preserves these relative sensitivities. Additional factorial experiments further indicate that errors arise from color-and-legend decoding, spatial reasoning, and the integration of thematic attributes with spatial structure. These findings show that conventional sequential ordering and sufficient contrast remain important for machine map understanding and provide empirical guidance for AI-friendly cartographic design.

</details>


### [135] [Propaganda Forensics: Recovering the Generation Pipeline of an AI-Driven Influence Campaign](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15746)
*Benjamin Icard,Elouan Vuichard,Louis Lefebvre,Lila Sainero,Thomas Girault,Alice Breton,Tanguy Launay,Gauvain Bourgne,Morgane Casanova,Guillaume Gadek,Victor Klötzer,Michel Le Nouy,Guillaume Gravier,Jean-Gabriel Ganascia,Paul Égré*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PROPAGIA: Forensic analysis of an AI-driven French influence campaign reveals propaganda techniques, prompt leaks, and evidence of both Llama 3 and Mistral model usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To conduct a forensic analysis of AI-generated propaganda in French influence campaigns, specifically the Storm-1516/CopyCop campaign disclosed by intelligence agencies, and to understand how AI models are being used to generate persuasive content at scale.

Method: Created PROPAGIA corpus (2,646 propagandist French articles) and compared with SIPA corpus (human-written mainstream press). Applied topic modeling, vagueness analysis, sentiment analysis, and source citation analysis. Analyzed prompt instruction leaks from websites and used rewriting-based detection for model attribution.

Result: PROPAGIA articles showed significantly higher vagueness, subjectivity, and negativity than mainstream press, with fewer sources cited. Found prompt instruction leaks on 50 of 84 websites, including a verbatim editorial specification explaining these stylistic differences. High cross-article redundancy observed. Detection methods support attribution to Llama 3 family but also suggest Mistral-family model involvement.

Conclusion: The study reveals systematic use of AI models for generating propaganda with identifiable persuasion techniques and stylistic patterns, demonstrating both technical detection methods and the importance of forensic analysis for understanding AI-driven influence operations.

Abstract: We present a forensic analysis of the generation pipeline behind a recent AI-driven influence campaign. We introduce PROPAGIA, a corpus of 2,646 propagandist French articles from the Storm-1516/CopyCop campaign disclosed by VIGINUM and INSIKT GROUP in 2025. For comparison, we rely on SIPA, a corpus of human-written French mainstream press from the same period. Using topic modeling, vagueness and sentiment analysis, we first isolate persuasion techniques characteristic of propaganda, with PROPAGIA far exceeding SIPA in vagueness, subjectivity and negativity, and citing fewer sources. We then find prompt instruction leaks on 50 of the 84 PROPAGIA websites, including a verbatim ten-point editorial specification accounting for several of these differences, together with high cross-article redundancy. Finally, we show that rewriting-based detection supports INSIKT GROUP's attribution to the Llama 3 family, but also suggests the involvement of Mistral-family models.

</details>


### [136] [Intent-Driven Situation Tracking for User-Centric Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15755)
*Meiling Tao,Yiling Tao,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IDSS is a training-free framework that maintains explicit situation states to help agents better track user intents, constraints, and facts in multi-turn dialogues, improving task completion and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing context-management methods rely on implicit inference from dialogue history rather than maintaining explicit situation states, making it difficult for agents to track grounded facts, task dependencies, and constraint satisfaction in evolving multi-turn interactions.

Method: IDSS maintains an explicit situation state alongside dialogue that: 1) parses tool returns into provenance-aware entities/attributes, 2) tracks user intents, required variables, constraints, and execution status, and 3) propagates new facts to update action executability, enabling agents to avoid infeasible actions and reuse relevant information.

Result: Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across eight LLMs show IDSS improves task completion, preference elicitation, and interaction efficiency, particularly for tasks involving multi-entity coordination, evolving user constraints, and constraint-aware replanning.

Conclusion: Explicit situation tracking through IDSS offers an effective alternative to history-centric context management for reliable user-centric multi-turn agents, with improvements stemming from the interaction between fact persistence, intent-centered state tracking, and constraint modeling.

Abstract: User-centric multi-turn agents must act on an evolving task situation shaped by changing user intents, accumulated tool-grounded facts, missing information, and execution constraints. Existing context-management methods improve the use of past interaction history, but rarely maintain an explicit situation state that separates grounded facts from task-state judgments. As a result, agents often need to infer fine-grained attributes, task dependencies, and constraint satisfaction implicitly from dialogue traces. We propose Intent-Driven Situation States (IDSS), a training-free framework that maintains an explicit situation state alongside the dialogue. IDSS parses tool returns into provenance-aware entities and attributes, tracks user intents, required variables, constraints, and execution status, and propagates new facts to task constraints to update action executability. This allows agents to avoid infeasible actions, advance dependent goals, and reuse relevant information without repeatedly searching raw history. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across eight LLMs show that IDSS improves task completion, preference elicitation, and interaction efficiency, with clear gains on tasks involving multi-entity coordination, evolving user constraints, and constraint-aware replanning. Ablations and error analyses show that these improvements come from the interaction between fact persistence, intent-centered state tracking, and constraint modeling. These results suggest that explicit situation tracking offers an effective alternative to history-centric context management for reliable user-centric multi-turn agents.

</details>


### [137] [Broken Symmetry in LLM Refusal: Answer Release Is More Local Than Refusal Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15772)
*Yiqi Liu,Yang Wang,Songxin Wang,Chenghao Xiao,Chenghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language model refusal doesn't erase correct answers but merely suppresses them; suppression is easier to remove than to impose, showing asymmetric control rather than symmetric switching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether language model refusal mechanisms truly erase correct answers from internal representations or merely suppress them at the output layer, and to investigate the symmetry of control over answering vs refusal behaviors.

Method: Use controlled withhold setting with perfectly matched answering and refusal trajectories for bidirectional activation patching. Conduct causal interventions using activation patching to examine intervention locality under matched conditions. Test recoverability of withheld answers from hidden states and examine the reversibility of refusal behaviors.

Result: 1) Correct answers remain linearly recoverable from hidden states even during clean refusals. 2) Releasing withheld answers requires only single-position patching (highly local), while reimposing suppression requires broader interventions across multiple positions. 3) An average answer-to-refusal displacement vector captures geometric differences but doesn't serve as a reliable reversible linear control toggle. 4) Assembling coherent refusal sequences is more difficult than releasing suppressed answers.

Conclusion: Refusal doesn't function as a simple symmetric switch - suppression is easier to remove than to impose. For safety and auditing, probe recoverability can overestimate true behavioral control, and locating refusal-relevant directions doesn't reliably enable steering from answering to coherent refusal.

Abstract: When a language model refuses to answer a prompt, it is unclear whether the correct answer is erased from its internal representations, or merely suppressed at the output layer. We investigate this mechanism using a controlled withhold setting, which yields perfectly matched answering and refusal trajectories for bidirectional activation patching. We uncover a causal asymmetry in intervention locality under matched causal interventions, which we term broken symmetry. Even when a model generates a clean refusal, the correct answer remains linearly recoverable from its hidden states. Furthermore, releasing this withheld answer is a highly local operation, requiring only a single-position patch. Conversely, the reverse operation is not equally local: reimposing suppression requires broader interventions across multiple positions, and assembling a coherent refusal sequence is more difficult still. We further demonstrate that while an average answer-to-refusal displacement vector marks the geometric difference between these states, it fails to act as a reliable, reversible linear control toggle between behaviours. Taken together, our findings show that refusal does not function as a simple symmetric switch. For safety and auditing, this implies that probe recoverability can overestimate true behavioural control, and locating refusal-relevant directions does not reliably grant the ability to steer a model from answering to coherent refusal.

</details>


### [138] [KV-Rescue: Recovering Reasoning Language Model KV Eviction Loss via Stepwise Interleaving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15797)
*Minsoo Cheong,Woosang Lim,Vincent-Daniel Yun,Sungjoo Yoo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KV-Rescue is a training-free inference framework that uses a lightweight full-context helper model to recover accuracy lost from KV-cache eviction, preventing runaway degeneration while reducing token generation costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV-cache eviction is necessary for memory efficiency in long reasoning tasks but causes accuracy loss and runaway degeneration (incoherent/repetitive tokens) due to missing context, which is an information gap rather than a capability limitation.

Method: KV-Rescue bridges the information gap by interleaving reasoning steps from an evicted base model with a lightweight full-context helper model, using an online detector with entropy and compressibility metrics to terminate incoherent/repetitive generation early.

Result: On five math benchmarks with Qwen2.5-Math 7B/72B models, KV-Rescue recovers 87% of accuracy lost to eviction at budget B=64, prevents runaway degeneration, and reduces base-model token generation by 43% on average.

Conclusion: The accuracy loss from KV-cache eviction is primarily an information gap rather than a capability gap, and KV-Rescue effectively bridges this gap using complementary models and early termination of degenerate generations, making long-context reasoning more efficient and reliable.

Abstract: KV-cache eviction caps the memory cost of long reasoning traces but is inherently lossy because the model decodes from a partial view of its history. Under aggressive budgets, this not only lowers accuracy but can also cause runaway degeneration, where the model produces incoherent or repetitive tokens until reaching the length limit. We characterize much of this loss as an information gapf caused by missing context, rather than a capability gap caused by limited model capacity. An evicted 7B model and a full-context 1.5B model make complementary errors, and an oracle choice between their answers recovers 79% of the accuracy gap to the full-KV 7B model. Based on this observation, we propose KV-Rescue, a training-free inference framework that bridges the information gap introduced by KV eviction using a lightweight full-context helper. KV-Rescue interleaves reasoning steps from the two models into a shared trajectory. An online detector uses entropy and compressibility to terminate the generation of incoherent or repetitive base-model candidates early. Across five math benchmarks with Qwen2.5-Math 7B and 72B, KV-Rescue recovers an average of 87% of the accuracy lost to eviction at eviction budget B=64. A decode-cost analysis further shows that preventing runaway degeneration cuts base-model token generation by 43% on average.

</details>


### [139] [Pricing the Risk of Runtime Compression: Anytime-Valid Admission and a Served-Output Law for Compressed Serving State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15810)
*Fanzhe Wei,Li Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A certified serving system replaces union-bound risk budgeting with anytime-valid ledgers and machine-checked design laws, providing priced guarantees for runtime compression of serving state with measurable quality-capacity tradeoffs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current runtime compression approaches for serving systems trade quality for capacity without formal guarantees - they adapt precision based on load signals without soundness statements, and certified approaches use union bounds that fail on long requests (100% failure rate in production).

Method: 1. Replace union budget with anytime-valid, physically accounted ledger that holds at every admission call; 2. Use machine-checked design law (TV <= tanh(a_q w_thr)) to turn served-TV target into threshold knob; 3. Implement three-layer audit with operator-norm query envelopes, measured-ellipsoid replacements, and gate operating points; 4. Apply exchangeable extrapolation across serving histories for order-statistic bounds.

Result: The anytime ledger bound holds at all 352,333 admission calls on live traffic and halves exact-fallback rate from 0.30 to 0.14 at matched risk. All probabilistic kernels are Lean 4-checked (228 theorems). The approach identifies that 1064x gap is localized to operating point, providing priced bounds that survive unseen requests with discriminating risk calibration (0.41 vs 0.51).

Conclusion: The system provides priced guarantees for runtime compression: risk you can spend, measurable gaps you can read from design laws, and bounds that survive unseen requests. The companion paper rejects alternative approaches like certifying routing, establishing this account-based methodology as the appropriate machinery.

Abstract: Runtime compression of serving state trades quality for capacity with no priced guarantee: systems adapt precision on load signals with no soundness statement, and certified approaches budget request-level risk by a union bound over a pre-declared event count. We show the union budget exhausts on every long request in a production serving stack (100% of requests), and replace it with an anytime-valid, physically accounted ledger whose bound holds at every one of 352,333 admission calls on live traffic and which, in a pre-registered held-out confirmatory round, halves the exact-fallback rate at matched risk (0.30 -> 0.14) -- coverage is bought at a price the account states. We then price the remaining distance from the certified witness to what a user experiences: a machine-checked design law (TV <= tanh(a_q w_thr)) turns the served-TV target into a threshold knob, and a three-layer audit of its instantiation -- an operator-norm query envelope measured 1.5x from tight, a measured-ellipsoid replacement for the Cauchy-Schwarz ball that buys nothing (0.89x, held-out sound), and the gate's operating point (~700x) -- localizes the entire 1064x gap to the operating point, a price the law now states rather than an unknown. A priced bound is worth nothing on a request one has not seen, so the third link is the quantifier: exchangeable extrapolation across 80 serving histories replaces binary conformal prediction's vacuous certificates with order-statistic bounds that discriminate (0.41 against 0.51 calibration risk). All probabilistic kernels are Lean 4-checked (228 exported theorems, no sorry); which object deserves this machinery at all is settled empirically in a companion paper that adjudicates -- and rejects -- the natural alternative of certifying routing. What ships is an account: risk you can spend, a gap you can read off a law, and a bound that survives the request you have not seen.

</details>


### [140] [RLCascadeRouter: Quality-Estimator-Free Cascade Routing via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15817)
*Shihong Huang,Shengjie Wang,Hong Ma,Zhou Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLCascadeRouter: A reinforcement learning framework for LLM cascade routing that directly optimizes performance-cost trade-offs without needing separate response quality estimators, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM cascade routing methods are inflexible - one-shot routers commit too early, while conventional cascades follow fixed model orders. Current predict-then-optimize approaches suffer from misaligned objectives where better prediction doesn't guarantee better routing decisions.

Method: Formulates cascade routing as a Markov decision process using reinforcement learning. Employs a Cascade Policy Network that models candidate complementarity for model selection and remaining-action value for stopping, eliminating the need for independent response-quality estimators. Directly optimizes performance-cost objectives using trajectory returns and advantages.

Result: Outperforms strong baselines across ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs, achieving superior performance-cost trade-offs. The framework can incorporate unseen models without retraining, and ablation studies validate both policy components.

Conclusion: RLCascadeRouter provides a more flexible and effective approach to LLM cascade routing by directly optimizing routing decisions through reinforcement learning, eliminating the limitations of predict-then-optimize pipelines and enabling better exploitation of heterogeneous LLM capabilities and costs.

Abstract: The growing ecosystem of large language models (LLMs) offers huge potential to optimize performance-cost trade-offs. However, their heterogeneous capabilities and inference costs make efficiently routing queries a significant challenge. Existing paradigms are inflexible: one-shot routers commit before observing responses, whereas conventional cascades stop adaptively but follow a fixed model order. Cascade routing removes both restrictions by reconsidering whether to stop or invoke another model after each response. Current methods use a predict-then-optimize pipeline estimating response quality and future model utility. However, prediction loss for quality or utility is not equivalent to routing-decision loss. A lower prediction error does not necessarily yield a better action; a small boundary-crossing error can reverse a ``stop'' or model-selection decision. Therefore, we propose RLCascadeRouter, a quality-estimator-free framework that formulates cascade routing as a Markov decision process with actions comprising ``stop'' and model selection. It uses trajectory returns and advantages to directly optimize the performance-cost objective. Its Cascade Policy Network models candidate complementarity for model selection and remaining-action value for stopping, eliminating independent post-hoc response-quality estimators. Evaluated across ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs, RLCascadeRouter outperforms strong baselines and achieves superior performance-cost trade-offs. It incorporates unseen models without retraining, and ablation studies validate both policy components.

</details>


### [141] [The Authority Resolution Framework: A Five-Domain Ontology for Governing Who and What Decides, at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15832)
*Parviz Shariff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Authority Resolution Framework (ARF), a five-domain ontology for representing and resolving authority across organizational structures to help AI systems determine whether actions are authorized in their context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems gain more autonomous capabilities, simply determining technical feasibility of actions is insufficient. AI systems must also determine whether actions are authorized within their operational context, requiring a systematic approach to authority resolution that accounts for organizational roles, informal influences, business processes, and real-world context.

Method: The paper introduces the Authority Resolution Framework (ARF), a five-domain ontology covering: 1) organizational roles and informal influence, 2) business concepts, 3) codified processes, 4) machine-readable permissions and executable systems, and 5) external real-world context. It defines the Authority Relation (AR) as a cross-domain primitive with components including actor, action, object, bounded context, justification chain, and DNA-Coefficient (calibration measure of divergence between documented and practiced authority). The framework provides JSON-LD representations and knowledge-graph query patterns for authority resolution.

Result: The framework provides a machine-interpretable representation of authority provenance and scope, with structured representations and query patterns for authority resolution. ARF is designed to enable AI agents to determine the provenance, scope, and contextual validity of authority before executing consequential actions.

Conclusion: The paper positions authority resolution as a knowledge-representation and reasoning problem at the intersection of ontology engineering, semantic AI, agentic AI, and AI governance. ARF provides a systematic framework to help autonomous AI systems navigate complex authority structures and make informed decisions about action authorization.

Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable of autonomous action, determining whether an agent is technically capable of performing an action is insufficient: the system must also determine whether the action is authorised in its context.
  This paper introduces the Authority Resolution Framework (ARF), a five-domain ontology for representing and resolving authority across organisational roles and informal influence, business concepts, codified processes, machine-readable permissions and executable systems, and external real-world context. ARF defines the Authority Relation (AR) as a cross-domain primitive binding an actor, action, object, bounded context, justification chain, and a calibration measure termed the DNA-Coefficient, which captures divergence between documented authority structures and authority as practiced.
  The framework provides a machine-interpretable representation of authority provenance and scope, with JSON-LD representations and knowledge-graph query patterns for authority resolution. ARF is designed to support AI agents in determining the provenance, scope and contextual validity of authority before executing consequential actions. The framework positions authority resolution as a knowledge-representation and reasoning problem at the intersection of ontology engineering, semantic AI, agentic AI and AI governance.

</details>


### [142] [Schema-Agnostic Graph Reasoning Agent for Hybrid Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15834)
*Marius Dragic,Ruben Ifrah,Alexandre Rio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRA (Graph Reasoning Agent) uses seven generic tools to explore hybrid knowledge graphs (textual concepts + relational tables), outperforming full-context agents on industrial benchmarks while reading significantly fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents navigate codebases with generic file operations (ls, cat, grep), but similar operations could apply to knowledge graphs. There's a need for more efficient agents that can explore structured data without exhaustive context consumption.

Method: GRA uses seven generic tools to explore hybrid knowledge graphs with textual concepts and relational tables. The agent discovers domain-specific information at runtime through selective navigation, treating graph operations similarly to file system operations (listing neighbors, reading node content, searching descriptions).

Result: On UFK-M (258 analytical questions with SQL-program gold answers), GRA achieves 88.4% accuracy vs 83.3% for full-context agent, while reading under a third of the input tokens. The improvement comes from selective agentic access rather than graph topology.

Conclusion: Selective navigation over structured substrates beats exhaustive context consumption. The agent answers better while seeing less, with performance dependent on the model's ability to drive tools reliably rather than just graph structure.

Abstract: Tool-calling LLM agents navigate unfamiliar codebases with a handful of generic primitives for listing, reading and searching files (ls, cat, grep). A knowledge graph admits the same interface: listing neighbours, reading node content and searching descriptions are the same operations on a different substrate. Building on this correspondence, we present GRA, a Graph Reasoning Agent that explores hybrid knowledge graphs, whose nodes are either textual concepts or relational tables, with seven generic tools, discovering everything domain-specific at run time. On UFK-M (Unified Factory Knowledge Model), an industrial benchmark of 258 analytical questions whose gold answers are produced by executing validated SQL programs, GRA beats a full-context agent by 5.1 pp (88.4% vs. 83.3%), while reading under a third of its input tokens. A graph-free control shows the gain comes chiefly from selective agentic access rather than graph topology, and that the effect depends on a model able to drive tools reliably. Seeing less, the agent answers better: selective navigation over a structured substrate beats exhaustive context.

</details>


### [143] [RAGas: Retrieval-Augmented Gas Optimization for Smart Contracts with Continuous Knowledge Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15857)
*Yishun Wang,Wenjin Yi,Wenkai Li,Zongwei Li,Xiaoqi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAGas is a novel retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses LLMs to automatically detect and fix Gas inefficiencies in Ethereum smart contracts, reducing Gas usage by up to 11%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ethereum smart contracts incur execution fees (Gas) that scale with computational complexity, and no existing system continuously exploits evolving Gas usage patterns to optimize Gas-intensive code while preserving functional equivalence.

Method: Systematic analysis of syntactic and semantic constructs driving excessive Gas use, resulting in six high-level categories covering twelve fine-grained antipatterns. These insights are operationalized with RAGas, a three-stage retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses large language models to pinpoint and automatically fix Gas inefficiencies.

Result: Experiments on deployed contracts demonstrate that RAGas reduces Gas usage by up to 11% and achieves high precision and recall in detecting code snippets exhibiting Gas wastage.

Conclusion: RAGas effectively addresses the critical need for automated Gas optimization in Ethereum smart contracts by combining systematic pattern analysis with advanced LLM-based code transformation techniques.

Abstract: Ethereum is now integral to mission-critical sectors, including finance, healthcare, and supply chain management. Execution fees, commonly referred to as Gas, scale with the computational complexity of their functions. Smart contracts on Ethereum incur execution fees, known as Gas, which increase with computational complexity. Thus, optimizing Gas-intensive code while preserving functional equivalence significantly lowers deployment costs. No existing system continuously exploits evolving Gas usage patterns. We systematically analyze syntactic and semantic constructs that drive excessive Gas use. This yields six high-level categories covering twelve fine-grained antipatterns underpinning a curated knowledge base. We operationalize these insights with RAGas, a three-stage retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a large language model to pinpoint and automatically fix Gas inefficiencies. Experiments on deployed contracts demonstrate that RAGas reduces Gas usage by up to 11% and achieves high precision and recall in detecting code snippets exhibiting Gas wastage.

</details>


### [144] [CoupVisor: Strategy Optimization by Round and Challenge Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15868)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoupVisor is a decision-support system for the card game Coup that helps players decide what actions to take and when to challenge opponents, using a unified game representation that supports manual play, replay, simulation, and learning-based policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need for decision support in hidden-information games like Coup, specifically helping players with two key decisions: what actions to take on their turn and when to challenge opponents' claims, which are challenging due to incomplete information.

Method: Built CoupVisor around a single unified description of game events shared across different functionalities (manual play, replay, simulation, belief tracking, advisor recommendations, learning-based policies). The system estimates claim truthfulness by combining role probabilities with remaining cards, and compares rule-following, learned, and heuristic players through extensive simulations against different opponent styles.

Result: The main finding is that the choice of reward function (short-term gains vs. ultimate winning) determines which learning approach performs best. A win-oriented reward produces a policy that outperforms all baselines, including rule-following and other learned/heuristic approaches.

Conclusion: CoupVisor successfully provides decision support for Coup by using a unified game representation and demonstrating that reward design is crucial for learning optimal policies in hidden-information games, with win-oriented rewards producing superior performance.

Abstract: This paper presents CoupVisor, a decision-support system for the hidden-information card game Coup. It addresses two questions: what a player should do on each turn, and when a player should challenge an opponent's claim. The system is built around a single description of game events, which is shared across manual play, replay of recorded games, simulation, belief tracking, advisor recommendations, and learning-based policies. CoupVisor estimates the chance that a claim is truthful by combining how likely each role is with how many cards the claimant still holds, which corrects a case where the very first claim of a game was flagged as suspicious despite no evidence. We compare a rule-following advisor and several learned and heuristic players across many simulated games and different opponent styles. Our main finding is that the choice of reward, whether it rewards short-term gains or ultimately winning the game, decides which learning approach performs best, and that a win-oriented reward produces a policy that outperforms all baselines.

</details>


### [145] [Dear Algo: A Precision-First Agentic Intent Layer for Unified Search and Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15877)
*Rui Wang,Jiazhou Wang,Zheng Wei,Chenglin Lu,Fangcheng Sun,Ivy Sun,Jin Sun,Hui Geng,Lillian Zhang,Chao Yang,Lei Chen,Shahin Sefati,Reem Helou,Joe Zhou,Babak Shakibi,Yiyi Pan,Bi Xue,Hong Yan,Shujian Bu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dear Algo on Threads is a deployed product that uses natural language requests to steer feed recommendations, combining search-like and recommendation-like capabilities through an agentic intent layer that achieves high precision in delivering relevant content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the boundary between search and recommendation systems, noting they serve similar discovery objectives but encode user intent differently. The motivation is to create a system where open-ended natural language requests can steer feed recommendations rather than just returning one-shot search results.

Method: The system uses an agentic intent layer that compiles explicit, inferred, negative, and compound user intent into a grounded executable plan. This layer invokes conventional retrieval and optional semantic/multimodal reranking. It shares an intent-to-retrieval contract without requiring a single model or serving path across search-like and recommendation-like modes.

Result: Evaluation under precision-first objective showed: 1) 94.4% exact-Relevant precision in blinded audit; 2) 7.73 judge-qualified candidates per 20 slots vs 6.61 for baseline (1.11 gain); 3) In candidate-randomized study, user-weighted judge-Irrelevant share was 2.80% vs 4.78% off (-1.97 points improvement), while Exact-Relevant share was 2.24 points higher.

Conclusion: The studies demonstrate that explicit natural-language intent can be effectively integrated into feed recommendation systems under a precision-first evaluation framework, bridging the gap between search and recommendation capabilities while maintaining high precision.

Abstract: Search and recommendation serve a shared discovery objective but encode intent differently. We study this boundary through Dear Algo on Threads, a deployed product where open-ended requests such as \emph{more NBA news} or \emph{less politics} steer subsequent feed recommendations rather than return a one-shot result list. Its agentic intent layer compiles explicit, inferred, negative, and compound intent into a grounded executable plan, then invokes conventional retrieval and optional semantic or multimodal reranking. The layer shares an intent-to-retrieval contract without requiring one model or serving path across search-like and recommendation-like modes.
  We evaluate Dear Algo under a precision-first objective. In a blinded audit of 300 public request-item pairs (296 evaluable), a strict categorical LLM-as-a-judge gate achieved 94.4\% exact-Relevant precision [88.8\%, 98.9\%]. Across 72 normalized request clusters, the full configuration produced 7.73 judge-qualified candidates per 20 slots versus 6.61 for an LLM-derived-query baseline, a gain of 1.11 [0.12, 2.12]. In a candidate-randomized serving-path study restricted to the reranker path's first 72 eligible hours, the user-weighted judge-Irrelevant share among judged admissions was 2.80\% versus 4.78\% off (-1.97 points [-3.02, -0.94]), while Exact-Relevant share was 2.24 points higher [0.08, 4.41].
  Together, these studies show how explicit natural-language intent can be carried into feed recommendation under a precision-first evaluation framework

</details>


### [146] [Bounded Agents: Delegation Security for Multi-Agent AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15888)
*Xabier Muruaga*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: APC is a dynamic authorization framework that tracks delegated authority across agent sessions to prevent abuse like prompt injection attacks by enforcing six authorization checks and limiting scope/budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based agents have static permissions evaluated per request without considering session history, allowing agents to combine permitted actions into prohibited outcomes, delegate authority unchecked, or act contrary to delegated tasks despite prompt injection vulnerabilities.

Method: APC tracks delegated authority through a chain from one principal to the next, evaluating each request against accumulated session state using six authorization checks, carrying forward and restricting delegated scope/budgets, and using composition closure to prevent prohibited combinations enforced outside the model.

Result: APC blocked all 544 InjecAgent data-stealing cases, reduced AgentDojo exfiltration from 75-100% to 0%, reduced destruction from 38.6% to 4.0% and manipulation from 90.5% to 12.1% with intent binding, had 0.24ms 99th percentile latency, and reduced utility by 8.6-13.9 percentage points.

Conclusion: Agent authorization is an architectural problem, not just a model problem; APC provides a provably sound framework for dynamic authorization that prevents session-based attacks while maintaining reasonable utility overhead, with publicly available implementation and evaluation tools.

Abstract: LLM-based agents can act on behalf of a user to access cloud services, call tools, or invoke agents.
