At session start, the agent's permissions are set but remain static, and each request is evaluated independently, without considering prior actions. Within its permissions, an agent may act contrary to the delegated task, combine individually permitted actions into a prohibited outcome, or delegate authority to a sub-agent without limiting it. A prompt injection poses a risk only if the agent has authority to perform such actions; this is therefore a problem of authorization architecture, not just the model. The Agentic Principal Chain (APC) tracks delegated authority from one principal to the next. APC evaluates each request against the accumulated session state using six authorization checks. APC carries forward and restricts delegated scope and budgets. Using composition closure, APC checks requests against prior actions to prevent prohibited combinations and enforces the decision outside the model. We prove Blast Radius Monotonicity and Composition Soundness for APC implementations; Composition Soundness is limited to prohibited combinations under a complete restriction set and serialized admission. We evaluated 3,154 instances including InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and ASB. Our compromised-model evaluation tests APC independently of model behavior by inserting the ground-truth attack call after the first legitimate tool call. AgentDojo exfiltration fell from 75-100% to 0% across all four domains; APC blocked all 544 InjecAgent data-stealing cases. Intent binding reduced destruction from 38.6% to 4.0% and manipulation from 90.5% to 12.1%. Authorization latency was 0.24 ms at the 99th percentile on an idle host; across 949 AgentDojo task-injection pairs, utility was 8.6 and 13.9 percentage points lower in the two settings. Implementation, evaluation tools, and data are publicly available.

</details>


### [147] [Breaking and Defending LLM-Powered Social Media Bot Detection Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15893)
*Nof Orenstein,Yoni Birman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based social media bot detection systems face new adversarial threats that exploit their semantic reasoning, but a multi-LLM ensemble defense (LSABRE) can significantly improve robustness while maintaining high detection accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social media bots pose persistent threats like misinformation and manipulation, and while LLMs have improved bot detection, they introduce new attack surfaces that adversaries can exploit through semantic targeting of reasoning mechanisms.

Method: Investigated offensive and defensive aspects of LLM-powered cybersecurity systems; introduced two novel adversarial attack strategies that exploit semantic/contextual weaknesses of LLM-based classifiers; proposed LSABRE - a robust multi-LLM defense architecture using ensemble methods to maintain detection reliability under adaptive adversarial conditions.

Result: Adversarial attacks degraded detection accuracy by up to 48%, but the LSABRE multi-LLM framework maintained 86% detection accuracy even under strong, adaptive adversarial pressure, substantially improving robustness across various attacks.

Conclusion: While LLMs introduce new vulnerabilities in cybersecurity applications, carefully designed multi-LLM ensemble architectures like LSABRE can provide effective defense against adversarial attacks, with broader applicability to phishing detection, email classification, and fraud analysis systems.

Abstract: The rise of social media bots poses a persistent threat, enabling misinformation, opinion manipulation, and the erosion of trust in online platforms. To combat this, machine learning systems have been developed to detect and limit bot activity, but attackers continuously adapt through techniques such as adversarial learning and behavior imitation, fueling an ongoing arms race between bots and detection tools. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved bot detection by enabling deeper semantic and contextual analysis of accounts and their content. However, this shift also introduces new attack surfaces, allowing adversaries to craft exploits that directly target the reasoning and generation mechanisms of LLM-based classifiers. Industry tools such as Anthropic's Claude Code Security similarly leverage LLMs for security-critical decisions, further motivating a careful study of their attack surfaces. In this work, we investigate both the offensive and defensive aspects of LLM-powered, threat-specific cybersecurity applications. While centered on the challenge of social media bot detection, our methodology and insights generalize to a broad class of LLM-powered cybersecurity systems, including phishing detection, email classification, and fraud analysis. We introduce two novel adversarial attack strategies that systematically exploit the semantic and contextual weaknesses of LLM-based classifiers, degrading their detection accuracy by up to 48%. To counter these threats, we propose a robust multi-LLM defense architecture designed to preserve detection reliability under adaptive adversarial conditions. Our solution, LSABRE (LLM-powered Social Adversarial Bot Recognition Ensemble), is a multi-LLM framework that substantially improves robustness across a range of attacks, maintaining 86% detection accuracy even under strong, adaptive adversarial pressure.

</details>


### [148] [Unified Pedestrian Path Prediction Using Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15929)
*Šimon Sukup,Ariyan Bighashdel,Pavol Jancura*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adapting STGAT to pedestrian path prediction with new formulations improves performance over standard supervised learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous studies compared learning-task formulations for pedestrian path prediction using shallow networks, but didn't extend this analysis to complex deep-learning models. There's a need to explore how reformulating decision processes and training objectives can improve advanced architectures.

Method: Adapted Spatial-Temporal Graph Attention Network (STGAT) to a unified pedestrian path prediction framework with specific state and action definitions for STGAT. Supported deterministic/stochastic policies, one-time/sequential decision-making, and reinforcement-learning algorithms (REINFORCE and PPO).

Result: The proposed learning-task formulations improved prediction performance across benchmark datasets compared with standard supervised-learning formulation.

Conclusion: Reformulating decision process and training objective can improve advanced pedestrian trajectory prediction architectures and may provide a path toward improving other graph-based prediction models.

Abstract: Pedestrian path prediction is crucial for enhancing the safety of autonomous vehicles and advanced driver-assistance systems. Previous studies explored different learning-task formulations for pedestrian path prediction and compared these formulations using shallow neural networks, but did not extend this analysis to more complex deep-learning models. This paper adapts the Spatial-Temporal Graph Attention Network (STGAT) to a unified pedestrian path prediction framework and introduces state and action definitions specific to STGAT. The resulting formulations support deterministic and stochastic policies, one-time and sequential decision-making, and reinforcement-learning algorithms including REINFORCE and proximal policy optimization. The proposed learning-task formulations improve prediction performance across the selected benchmark datasets compared with the standard supervised-learning formulation. These results demonstrate that reformulating the decision process and training objective can improve an advanced pedestrian trajectory prediction architecture and may provide a path toward improving other graph-based prediction models.

</details>


### [149] [UI-Mate: Advancing Open-Weight Foundation GUI Agents with In-Context Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15930)
*Zihan Ding,Longxu Dou,Qi Gao,Xiangwu Guo,Shengchao Hu,Zilong Huang,Zihang Jiang,Lei Ke,Mengcheng Lan,Weixian Lei,Hanxuan Li,Honglin Li,Xiyun Li,Zaitang Li,Leowei Liang,Xin Luo,Haozhe Ma,Jiayi Mao,Zhoujie Pan,Can Qin,Tianyuan Qu,Weiqi Wang,Wenkai Wang,Yonglin Wang,Yuxin Wang,Chenxu Wu,Yingchen Yu,Chenyu Zhang,Yuhao Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UI-Mate is a foundation GUI agent that addresses challenges in GUI automation by combining environment-grounded training with in-context demonstration learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on computer-use benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation GUI agents face deployment challenges due to scarce/biased training data, ambiguous prompts, and unreliable execution. Routine workflows rely on user-specific tools and tacit conventions, leading to arbitrary variations across runs.

Method: UI-Mate integrates an environment-grounded training stack with in-context demonstration learning. The training stack uses a closed-loop data engine for automated task generation, environment construction, rollout, filtering, capability balancing, SFT, and online RL. Demonstration learning transforms multimodal demonstrations into flexible subtask workflows and supports re-planning from live interfaces.

Result: UI-Mate-27B achieves 77.0% on OSWorld-Verified and 66.2% on WindowsAgentArena, setting new open-weight SOTA. On OSWorkerBench, it reaches 41.0% strict success and 76.9% progress, outperforming Qwen3.6-27B by 17.7 and 24.5 points. With one demonstration, success improves from 17.2% to 35.4% and progress from 67.9% to 81.1%.

Conclusion: UI-Mate demonstrates that environment-grounded training combined with in-context demonstration learning substantially improves GUI agent performance, particularly for long-horizon tasks, addressing key challenges in reliable workflow automation.

Abstract: Foundation GUI agents can automate complex digital tasks, but deployment is hindered by scarce and biased training data, ambiguous prompts, and unreliable execution. Routine workflows rely on user-specific tools and tacit conventions, so unstated instructions can produce arbitrary variations across runs. We present UI-Mate, a foundation GUI agent that integrates an environment-grounded training stack with in-context demonstration learning. UI-Mate makes three contributions: A Scalable Environment-Grounded Training Stack: A closed-loop data engine automates task generation, environment construction, rollout, filtering, capability balancing, SFT, and online RL across massively parallel environments via unified task-verifier bundles. In-Context Demonstration Learning: A mechanism that transforms multimodal demonstrations into flexible subtask-level workflows, follows relevant demonstrated steps, and re-plans from the live interface. OSWorkerBench Benchmark and Insights: A benchmark of 100 long-horizon office tasks across 41 applications that supports instruction-only and demonstration-guided evaluation. Its demonstration resources separate a 33-task self-demo setting, built from successful strong-agent rollouts of the same targets, from a 45-task variant-demo setting, built from human recordings of related but non-identical tasks. Experiments show that UI-Mate-27B sets a new open-weight state of the art on general computer-use benchmarks, scoring 77.0% on OSWorld-Verified and 66.2% on WindowsAgentArena. On OSWorkerBench, it reaches 41.0% strict success and 76.9% progress, outperforming its Qwen3.6-27B base by 17.7 and 24.5 points. On the 33-task self-demo subset, one demonstration raises strict success from 17.2% to 35.4% and progress from 67.9% to 81.1%, substantially improving long-horizon reliability. Project page: https://ui-mate.github.io.

</details>


### [150] [Augmenting Text to Increase Translation Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15932)
*William Kalikman,Šimon Sukup,Michal Tešnar,Vilém Zouhar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATO generates more challenging translation test sets by combining adversarial optimization with difficulty estimation to replace tokens, making benchmarks harder without using LLMs or human curation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current machine translation benchmarks are becoming saturated, making it difficult to distinguish between models of varying quality. There's a need for more challenging evaluation datasets that can better discriminate model performance.

Method: Adversarial Translation Optimization (ATO) combines adversarial optimization with a differentiable translation difficulty estimator. It uses gradients from combined difficulty and fluency objectives to iteratively replace tokens. Due to branching over candidate substitutions, optimization becomes a tree search problem addressed with Beam Search.

Result: ATO-modified benchmarks lower average translation quality (xCOMET) from 0.93 to 0.82 (compared to 0.88 for paraphrasing and 0.86 for zero-shot baseline). Human evaluation shows modified texts are somewhat less natural but remain reasonably grammatical and plausible while being substantially harder to translate.

Conclusion: ATO provides an effective gradient-based alternative to LLM-based dataset creation that can generate more challenging translation benchmarks without LLM prompting, expensive human curation, or task-specific model training. The released datasets demonstrate the method's practical utility.

Abstract: As state-of-the-art machine translation models saturate standard benchmarks, the field needs more challenging evaluations to distinguish between models of varying quality. We propose augmenting existing benchmarks to increase translation difficulty by combining adversarial optimization with a differentiable translation difficulty estimator. Our Adversarial Translation Optimization (ATO) uses gradients from a combined difficulty and fluency objective to iteratively replace tokens. Because each step branches over candidate substitutions at every position, optimization becomes a tree search problem, which we address with Beam Search. ATO offers a gradient-based alternative to LLM-based dataset creation without LLM prompting, expensive human curation, or task-specific model training. Our ATO-modified benchmark lowers average translation quality (xCOMET) from 0.93 to 0.82, compared to 0.88 for paraphrasing and 0.86 for a zero-shot baseline. Human evaluation shows the modified texts are somewhat less natural than the baselines but remain reasonably grammatical and plausible while being substantially harder to translate. We release two datasets of 350 English texts each, generated by our methods, as well as the code.

</details>


### [151] [Navigation-Informed Embeddings: Dense-Retriever Adaptation from Agent Search Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15956)
*Shrey Shah,Levent Ozgur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Navigation-Informed Embeddings (NIE) adapt dense retrievers to changing workflow distributions using query/retrieval/stopping traces without new labels, achieving significant performance improvements with zero labeling cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed dense retrievers need adaptation to changing workflow distributions, but obtaining new relevance labels, synthetic queries, or LLM judgments is costly. Agentic retrieval workflows naturally produce traces that could be leveraged for adaptation without additional labeling.

Method: NIE uses trace-derived objectives from retrieval workflows. NIE-Stop treats the stopping document as a soft positive. NIE-Path uses preceding path documents as hard comparisons with ordinal constraints and geometric decay, adapting BGE encoders from retained source trajectories.

Result: Adapted encoder improved support Recall@20 from 72.2 to 78.0 on target benchmark. NIE-Stop reached 76.9 overall and 52.3 on long paths; NIE-Path improved long-path performance to 55.4 vs 46.7 unadapted. Also improved nDCG@10 by 1.9 points on BEIR HotpotQA without public-benchmark training.

Conclusion: NIE provides effective, lightweight adaptation for dense retrievers using naturally occurring retrieval traces, eliminating labeling costs while significantly improving performance on both support and standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Agentic retrieval workflows produce query, retrieval, and stopping traces as a byproduct of answering questions. We study how these traces can adapt a deployed dense retriever to changing workflow distributions without new relevance labels, synthetic queries, or LLM judgments. We introduce Navigation-Informed Embeddings (NIE), a family of trace-derived objectives. NIE-Stop turns the stopping document into a soft positive; NIE-Path additionally uses preceding path documents as hard comparisons and imposes ordinal constraints with geometric decay. A BGE encoder adapted from retained source trajectories improves support Recall@20 on an independent target benchmark from 72.2 to 78.0 overall. NIE-Stop reaches 76.9 overall and 52.3 on long paths; NIE-Path raises long-path performance to 55.4, compared with 46.7 for the unadapted encoder. A shuffled-order control under the full path objective loses 3.2 points. Without public-benchmark training, the same adapter also improves nDCG@10 by 1.9 points on standard BEIR HotpotQA. NIE therefore provides a lightweight adaptation channel for settings where trajectories are already retained, with zero incremental labeling cost.

</details>


### [152] [Solvable Sokoban Without a Solver via Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15958)
*Sina Baghal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A transformer-based discrete diffusion model trained only on tile completion tasks achieves 77.4% solvability rate for Sokoban puzzles without any solvability supervision, demonstrating that global puzzle properties emerge from local training objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sokoban puzzle solvability is PSPACE-complete with exponentially long solutions and no short certificates. Solvability is fragile - even a single misplaced wall can make puzzles unsolvable. The paper aims to show whether global, search-heavy properties can emerge from local training objectives without explicit solvability supervision.

Method: The authors use a transformer-based discrete diffusion model trained purely on tile completion tasks on the Boxoban dataset. The model uses masked diffusion that learns to predict missing cells given any random subset of revealed cells, unlike autoregressive models that use fixed generation orders. This allows cells to be revealed in any order, each conditioned on all already-placed cells.

Result: The model achieves 77.4% solvability rate despite no training on solvers, rewards, or solvability labels. Of the remaining 22.6% unsolvable puzzles, 94.5% become solvable by removing just a single wall, indicating the model has learned meaningful global constraints. The flexible generation order matches the non-local nature of puzzle constraints.

Conclusion: Global puzzle properties like solvability can emerge from purely local training objectives. The masked diffusion approach, with its flexible generation order conditioned on any subset of revealed cells, provides a better structural match for puzzle generation than fixed-order autoregressive models. The model inherits solvability without explicit supervision.

Abstract: Deciding whether a Sokoban puzzle is solvable is PSPACE-complete (Culberson, 1997): solutions can be exponentially long and there is no short certificate to check. Solvability is also a fragile property, since even a single misplaced wall can silently render an entire puzzle unsolvable.
  In this work, we show that a transformer-based discrete diffusion model trained purely on tile completion, with no access to solvers, rewards, or solvability labels, achieves a solvability rate of 77.4%, with 94.5% of the remaining failures rendered solvable by removing a single wall. In other words, a global, search-heavy property follows from a local training objective: trained only to fill in masked cells, the model inherits solvability it was never trained on.
  An autoregressive model factorizes as $p(c_k \mid c_1 \dots c_{k-1})$, meaning a fixed order, always conditioned on a prefix. Masked diffusion does not: it hides a random subset of cells and learns $p(c_k \mid \text{any subset})$, so at generation time it can reveal cells in any order, each one conditioned on everything already placed, wherever it sits on the board. A puzzle's difficulty comes from exactly this kind of non-local interaction, a decision in one part of the grid constraining what will work somewhere else entirely. A generator that is not locked into a single fixed order is therefore a better structural match for the problem than one that is.
  The training pipeline is adapted from MD4 (Shi et al., 2024) and the dataset is DeepMind's Boxoban (Guez et al., 2019). The trained model and instructions for generating puzzles are publicly available.

</details>


### [153] [ALPS: Measuring Valid Creativity in Large Language Models with Mathematical Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15979)
*Eric Xie,Wenqian Ye,Aidong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ALPS benchmark measures valid creativity in LLMs using equational laws that require either constructing infinite mathematical structures or proving non-existence, with automated verification and infinite problem generation to prevent training data contamination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's no reliable way to determine if LLMs' "creative" outputs (like new proofs or discoveries) are truly original and effective, as current evaluation methods suffer from subjective judgment, potential training data replication, or overly simple tasks.

Method: Create ALPS benchmark with automatically generated equational laws, each requiring either constructing an infinite mathematical structure satisfying the law or proving no such structure exists. Use automated proof checking for verification and public generator to produce infinite new instances. Test with portfolio of automated provers and LLM-based reasoning models.

Result: Automated provers solve only 2.2% of 4,141 laws, with 20x budget adding just 0.6%. Top reasoning model succeeds in 14% of proof-side instances but 0% on construction side. 97.2% of problems remain unsolved across all tested configurations and budgets, indicating fundamental methodological limitations rather than computational constraints.

Conclusion: ALPS reveals severe limitations in current AI systems' ability to demonstrate valid creativity in mathematically rigorous tasks. The benchmark provides an objective, scalable way to measure genuine creative reasoning that requires both originality and correctness, with most problems proving unsolvable by existing methods.

Abstract: Large language models produce outputs presented as discoveries - new proofs, conjectures, or molecules. Whether such an output that appears creative is truly original and effective is hard to establish: open-ended outputs require subjective judgment, the output may replicate something seen in training, or the task may be too simple to need creativity. We present ALPS (Austin-Law Proof-Synthesis), a benchmark that designs a task to measure valid creativity: producing a solution that is original and can be proven correct. Each instance is a single equational law, certified to require either the construction of an infinite mathematical structure satisfying the law, or a proof that no such structure exists. Submissions are verified by automated proof checking with no human involvement, and a public generator produces new instances without limit, so LLMs are never evaluated on problems they may have seen. A portfolio of eight configurations of leading automated provers resolves 2.2% of the 4,141-law evaluation pool, and a twentyfold budget increase adds 0.6%: the obstacle is not compute, but the absence of any method that produces the tailored structure each law requires. Under a fixed protocol, the strongest reasoning model we test succeeds in 14% of instances on the proof side, but none on the construction side. The remaining 97.2% of the pool is unresolved at every configuration and budget we test. We release ALPS in full: the corpus, the generator, and the automated judge.

</details>


### [154] [MUPA$^{2}$E: Multimodal Unified Perception with Asymmetric Attention for Emotion Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15999)
*Stefanos Gkikas,Eric Nichols,Christian Arzate Cruz,Randy Gomez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MUPA²E is a unified framework that processes facial video and EEG signals through a shared asymmetric-attention backbone, achieving 70.07% accuracy on emotion assessment but drops to 62.71% when controlling for duration-related cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal emotion assessment approaches often rely on separate, modality-specific feature extraction pipelines before fusion, which can be inefficient. There's a need for a unified framework that can directly process structurally different neural (EEG) and visual (facial video) signals together.

Method: MUPA²E uses a single shared asymmetric-attention backbone to process both facial video (represented as axis-folded frame tokens) and EEG (processed as raw multichannel waveforms or projected into spatial domain). The framework supports unimodal video, unimodal EEG, and fused video-EEG configurations, evaluated on the DMER dataset under stratified subject-independent protocols.

Result: With original recordings (shorter trials zero-padded), merged fusion at stride 30 achieved 70.07% test accuracy. However, when controlling for duration-related cues by cropping all recordings to 20 seconds, accuracy dropped to 62.71%. The analysis revealed that recording duration was unevenly distributed across affective classes, making padding patterns a potential classification cue.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates the feasibility of processing structurally different neural and visual signals within a compact unified architecture while highlighting the importance of controlling duration-related cues in affective datasets to avoid biased performance assessments.

Abstract: Automatic emotion assessment can benefit from combining neural and behavioral signals, but many multimodal approaches rely on separate, modality-specific feature-extraction pipelines before fusion. This paper presents MUPA\textsuperscript{2}E, a unified perception framework that processes facial video and electroencephalography (EEG) through a single shared asymmetric-attention backbone. Facial video is represented through axis-folded frame tokens, while EEG is processed either as a raw multichannel waveform or projected into the spatial domain for multimodal fusion. The framework is evaluated on the DMER dataset under a stratified subject-independent protocol, comparing unimodal video, unimodal EEG, and fused video--EEG configurations with per-channel and merged EEG projections. Using the original recordings, with shorter trials zero-padded to match the longest duration, merged fusion at stride~$30$ achieves the highest validation performance and a test accuracy of $70.07\%$. Further analysis revealed that recording duration is unevenly distributed across the affective classes, making the padding pattern a potential classification cue. Controlling for this factor by cropping all recordings to a common duration of $20$ seconds yielded a test accuracy of $62.71\%$, providing a stricter duration-controlled assessment of the framework in which differences in recording length are removed as a potential classification cue. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of processing structurally different neural and visual signals within a compact unified architecture while highlighting the importance of controlling duration-related cues in affective datasets.

</details>


### [155] [Prior Audit-Repair Context Shifts LLM Verifier Thresholds Toward Leniency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16003)
*Parsa Mazaheri,Kasra Mazaheri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Models acting as checkers report fewer false alarms when they have previously audited and repaired the same problem in their context, suggesting checker behavior changes based on their own previous actions rather than following expected accumulation effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether the architecture of automated checking pipelines - where one language model acts as checker and another (or the same) as fixer - affects what the checker reports. There's a concern that this configuration might change the checker's behavior in ways that aren't understood or predicted by existing literature.

Method: The researchers measured false alarms on human-verified-correct ProcessBench traces with identical tasks. They compared checker behavior with and without previous audit-repair episodes in context. They tested 15 model x wording combinations, analyzed signal detection parameters (d' and threshold), and conducted a hand audit of 50 false alarms. They also tested with reasoning enabled on both models.

Result: Previous audit-repair episodes lowered false alarms in all 15 model x wording combinations (2.8-11.5 percentage points reduction, 9-25% relative to control). Surprisingly, episodes where the audit reported an error lowered false alarms further, contrary to negativity asymmetry predictions. Signal detection analysis showed the change occurred in threshold (criterion shift) rather than discrimination (d'), with threshold surviving correction in 13 of 15 cases. Hand audit revealed 82% of false alarms were simply wrong. The effect persisted with reasoning enabled.

Conclusion: Checker behavior systematically changes based on having previously audited and repaired the same problem, with the effect manifesting as a threshold shift rather than improved discrimination. This suggests current automated checking pipelines may operate differently than expected, and checker models' judgments depend on their own prior actions in ways that contradict accumulated-message literature predictions.

Abstract: Automated checking pipelines increasingly place one language model as the checker and another (or the same one) as the fixer. We ask whether that wiring changes what the checker reports. Measuring false alarms on human-verified-correct ProcessBench traces with the present task held byte-identical, we find that a completed audit -> repair episode already in the model's context lowers false alarms in 15 of 15 model x wording combinations, by 2.8 to 11.5 percentage points against a length-matched non-audit control, a 9 to 25% reduction relative to that control. The direction contradicts what the accumulated-message literature predicts: an episode whose audit reported an error lowers false alarms further still, at all five wordings on the model where that manipulation lands cleanly, though a negativity asymmetry predicts more flagging. Decomposing the episode finds repair content and audit verdict complementary: different components carry the effect on different model families. Signal-detection analysis locates the change in the threshold rather than in discrimination -- the criterion moves in 15 of 15 combinations and survives correction in 13 while d' survives in none, though the d' test is half as sensitive by construction -- and a hand audit of 50 false alarms finds 82% simply wrong, so at this operating point the shift need not be harmful. With reasoning enabled the effect keeps its relative size on both models tested, and the threshold reading holds there too.

</details>


### [156] [Governance at the Boundary: How Agent Decomposition Degrades Policy Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16055)
*Bowen Li,Guojun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent decomposition architectures degrade financial governance by attenuating policy-relevant facts at handoff boundaries, causing both under- and over-escalation in KYC/AML tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks only measure whether agents complete tasks, not whether they comply with policy. There's a need to study how agent decomposition architectures affect governability in financial applications.

Method: Developed Fiducia-bench, a benchmark for financial agent governability. Conducted 626-episode experiment across 100 KYC/AML task variants, testing two models (32B open-weights and GPT-4.1-mini) and three architectures (single-loop baseline, fixed pipeline, orchestrator-subagent).

Result: Agent decomposition degrades governance by attenuating policy-relevant facts at handoff boundaries: 32B model attenuated 0% facts (single-loop), 56% (pipeline), 85% (orchestrator-subagent). GPT-4.1-mini attenuated 3-6% across architectures. Same mechanism causes both under-escalation (dropped risk signals) and over-escalation (dropped exculpating facts).

Conclusion: Decomposition architectures introduce governance risks through fact attenuation at component boundaries. Model capability mitigates but doesn't eliminate this degradation. Governance costs must be considered when designing agent architectures, especially for financial compliance tasks.

Abstract: Existing agent benchmarks ask whether the agent finished the task. We ask whether it finished it within policy. We introduce Fiducia-bench, a benchmark for the governability of financial agents---whether they escalate when obligated, abstain when required, and leave an auditable trail---and use it to study a question no prior benchmark addresses: does decomposing an agent into components degrade its governance? It does, and the mechanism is specific. Policy-relevant facts discovered by one component are attenuated at the handoff boundary before reaching the component that must act on them. In a 626-episode experiment across 100 KYC/AML task variants, two models, and three architectures, a 32B open-weights model attenuated 0% of discovered facts under a single-loop baseline, 56% under a fixed pipeline, and 85% under an orchestrator-subagent architecture (all at constraint distance 2). A stronger model (gpt-4.1-mini) attenuated 3-6% under the same conditions, suggesting the governance cost of decomposition is partly a function of model capability. Critically, the same mechanism produces both under-escalation and over-escalation, depending on whether the dropped fact was a risk signal or an exculpating one. The benchmark, all tasks, and the verification harness are open-source

</details>


### [157] [Eigenanalysis framework for autoregressive neural emulators of multi-scale chaotic dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16084)
*Conrad Ainslie,Pedram Hassanzadeh,Michael W. Mahoney,Ashesh Chattopadhyay*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops an eigenanalysis framework to understand error growth in neural emulators of chaotic systems, showing that spectral radius of the learned Jacobian determines stability, and introduces a stability-promoting loss that improves forecasts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural autoregressive models are powerful emulators for high-dimensional chaotic systems but suffer from long-term instability and poorly understood error growth, leading to ad-hoc solutions that lack theoretical foundation.

Method: Develops an eigenanalysis framework analyzing the Jacobian of the learned one-step update map. Compares direct-step vs integration-constrained architectures, showing their spectral properties determine stability. Introduces a stability-promoting loss that regularizes Jacobian-driven error amplification.

Result: Direct-step architectures have unstable eigenvalues (>1), causing rapid divergence, while integration-constrained models collapse eigenspectrum to unit circle, yielding neutral stability. Largest eigenvalue serves as a priori diagnostic for skill and stability. Stability-promoting loss improves forecast accuracy and robustness across 29 tested models on Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system.

Conclusion: Provides theoretical foundation for neural emulator design, establishing spectral radius as key stability metric and enabling a priori stability analysis similar to numerical analysis of differential equations, addressing a current gap in scientific machine learning.

Abstract: Neural autoregressive models have rapidly emerged as powerful emulators of high-dimensional chaotic systems, yet their long-term instability and error growth remain poorly understood, leading to ad-hoc solutions. Here, we develop an eigenanalysis framework that reveals the dynamical origin of this error growth. By analyzing the Jacobian of the learned one-step update map with respect to the state, we show how inference-time error growth, and thus model stability, is governed by its spectral radius. Direct-step architectures (models that predict the next state from the previous one) generically admit unstable eigenvalues with magnitudes exceeding one, explaining the rapid divergence of these widely used models. In contrast, integration-constrained models (where the time derivative is estimated and integrated with a higher-order integrator) collapse their eigenspectrum onto the unit circle, yielding neutral stability and a universal linear error-scaling law. The largest eigenvalue of this Jacobian provides an architecture-agnostic, a priori diagnostic of short-term skill, long-term stability, and spectral bias, without requiring an expensive rollout. Leveraging this theory, we introduce a stability-promoting loss that explicitly regularizes Jacobian-driven error amplification, improving both forecast accuracy and dynamical robustness. Demonstrated across $29$ models spanning two architectures, several explicit and implicit integrators, and multiple loss functions on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system, our results establish a theoretical foundation for the design and evaluation of neural emulators of chaotic multi-scale dynamics. More broadly, our framework is a step toward the kind of a priori stability analysis that numerical analysis provides for discretizations of differential equations and that scientific machine learning currently lacks.

</details>


### [158] [Protein Structure Prediction: From Evolutionary Constraints to Generative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16094)
*Wengan He,Yongsheng Luo,Lihong Jiang,Wenhui Xu,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This review examines the methodological evolution of protein structure prediction, tracing its progression through four phases and three key transitions: from MSA-based monomer folding to learned sequence representations, then to modeling heterogeneous systems, and finally to generative design frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a clearer understanding of how methodological shifts have shaped the capabilities, limitations, and practical roles of recent protein structure prediction models, building on existing reviews that focus on representative models, application domains, and protein design.

Method: The review examines developments through three dimensions: representations and data, architectures and learning strategies, and confidence and evaluation. It organizes the field into four methodological phases and three cross-cutting transitions, analyzing key models like AlphaFold2, RoseTTAFold, ESMFold, AlphaFold-Multimer, RoseTTAFoldNA, AlphaFold3, and RFdiffusion.

Result: The analysis reveals three major transitions: 1) from explicit evolutionary coupling features to learned sequence representations in models like AlphaFold2, 2) from protein-only monomer folding to integrated modeling of heterogeneous molecular systems, and 3) from prediction-oriented structure inference to design-oriented generative modeling.

Conclusion: This framework provides a structured understanding of how methodological evolution has transformed protein structure prediction from MSA-driven monomer folding into broader capabilities for modeling complexes, heterogeneous systems, and generative design, highlighting the field's progression and future directions.

Abstract: Accurate protein structure prediction is fundamental to structural biology because protein structure underlies molecular function and provides a basis for mechanistic interpretation. Recent advances in deep learning have transformed the field from multiple sequence alignment (MSA)-driven monomer folding into broader frameworks capable of modeling protein complexes and increasingly heterogeneous molecular systems. Existing reviews have summarized this progress from the perspectives of representative models, application domains, and protein design. Building on these efforts, this review focuses on the methodological evolution of the field itself. It examines recent developments through three closely related dimensions: representations and data, architectures and learning strategies, and confidence and evaluation. Within this perspective, the field is organized into four methodological phases and three cross-cutting transitions: from explicit evolutionary coupling features and early contact prediction to learned sequence representations in AlphaFold2, RoseTTAFold, and ESMFold; from protein-only monomer folding to increasingly integrated modeling of heterogeneous molecular systems in AlphaFold-Multimer, RoseTTAFoldNA, and AlphaFold3; and, more recently, from prediction-oriented structure inference to design-oriented generative modeling in RFdiffusion and related frameworks. This framework provides a clearer understanding of how methodological shifts have shaped the capabilities, limitations, and practical roles of recent models.

</details>


### [159] [Assessing LLMs' mathematical abilities requires understanding the various mechanisms of mathematical creativity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16118)
*Silvère Gangloff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that mathematical invention involves multiple distinct creative modes, and current LLMs excel primarily at recombination/search of existing patterns while lacking other crucial modes like analogical import and strategic meaning-making, suggesting evaluation should focus on this taxonomy rather than aggregate benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current assessments of LLM mathematical ability are underspecified, conflating multiple mechanistically distinct modes of mathematical creativity. Mathematical invention is not a single capacity but involves several distinct ways of creating meaning that may be non-substitutable.

Method: Develops a taxonomy of mathematical creativity modes: reflexive introspection, analogical import, problem-driven construction, bridging distant domains, plus cross-cutting distinction between pattern-driven and strategically-wanted meaning. Grounds each mode in historical case studies and architecture-level analysis of transformer-based systems.

Result: Current transformer-based models concentrate competence in modes shaped by recombination and search over existing building blocks. The remaining creative modes are potentially out of reach in principle for current architectures. As AI improves at proof generation, mathematical value is migrating toward modes current systems cannot perform.

Conclusion: Evaluations of AI mathematical ability should be organized around the taxonomy of distinct creative modes rather than aggregate benchmarks that conflate different types of mathematical invention. Whether current systems can achieve the other modes remains an open empirical question.

Abstract: How should we assess whether large language models can perform mathematical invention? I argue that this question is currently underspecified: mathematical creativity is not one capacity but several mechanistically distinct modes of meaning-making - reflexive introspection on mathematical practice, analogical import from the sciences, problem-driven construction, and the bridging of distant domains - together with a further, cross-cutting distinction between meaning pursued because a pattern was observed and meaning pursued because it is strategically wanted, a distinction I develop through the case of conjecture-formation. These mechanisms are likely non-substitutable, so that competence in one does not transfer to the others. Grounding each in a historical case study and in an architecture-level account of current transformer-based systems, I suggest that today's models concentrate their competence in modes shaped by recombination and search over existing building blocks; if that description holds, the remaining modes are out of reach in principle, not just slower - though whether it holds is itself the open, empirical part. Because proof is getting cheaper as AI improves at generating it - a shift the field's own leading voices are now diagnosing - mathematical value is migrating toward the modes current systems cannot yet perform, and evaluations of AI mathematical ability should be organized around this taxonomy rather than around aggregate benchmarks that conflate it.

</details>


### [160] [When Single-Dataset Conclusions Fail: A 45-Task Study of Threshold Tuning and Resampling for Imbalanced Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16147)
*Diyorbek Musaev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that evaluating class-imbalance handling methods on single datasets is misleading, demonstrating contradictory results between a popular credit-card fraud dataset and a broader 45-dataset benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice evaluates class-imbalance handling methods on single benchmark datasets and treats the results as general properties of the methods, which the authors argue is unsafe and potentially misleading.

Method: Used a leakage-free nested cross-validation protocol with threshold selection on held-out inner validation folds. Applied this to 45 binary classification tasks spanning imbalance ratios from 1:1.5 to 1:178, totaling 2,025 model fits across four model families.

Result: On the fraud dataset (1:577 imbalance), Random Forest showed no benefit from threshold tuning, but across 45 datasets, it benefited most (+0.101 F1 improvement). SMOTE helped across the suite despite harming fraud dataset performance. Threshold-tuning benefit is non-monotonic with imbalance ratio, peaking at moderate imbalances and explaining why fraud dataset is unrepresentative.

Conclusion: Single-dataset evaluations of class-imbalance methods are unreliable; broader benchmarking reveals contradictory findings. The fraud dataset is particularly unrepresentative for studying imbalance issues due to its extreme ratio. Calibration diagnostics don't predict threshold-tuning benefit, challenging intuitive heuristics.

Abstract: Class-imbalance handling is routinely evaluated on a single benchmark dataset, and the resulting conclusions are reported as if they were properties of the method. We show this practice is unsafe. On the public Kaggle credit-card fraud dataset, under a leakage-free nested cross-validation protocol in which the decision threshold is selected on a held-out inner validation fold, a plain Random Forest at the default 0.5 threshold attains F1 = 0.861 +/- 0.021, and threshold tuning yields it no benefit (delta-F1 = -0.002). Read alone, this supports an appealing conclusion: for a well-calibrated ensemble, imbalance handling is unnecessary.
  We then apply the identical protocol to 45 binary tasks spanning imbalance ratios from 1:1.5 to 1:178 (2,025 model fits, four model families). The conclusion reverses. Random Forest benefits most from threshold tuning across the suite (delta-F1 = +0.101 +/- 0.134), not least, while three other families replicate their fraud-dataset behaviour almost exactly. SMOTE likewise harms the fraud dataset but helps across the suite (mean delta-F1 = +0.076; 138 wins, 39 losses; Wilcoxon p = 2.7e-17).
  Two further results. Threshold-tuning benefit is non-monotonic in the imbalance ratio: near zero below 1:5, peaking at +0.120 in the 1:15-1:40 band, declining to +0.045 beyond 1:100 - explaining why the fraud dataset, at 1:577, is an unrepresentative place to study the question. And we reject an intuitive heuristic: validation-set calibration error does not predict tuning benefit (expected calibration error r = -0.087; Brier r = +0.137), so calibration diagnostics cannot tell a practitioner whether tuning is worthwhile. We release the protocol, the 45-task harness, and all per-run metrics.

</details>


### [161] [FeatureHospital: A Skill-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Algorithm Customization in Multi-View Multi-Label Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16148)
*Junxuan Li,Zhiqi Chen,Yuzhou Liu,Peng Zhang,Huaxiao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FeatureHospital is an automated multi-agent framework that designs customized feature selection algorithms for multi-view multi-label datasets by diagnosing dataset characteristics and assembling appropriate optimization strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-view multi-label feature selection methods require expert knowledge and manual effort to design algorithms for diverse datasets, which is time-consuming and impractical for real-world adoption.

Method: FeatureHospital uses a skill-driven multi-agent framework that: 1) diagnoses target datasets to identify feature selection issues, 2) employs specialist agents with domain skills to prescribe optimization strategies and loss terms, 3) reconciles prescriptions to remove overlaps and resolve conflicts, and 4) integrates them into a compact dataset-specific objective that is optimized to select features.

Result: Experimental results show that FeatureHospital can effectively construct feature selection algorithms tailored to different datasets based on their individual characteristics.

Conclusion: The proposed framework automates feature selection algorithm design, reducing reliance on expert knowledge and manual effort, making feature selection more practical and adaptable to diverse datasets.

Abstract: Multi-view multi-label feature selection aims to identify a compact and informative feature subset from heterogeneous views while preserving discriminative information for multiple labels. Existing methods are generally developed from specific modeling perspectives and incorporate mechanisms tailored to particular data characteristics. Designing suitable feature selection algorithms across datasets with diverse and heterogeneous characteristics still relies heavily on expert knowledge and substantial manual effort, imposing considerable time and labor costs that severely hinder the practical adoption of feature selection. To address this problem, we propose FeatureHospital, a Skill-driven multi-agent framework for automated multi-view multi-label feature selection algorithm design. FeatureHospital first diagnoses the target dataset to identify its feature selection issues. Based on the diagnosis, specialist agents equipped with domain Skills then prescribe corresponding optimization strategies and Loss terms for different issues. After that, the resulting prescriptions are reconciled to remove overlaps and resolve conflicts before being integrated into a compact dataset-specific objective. Finally, the constructed objective is optimized to select the final feature subset. Experimental results demonstrate that FeatureHospital can construct effective feature selection algorithms for different datasets based on their individual characteristics.

</details>


### [162] [TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16156)
*Huan Zhang,Mingju Chen,Dongxu Zhou,Can Lv,Heng Chang,Sen Cui,Faguo Wu,Shiji Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRCA introduces transition-wise rubric credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents, using evidence, execution, and invalidity rubrics to provide fine-grained step-level rewards without requiring successful trajectories or learned evaluators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents face difficulty with credit assignment due to sparse terminal outcomes. Existing methods either require expensive process evaluators or rely on successful trajectories, which are scarce during early-stage reinforcement learning, limiting learning efficiency.

Method: TRCA (Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment) evaluates each transition using three rubrics: Evidence (task-relevant information acquisition), Execution (valid task execution), and Invalidity (invalid/regressive behavior). From these, it produces Foundational Rubric Reward for local transition quality and Breakthrough Rubric Reward for tracking newly covered conditions to reward incremental progress.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and seven search-augmented QA benchmarks show consistent improvements. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TRCA improves WebShop score by 6.0%-12.6%; with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, it improves average SearchQA score by 1.9%-18.3%.

Conclusion: TRCA effectively addresses credit assignment for long-horizon tasks with sparse successful anchors by providing fine-grained step-level supervision directly from action-induced transitions, without requiring learned evaluators or successful trajectories.

Abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents are typically optimized with sparse terminal outcomes, making fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step interactions difficult. Existing approaches either rely on process evaluators, which incur annotation and inference costs, or derive step-level credit from successful trajectories. However, successful trajectories are extremely scarce during early-stage reinforcement learning, substantially weakening anchor-based methods. We propose Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment (TRCA), which derives step-level supervision directly from action-induced transitions without learned evaluators or successful anchors. TRCA evaluates each transition using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics to capture task-relevant information acquisition, valid task execution, and invalid or regressive behavior. From these judgments, Foundational Rubric Reward measures local transition quality, while Breakthrough Rubric Reward tracks newly covered Evidence and Execution conditions to reward incremental task progress. Combined with terminal outcomes, these signals produce fine-grained step-level advantages for policy optimization. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and seven search-augmented question-answering benchmarks show consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TRCA improves the WebShop score by 6.0%-12.6%; with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, it improves the average SearchQA score by 1.9%-18.3%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of transition-wise rubric credit assignment for long-horizon tasks with sparse successful anchors.

</details>


### [163] [Trajectory-Level Automatic Curriculum Learning for Legged Locomotion on Unstructured Terrain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16164)
*Rocky Liu,Tengyu Liu,Baoxiong Jia,Fangwei Zhong,Xinyi Tong,Hongzhao Xie,Siyuan Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TALC: Trajectory-level Automatic Curriculum Learning framework that generates training tasks directly from unstructured terrain maps without heuristic parameterization, improving generalization in locomotion policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training locomotion policies for complex unstructured terrain requires curriculum learning, but existing methods use heuristic curricula over parameterized terrains which limits generalization and causes policies to overadapt to fixed perceptual patterns.

Method: Proposes TALC - a trajectory-level automatic curriculum learning framework with two components: 1) an evaluator that learns a difficulty function mapping trajectories to scores for the current policy, and 2) a sampler that proposes new trajectories guided by the evaluator as curriculum for next policy update, forming a closed loop where curriculum iteratively matches evolving policy.

Result: TALC continuously provides effective curricula on unstructured terrain, improving trajectory success rate by 56.3% over direct training without curriculum. Compared to handcrafted curriculum learning, improves success rate by 18.5% on hardest terrain tasks and up to 39.74% when evaluating traversal from diverse approach directions on same obstacle type.

Conclusion: TALC successfully addresses the curriculum generation problem for unstructured terrain by creating an automatic closed-loop system that dynamically adapts training tasks to the policy's evolving capabilities, enabling better generalization and performance compared to heuristic approaches.

Abstract: Training locomotion policies for complex unstructured terrain requires a curriculum to avoid early exploration failures. However, since unstructured terrain lacks explicit difficulty ordering for curriculum design, existing methods resort to heuristic curricula over parameterized terrains. This abstraction limits generalization, as policies can overadapt to near-fixed perceptual patterns. To address this, we propose \textbf{\ourname{}}, an \textbf{T}rajectory-level \textbf{A}utomatic \textbf{C}urriculum \textbf{L}earning framework that generates training tasks directly from unstructured terrain maps. At each curriculum update, the evaluator learns a difficulty function for the current policy that maps a given trajectory task to a difficulty score. The sampler then proposes new trajectories guided by the learned evaluator as the curriculum for the next policy update. This forms a closed loop in which the curriculum is iteratively matched to the evolving policy. Quantitative and qualitative experiments show that \ourname{} continuously provides effective curricula on unstructured terrain, improving trajectory success rate by \(56.3\%\) over direct training without curriculum. Compared with handcrafted curriculum learning, our method improves success rate by \(18.5\%\) on the hardest terrain tasks and by up to \(39.74\%\) when evaluating traversal from diverse approach directions on the same obstacle type.

</details>


### [164] [Baseline-Relative Counterfactual Refinement for Bit-Aware Visual Token Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16192)
*Jia Guo,Xiaohan Zhao,Changwang Liu,Shuqing He,Chenyang Zhang,Bingchuan Zhao,Jinqi Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GCR-C is a token-selection method for generative visual communication that uses counterfactual refinement to improve reconstruction quality without increasing transmission rate, at the cost of additional computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing token-selection methods for generative visual communication (based on local uncertainty, importance, or diversity) don't directly optimize for whether changing token selection improves final reconstruction given the same packet budget. There's a need for better criteria that evaluate selection impact on reconstruction quality.

Method: GCR-C (Gated Counterfactual Refinement for Communication) is a rollout-style correction layer over Local-MDL. It builds a compact diversified candidate set of tokens, evaluates each candidate by simulating full-budget Local-MDL continuation, and only replaces the baseline action when there's a positive baseline-relative reconstruction gain. This provides a way to counterfactually assess if different token selections would improve reconstruction.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, STL-10, a 5G-LDPC link, and Kodak transfer show GCR-C consistently improves reconstruction quality at active low- and medium-rate operating points without increasing packet rate. It remains effective across changes in dataset, channel conditions, resolution, token grid, and tokenizer. Results reveal a clear quality-computation tradeoff due to counterfactual evaluation overhead.

Conclusion: GCR-C successfully addresses the problem of directly evaluating token selection impact on reconstruction quality, demonstrating consistent improvements across diverse conditions without increasing transmission load, though at the cost of additional encoder-side computation.

Abstract: Generative visual-token communication reduces transmission load by sending only selected discrete tokens and reconstructing missing content at the receiver. However, existing token-selection criteria based on local uncertainty, importance, or diversity do not directly determine whether changing the current selection improves the final reconstruction under the same packet budget. To address this problem, we propose Gated Counterfactual Refinement for Communication (GCR-C), a rollout-style correction layer over Local-MDL. GCR-C constructs a compact diversified candidate set, evaluates each candidate through matched full-budget Local-MDL continuation, and replaces the baseline action only when a positive baseline-relative reconstruction gain is obtained. Experiments on CIFAR-10, STL-10, a coded 5G-LDPC link, and a limited high-resolution Kodak transfer show that GCR-C consistently improves reconstruction quality at active low- and medium-rate operating points without increasing the realized packet rate, while remaining effective across changes in dataset, channel condition, resolution, token grid, and tokenizer. The results also reveal a clear quality--computation tradeoff due to the additional encoder-side counterfactual evaluation.

</details>


### [165] [Beyond Asking: A Pipeline for Personalized Game Generation that Reads Players from Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16196)
*Yifan Lu,Xiaopeng Yuan,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark for evaluating player trait inference from gameplay, using synthetic players with ground-truth traits and opportunity-aware behavior representation, showing LLMs outperform baselines but supervised models remain strongest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized game generation needs reliable player profiling, but current methods lack verification - latent traits are unobservable, questionnaires are noisy, and behavior is ambiguous without context. There's a need for a benchmark with ground-truth traits to properly evaluate inference methods.

Method: 1) Construct synthetic player population with explicit bot parameters as ground-truth traits, validated through controlled manipulation. 2) Create opportunity-aware decision-moment representation that disentangles preference from opportunity. 3) Evaluate few-shot LLM inference against embedding- and rule-based baselines. 4) Use inferred profiles for difficulty adaptation and test with human study.

Result: Few-shot LLM inference outperforms embedding- and rule-based baselines on most traits, but feature-based supervised regressors remain stronger overall. The opportunity-aware representation improves opportunity-dependent trait inference. Inferred profiles successfully drive difficulty adaptation when evaluated against ground-truth references.

Conclusion: The paper presents a verified benchmark for player trait inference with ground-truth validation, showing LLMs can effectively infer traits from behavioral transcripts alone. The opportunity-aware representation addresses behavioral ambiguity, and the approach enables reliable personalized adaptation, with promising transfer to real players.

Abstract: Personalized game generation requires inferring a player's abilities and behavioral style from how they play. Large language models have made this inference more attainable than ever: an LLM can read a raw gameplay transcript and produce a fluent, plausible profile of the player. Plausible, however, is not verified, and verification is precisely what the field lacks: latent traits are unobservable; questionnaires provide noisy proxies and become circular when self-reports are used to validate behavior-based inference; and behavior itself is ambiguous without context -- a player who never collects an item may not want it, or may never have had the chance. We address both problems. First, we construct a synthetic player population whose traits are ground truth by construction: each trait is an explicit bot parameter, accepted only after controlled manipulation produces consistent, trait-specific behavioral change. Unlike prior parameter-recovery work that inverts a known decision model, our benchmark evaluates policy-agnostic inference from behavioral transcripts alone. Second, we introduce an opportunity-aware decision-moment representation that disentangles preference from the chance to express it; ablating it selectively degrades opportunity-dependent traits. On this benchmark, few-shot LLM inference outperforms embedding- and rule-based baselines on most traits, though feature-based supervised regressors remain stronger overall. Finally, we close the loop: inferred profiles drive difficulty adaptation, evaluated against ground-truth references and mismatched-profile controls, and an exploratory human study examines whether these findings transfer to real players.

</details>


### [166] [Competing at Every Price Point with Agentic Evolution over a Menu of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16207)
*Andrew Borthwick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RoboPhD is an evolutionary meta-agent that evolves complete agent programs to Pareto-dominate competitors on agentic tasks, achieving superior accuracy at every competitor price point using minimal training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to create firms that can survey competition and offer superior accuracy at every competitor price point, eliminating rational customer reasons to buy elsewhere by achieving Pareto dominance.

Method: RoboPhD uses agentic evolution over a menu of LLMs with minimal training (pools of at most 100 examples). Given a priced menu of nine LLM endpoints, task documentation, a seed agent, and a per-problem cost target, it evolves complete agent programs through evolutionary methods.

Result: The approach achieves almost complete Pareto domination on two semantically dissimilar tasks: DS-1000 (execution-checked code generation) and PaperFindingBench (LLM-judged scientific document retrieval). Officially scored submissions hold every Pareto-frontier slot but one on both tasks' leaderboards, including Pareto domination of both top-scoring and lowest-cost competing points.

Conclusion: RoboPhD demonstrates a viable path to achieving Pareto dominance over competitors on agentic tasks using evolutionary methods with minimal training data, enabling firms to offer superior accuracy across all competitor price points.

Abstract: Consider a firm that surveys its competition for a particular agentic task and seeks to offer superior accuracy at every competitor price point. A firm that Pareto-dominated its competitors would leave no rational customer a reason to buy elsewhere. This paper shows a path to this kind of capability via agentic evolution over a menu of LLMs, from training pools of at most 100 examples. Given a priced menu of nine LLM endpoints; brief documentation of the task, objective, and API; a simple seed agent; and an operator-chosen per-problem cost target - usually set at an incumbent's own price - RoboPhD, an evolutionary meta-agent, evolves complete agent programs that attack the public frontiers of two semantically dissimilar tasks point by point: DS-1000 (execution-checked code generation) and PaperFindingBench (LLM-judged scientific document retrieval). Our officially scored submissions hold every Pareto-frontier slot but one on the two tasks' leaderboards, including Pareto domination of both the top-scoring and the lowest-cost competing points.

</details>


### [167] [BaT: Towards Self-Evolving Medical Research Agent with Stage Rubrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16211)
*Junqi Liu,Yufan He,Yexiao He,Pengfei Guo,Dong Yang,Andriy Myronenko,Can Zhao,Hanrong Ye,Tianhao Qi,Yuyin Zhou,Daguang Xu,Yucheng Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BaT (Benchmark-as-Teacher) is a self-improving system for training AI agents on multi-stage medical imaging workflows that uses a recursive feedback loop between benchmark evaluation and policy training to dramatically improve performance over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical imaging workflows are complex, multi-stage, and data-sensitive, with scarce expert trajectories that are difficult to share. Standard post-training methods discard valuable diagnostic feedback from structured benchmarks, preventing continuous improvement.

Method: BaT consists of two components: 1) Stage Bank - an asynchronous data pipeline that synthesizes content-isolated training states outside the policy-update loop, and 2) BiCuRL (Bilevel Curriculum Reinforcement Learning) - a self-improving post-training method that uses fixed evaluation to select stage curricula, verifies rollouts with task rubrics, updates policy with GRPO, and returns candidate checkpoints to evaluation.

Result: On AutoMedBench-Lite, BaT-4B and BaT-9B models more than doubled the Overall scores of their Qwen Instruct baselines. The BaT-9B Agent achieved 79.6 Overall score, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6 with Claude Code (77.5).

Conclusion: BaT demonstrates that recursive self-improvement using benchmark feedback can significantly enhance agent performance on complex multi-stage workflows, achieving state-of-the-art results on medical imaging benchmarks through structured curriculum learning and continuous feedback integration.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents are beginning to automate complete workflows that produce code, reports, and research artifacts. Medical imaging workflows are multi-stage and data-sensitive, while expert trajectories remain scarce and difficult to share. Structured benchmarks can localize failures through stage-level rubrics, but standard post-training discards these diagnostics before the next training round. We present Benchmark-as-Teacher (BaT), a recursive self-improvement system for agent post-training. BaT contains two linked components: the asynchronous Stage Bank data pipeline and BiCuRL (Bilevel Curriculum Reinforcement Learning), its self-improving post-training method. Stage Bank synthesizes content-isolated training states outside the policy-update loop. BiCuRL uses a fixed held-out evaluation to select the next stage curriculum, verifies rollouts with task rubrics, updates the policy with GRPO, and returns the candidate checkpoint to evaluation. On AutoMedBench-Lite, BaT-4B and BaT-9B more than double the Overall scores of their Qwen Instruct baselines. BaT-9B Agent reaches 79.6 Overall, exceeding Claude Opus 4.6 with Claude Code at 77.5.

</details>


### [168] [Process-Constituted Intelligence: A Shared Criterion for Humans and Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16213)
*Michael J. Richardson,Ayeh Alhasan,Cassandra Crone,M. Paula Diaz Monfort,Patrick Nalepka,Mark Dras,Rachel W. Kallen,David M. Kaplan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TLDR: Intelligence is about cognitive processes, not just outputs. Current generative AI produces outputs similar to human reasoning but lacks the underlying cognitive processes. The paper proposes a framework for "strong equivalence" that requires AI to have human-like cognitive processes, not just produce similar outputs, to prevent erosion of human capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the fundamental disconnect between human intelligence (which involves active cognitive processes) and current generative AI (which merely reproduces outputs without engaging in genuine cognitive activity). The authors are concerned that AI tools that simply mimic outputs without engaging in processes may erode human cognitive abilities and judgment.

Method: The method involves defining "strong equivalence" across seven process features that can be assessed against both human and machine cognition. The authors develop a process-based account of intelligence and propose design principles for generative AI that incorporate more genuine cognitive processes, along with process audits to make strong equivalence testable.

Result: The paper establishes a framework distinguishing weak equivalence (matching outputs) from strong equivalence (matching cognitive processes). It identifies the risk that generative AI may erode human capacities by outsourcing generative processes, and provides specific design principles and process audits to help AI systems preserve rather than undermine human judgment and creativity.

Conclusion: Current generative AI lacks strong equivalence with human cognition as it reproduces outputs without genuine cognitive processes. To prevent erosion of human capabilities, AI systems should be designed with process-based approaches that maintain and enhance human judgment and creativity, with testable frameworks for evaluating strong equivalence.

Abstract: Intelligence is constituted by \textit{process} (iterative activity through which output emerges), not in the output itself. Generative AI (GenAI) is trained on \textit{traces} (textual and visual residues of human cognitive processes), reproducing samples from a distribution of those traces. Its outputs resemble reasoning, problem-solving, and creativity, yet the activity that produces such outputs in humans remains largely absent. Current GenAI is, therefore, weakly equivalent to the cognition it imitates, matching outputs while process stays absent or opaque. The cognitive sciences have long distinguished between weak and strong equivalence. Here, we define \textit{strong} equivalence across seven process features, assessable against human and machine cognition. Our process-based account addresses a symmetric risk: GenAI tools that outsource a person's generative processes may leave critical capacities unbuilt. We specify design principles for GenAI that instantiate more process and preserve rather than erode human judgment and creativity, and outline process audits that make strong equivalence testable.

</details>


### [169] [AeroCopilotBench: A Two-Tier Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents as Aviation Copilots in an Interactive Virtual Cockpit Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16349)
*Yuchen Yuan,Zhenghuang Wu,Yuangan Li,Liang Ma,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AeroCopilot Operational Environment (ACOE) and AeroCopilotBench provide an interactive virtual cockpit environment and benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' aviation procedural execution and safety compliance, revealing gaps between static knowledge and actual task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing aviation evaluations focus only on static knowledge testing, which doesn't adequately assess LLM agents' ability to execute complex procedures and maintain safety compliance in interactive cockpit environments. There's a need for systematic testing of procedural execution and safety in dynamic, operational settings.

Method: Created ACOE, a reproducible interactive virtual cockpit environment that converts natural-language procedures into executable state transitions, final-state goals, and hard safety constraints. Developed AeroCopilotBench with two tiers: Tier-1 with 1,200 multiple-choice questions for aviation knowledge, and Tier-2 with 73 emergency/abnormal tasks from manufacturers' Pilot's Operating Handbooks instantiated in ACOE. Established a safety-gated evaluation framework where success requires achieving all task goals without violating safety constraints.

Result: Across 12 models, the highest Tier-2 success rate was 72.6%, demonstrating that static knowledge performance doesn't consistently translate to procedural execution. Analysis of 451 failed episodes from 3 representative models identified recurring failures in procedural completeness, use of state feedback, and long-horizon execution management.

Conclusion: The findings motivate state-aware agent orchestration, joint assessment of task completion and trajectory safety, and repeated regression testing. ACOE and AeroCopilotBench provide a reproducible foundation for testing knowledge application, interactive execution, and operational safety in aviation agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents may assist flight crews with complex decisions and task execution, but existing aviation evaluations centered on static knowledge do not support systematic testing of procedural execution and safety compliance in interactive environments. This paper presents the AeroCopilot Operational Environment (ACOE), a reproducible interactive virtual-cockpit test environment, and AeroCopilotBench, a two-tier aviation agent evaluation benchmark. Tier-1 evaluates aviation knowledge using 1,200 multiple-choice questions, while Tier-2 comprises 73 emergency and abnormal tasks derived from the manufacturers' Pilot's Operating Handbooks (POHs) and instantiated in ACOE. ACOE converts natural-language procedures into executable state transitions, final-state goal conditions, and hard safety constraints, enabling models to interpret cockpit state, diagnose faults, and operate aircraft systems through standardized tool interfaces. We establish a safety-gated evaluation framework in which a trajectory succeeds only when all task goals are achieved without violating any hard safety constraint, while safe goal progress and trajectory safety are measured separately. Across 12 models, the highest Tier-2 success rate is 72.6%, while static knowledge performance does not consistently translate into procedural execution. Analysis of 451 failed episodes from 3 representative models identifies recurring failures in procedural completeness, use of state feedback, and long-horizon execution management. These findings motivate state-aware agent orchestration, joint assessment of task completion and trajectory safety, and repeated regression testing. ACOE and AeroCopilotBench provide a reproducible foundation for testing knowledge application, interactive execution, and operational safety in aviation agents.

</details>


### [170] [DriveCache: Action-Aware Caching for Driving World Model Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16354)
*Jianchun Yang,Jian Liang,Xianda Guo,Pinhan Fu,Yanlun Peng,Conglang Zhang,Wenke Huang,Mang Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DriveCache is a training-free controller for accelerating diffusion-based driving video generation by intelligently caching denoising steps based on planned motion signals, improving the fidelity-efficiency trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based driving video generation models are computationally expensive due to repeated evaluation of large backbones across many denoising steps. Existing acceleration methods don't leverage available driving signals like ego speed and planned trajectories, which could inform smarter caching strategies.

Method: DriveCache is a training-free, action-aware controller that uses planned motion to allocate feature reuse across scenes and employs dynamic programming to place caches across denoising steps within a calibrated response budget. It includes a causal drift check that refreshes features and replans the schedule when generation quality degrades.

Result: Experiments show that cache tolerance varies with ego translation/rotation, denoising progress, and consecutive reuse length. Across three generator configurations, DriveCache improves the overall fidelity-efficiency trade-off compared to evaluated cache methods.
