Result: Numerical experiments show FENs consistently achieve higher accuracy than ELMs across various activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, swish) when properly scaled.

Conclusion: FENs provide a superior alternative to ELMs by leveraging Fourier features instead of affine transformations, offering higher accuracy while maintaining the simplicity of single-hidden-layer neural network architecture.

Abstract: Building on the foundation of single-hidden-layer neural networks, Fourier Feature Networks (FENs) are proposed, which incorporate Fourier features using $\cos$, $\sin$, or a combination of both. Similar to Extreme Learning Machines (ELMs), FENs employ a single-hidden-layer architecture to generate a set of basis functions. The target function is then approximated as a linear combination of these basis functions, with the coefficients determined using the least squares method. However, unlike ELMs, which often rely on affine transformations to improve representational power, FENs can achieve high-precision solutions without requiring such transformations on the input variables. To evaluate the representational capacity of these networks, we search for an optimal scaling factor within a predefined range for the randomly initialized and fixed weights and biases. By adjusting this scaling factor, we ensure a fair comparison between FENs and ELMs using various activation functions, such as $\text{sigmoid}$, $\tanh$, and $\text{swish}$. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that FENs consistently achieve higher accuracy than ELMs.

</details>


### [244] [Unraveling the Size Determination Mechanism of Nanocrystal Synthesis via Interpretable Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14734)
*Kai Gu,Haizheng Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NanoEQL is a white-box neural network that learns interpretable mathematical equations to predict and explain nanocrystal size/shape by encoding precursor properties and reaction conditions, revealing synthetic mechanisms through three interpretable scalars.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep learning models for nanocrystal synthesis are black-box, preventing deep understanding of underlying synthetic mechanisms despite accurate predictions. There's a need for interpretable models that can reveal the fundamental principles governing nanocrystal formation.

Method: Developed Nanocrystal Equation Learner (NanoEQL), a fully white-box neural network based on EQL architecture. Introduced eight operators to replace standard activation functions to fit nanocrystal synthesis equations, with three smoothed operators to address gradient explosion. Used temperature-gated attention pooling to evaluate precursor weights and encode chemical synthesis mechanisms.

Result: NanoEQL successfully learned that final nanocrystal size can be described by a linear equation composed of three interpretable scalars: nanocrystallization capability (-Zp), growth capability (Zrea), and external input potential (-Zops). The model provides mechanistic insights into synthetic processes.

Conclusion: NanoEQL establishes a generalizable paradigm for deciphering chemical reaction mechanisms through white-box machine learning, advancing rational design of nanocrystal synthesis by providing interpretable mathematical understanding rather than just predictive accuracy.

Abstract: Deep learning models of nanocrystal synthesis enable the prediction of size and shape by encoding precursors and reaction conditions. However, their black-box nature hinders gaining deep insights into the underlying synthetic mechanisms. Here, we develop the Nanocrystal Equation Learner (NanoEQL), a fully white-box neural network to unravel the size determination mechanisms of nanocrystal synthesis. Building on the EQL architecture, eight operators are introduced to replace standard activation functions to fit the mathematical equations in nanocrystal synthesis. Among these operators, three smoothed operators address the gradient explosion of singular operators at zero. To evaluate the weights of different precursors, we develop a temperature-gated attention pooling strategy that encodes concentration-driven and reactivity-driven chemical synthesis mechanisms into the temperature gate. The NanoEQL model illustrates that the final nanocrystal size can be described by a linear equation composed of three scalars representing nanocrystallization capability (-Zp), growth capability (Zrea), and external input potential (-Zops). These interpretable scalars not only advance the rational design of nanocrystal synthesis but also establish a generalizable paradigm for deciphering chemical reaction mechanisms through white-box machine learning.

</details>


### [245] [Generative Learning of Separatrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14743)
*Ellis R. Crabtree,Dimitris G. Giovanis,Anastasia Georgiou,George Datseris,Ioannis G. Kevrekidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-driven framework combining neural network classifiers and score-based generative models to identify and reconstruct separatrix manifolds between basins of attraction in multistable dynamical systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identifying and reconstructing boundaries between basins of attraction in multistable dynamical systems is challenging. Traditional approaches face computational limitations in high dimensions and require system equations, while random sampling fails to capture separatrix structures that govern transition pathways.

Method: 1. Train neural network classifiers on uniformly/randomly sampled initial conditions labeled by their basins. 2. Use classifier uncertainty metrics to identify high-uncertainty regions as approximate separatrices. 3. Train score-based generative models specifically on samples from high-uncertainty regions to generate densities consistent with the empirical density near separatrix manifolds.

Result: The approach leverages discriminative models for global phase space partitioning and generative models for detailed geometric sampling, creating a systematic, iterative, data-driven framework that produces empirically consistent reconstructions of approximate separatrix manifolds.

Conclusion: This hybrid framework combines supervised classification and generative modeling to address the fundamental challenge of identifying basin boundaries in multistable systems without requiring prior knowledge of system equations or extensive computational resources.

Abstract: The identification and reconstruction of the boundaries separating basins of attraction in multistable, multidimensional dynamical systems presents a fundamental challenge in computational dynamics. These structures govern transition pathways and other important large timescale behavior, yet they remain typically under-sampled since their neighborhood does not get routinely visited during direct simulations. Traditional computational approaches face computational limitations in high-dimensional systems and require a priori knowledge of the dynamical system and its equations. Simplistic sampling methods such as random or uniform sampling of the phase space typically fail to quantitatively approximate separatrices and their structure altogether.
  We introduce and implement a framework that combines supervised classification with generative modeling to address this challenge. Our approach first trains neural network classifiers on uniformly or randomly sampled initial conditions labeled by their corresponding basins of attraction in the system of interest. Using uncertainty metrics of the trained classifier to quantify decision boundaries, the method then identifies these high uncertainty regions and boundaries of the classifier as preliminary approximate separatrices. Subsequently, score-based generative models are trained specifically on samples from high-uncertainty regions, ultimately generating densities of samples consistent with the empirical density of samples on or close to the manifold that constitutes the separatrix between basins in the sampled region. This approach leverages the complementary strengths of (a) discriminative models for global phase space partitioning and (b) generative models for detailed geometric sampling, resulting in a systematic, iterative, data-driven framework that produces empirically consistent reconstructions of (approximate) separatrix manifolds.

</details>


### [246] [Iterative Refinement Diffusion for Super-Resolved Data Assimilation of Multiscale Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14744)
*Mrigank Dhingra,Ramchandran Muthukumar,Rebecca Willett,Omer San*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IR (Iterative Refinement) is a learned data assimilation framework that combines hierarchical forecast-analysis cycles with generative super-resolution, outperforming traditional methods on complex multiscale systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of recovering high-resolution states from sparse, low-resolution observations. Classical data assimilation requires expensive high-resolution forecast models, while one-shot generative super-resolution doesn't fully exploit temporal constraints from past states. There's a need for a method that combines temporal information with efficient high-resolution recovery.

Method: IR decomposes the reconstruction task into resolution-wise forecast-analysis operations across a multiresolution hierarchy. It uses: 1) a shared neural operator with resolution-dependent spectral mode slicing for dynamical priors, and 2) a shared conditional diffusion corrector that uses current coarser-resolution states to produce refined posteriors at finer resolutions.

Result: On 256x256 Kraichnan turbulence benchmark: IR achieves RMSE 0.184 and SSIM 0.836, outperforming spectral upsampling, one-shot diffusion super-resolution, enhanced deep super-resolution, and autoregressive forecaster. On 1D Burgers dynamics: IR remains competitive with one-shot diffusion (which achieves lowest RMSE).

Conclusion: One-shot generative reconstruction works well for simpler settings, while hierarchical forecast-analysis refinement becomes advantageous in strongly multiscale and underdetermined regimes. IR successfully combines temporal priors, generative correction, and multiresolution reconstruction for learned data assimilation in complex physical systems.

Abstract: Recovering high-resolution states from sparse, low-resolution observations is a central challenge in scientific machine learning and data assimilation. Classical data assimilation exploits temporal information through forecast-analysis cycles, but often requires repeated access to expensive high-resolution forecast models. Generative super-resolution can recover unresolved structure from coarse observations, but is commonly used as a one-shot mapping that does not fully exploit constraints from past states. We introduce Iterative Refinement (IR), a learned data assimilation framework that combines these perspectives. Instead of performing a single coarse-to-fine reconstruction, IR decomposes the task into resolution-wise forecast-analysis operations across a multiresolution hierarchy. At each stage, a shared neural operator with resolution-dependent spectral mode slicing provides a dynamical prior, while a shared conditional diffusion corrector uses the current coarser-resolution state to produce a refined posterior at the next finer resolution. We evaluate IR on one-dimensional stochastically forced Burgers dynamics and two-dimensional Kraichnan turbulence. On the challenging 256x256 Kraichnan benchmark, IR achieves an RMSE of 0.184 and an SSIM of 0.836, outperforming spectral upsampling, one-shot diffusion super-resolution, enhanced deep super-resolution, and an autoregressive forecaster. On the more constrained Burgers testbed, IR remains competitive with one-shot diffusion, which achieves the lowest RMSE. These results show that one-shot generative reconstruction can be effective for simpler settings, while hierarchical forecast-analysis refinement becomes advantageous in strongly multiscale and underdetermined regimes. Overall, IR combines temporal priors, generative correction, and multiresolution reconstruction for learned data assimilation in complex physical systems.

</details>


### [247] [WANDR: A Benchmark for Wide and Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14747)
*Vitaliy Polshkov,Marcin Pitera,Jeremy Yang,Kirill Priemko,Maksim Gaiduk,Aleksandr Nikolenko,Denis Bykov,Clare Southern,Denis Yarats,Jerry Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WANDR is a benchmark of 500 realistic web research tasks that require discovering entities (breadth), investigating each through coordinated searches (depth), and returning verifiable records with sources, using hierarchical qualification structures for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks don't adequately evaluate real-world research agents that need to combine breadth (discovering many entities) with depth (investigating each entity thoroughly), and lack dynamic verification mechanisms for changing facts and comprehensive evidence collection.

Method: Creates 500 tasks using qualification key hierarchies that specify entities, relationships, evidence, and required counts. Uses task-specific judges that refetch cited pages to verify each record dynamically. Includes automated checks, empirical audits, and human review for task creation.

Result: Benchmark is far from saturated - best system reaches only 0.363 soft F1 and 0.133 hard F1. Performance degrades with increasing target volume and hierarchy depth, with incomplete discovery, missing enrichment, and incomplete evidence construction as major bottlenecks.

Conclusion: WANDR provides a challenging, realistic benchmark for research agents that requires both breadth and depth, with dynamic verification that adapts to changing facts, highlighting significant performance gaps and research opportunities in automated web research systems.

Abstract: WANDR (Wide ANd Deep Research) is a benchmark of 500 realistic, challenging data-collection tasks for research agents. Each task requires a system to discover a large set of entities that satisfy specified criteria (breadth), investigate each entity through multiple coordinated web searches (depth), and return independently verifiable records with supporting sources and excerpts. Tasks are represented as qualification key hierarchies that specify the entities, relationships, evidence, and required count at each level; a hierarchy with n companies, m employees per company, and k sources per employee requires n x m x k records. This structure supports diverse workflows such as market mapping, due diligence, literature review, product comparison, and talent sourcing, with targets ranging from dozens to thousands of records. WANDR replaces static gold answer sets with task-specific judges that refetch cited pages and verify each record against its evidence, allowing evaluation of current and changing facts. Record verdicts are aggregated into soft and hard precision, recall, and F1 scores that distinguish factual quality, coverage, and hierarchical completeness. The tasks are derived from de-identified product-usage logs and produced through a semi-automated pipeline with automated checks, empirical audits, and human review where needed. We evaluate six production research systems and find that the benchmark is far from saturated: at high effort, the strongest system reaches only 0.363 soft F1 and 0.133 hard F1. Performance degrades as target volume and hierarchy depth increase, with incomplete discovery, missing enrichment, and incomplete evidence construction remaining major bottlenecks. The benchmark and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/perplexityai/wandr.

</details>


### [248] [Real-Time State-of-Health Estimation and Online Degradation Prognosis from Partial Battery Discharge Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14764)
*Begoña Ispizua,Serio Gil-López,Leire Arrizabalaga,Ibai Laña*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-informed deep learning for lithium-ion battery SOH prediction using incomplete discharge curves from arbitrary voltage ranges, achieving <4% MAPE with real-time degradation trend estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With increasing renewable energy integration, accurate State of Health (SOH) estimation and degradation behavior prediction for energy storage systems have become critical. Current methods rely on fixed testing protocols or early, non-adaptive predictions, limiting their applicability in realistic, heterogeneous operating conditions.

Method: Proposes a physics-informed deep learning approach that combines data-driven learning with physically motivated degradation dynamics. Uses incomplete discharge curves extracted from arbitrary voltage ranges to reflect realistic conditions. Also introduces a real-time degradation trend estimation strategy that detects key aging transitions without requiring prior knowledge or historical data.

Result: Achieves Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) below 4% for SOH prediction using partial discharge information. The method enables SOH estimation from arbitrary discharge segments and provides real-time degradation forecasting that continuously integrates all usage data.

Conclusion: The approach overcomes limitations of previous methods by enabling reliable SOH estimation from partial discharge curves and providing adaptive, real-time degradation forecasting applicable to a wide range of batteries under heterogeneous operating conditions.

Abstract: With the increasing integration of renewable energy sources, energy storage systems have become essential, making the accurate estimation of their State of Health (SOH) and degradation behavior critical. In this work, we propose a physics-informed deep learning approach for lithium-ion battery SOH prediction using incomplete discharge curves extracted from arbitrary voltage ranges, thereby reflecting realistic and heterogeneous operating conditions. The proposed method combines data-driven learning with physically motivated degradation dynamics to ensure consistent and reliable SOH estimation from partial discharge information, achieving a MAPE below 4$\%$. In addition, a real-time degradation trend estimation strategy is introduced to detect key aging transitions without requiring prior knowledge or historical data, making it applicable to a wide range of batteries. Overall, our approach enables SOH estimation from arbitrary discharge segments and a real-time degradation forecast that continuously integrates all usage, overcoming previous methods that rely on fixed protocols or early, non-adaptive predictions.

</details>


### [249] [ER-KANs: Efficient and Robust Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Data-Scarce Scientific Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14773)
*Harshil Lodhiya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ER-KAN is a noise-robust Kolmogorov-Arnold Network that outperforms existing KAN variants and MLPs on noisy, data-scarce tasks through three design choices: shared RBF bases, curriculum noise injection, and entropy-weighted regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current efficient-KAN literature has been benchmarked almost entirely on clean data, concealing large capability differences between architectures when faced with real-world noisy data. ChebyKAN shows severe performance degradation (10.6x worse) with noise compared to minimal degradation for MLPs (1.7x).

Method: ER-KAN combines three design choices: 1) shared Gaussian RBF bases across all edges in a layer for locality and efficient parameterization, 2) curriculum noise injection during training to explicitly teach noise robustness, and 3) entropy-weighted adaptive regularization to prevent overfitting at small data sizes. The architecture has only 595 parameters.

Result: ER-KAN matches MLP accuracy at moderate noise and degrades far more gracefully as noise grows. On eight analytic functions, it outperforms other KAN variants. In a damped harmonic oscillator PINN, ER-KAN achieves 4.2x lower solution MSE than MLP. The authors also report limitations where all models fail to converge on Burgers' equation PINN.

Conclusion: ER-KAN demonstrates superior noise robustness compared to existing efficient-KAN architectures and MLPs. The paper introduces the noise degradation ratio as a key metric for evaluating noise robustness and recommends it become standard reporting for efficient-KAN papers, while honestly reporting model limitations where convergence fails.

Abstract: The efficient-KAN literature---covering Chebyshev, wavelet, and radial-basis-function variants of the original Kolmogorov-Arnold Network---has been benchmarked almost entirely on clean data. We show that this choice conceals a large capability difference between architectures: ChebyKAN's test MSE (evaluated against clean ground truth) increases by a factor of 10.6x when training data is corrupted with sigma=0.1 noise, versus 7.9x for vanilla KAN, 1.7x for a standard MLP, and just 1.4x for our proposed ER-KAN.
  ER-KAN combines three design choices targeting the noisy, data-scarce setting: shared Gaussian RBF bases across all edges in a layer (providing locality and efficient parameterisation), curriculum noise injection during training (explicitly teaching noise robustness), and entropy-weighted adaptive regularisation (preventing overfitting at small N). The result is a 595-parameter network that matches MLP accuracy at moderate noise while degrading far more gracefully as noise grows.
  We evaluate on eight analytic functions (N in {50, 200, 500}, sigma in {0, 0.03, 0.1}), on a damped harmonic oscillator physics-informed neural network where ER-KAN achieves 4.2x lower solution MSE than MLP, and on a Burgers' equation PINN where all models fail to converge---a genuine limitation we report rather than suppress. We introduce the noise degradation ratio as a simple complementary metric and recommend it become a standard reporting requirement for efficient-KAN papers.

</details>


### [250] [p-Spin Glass Network Efficient Single-Batch Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14774)
*Vladimer Khasia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel $p$-Spin Glass Network architecture achieves memory and sample efficiency with stable single-batch training, enabling continuous learning and edge AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern sequence models suffer from massive memory footprints and reliance on large-batch optimization, which restricts sample efficiency and prevents continual learning applications.

Method: Introduces the $p$-Spin Glass Network architecture featuring native ternary quantization for 8× parameter compression, exact implicit gradients that bound activation memory to $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot T \cdot D)$, and structural variance management enabling stable single-batch training.

Result: The architecture achieves: 1) 8× parameter compression via ternary quantization, 2) matches Transformer performance with 8× fewer training sequences, 3) stable convergence with micro-batch size of 1, and 4) modality-agnostic robust temporal credit assignment across both discrete subword and raw byte streams.

Conclusion: The $p$-Spin Glass Network removes the large-batch requirement for stable deep learning, establishing a foundation for continuous learning and edge AI applications.

Abstract: Modern sequence models heavily rely on massive memory footprints and large-batch stochastic optimization, barriers that restrict sample efficiency and continual learning. We introduce the $p$-Spin Glass Network, a novel architecture that overcomes these limitations, structurally manages optimization variance and yields four noticeable capabilities: 1. It enforces memory efficiency: native ternary quantization compresses internal parameters by $8\times$, while exact implicit gradients strictly bound activation memory to $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot T \cdot D)$. 2. it demonstrates sample efficiency, matching the asymptotic performance of a Transformer baseline while utilizing $8\times$ fewer training sequences. 3. Method enables single-batch stability and smooth, monotonic convergence at a stochastic micro-batch size of $1$. 4. Finally, this stability proves modality-agnostic, maintaining robust temporal credit assignment across both discrete subword and long horizon uncompressed raw byte streams. Ultimately, this work removes large batch requirement for stable deep learning, establishing a foundation for continuous learning and edge AI.

</details>


### [251] [NRCD: An Open Database of Collegiate Running with Unified Performance Standardization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14776)
*Jonathan A. Karr,Ryan M. Fryer,Ben Darden,Nicholas Pell,Kayla Ambrose,Evan Hall,Ramzi K. Bualuan,Nitesh V. Chawla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces NRCD - the first large-scale public dataset for collegiate running results, containing 128,963 performances with standardized adjustments for distance, elevation, and weather, enabling comprehensive longitudinal and gender-equity research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collegiate running generates thousands of race results annually, but no large-scale dataset has been publicly available. Existing websites restrict bulk downloads, limiting analyses to ~500 performances and skewing studies toward male athletes. Researchers need comprehensive data for longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental studies, and gender-equity research.

Method: Created the National Running Club Database (NRCD) - a community-governed, openly available dataset with 128,963 performances from 28,913 athletes across 1,336 meets. Developed a unified performance standardization framework with distance, elevation, and heat adjustments. Used a Python package 'nrcd' for implementation following FAIR principles.

Result: Dataset contains 36.3% women's performances with comprehensive metadata (course distance, elevation, weather) for meets from August 2023 onward. Standardization pipeline reduces within-athlete cross-meet variability by 51.0% (women) and 34.4% (men) in cross country versus raw times. The dataset spans 2004-2026 with yearly growth.

Conclusion: NRCD provides the first comprehensive, standardized collegiate running dataset, enabling large-scale research previously impossible due to data access limitations. The dataset and pipeline support longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental-confounder studies, and gender-equity research in collegiate sports.

Abstract: Collegiate running in the United States generates thousands of race results annually in cross country and track and field, yet no large-scale dataset has been publicly available for research. Existing websites such as Athletic.net, MileSplit, and TFRRS host results but do not support bulk download, restricting prior analyses to ~500 performances, often skewing studies toward male athletes. We introduce the National Running Club Database (NRCD), the first openly available collegiate running dataset at scale: 128,963 approved performances from 28,913 athletes across 1,336 meets in four sports (cross country (XC), indoor and outdoor track, and road races), 36.3% women, spanning 2004 through 2026. Within that single export, meets from August 2023 onward carry comprehensive course distance, elevation gain and loss, weather at race time, and track venue metadata (97.7% of XC rows with weather fields); earlier seasons back to 2004 are included with sparser metadata. NRCD is community-governed through open submission and expert approval and is maintained as a live database whose meet volume has grown yearly. We release a unified performance standardization framework that operationalizes established distance, elevation, and heat adjustments in one pipeline. Furthermore, we recommend gender-stratified modeling. On XC, full standardization lowers median within-athlete cross-meet variability by 51.0% (women) and 34.4% (men) versus raw times. We release the dataset and pipeline with a python package `nrcd' under FAIR principles, supporting longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental-confounder studies, and gender-equity research in collegiate sport.

</details>


### [252] [Is Grokking a Loss of Normal Hyperbolicity of the Interpolation Manifold?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14803)
*Suvinava Basak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analysis of grokking as constrained optimization shows the generalization transition is not due to loss of normal hyperbolicity (bifurcation), but rather smooth contraction along the interpolation manifold.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to resolve whether the sharp generalization transition in grokking results from a bifurcation event (loss of normal hyperbolicity) or smooth drift along the interpolation manifold. Existing literature frames grokking as constrained optimization but hasn't addressed this specific mechanistic question.

Method: Proposes an optimizer-agnostic diagnostic: the smallest nonzero singular value σ⁺_min(J) of the residual Jacobian, which equals the slowest normal restoring rate of the interpolation manifold. Tests this on a two-layer ReLU network trained to perform modular addition under squared loss across five random seeds.

Result: σ⁺_min(J) does NOT collapse at the generalization transition - it's near zero only before memorization and reaches largest values during the transition. The behavior is consistent across seeds, and multiple smallest singular values behave identically (no subspace-local collapse).

Conclusion: Preliminary evidence against bifurcation hypothesis and in favor of smooth contraction picture. However, authors note limitations - a single gradual-transition experiment under Adam doesn't prove absence of bifurcation, only constrains where one could be hidden.

Abstract: A recent line of work recasts the post-memorization phase of grokking as constrained optimization: once a network interpolates the training set, weight decay drives a slow drift along the zero-loss manifold toward lower norm. In the language of dynamical systems, this is a fast-slow system in which the interpolation manifold plays the role of a slow manifold. We ask a question that this framing makes natural but the existing literature does not address: is the sharp generalization transition a loss of normal hyperbolicity of that manifold: a fold- or bifurcation-like event in which a normal restoring direction goes flat? Or does the manifold stay uniformly attracting while generalization happens by smooth drift? We propose a simple, optimizer-agnostic diagnostic: the smallest nonzero singular value $σ_{\min}^{+}(\mathbf J)$ of the residual Jacobian, which, for the squared loss, equals the slowest normal restoring rate of the manifold. On a two-layer ReLU network trained to grok modular addition under squared loss, $σ_{\min}^{+}(\mathbf J)$ does not collapse at the transition; it is near zero only before memorization and attains its largest values during the transition. The result holds across five seeds, and the six smallest singular values behave identically; there is no subspace-local collapse either. This is preliminary evidence against the bifurcation hypothesis and in favor of the smooth-contraction picture. We are explicit that a single-setting, gradual-transition experiment under Adam optimizer does not prove the absence of a bifurcation; it constrains where one could hide.

</details>


### [253] [Disentangling Homophily and Rarity: Explaining Failure in Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14823)
*Preben M. Ness,Fariz Ikhwantri,Dusica Marijan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Heterophilic node classification difficulty in GNNs is not just about rarity but actual structural properties; classification heads can often be retrained to correctly classify heterophilic nodes even when initial training fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether heterophilic nodes in graphs are harder to classify primarily because they are rare (subgroup generalization problem) or because they have different structural properties (neighborhood aggregation problem), and to reconcile these two competing explanations.

Method: Conducted detailed evaluation of six different Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on five datasets with varying degrees of homophily. Explored whether classification difficulty persists even when homophilic nodes are rare and heterophilic nodes are common. Tested information recovery by retraining just the classification head or final linear layer of models.

Result: Homophilic nodes are generally easier to classify even when they are rare, challenging the subgroup framing explanation. However, the information needed to correctly classify heterophilic nodes is often recoverable by retraining only the classification head or final linear layer, suggesting GNN representations capture relevant information but the classification part fails to utilize it properly.

Conclusion: Heterophilic node classification difficulty stems from structural properties rather than just rarity. While GNN representations often contain sufficient information to classify heterophilic nodes correctly, the classification heads fail to properly leverage this information, suggesting improvements in classifier design rather than fundamental GNN limitations.

Abstract: Are heterophilic nodes in a graph harder to classify because they are heterophilic or because they are rare? Some existing work frames classification of such nodes as a subgroup generalisation problem, where a model performs well on the majority group at the expense of the rare group. Others explain this as a problem of neighbourhood aggregation in graph neural networks (GNNs). We assess these two viewpoints through a detailed evaluation of six GNNs on five datasets of varying homophily, and find that homophilic nodes tend to be easier to classify, even when they are rare---challenging the subgroup framing. However, our findings also nuance existing beliefs about how GNNs misrepresent heterophilic nodes. We demonstrate that the information needed to classify heterophilic nodes correctly is often recoverable by retraining the classification head of a model, or even just the final linear classification layer.

</details>


### [254] [M-LINKX: Multiview Graph Learning for Brain Cognitive Disease Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14847)
*An Phan,Yufei Jin,Xingquan Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M-LINKX: A multi-view graph learning framework for EEG-based dementia classification using functional connectivity graphs from different connectivity metrics, frequency bands, and topology filters, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two three-class EEG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG-based classification of dementia-related conditions (AD, MCI, FTD) is challenging due to noisy, non-stationary EEG signals with high inter-subject variability. Existing methods need to better capture both within-channel information and between-channel interactions for improved dementia classification.

Method: Proposed M-LINKX framework: 1) Extract channel-level node features from EEG segments, 2) Construct multiple functional connectivity graph views using different connectivity metrics, frequency bands, and topology filters, 3) Use simple design modeling node features and adjacency-based connectivity (instead of message passing), 4) Fuse graph-view representations with trainable view weights, 5) Average segment-level probabilities for subject-level prediction.

Result: M-LINKX achieves best subject-level performance on two three-class EEG datasets: CAUEEG (HC/MCI/Dementia) and AHEAP (HC/AD/FTD) under main experimental settings, demonstrating improved classification accuracy for dementia-related conditions.

Conclusion: Multi-view functional connectivity can significantly improve EEG-based dementia classification when integrated with appropriate graph-learning architectures like M-LINKX. The framework shows promise for practical applications with available code and data.

Abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) is a non-invasive and relatively low-cost procedure that measures brain electricity for the detection of cognitive diseases. EEG-based classification of dementia-related conditions, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), remains challenging because EEG signals are noisy, non-stationary, and vary across subjects. Segment-based learning provides a practical way to model long EEG recordings by converting them into fixed-length inputs. For each segment, discriminative information may be explored by using signals within each channel (i.e. electrode), as well as interactions between EEG channels. In this paper, we propose M-LINKX, a multi-view graph learning framework for EEG-based dementia classification. For each segment, we extract channel-level node features and construct multiple functional-connectivity (FC) graph views, where each view is defined by a specific combination of connectivity metric, frequency band, and topology filter, respectively. Instead of relying on message passing over the constructed graphs, M-LINKX follows a simple design in modeling node features and adjacency-based connectivity representations. The graph-view representations are fused using global trainable view weights, and subject-level prediction is obtained by averaging segment-level probabilities. Experiments on two three-class EEG datasets with different diagnostic groups, CAUEEG (HC/MCI/Dementia) and AHEAP (HC/AD/FTD), show that M-LINKX achieves the best subject-level performance under the main experimental settings. Our study suggests that multi-view functional connectivity can improve EEG-based dementia classification when integrated with an appropriate graph-learning architecture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/anphantt/MLINKX.

</details>


### [255] [Can Neural Networks Learn by Experimenting on Themselves? Self-Interventional Learning from Functional Consequences to Predictive Self-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14894)
*Michał Tomaszewski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A neural system learns to predict the effects of perturbing its own internal structure through self-interventions, enabling it to build a predictive self-model, though this approach doesn't outperform simpler direct strategies in all cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional machine learning systems model external data but don't introspect their own internal functional organization. The authors aim to develop a method where neural systems can actively investigate and understand their own functional structure through self-experimentation.

Method: Self-Interventional Learning (SIL) involves: 1) a neural system perturbing its own functional structure, 2) observing the consequences of these perturbations, 3) learning a predictive self-model, 4) generalizing to unexecuted interventions, and 5) using predictions to guide later structural actions. The approach was tested in both synthetic systems and practical settings including CIFAR-10/ResNet validations.

Result: SIL successfully recovered critical structure, redundancy, and replaceability in synthetic systems, though synergy was not reliably recovered. Increasing intervention budgets improved prediction accuracy (error reduced from 0.0335 to 0.0148) and correlation (Spearman increased from 0.629 to 0.883). In ablation studies, preserving correct intervention-consequence mapping reduced error by 81.3%, and using the learned self-model reduced normalized regret by 31.7%. However, model-guided action didn't significantly outperform direct empirical-memory policies, and showed no robustness advantage over direct repair search in CIFAR-10/ResNet validation.

Conclusion: SIL provides a viable intervention-driven framework for neural systems to learn predictive knowledge about their own functional organization, demonstrating that self-models can be learned from limited data. However, these self-models remain incomplete and don't universally outperform simpler direct strategies, suggesting practical limitations to introspection-based approaches in certain contexts.

Abstract: Machine-learning systems usually model external data, while their internal functional organization is analyzed by external observers. This work introduces Self-Interventional Learning (SIL), in which a neural system perturbs its own functional structure, observes consequences, learns a predictive self-model, generalizes to unexecuted interventions, and uses predictions to guide later structural action. In a construction-known synthetic system, SIL recovered critical structure, redundancy, and replaceability, while synergy was not reliably recovered. Across 30 fresh confirmatory seeds, increasing the pairwise intervention budget from 4 to 56 reduced held-out prediction error from 0.0335 to 0.0148 and increased Spearman correlation from 0.629 to 0.883. In a matched ablation, preserving the correct intervention--consequence mapping reduced prospective prediction error by 81.3%, while using the same learned self-model for action reduced normalized regret by 31.7% relative to ignoring it. However, model-guided action did not significantly outperform a direct empirical-memory policy, and powered CIFAR-10/ResNet validation showed no robustness advantage over equal-budget direct repair search. These results support SIL as an intervention-driven framework for learning predictive knowledge about a network's own functional organization, while showing that the self-model remains incomplete and is not universally superior to simpler direct strategies.

</details>


### [256] [Degeneracy Counting Quantum Algorithm using Decoherence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14941)
*Malay Marut Das,Mark A. Novotny,Yaroslav Koshka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces CTPQsd#, a quantum algorithm that counts the number of global minima in classical optimization problems by measuring only a small probe qubit system rather than the full problem space, using thermal quantum states and exploiting perturbative relations between decoherence and degeneracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counting the number of global optima in classical optimization problems is computationally hard (#P-hard), making it infeasible for classical computers. Current approaches require finding individual minima, which is inefficient. There's a need for quantum algorithms that can determine degeneracy counts without full problem space exploration.

Method: The CTPQsd# algorithm uses canonical thermal pure quantum (CTPQ) states to relate a probe system S's decoherence measure to the degeneracy of optimization problem P. The method only requires measurements on the small probe S (represented by four qubits in simulations), avoiding full tomography of the exponentially large problem Hilbert space. Temperature parameters and Hamiltonian properties are tuned to extract degeneracy information.

Result: Numerical simulations on random-energy Hamiltonians (acting as testbeds for binary optimization) with up to 20 problem qubits demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Two temperature thresholds are identified: one for exact degeneracy counting and a lower threshold for counting near-degenerate minima within user-defined energy tolerances. The algorithm successfully counts global minima by measuring only a 4-qubit probe.

Conclusion: The CTPQsd# algorithm provides a practical quantum approach to the #P-hard problem of counting global optima, dramatically reducing measurement requirements from exponential problem space tomography to small probe measurements. This represents an efficient quantum advantage for degeneracy counting in classical optimization problems.

Abstract: Counting the global optima of a classical optimization problem is a #P-hard task. We develop the canonical thermal pure quantum (CTPQ) state-based degeneracy counting (CTPQsd#) algorithm that determines the number of global optima of a classical optimization problem P by measuring only a small probe S, without finding individual minima. The method exploits a perturbative relation between the decoherence measure of S and the degeneracy of P when S and P are together in a CTPQ state. We provide the first numerical demonstration that this relation can be used to count the global minima, applying it to problems encoded by diagonal random-energy Hamiltonians as a maximally unstructured testbed for classical binary optimization problems. Classical simulations of up to 20 problem qubits quantify the algorithm's sensitivity to variations in the temperature of the CTPQ state, the Hamiltonian energy range, the problem size, and degeneracy. We establish the temperature threshold for determining the exact degeneracy and identify a second, lower threshold that provides a temperature window to count near-degenerate minima within a user-defined energy tolerance. By confining measurement to S, the protocol replaces tomography over the exponentially large problem Hilbert space with tomography over a small probe represented by only four qubits.

</details>


### [257] [PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14951)
*Ying-Qiu Zheng,Alex Fung,Stephen M Smith,Rogier B Mars,Saad Jbabdi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PathFinder is a novel method for joint low-rank matrix decomposition that can analyze multimodal datasets even when they don't all share common dimensions, as long as there are connecting paths between subsets of matrices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing joint low-rank decomposition methods require all multimodal datasets to share one or more dimensions, which limits their applicability to datasets where complete dimension mapping across all modalities isn't available.

Method: PathFinder extends joint matrix decomposition by connecting datasets through pairwise or subgroup dimension sharing, forming a network path that enables global joint decomposition across all datasets even without universal dimension sharing.

Result: The method provides a general framework that encompasses many existing matrix decomposition methods as special cases, enables discovery of common patterns across disparate datasets, and allows predictions for missing data or modalities.

Conclusion: PathFinder offers a flexible and powerful approach for multimodal data analysis that overcomes the limitation of requiring complete dimension sharing across all datasets, expanding applications to more complex real-world scenarios where direct dimension mapping isn't available.

Abstract: Low-rank matrix decompositions can uncover patterns and structure in data and have a number of different applications across many disciplines. Extensions to "joint" low-rank decompositions have been proposed to link datasets from different modalities. While these methods enable the discovery of common patterns across modalities, they require that all the multimodal data share one or more dimensions. We propose a new analysis method, PathFinder, that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily all share a dimension. The key insight is that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices do share some dimension, and that there are one or more paths that link across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This enables the joint estimation of common patterns across different modalities, species, or scales, where a one-to-one mapping across all data along some dimension is not necessarily available. We show that PathFinder is a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases. It can be used to discover common patterns across disparate datasets and to make predictions for missing data or modalities.

</details>


### [258] [LLM-based Framework for Generating and Verifying Parallel DEVS Statecharts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14956)
*Vamsi Krishna Vasa,Hessam S. Sarjoughian,Edward J. Yellig*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Agentic PDEVS-LLM framework assists modelers in generating and verifying PDEVS statecharts for atomic models through iterative correction and verification of plausible facts against behavioral conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Models require accurate representation of system dynamics and verifiability. Developing models needs both modeling/simulation expertise and domain knowledge. The paper aims to help human modelers generate and verify PDEVS statecharts more effectively.

Method: Proposes an agentic PDEVS-LLM framework that: 1) generates plausible facts from system description prompts, 2) uses controlled-correction mechanism to verify logical consistency of facts, 3) generates behavioral conditions from prompts, 4) verifies facts against conditions using propositional logic entailment, 5) generates modification prompts to reduce errors, and 6) converts statecharts to Timed Automata for deadlock and reachability verification.

Result: The verification mechanism shows substantial improvement in logical consistency of generated statecharts. A basic correctness metric quantifies completeness/accuracy of behavioral traits. Example systems demonstrate LLM capabilities and limitations.

Conclusion: The agentic PDEVS-LLM framework successfully assists modelers in iterative generation and verification of PDEVS statecharts, improving logical consistency and enabling human-in-the-loop refinement with verification feedback.

Abstract: The development of models demands sound modeling and simulation knowledge as well as domain knowledge. Every model should accurately represent a system's dynamics and be verifiable. Toward this objective, this research introduces an agentic PDEVS-LLM framework to assist human modelers in generating and verifying PDEVS statecharts for behavior modeling of atomic Parallel Discrete Event System Specification (PDEVS) models. The framework supports (re)generating plausible facts from a system description prompt using the agentic LLM used for generating plausible facts. Inconsistencies in plausible facts lead to incorrect PDEVS statecharts having logical structure and behavioral inaccuracies. A controlled-correction mechanism is developed to verify the logical consistency of the plausible facts. The agentic LLM is used to generate key behavioral conditions from the system description prompt. The plausible facts are then verified against the behavioral conditions using propositional logic entailment for a finite number of times. The verification results enable the generation of modification prompts that can reduce errors in generated plausible facts, resulting in more accurate PDEVS statecharts. To verify a statechart's logical correctness, its Timed Automata counterpart is manually created and verified for deadlock and reachability properties. The human modeler may regenerate plausible facts and PDEVS statecharts iteratively and incrementally. A basic correctness metric is introduced to quantify the completeness and accuracy of the expected behavioral traits of the PDEVS statechart models. A collection of example systems with varying levels of complexity is developed to demonstrate the capabilities and limitations of LLMs. The evaluation of the proposed verification mechanism shows a substantial improvement in the logical consistency of generated statecharts.

</details>


### [259] [Command-Space Counterfactual Explanations for Pareto-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14963)
*Joanikij Chulev,Hendrik Baier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CF-ZOO generates counterfactual explanations for Pareto Conditioned Networks by finding minimally changed return commands that would cause a policy to choose different actions, explaining RL behavior in terms of user preference trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pareto Conditioned Networks learn multi-objective RL behaviors but their decision-making process from command and state to action remains opaque. There's a need for explainable AI methods that can reveal why certain actions were chosen and what would need to change in user preferences for different decisions.

Method: The authors propose CF-ZOO, which formulates PCN explanations as return-command interventions using a return-only variant of PCNs. They adapt adversarial ML methods to RL explanations and introduce a boundary-seeded directional search that improves over purely local optimization in the command-action landscape.

Result: The approach generates actionable counterfactual explanations expressed in user preference terms, allowing statements like "If your trade-off had shifted slightly towards X, the agent would have chosen Y." The method provides interpretable insights into PCN decision-making.

Conclusion: CF-ZOO enables transparent explanation of multi-objective RL policies by finding minimal changes to desired return commands that would lead to different actions, making RL behavior understandable in terms of user preference trade-offs.

Abstract: Pareto Conditioned Networks learn multiple multi-objective reinforcement learning behaviours by conditioning a single policy on a desired return command. However, the local mapping from command and state to action remains opaque. We propose command-space counterfactual explanations for PCNs: given a fixed state, original command, and foil action, we search, in a black-box setting, for a minimally changed desired-return command under which the same trained policy would choose the foil. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate PCN explanations as return-command interventions, using a return-only PCN variant that avoids the added ambiguity of horizon-conditioning. Second, we adapt adversarial machine learning methods to reinforcement-learning explanations. Third, we introduce a boundary-seeded directional search that improves over purely local optimization in the command-action landscape, resulting in our proposed approach CF-ZOO. The resulting explanations are actionable and intuitively expressed in the user's own preferences: "If your trade-off had shifted slightly towards X, the agent would have chosen Y."

</details>


### [260] [A Physiology-Informed Digital Twin Framework for Simulating Liver Health Progression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14969)
*Sumaiya Afroz Mila,Sandip Ray*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HEPATWIN is a physiology-informed digital twin of the human liver that simulates liver function and disease progression using mechanistic models and patient-specific inputs to generate clinically observable biomarker trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create a personalized, non-invasive tool for liver health monitoring that goes beyond purely data-driven approaches by incorporating mechanistic physiology to simulate disease progression over time.

Method: Integrated key hepatic processes (carbohydrate, lipid, protein metabolism, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, detoxification) in a systems-level framework with patient-specific inputs. Introduced stage-transition-driven calibration mechanism to align with population-level biomarker distributions across disease stages.

Result: HEPATWIN produces longitudinal biomarker estimates within clinically acceptable ranges and forecasts trajectories over multi-year horizons. Simulated biomarkers retain sufficient clinical signal for competitive NASH detection performance compared to models using ground-truth laboratory data.

Conclusion: Physiology-informed digital twins show strong potential for personalized, non-invasive diagnosis and prediction of organ health, particularly for liver health monitoring and disease progression tracking.

Abstract: We present a physiology-informed digital twin of the human liver designed for longitudinal simulation of liver function and early-stage disease progression. The model, referred to as HEPATWIN, integrates key hepatic processes, including carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, and detoxification, within a unified systems-level framework to generate clinically observable biomarker trajectories. Unlike purely data-driven approaches, HEPATWIN incorporates mechanistic representations of liver physiology and patient-specific inputs such as diet, activity, and baseline biomarkers to simulate disease evolution over time. To ensure consistency with clinical progression patterns, we introduce a stage-transition-driven calibration mechanism that aligns simulated outputs with population-level biomarker distributions across disease stages, including NAFLD, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Validation using the NIDDK NAFLD dataset demonstrates that HEPATWIN produces longitudinal biomarker estimates within clinically acceptable ranges and can forecast trajectories over multi-year horizons. Furthermore, simulated biomarkers retain sufficient clinical signal to support downstream NASH detection with competitive performance relative to models using ground-truth laboratory data. These results highlight the potential of physiology-informed digital twins for personalized, non-invasive diagnosis and prediction of organ health in general and liver health monitoring in particular.

</details>


### [261] [Do Geometry-Aware Positional Encodings Help Transformers in Spatial Imperfect-Information Games?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14982)
*Wenji Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HexRoPE, a hexagonal relative positional encoding, improves belief tracking and data-efficient imitation in transformers for spatial imperfect-information games, but these representation gains don't translate to better overall gameplay performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers need to represent map geometry while tracking hidden entities in spatial imperfect-information games. The paper investigates whether geometry-aware positional encodings (without claiming a new encoding) can improve these capabilities.

Method: Constructed a four-level benchmark on a hexagonal naval pursuit game: 1) controlled geometry and topology probes, 2) exact-Bayes hidden-target tracking task, 3) offline policy imitation at 1k and 10k games, and 4) 7,200 fixed-seed games against three legacy opponents. Tested HexRoPE across matched Transformer backbones compared to no positional encoding and rectangular relative bias.

Result: HexRoPE significantly reduces exact-belief posterior cross-entropy (0.278-0.329 improvement), improves policy action accuracy at 1k games (4.63pp over no encoding, 2.05pp over rectangular bias), but gains shrink at 10k games. However, HexRoPE doesn't improve aggregate gameplay win rate (-1.56pp effect over no encoding). Rectangular bias fails when extrapolating from radius 3 to 4.

Conclusion: Geometric inductive bias improves belief estimation and data-efficient imitation learning in transformers for spatial games, but these representation gains don't automatically produce stronger closed-loop gameplay performance.

Abstract: Transformers applied to spatial imperfect-information games must represent map geometry while tracking hidden entities through time. We ask whether geometry-aware positional encodings improve these capabilities, without claiming a new positional encoding. We construct a four-level benchmark on a hexagonal naval pursuit game: controlled geometry and topology probes, an exact-Bayes hidden-target tracking task, offline policy imitation at 1k and 10k games, and 7,200 fixed-seed games against three legacy opponents. Across matched Transformer backbones, HexRoPE reduces exact-belief posterior cross-entropy relative to no positional encoding by 0.278 on D6-transformed test orbits and 0.329 on a larger map; both hierarchical-bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero, and both Holm-adjusted p-values are below 0.001. At 1k games, HexRoPE improves policy action accuracy by 4.63 percentage points over no encoding and 2.05 points over rectangular relative bias; the gains shrink to 1.55 and 0.41 points at 10k games. However, HexRoPE does not improve aggregate gameplay win rate: its paired effect over no encoding is -1.56 percentage points (95% CI [-4.50, 1.17]). Rectangular relative bias is strongest on D6 belief consistency but fails sharply when extrapolating from radius 3 to radius 4, while graph bias provides only a small blocked-edge gain. The results show that geometric inductive bias improves belief estimation and data-efficient imitation, but those representation gains do not automatically produce stronger closed-loop play.

</details>


### [262] [Lipschitz Bandits with Arbitrary Feedback Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15036)
*Yuhao Liu,Yu Chen,Longbo Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Lipschitz bandits with arbitrary feedback delays: new algorithms for both stochastic and adversarial settings achieve $\tilde{O}(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}+\sqrt{D})$ regret, matching delay-free bounds plus $\sqrt{D}$ delay penalty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Lipschitz bandits assume immediate feedback, but real-world scenarios often involve delays. The paper aims to extend Lipschitz bandits to handle arbitrary feedback delays in both stochastic and adversarial reward settings.

Method: For stochastic rewards: propose an elimination-based algorithm. For adversarial rewards: propose an EXP3-based algorithm. Both algorithms handle arbitrary feedback delays.

Result: Achieve regret bound $\tilde{O}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}+\sqrt{D}\right)$ for both settings, where $T$ is time horizon, $D$ is total delay, and $d_z$ is zooming dimension (defined differently for each setting).

Conclusion: The algorithms match existing delay-free regret guarantees for Lipschitz bandits while quantifying the additional $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{D})$ cost of feedback delays. The work successfully extends Lipschitz bandits to delayed feedback scenarios.

Abstract: The Lipschitz bandit problem extends the traditional multi-armed bandit framework to continuous action spaces by assuming that the reward functions satisfy a Lipschitz condition. This work investigates Lipschitz bandits under arbitrary feedback delays, where reward signals are not received immediately upon taking an action but after an arbitrarily chosen delay. We consider both stochastic and adversarial reward settings, proposing an elimination-based algorithm and an EXP3-based algorithm, respectively. For both settings, our algorithms achieve a regret bound of $\tilde{O}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}+\sqrt{D}\right)$ over a time horizon $T$ with total delay $D$, where the main difference between settings lies in the definition of the zooming dimension $d_z$. Our bounds match existing delay-free regret guarantees for Lipschitz bandits and characterize the additional $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{D})$ impact introduced by feedback delays.

</details>


### [263] [Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15046)
*Amogh Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper critiques current practices for claiming model equivalence after compression, showing that traditional accuracy deltas mask significant per-item churn, and proposes a rigorous paired equivalence testing framework with specific reporting standards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current claims of model equivalence after compression rely on minor accuracy deltas, which can mask significant disagreement at the per-item level. The paper argues that these practices lack rigor and transparency, as researchers typically don't specify equivalence margins, release per-item outputs, or account for the substantial churn that occurs even when models appear identical at the aggregate level.

Method: The authors conducted a large-scale analysis of 1,707 paired model-by-task cells from public evaluation data (models ranging from 1.3B to 405B parameters). They performed a preregistered audit of 17 equivalence claims across three publication types, developed a paired equivalence testing framework with declared margins, and ran controlled experiments comparing GPTQ and AWQ compression methods across five random seeds.

Result: Analysis revealed churn is roughly 5x the net accuracy delta, with models showing identical aggregate scores still disagreeing on individual items. Only 1 of 17 equivalence claims provided sufficient evidence for verification. Controlled experiments showed that changing calibration draws was sufficient to reverse method ordering in 5 out of 8 cases. Most claims lacked numerical equivalence margins and didn't release task-matched per-item outputs.

Conclusion: The paper proposes a new reporting standard requiring: declared equivalence margins, paired statistical testing, reporting churn alongside net delta, citing achieved sample size, and releasing per-item outputs. This framework applies to any comparison between similar models and aims to bring rigor to equivalence claims, with all data, protocols, and code released for transparency.

Abstract: A fraction of a point of benchmark accuracy is the usual evidence that a compressed model is equivalent to its original. That quantity is least informative when two models are most alike: a net delta is what survives cancellation between opposing per-item changes, and cancellation is most complete in the regime equivalence claims occupy. Across an atlas of 1,707 paired model-by-task cells mined from public per-item evaluation dumps (1.3B-405B), churn runs roughly five times the net accuracy delta, and cells scoring identically to their baseline still disagree on individual items. In a preregistered audit of 17 equivalence claims from three registered frames (method papers, model cards, vendor documentation), 16 are eligible. None states a prospective numerical equivalence margin, and none releases task-matched per-item outputs, though 3 release outputs for other tasks only; 5 report too little to assess numerically, so a reader cannot check them at any sample size. We audit evidential sufficiency, not truth: no claim is called false. We supply the missing instrument: paired equivalence testing at a declared margin, with certification tables giving the items an evaluation needs, computed from disagreement observed under compression, not from independent-binomial variance. A controlled experiment pairs GPTQ and AWQ on byte-identical calibration samples across five seeds. Under the frozen eight-cell decision rule H3 is supported: changing the calibration draw was sufficient to reverse the observed method ordering in 5 of 8 confirmatory cells. The reporting standard we propose is five lines: declare a margin, run the paired test, report churn beside net delta, cite the sample size you met, release per-item outputs. It applies to any comparison between two models alike enough to be worth comparing. All per-item outputs, protocols and code are released.

</details>


### [264] [Online Convex Optimization with Dueling Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15050)
*Yiyang Lu,Hareshkumar Jadav,Mohammad Pedramfar,Ranveer Singh,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First-order methods for online convex optimization with dueling feedback achieve sublinear regret across various function classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dueling feedback (pairwise comparison) is well-studied in discrete/stochastic settings, but adversarial convex optimization with this feedback type was unexplored, creating a gap in understanding online learning with limited feedback.

Method: Proposes a reduction that converts dueling feedback into approximate gradients, enabling use of standard first-order optimization methods. The reduction allows regret guarantees to transfer from full-gradient settings to dueling feedback settings.

Result: Achieves O(T^{3/4}) static, adaptive, and dynamic regret in general convex setting; improved rates of O(T^{2/3}) for smooth objectives and O(√(T log T)) for strongly convex functions under additional structure.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that first-order methods can effectively handle dueling feedback in adversarial convex optimization, establishing fundamental regret bounds and showing improved rates with additional structure on objective functions.

Abstract: We study online convex optimization with dueling (pairwise comparison) feedback, where the learner observes only a binary preference between two queried points. While dueling feedback is well understood in discrete or stochastic settings, the adversarial convex setting has remained unexplored. We propose a simple reduction that converts dueling feedback into approximate gradients, enabling the use of standard first-order methods. We show that regret guarantees transfer under this reduction, yielding the first results for this setting, including $\mathcal{O}(T^{3/4})$ static, adaptive, and dynamic regret. Under additional structure, we obtain improved rates of $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ for smooth objectives and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \log T})$ for strongly convex functions.

</details>


### [265] [A Unified Mamba--MoE Surrogate for Closed-Loop Simulation and Measurement-Window Forecasting of Inverter Transients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15051)
*Haoguang Wang,Huy Hoang Le,Akhila Kandivalasa,Christian Moya,Marcos Netto,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Mamba-MoE surrogate model for inverter transient dynamics that performs both closed-loop simulation and forecasting using a single architecture with task conditioning, achieving comparable accuracy to specialist models with fewer parameters and providing reliable prediction intervals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for efficient modeling of inverter-based resource transient dynamics that can handle both closed-loop simulation and measurement-window forecasting tasks without requiring separate specialized models, while providing uncertainty quantification.

Method: Proposes a unified Mamba architecture with mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing and task conditioning. Uses a single Mamba backbone with MoE routing to handle both tasks, replacing separate specialists. Incorporates task-matched objectives for each prediction form and an adaptive conformal layer for prediction intervals.

Result: The unified model achieves same low-error regime as specialist Mamba pair while using 13% fewer parameters. Prediction intervals achieve 94-96% empirical mean marginal coverage. Outperforms shared Mamba backbone without expert routing for transient dynamics. Controller hardware-in-the-loop validation shows reduced forecasting error with limited adaptation data.

Conclusion: The Mamba-MoE surrogate model successfully unifies two prediction tasks for inverter transient dynamics, providing efficiency (fewer parameters), accuracy comparable to specialists, reliable uncertainty quantification, and better performance than non-expert-routed alternatives, validated by hardware-in-the-loop simulations.

Abstract: This paper proposes a Mamba surrogate model with mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing to represent the transient dynamics of inverter-based resources. A Mamba surrogate model is a predictive machine learning model built on the Mamba architecture. MoE routing uses a router network to assign data-dependent weights to specialized subnetworks (experts). The resulting Mamba--MoE surrogate can perform two tasks: (i) closed-loop simulation and (ii) measurement-window forecasting of inverter transients. A single Mamba backbone with task conditioning and expert routing serves both tasks, replacing two separate specialists. Task-matched objectives fit each prediction form, and an adaptive conformal layer provides prediction intervals for both tasks. For the considered grid-following inverter, the unified surrogate model remains in the same low-error regime as a Mamba specialist pair while using 13% fewer parameters. The prediction intervals achieve 94--96% empirical mean marginal coverage across the two tasks. For transient dynamics---that is, beyond the vicinity of an equilibrium point---our surrogate model with MoE routing yields lower errors across all outputs in both tasks compared to a shared Mamba backbone without expert routing. A controller hardware-in-the-loop simulation validates our results and shows that adapting only the shared output head with limited measured data reduces held-out forecasting error.

</details>


### [266] [GATTA: Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15084)
*Zsombor Bánfi,András Gézsi,András Formanek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GATTA improves graph active learning by using test-time augmentation with consistency filtering to enhance uncertainty estimation, making simple methods competitive with complex approaches at lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test-time augmentation has been effective in computer vision but remains unexplored for graph-structured data. Current active learning methods for graphs rely on complex acquisition functions that are computationally expensive, while simple uncertainty-based methods underperform. There's a need for efficient uncertainty estimation in graph active learning that can leverage data augmentation while preserving label integrity.

Method: GATTA framework applies test-time augmentation to graph data by generating multiple augmented views of test samples and aggregating predictions across these views. It includes a consistency-based filtering mechanism to discard unreliable augmented views that don't preserve label integrity. The system is evaluated across various graph datasets, GNN architectures, and acquisition strategies.

Result: Simple uncertainty-based methods (Entropy and Least Confidence) benefit most from TTA, achieving performance competitive with sophisticated approaches. GATTA generalizes across architectures, outperforms MC Dropout, and scales efficiently with ensemble and graph sizes. Analysis provides guidelines on augmentation types, strengths, and filtering strategies.

Conclusion: Augmenting simple methods with test-time augmentation offers a more efficient path to strong active learning performance than engineering complex acquisition functions, enabling competitive results with lower computational overhead and reduced implementation complexity.

Abstract: Test-time augmentation (TTA) has proven effective for improving model robustness and uncertainty estimation in computer vision, yet its application to graph-structured data remains largely unexplored. We introduce GATTA (Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation), a framework for enhancing active learning by aggregating predictions across multiple augmented views to produce more reliable uncertainty estimates. To address the challenge of label-preserving graph augmentations, GATTA incorporates a consistency-based filtering mechanism that discards augmented views yielding unreliable predictions. We systematically evaluate GATTA across multiple graph datasets, GNN architectures, and acquisition strategies. Our results show that simple uncertainty-based methods, such as Entropy and Least Confidence, benefit most from TTA, achieving performance competitive with more sophisticated and computationally expensive approaches. GATTA generalizes across architectures, outperforms model-side ensemble methods such as MC Dropout. We further show that GATTA scales efficiently with both ensemble size and graph size. Extensive analysis of augmentation types, strengths, and filtering strategies provides practical guidelines for effective deployment. Our findings demonstrate that augmenting simple methods with TTA offers a more efficient path to strong active learning performance than engineering complex acquisition functions, enabling practitioners to achieve competitive results with lower computational overhead and reduced implementation complexity.

</details>


### [267] [EMASAM: a Computationally Efficient Sharpness-Aware Minimization via EMA-Guided Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15105)
*Tanapat Ratchatorn,Masayuki Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EMASAM is a computationally efficient variant of SAM that uses EMA shadow model discrepancy instead of gradient computations for perturbation, reducing computational cost while maintaining generalization benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SAM suffers from twice the computational cost due to extra gradient computation in the perturbation step, which limits its practical efficiency despite promising generalization performance.

Method: EMASAM defines perturbation direction based on the discrepancy between the main model and the EMA shadow model, moving away from stable average positions toward less stable areas, eliminating the need for extra backpropagation.

Result: Experiments confirm EMASAM's efficiency and robustness, showing it eliminates the computational overhead of SAM while preserving its generalization ability and mitigating gradient-induced instability.

Conclusion: EMASAM provides a computationally efficient alternative to SAM that maintains generalization benefits through EMA-based perturbations instead of gradient-based worst-case scenario perturbations.

Abstract: Recent progress in optimization research has highlighted the sharpness of the loss landscape as a key factor in narrowing the generalization gap. Motivated by this insight, Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) was proposed as a training strategy that enhances generalization. Despite the promising performance, SAM suffers from its twice computational cost due to its core algorithm requiring an extra gradient computation during the perturbation step. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Exponential Moving Average Sharpness-Aware Minimization (EMASAM), a computationally efficient variant of SAM. EMASAM does not require the loss gradient in the perturbation step. Instead, EMASAM defines the perturbation direction based on the discrepancy between the main model and the EMA shadow model. This perturbation travels away from the stable average position toward the less stable area, acting as a softer yet cheaper alternative to SAM's worst-case scenario perturbation. Moreover, since EMASAM's perturbation does not rely on noisy mini-batch gradients, it mitigates the gradient-induced instability inherent in SAM. Hence, EMASAM eliminates the need for an extra backpropagation while also preserving the generalization ability of the SAM-style training. Several experiments have been performed and confirm the efficiency and robustness of our method.

</details>


### [268] [Global Federated Learning Strategies for Building Efficient Personalized Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15107)
*Seongyoon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents methods for efficient personalized federated learning by addressing representation collapse, balancing local alignment with global knowledge preservation, and redefining the role of global initialization under data heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning suffers from performance degradation in both global and personalized models due to data heterogeneity across users, necessitating new approaches that can maintain global knowledge while achieving effective personalization.
