By mitigating spurious homophilic correlations and embracing the heterogeneity of normal patterns, RagGAD identifies anomalies as low-density regions within a structure-aware distribution space. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RagGAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [342] [Group ICA 2.0: Closing the Gap Between Subjects and Group Latent Decomposition with Copula-Linked Group ICA (CoLiG-ICA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16029)
*Oktay Agcaoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoLiG-ICA is a new Group ICA method that extends beyond conventional group-level analysis to jointly estimate template-linked, cohort-only, and subject-only brain networks using copula modeling and deep learning, better capturing individual variability in fMRI data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional Group ICA (gICA) primarily identifies components shared across all subjects, which limits recovery of networks present only in individuals or subject subsets. This reduces sensitivity to intersubject heterogeneity, particularly problematic in clinical neuroimaging where individual differences matter.

Method: CoLiG-ICA combines ICA-based spatial decomposition, copula-based dependence modeling, and deep learning optimization within the Group ICA 2.0 framework. It jointly estimates three types of networks: template-linked (shared with reference), cohort-only (shared within cohort), and subject-only (individual-specific) in a unified model.

Result: On UCLA-CNP resting-state fMRI data, CoLiG-ICA showed significantly lower intercomponent spatial dependence (improved independence) and reduced motion-related variance in template-linked components compared to MOO-ICAR. In schizophrenia-only analysis, it identified three additional resting-state networks beyond the 53 template-linked NeuroMark components.

Conclusion: CoLiG-ICA successfully addresses limitations of conventional gICA by capturing individual variability beyond shared group priors while maintaining interpretability, making it particularly valuable for clinical neuroimaging studies where intersubject heterogeneity is important.

Abstract: Group Independent Component Analysis (gICA) is widely used to decompose high-dimensional functional MRI data into interpretable brain networks. However, conventional gICA primarily identifies components shared across subjects. This group-level assumption can limit the recovery of networks present only in individuals or subject subsets, reducing sensitivity to intersubject heterogeneity in clinical neuroimaging datasets. We introduce Copula-Linked Group ICA (CoLiG-ICA), an algorithm in the Group ICA 2.0 framework that jointly estimates template-linked, cohort-only, and subject-only brain networks within a unified model. CoLiG-ICA combines ICA-based spatial decomposition, copula-based dependence modeling, and deep learning optimization to preserve the consistency and interpretability of template-constrained ICA while enabling free components beyond the reference networks. By linking subject decompositions to shared templates and jointly estimating cohort-only and subject-only sources, CoLiG-ICA represents individual variability not captured by conventional group priors. We evaluate CoLiG-ICA using resting-state fMRI data from the UCLA-CNP dataset and compare it with conventional constrained ICA in estimating template-linked components, discovering additional free components, improving component independence, and capturing subject-level variability beyond the shared group prior. Compared with MOO-ICAR, CoLiG-ICA showed significantly lower intercomponent spatial dependence, indicating improved subject-level component independence, and significantly reduced motion-related variance in the template-linked components. Additionally, in a schizophrenia-only group analysis, CoLiG-ICA identified three additional resting-state networks beyond the 53 template-linked NeuroMark components: one sensorimotor and two visual networks.

</details>


### [343] [AdROD: HyperNetwork-based Adversarially Robust Object Detection for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16031)
*Yuting Wu,Dongfang Guo,Xiangzhong Luo,Qun Song,Rui Tan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AdROD is an embedded stochastic ensemble defense that uses lightweight hypernetworks to generate diverse object detectors per frame, making it hard for attackers to adapt, with two serving modes balancing robustness and runtime overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camera-based object detectors are vulnerable to physical adversarial attacks that suppress detections. Existing defenses like adversarial training and input purification often overfit to specific attack patterns and fail against adaptive adversaries, highlighting the need for more robust and generalizable protection.

Method: AdROD employs low-rank HyperNetworks (requiring only 1.6% of standard HyperNetwork parameters) to generate diverse object detectors at a per-frame rate. It incorporates a novel functional diversity mechanism that couples stochastic weight updates with unique input-space transformations. The system has two serving modes: AdROD-I (continuous protection mode) that leverages inter-detector disagreement to recover compromised detections, and AdROD-II (on-demand mode) triggered by kinematic discontinuities in object tracking.

Result: AdROD outperforms five baseline defenses and exhibits superior generalizability compared to adversarial-training baselines. It maintains real-time performance for safely stopping vehicles at stop signs instrumented with adversarial patches. Comprehensive evaluation includes synthetic benchmarks, physically deployed adversarial patches, and end-to-end safety tests in the OpenCDA co-simulator.

Conclusion: AdROD provides an effective embedded defense against physical adversarial attacks on object detectors in autonomous driving, offering both continuous protection and on-demand modes that balance robustness with computational overhead while maintaining real-time safety performance.

Abstract: Camera-based object detectors are vulnerable to physical adversarial attacks designed to suppress detections. While adversarial training and input purification offer some protection, they often overfit to specific attack distributions and fail on adaptive adversaries. This paper presents AdROD, an embedded, stochastic ensemble defense software designed for autonomous driving. AdROD employs {\em low-rank HyperNetworks}, which require only 1.6\% of the parameter footprint of standard HyperNetworks, to generate diverse detectors at a per-frame rate, making it impractical for attackers to obtain the deployed detectors in time. To further improve adversarial robustness, AdROD incorporates a novel \emph{functional diversity} mechanism, which couples stochastic weight updates with unique input-space transformations. We design two serving modes of AdROD that strike different trade-offs between robustness and runtime overhead: AdROD-I, a continuous protection mode for maximum resilience that leverages inter-detector disagreement to recover compromised detections, and AdROD-II, an on-demand mode triggered by kinematic discontinuities in object tracking. Through comprehensive evaluation with synthetic benchmarks, physically deployed adversarial patches, and end-to-end safety tests in the OpenCDA co-simulator, AdROD outperforms five baseline defenses and exhibits superior generalizability compared with the evaluated adversarial-training baselines, while maintaining real-time performance for safely stopping the vehicle at a stop sign instrumented with adversarial patches.

</details>


### [344] [NICE: Scale-Stable Perturbations for Graph Neural Network Explanations via Noise Corruption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16038)
*Ziluowen Luo,Jun Yin,Ruochen Liu,Ming Cheng,Shirui Pan,Chengqi Zhang,Senzhang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NICE introduces Noise Corruption as a scale-stable alternative to Element-wise Masking for GNN explanation, addressing Scale Drift issues in perturbation-based explainers and improving faithfulness through boundary-based attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Perturb-Query GNN explainers using Element-wise Masking introduce substantial distribution shift that undermines explanation reliability. The authors identify that Element-wise Masking causes deterministic scale contraction (Scale Drift) across message-passing layers, conflating information corruption with propagation scale deviations.

Method: Proposes Noise Corruption (NC) as scale-stable alternative to Element-wise Masking, which perturbs messages through matched-norm random-direction corruption while preserving expected squared message norm. Builds NICE framework that learns Stochastic Restoration Boundary (SRB) under NC-induced uncertainty, balancing prediction restoration with compactness. Uses Boundary-Integrated Gradient (BIG) to convert boundary into edge attributions by accumulating edge contributions along restoration path.

Result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate stronger explanation performance and model faithfulness compared to existing methods. Confirms that Noise Corruption substantially reduces Scale Drift induced by masking-based perturbations.

Conclusion: Addressing perturbation-induced Scale Drift through Noise Corruption provides more reliable and faithful GNN explanations, improving upon current perturbation-based explainers by properly separating information corruption from propagation scale effects.

Abstract: Post-hoc Graph Neural Network (GNN) explainers commonly follow a Perturb-Query paradigm, inferring the importance of graph elements based on queried predictions to perturbed inputs. However, such perturbations often introduce substantial distribution shift, undermining the reliability of the queried predictions used to derive explanations. While existing efforts mainly improve perturbed graphs or stabilize model predictions on them, we revisit the perturbation mechanism itself. We show that the widely used Element-wise Masking(EM) suppresses edge-induced messages toward zero, causing deterministic scale contraction that accumulates across message-passing layers, a phenomenon we term Scale Drift. Consequently, prediction changes under EM may conflate information corruption with deviations in propagation scale. As a scale-stable alternative to EM, we introduce Noise Corruption (NC), which perturbs each message through matched-norm random-direction corruption while preserving the expected squared message norm. Building on NC, we propose NICE, a Noise Corruption-based explanation framework, which learns a Stochastic Restoration Boundary (SRB) under NC-induced uncertainty, balancing target-prediction restoration against compactness. Furthermore, Boundary-Integrated Gradient (BIG) converts this boundary into edge attributions by accumulating each edge's contribution to reducing restoration risk along the restoration path. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate stronger explanation performance and model faithfulness while confirming that NC substantially reduces the Scale Drift induced by masking.

</details>


### [345] [OceanLight: Efficient Global Ocean Forecasting via Geometry-Adaptive Unstructured Mesh Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16070)
*Wei Wu,Xiang Wang,Hongze Leng,Qingye Min,Junxing Zhu,Junqiang Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OceanLight is an efficient global ocean forecasting framework that uses geometry-adaptive unstructured mesh tokenization with a graph neural network, achieving better accuracy with 62% less GPU memory and 70% fewer FLOPs than structured-grid models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based ocean forecasting models are computationally prohibitive, while existing deep learning approaches use structured-grid architectures that waste computation on land cells and enforce uniform resolution across dynamically heterogeneous ocean regions, regardless of local flow complexity.

Method: Combines geometry-adaptive unstructured mesh tokenization with a graph neural network (GNN) backbone, using unstructured mesh representation to avoid unnecessary computation on land cells and enable adaptive resolution.

Result: Achieves superior pointwise forecast accuracy and kinetic energy spectral fidelity compared to operational numerical analyses and state-of-the-art AI models, with best-in-class geostrophic balance consistency. Also demonstrates reliable mesoscale eddy representation. Delivers 62% reduction in GPU memory consumption and 70% reduction in FLOPs relative to structured-grid baselines.

Conclusion: OceanLight's unstructured mesh representation establishes a generalizable paradigm for scalable data-driven oceanography, offering efficient and accurate global ocean forecasting capabilities that surpass existing approaches.

Abstract: Reliable global ocean forecasting is critical for climate monitoring, marine navigation, and extreme event early warning. Physics-based ocean forecasting models impose prohibitive computational costs, while existing deep learning approaches predominantly rely on structured-grid architectures, incurring unnecessary computation on masked land cells and enforcing uniform resolution across dynamically heterogeneous ocean regions regardless of local flow complexity. Here we present OceanLight, an efficient global ocean forecasting framework innovatively combining geometry-adaptive unstructured mesh tokenization with a graph neural network (GNN) backbone. OceanLight achieves pointwise forecast accuracy and kinetic energy spectral fidelity exceeding both operational numerical analyses and state-of-the-art AI-based models, while surpassing all AI-based ocean models in geostrophic balance consistency. Furthermore, OceanLight demonstrates reliable mesoscale eddy representation, capturing coherent ocean structures beyond pointwise statistical optimization. These capabilities are delivered with a 62% reduction in GPU memory consumption and 70\% reduction in FLOPs relative to structured-grid baselines. Our unstructured mesh representation establishes a generalizable paradigm for scalable data-driven oceanography.

</details>


### [346] [Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072)
*Yixuan Wang,Yifei Chen,Haichao Zhang,Haozheng Luo,Xander Wu,Jie Ni,Yun Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos,Yijiang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SA-MRPO introduces saturation-aware advantage reweighting for multi-reward RL in language models, dynamically allocating optimization effort to under-optimized objectives instead of using fixed weighted sums.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-reward RL methods for language models use fixed weighted sums before group-wise standardization, causing two problems: different reward profiles can get identical advantages, and objectives continue to be optimized with fixed weights regardless of saturation levels, wasting gradient budget on already-solved objectives.

Method: SA-MRPO standardizes each reward objective independently and adaptively discounts each objective's contribution based on batch-level estimates of objective saturation. This dynamic reallocation focuses optimization effort on under-optimized objectives while maintaining performance on well-satisfied ones, and can even reverse update signs rather than just rescale magnitudes.

Result: SA-MRPO improves harder correctness objectives over GDPO in 12 of 15 mathematical reasoning benchmarks (up to 5% on AIME24), improves accuracy on all five adaptive reasoning benchmarks (average 3.8%, up to 9.2% on AMC23), and improves pass rate on coding benchmarks by up to 2.3%, while maintaining easier objectives near their satisfied levels.

Conclusion: Saturation-aware advantage reweighting (SA-MRPO) effectively addresses fundamental limitations of fixed-weight multi-reward RL, dynamically reallocating optimization effort to maximize overall performance by focusing on objectives with greater remaining improvement potential.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with group-relative advantages has become the de facto standard for post-training language model reasoners. However, when optimizing multiple reward objectives, existing methods typically scalarize the reward vector with a fixed weighted sum before group-wise standardization. We show that this design leads to two fundamental problems: rollouts with distinct reward profiles can receive identical advantages, and all objectives are optimized with fixed relative weights regardless of their current level of saturation. As a result, training continues to allocate gradient budget to already-solved objectives instead of focusing on those with greater remaining headroom. We introduce \textbf{Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization} (SA-MRPO), which standardizes each reward objective independently and adaptively discounts its contribution according to a batch-level estimate of objective saturation. This dynamically reallocates optimization effort toward under-optimized objectives while empirically maintaining performance on those that are already well satisfied. We further show that saturation-aware reweighting can reverse the sign of an update, rather than merely rescale its magnitude. Across mathematical reasoning with two- and three-objective reward combinations, SA-MRPO improves the harder correctness objective over GDPO in 12 of 15 benchmark comparisons, with gains of up to $5\%$ on AIME24. On adaptive reasoning it improves accuracy on all five benchmarks, by $3.8\%$ on average and up to $9.2 \%$ on AMC23, and on coding benchmarks it improves pass rate by up to $2.3\%$, while in all settings maintaining the easier objectives near their already satisfied levels.

</details>


### [347] [DeepOHeat-v2: Self-Improving Operator Learning for Fast and Trustworthy Thermal Optimization in 3D-IC Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16080)
*Xinling Yu,Yixing Li,Ziyue Liu,Xin Ai,Zhiyu Zeng,Hai Li,Zheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeepOHeat-v2 enables thermal-aware optimization of high-contrast multi-die 3D ICs using operator-learning surrogates with discretized physics loss and self-improving framework, achieving 56× speedup over traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thermal optimization of multi-die 3D integrated circuits requires solving heat equations for many designs, which is computationally expensive. While operator-learning surrogates (like DeepOHeat-v1) can replace these solves with fast forward passes, they fail on high-contrast multi-die stacks due to discontinuous conductivities and ill-conditioning problems.

Method: 1) Use discretized physics loss that handles material interface discontinuities natively. 2) Employ energy form to reduce loss-Hessian conditioning from κ² to κ. 3) Apply matrix-preconditioned optimizer to reduce temperature errors. 4) Implement self-improving framework with hotspot trust gate that sends flagged placements to reference solver and incrementally retrains surrogate on refined solutions.

Result: On multi-die benchmark: mean peak temperature error reduced from over 30K to 0.55K; surrogate-true peak gap on returned design fell from 1.12K to 0.11K; performance matches solve-at-every-step optimizer while running 56× faster.

Conclusion: DeepOHeat-v2 successfully overcomes limitations of previous operator-learning surrogates for high-contrast multi-die 3D ICs, combining discretized physics loss with self-improving framework to achieve both accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling practical thermal-aware optimization.

Abstract: Thermal-aware optimization of multi-die 3D integrated circuits evaluates many designs, each a costly heat-equation solve. Operator-learning surrogates replace this solve with a fast forward pass, ideally trained from physics alone, without labeled data. DeepOHeat-v1 made such surrogates fast and trustworthy, but only on low-contrast geometries. High-contrast multi-die stacks break it in two ways: discontinuous conductivities make the continuous physics loss ill-defined at material interfaces, and ill-conditioning ($κ_2(A_h) \approx 6 \times 10^4$) puts the discretized strong-form loss beyond first-order optimization. We propose DeepOHeat-v2 to overcome both. First, we train on a discretized physics loss that handles the discontinuities natively; its energy form reduces the prediction-space loss-Hessian conditioning from $κ^2$ to $κ$, and a matrix-preconditioned optimizer cuts the mean peak temperature error from over 30 K to 0.55 K. Second, because optimization leaves the training distribution, we propose a self-improving framework: a hotspot trust gate sends flagged placements to a reference solver, and the surrogate incrementally retrains on the refined solutions, keeping an update only when it improves held-out validation error. On a multi-die benchmark, the surrogate-true peak gap on the returned design falls from 1.12 K to 0.11 K, matching a solve-at-every-step optimizer while running $56\times$ faster.

</details>


### [348] [Towards Reasonable Molecular Structure Elucidation from Infrared Spectroscopy with Chemical Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16082)
*Yusen Tan,Hongyu Zhan,Hai-tao Yu,Changxi Chi,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FIRMPO is a chemical feedback-driven preference optimization framework that improves molecular structure elucidation from IR spectra by prioritizing candidates with exact formula matches and consistent theoretical IR spectra.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current machine learning methods for molecular structure elucidation from IR spectra often produce unreasonable candidate structures that don't match the input molecular formula and have inconsistent theoretical IR spectra with observed spectra, leading to unreliable predictions.

Method: FIRMPO (Formula- and IR-Matched Preference Optimization) incorporates chemical feedback as preference signals based on exact molecular formula matching and IR spectral consistency to guide structure predictions. It's a plug-and-play, model-agnostic framework that can be integrated with different structure prediction models.

Result: Extensive experiments on three widely used IR datasets show that FIRMPO significantly improves molecular structure elucidation accuracy over existing baselines, particularly enhancing the accuracy of top-ranked predictions.

Conclusion: FIRMPO provides an effective chemical feedback-driven preference optimization approach that addresses key limitations in molecular structure elucidation from IR spectra, enabling more reliable and chemically reasonable predictions while remaining flexible and model-agnostic.

Abstract: Infrared (IR) spectra provide characteristic signals of molecular structure, which are often interpreted by experts via functional-group identification or library matching, making the process time-consuming and ambiguous. Recent machine learning methods have made progress in molecular structure elucidation using molecular formulas and IR spectra. However, these models often infer unreasonable candidate molecular structures, including top-ranked predictions. More specifically, the molecular formula implied by a candidate structure often fails to match the input molecular formula, and the candidate's theoretical IR spectrum is often inconsistent with the observed IR spectrum. To address these issues, we propose Formula- and IR-Matched Preference Optimization (FIRMPO), a general and plug-and-play chemical feedback-driven preference optimization framework for molecular structure elucidation. FIRMPO incorporates chemical feedback as preference signals based on exact molecular formula matching and IR spectral consistency to guide reasonable structure predictions. Unlike generic preference optimization methods, FIRMPO is tailored to molecular structure elucidation while remaining model-agnostic, enabling it to be readily integrated with different structure prediction models in this class. This encourages models to prioritize structures that satisfy the chemical feedback, leading to a substantial improvement in the accuracy of top-ranked predictions. Extensive experiments on three widely used IR datasets show that FIRMPO significantly improves molecular structure elucidation accuracy over existing baselines.

</details>


### [349] [Behaviour Is an Incomplete Measure of Reasoning Development: Cross-surface pre-arrival accessibility and the limits of developmental inference in a recurrent-depth reasoner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16085)
*Simon Lam-Muir*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that behavioral competence, internal decoder accessibility, and training-time development are distinct phenomena in reasoning networks, with internal knowledge emerging before behavioral competence and not tracking cleanly across training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional approaches infer capability development from behavioral thresholds, final checkpoints, or decoder readouts, but these need not identify the same events. The study aims to disentangle these different observables in reasoning systems.

Method: Used a 30M-parameter recurrent-depth relational reasoner in a closed world with dense behavioral trajectories, two training surfaces (symbolic and verbal), preregistered pre-arrival hidden-state probes, prospectively checked evaluability, and explicit controls. Separated training-time and inference-time axes throughout.

Result: Behavioral competence required vastly different training: 70 epochs for 3-hop symbolic vs 13,055 epochs for verbal. Internal probes recovered answer identity before behavioral arrival with statistical significance (p=0.012987, 16/40 classes contributing). Similar pre-arrival accessibility survived surface changes with p=0.000999. Tracking accessibility across training wasn't cleanly evaluable due to probe eligibility being defined by behavioral arrival.

Conclusion: Behavioral competence, internal accessibility, and training-time development are distinct observables. Neither behavior nor decoder accessibility identifies what computation training acquired; causal intervention is necessary as the next step.

Abstract: Capability development is routinely inferred from behavioural thresholds, from final checkpoints, or from what a decoder can read out of a hidden state. These quantities need not identify the same event. We study a 30M-parameter recurrent-depth relational reasoner in a closed, oracle-defined world, using dense behavioural trajectories, two training surfaces, preregistered pre-arrival hidden-state probes, prospectively checked evaluability, and explicit untrained and negative controls, holding the training-time and inference-time axes separate throughout. Behaviour first: under one frozen acquisition criterion, three-hop competence cost 70 logical epochs on the symbolic surface and 13,055 on the verbal surface, a 186.5-fold contrast, after which verbal four-hop competence cleared in 8 logical epochs. Across the 13,055-epoch grind, four-hop held-out behaviour never exceeded 3/40 and ended at 0/40. Internal measurement next: on the verbal surface a linear probe recovered future-answer identity before behavioural arrival at 0.056159 against uniform chance 0.025, an untrained control of 0.024758 and a population frequency baseline of 0.048309 (p = 0.012987; 16/40 answer classes contributing). Analogous pre-arrival accessibility survived the surface change, reaching 0.1020 against a zero-step control of 0.0460 (p = 0.000999) at the upstream structural position and 0.0618 at the readout comparator (p = 0.004), with 21/40 classes contributing. Finally, the natural attempt to track that accessibility across training was not cleanly evaluable: probe eligibility is defined by behavioural arrival, so the measured population changes with the measurand. Behavioural competence, internal accessibility, and training-time development are distinct observables, and neither behaviour nor decoder accessibility identifies the computation training acquired; causal intervention is the necessary next step.

</details>


### [350] [Unifying Graph Neural Networks Through a Common Layer Equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16097)
*Sai Karthik Navuluru,Siddhartha Shankar Das,Bo Ni,Hongjie Chen,Yu Wang,Baris Coskunuzer,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Franck Dernoncourt,Mahantesh Halappanavar,Tyler Derr,Ryan A. Rossi,Lakshman Tamil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified mathematical framework for graph neural networks that decomposes architectures into seven components, enabling systematic analysis of 200+ models and connecting architectural choices to graph properties and performance issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph neural networks are described with family-specific notation that obscures shared computations and structural differences, making it difficult to compare architectures systematically and understand their fundamental components.

Method: Introduces a common layer equation with seven components: update domain, channel set, propagation bank, per-channel message maps, channel-fusion operator, ego/residual map, and update map. Uses a central factorization separating information movement (propagation bank) from content (message maps). Provides worked reductions of canonical layers and component assignments spanning seven architectural families.

Result: Organizes over 200 architectures in a common design space, enables component-wise comparison and generation of structurally consistent architectures, and connects propagation choices to issues like oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and expressivity. Provides theoretical insights about dependency bounds and mixing requirements.

Conclusion: The framework exposes the empirical inverse problem of mapping measurable graph and task properties to validated component choices, establishing a systematic approach to GNN design and analysis that reveals the design space's structure and component-level trade-offs.

Abstract: Graph neural networks are commonly described through family-specific equations whose notation obscures shared computations and structural differences. We introduce a common layer equation that represents covered architectures through seven components: an update domain, channel set, propagation bank, per-channel message maps, channel-fusion operator, ego/residual map, and update map. The central factorization separates where information moves, encoded by the propagation bank, from what moves, encoded by the message maps. Function-valued fillings extend the same equation across local message passing, attention, spectral filtering, global communication, relation-specific channels, higher-order domains, and geometric messages.
  We make this unification explicit and checkable through worked reductions of canonical layers and component assignments spanning seven nonexclusive architectural families. A fixed slot discipline assigns operations by computational role and defines the framework's coverage boundary. The decomposition also yields component-level theoretical insights: under endpoint-local messages and node-local updates, operator support bounds one-layer dependencies, and one-layer global mixing requires a full effective operator row under the stated hypotheses.
  The resulting framework organizes more than 200 architectures in a common design space, enables component-wise comparison and generation of structurally consistent architectures, and connects propagation choices to oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and expressivity. It further exposes the empirical inverse problem of mapping measurable graph and task properties to validated component choices.

</details>


### [351] [AsyTO: Asymmetric Temporal Operator for Parameter-Efficient Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16098)
*Xiachong Lin,Du Yin,Hao Xue,Wen Hu,Imran Razzak,Arian Prabowo,Matthew Amos,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AsyTO solves multivariate forecasting dilemma by factorizing temporal operators into asymmetric history/future modes with periodic components, achieving lightweight SOTA performance with linear parameter growth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multivariate time-series forecasting faces a structural dilemma: shared predictors force heterogeneous variables through identical history-to-future maps, while independent predictors are computationally expensive as costs grow with variable count, context length, and horizon.

Method: AsyTO (Asymmetric Temporal Operator) factorizes per-variable operators into shared history-reading and future-writing temporal modes with per-variable gains, plus a low-rank periodic prototype and cycle-separable factorization of temporal modes.

Result: AsyTO achieves best lightweight error in 30 of 44 dataset-horizon settings across 11 benchmarks, locating at the accuracy-compute Pareto frontier with parameters/compute growing linearly with variable count.

Conclusion: AsyTO provides an efficient solution to the multivariate time-series forecasting dilemma by factorizing temporal operators rather than compressing data series. It achieves state-of-the-art lightweight performance while maintaining linear parameter/compute growth with variable count.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series forecasting faces a structural dilemma: sharing one temporal predictor across variables is parameter-efficient but forces heterogeneous variables through an identical history-to-future map, whereas learning an independent predictor per variable restores flexibility at a cost that grows with the product of variable count, context length, and horizon. We argue that this dilemma dissolves once the object being compressed is the forecasting operator rather than the observed series. Auditing per-variable linear history-to-future maps across standard benchmarks, we find that a phase-locked seasonal component paired with a compact residual operator outperforms a dense phase-blind reference in most audited settings. The residual transport is also directional: lag-invariant alternatives consistently underperform asymmetric history-to-future maps. Guided by this structure, we propose AsyTO, an Asymmetric Temporal Operator that factorizes the tensor of per-variable operators into shared but distinct history-reading and future-writing temporal modes with per-variable mode-wise gains, complemented by a low-rank periodic prototype and a cycle-separable factorization of the temporal modes. Each forecast reads only its own variable's history, so parameters and compute grow linearly in the number of variables. Across eleven benchmarks and multiple forecast horizons, AsyTO attains the best lightweight error in 30 of 44 dataset-horizon settings, locating at the accuracy-compute Pareto frontier.

</details>


### [352] [RetroMPA: A Molecular Property-Aware Auxiliary Framework for Enhancing Retrosynthesis Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16111)
*Mianzhi Liu,Fan Xiao,Zhiliang Yu,Huayang Huang,Yuke Li,Yi Yang,Wenbo Liu,Yu Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RetroMPA is a post-hoc, model-agnostic chemical filter module that injects molecular property awareness into existing retrosynthesis models, improving their accuracy without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep learning models for retrosynthesis autonomously learn from large datasets with limited integration of established chemical knowledge as priors, creating a gap between data-driven approaches and chemical expertise.

Method: Developed RetroMPA as a plug-and-play, post-hoc enhancement module that operates as a chemical filter. It leverages a property-aware latent embedding space to recalibrate predictions from existing retrosynthesis models without modifying their architecture or requiring retraining.

Result: Improved top-1 accuracy by an average of 5.50% across eight representative models on USPTO-50K, and about 2.03% on large-scale USPTO-Full dataset across both template-based and template-free architectures. Wet-lab experiments confirmed viable, previously unreported substrate combinations for classic reactions.

Conclusion: RetroMPA successfully bridges the gap between data-driven learning and chemical knowledge by providing a practical, model-agnostic framework that enhances existing retrosynthesis algorithms without architectural changes, demonstrating real-world utility beyond data fitting.

Abstract: Retrosynthesis is a cornerstone of drug discovery and organic synthesis. While data-driven deep learning models have shown remarkable progress, they autonomously learn reaction patterns from extensive datasets with limited integration of established chemical knowledge as priors.
  To address this limitation, we introduce RetroMPA, a molecular property-aware, post-hoc enhancement module that injects chemical knowledge into the retrosynthesis pipeline. Rather than functioning as an independent SMILES sequence generator, RetroMPA is a broadly applicable, model-agnostic chemical filter designed to recalibrate and optimize the predictive pathways of existing algorithms.
  This plug-and-play framework integrates seamlessly with a range of data-driven retrosynthesis methods, enhancing outputs without modifying model architecture or requiring resource-intensive retraining. By leveraging a property-aware latent embedding space, RetroMPA consistently improves top-1 accuracy across eight representative retrosynthesis models by an average of 5.50% on USPTO-50K.
  Furthermore, we validate its scalability on the large-scale USPTO-Full dataset, achieving an average improvement of about 2.03% across both template-based and template-free architectures.
  Wet-lab experiments provide preliminary support for the practical utility of the framework. These syntheses confirmed viable, previously unreported substrate combinations for classic reaction paradigms---specifically, Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, Bucherer reaction, and Friedel-Crafts acylation---suggesting that RetroMPA can operate beyond mere data fitting. The code is open-sourced at https://github.com/MengzhouLu/RetroMPA.

</details>


### [353] [Multi-Feature Riemannian Hypergraph for Online Test-Time Adaptation of Motor Imagery Brain-Computer Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16134)
*Siqi Li,Zhi Li,Tong Liu,Shuai Zhang,Yanfei Jia,Zhiqiang Yi,Jue Xie,Ni Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MRieHy is a new framework for online motor imagery BCI decoding that combines Riemannian geometry and hypergraph learning to improve cross-day transferability and online adaptation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two critical challenges in clinical MI-BCI decoding are cross-day transferability and online operation. While hypergraphs can improve transferability by capturing higher-order relationships, existing hypergraph methods for emotion recognition neglect the cross-day benefits of Riemannian geometry that's widely used in EEG transfer learning.

Method: MRieHy first computes Riemannian means of covariance matrices from cross-day training data to align multi-day distributions. It constructs two hypergraphs: one over covariance matrices using Riemannian distance, and another over deep features using cosine similarity. These are fused via adaptively learned weights and jointly optimized with label projection matrices. During online testing, it maintains a FIFO buffer of recent samples, performs Riemannian alignment on buffered data, and decodes with the learned hypergraph.

Result: Extensive experiments on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets show that MRieHy achieves notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed MRieHy framework successfully bridges the gap between hypergraph methods and Riemannian geometry for MI-BCI decoding, effectively addressing cross-day transferability challenges while enabling online test-time adaptation with superior performance compared to existing methods.

Abstract: In clinical motor imagery brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) decoding, cross-day transferability and online operation remain two critical challenges. Hypergraphs can improve transferability by capturing higher-order sample relationships, yet existing hypergraph-based methods for online emotion recognition neglect the cross-day benefits of Riemannian geometry widely adopted in EEG transfer learning. To bridge this gap, we propose the Multi-feature Riemannian Hypergraph (MRieHy), a framework tailored for online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding that leverages Riemannian geometry to strengthen cross-day transferability. MRieHy first computes Riemannian means of covariance matrices from cross-day training data to align multi-day distributions. It then constructs a hypergraph over covariance matrices using Riemannian distance, complemented by a second hypergraph over deep features built with cosine similarity. The two hypergraphs are fused via adaptively learned combination weights, jointly optimized with the label projection matrices. During online testing, MRieHy maintains a first-in-first-out buffer of recent samples, performs Riemannian alignment on the buffered data, and decodes with the learned hypergraph. Extensive experiments on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets validate that MRieHy achieves notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [354] [REFLEX: Reflexive Equilibrium Fixed-point Learning for Endogenous eXchanges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16155)
*Vignesh Nagarajan,Shriraghav Ashok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REFLEX is a framework that provides dealers with a pre-deployment stability margin to predict whether repeated retraining of quoting ML models will converge or become unstable, addressing feedback loops in over-the-counter bond markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dealers increasingly use machine learning to set bond quotes, creating feedback loops where models retrain on trades their own quotes attract. The key question is not just model performance but whether the market it creates stays stable as the model learns from it. Existing performative prediction theory provides stability conditions but relies on unobservable quantities that trading desks can't measure before deployment.

Method: Introduces REFLEX framework that replaces unobservable quantities with three measurable dealer behavior features: 1) how strongly trading volume responds to tighter quotes, 2) how sharply the dealer's objective bends around its optimum, and 3) how quickly informed flow increases as spreads narrow. These combine into a single retraining modulus, a pre-deployment stability margin estimated from a desk's quote and execution history.

Result: Predicted and measured stability agree within 8% in simulation. Competing dealers increase instability by 1.74x with two and 3.16x with three dealers. Ordinary retraining becomes unstable at modulus 1.21, while structurally anchored correction converges where blind retraining collapses. Stability headroom falls roughly 4.4x for investment grade and 4.3x for high yield bonds from calm to crisis regimes over 36 years of market data.

Conclusion: REFLEX turns abstract convergence theory into a practical market-level safety margin that dealers can measure before deploying ML quoting models, addressing stability concerns in over-the-counter bond markets where feedback loops between model retraining and market outcomes create potential instability.

Abstract: In over-the-counter corporate bond markets, dealers compete for client trades by quoting bid and ask prices. Tighter quotes attract more business, but also informed customers more likely to trade ahead of adverse price moves, leaving the dealer holding the risk. As dealers increasingly use machine learning to set quotes, they retrain these models on the trades their own quotes attract, creating a feedback loop in which each model reshapes the market that generates its next training data. The question is therefore not only whether a quoting model performs well, but whether the market it creates stays stable as the model learns from it. Existing performative prediction theory gives a sharp stability condition, yet expresses it through abstract properties of the learning objective a trading desk cannot measure before deployment. We introduce REFLEX, a framework that replaces those unobservable quantities with three measurable features of dealer behavior: how strongly trading volume responds to tighter quotes, how sharply the dealer's objective bends around its optimum, and how quickly informed flow increases as spreads narrow. REFLEX combines these into a single retraining modulus, a pre-deployment stability margin estimated from a desk's own quote and execution history that predicts whether repeated retraining will converge or amplify itself. In simulation, predicted and measured stability agree within 8%, and competing dealers increase instability by 1.74x with two and 3.16x with three, as predicted. Where ordinary retraining becomes unstable at modulus 1.21, a structurally anchored correction converges as blind retraining collapses. Calibrated over 36 years of public market data, stability headroom falls roughly 4.4x for investment grade and 4.3x for high yield from calm to crisis regimes. Ultimately, REFLEX turns an abstract convergence theorem into a market-level safety margin.

</details>


### [355] [A Tree-Structured Approach for Phishing Template and Attacker Attribution Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16158)
*Unai Agirre,Imanol Jerico,Felipe Castaño,Andrea Venturi,Francesco Zola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using DOM tree structures as fingerprints to detect phishing template reuse through unsupervised clustering, enabling identification of coordinated phishing campaigns and zero-day templates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Phishing attacks are industrializing with widespread availability of phishing kits and reusable templates, allowing rapid generation of fraudulent webpages. Existing defenses focus on individual instances rather than structural similarities, limiting ability to detect template reuse and coordinated campaigns.

Method: Model webpages as DOM trees and extract structural features, optionally enriched with HTML tag-based content information. Use unsupervised learning to cluster structurally similar webpages, evaluating three clustering algorithms and analyzing DOM-tree depth impact on clustering performance.

Result: Structural representations effectively reveal hidden similarities across phishing sites, enabling detection of emerging and zero-day templates and supporting coordinated phishing threat analysis. Cluster quality validated both quantitatively (novel level-wise Jaccard Distance Score) and qualitatively through visualization tools.

Conclusion: HTML structure serves as a robust fingerprint for identifying phishing template reuse, offering a proactive approach to detect coordinated phishing campaigns that goes beyond traditional reactive defenses.

Abstract: Phishing remains a persistent and evolving cybersecurity threat, with attack volumes reaching record levels. This growth is driven by the industrialization of phishing through widely available phishing kits and reusable templates, which enable cybercriminals to rapidly generate and deploy large numbers of fraudulent webpages. Although surface-level attributes may differ across these websites, their underlying structures often exhibit significant similarities. However, most existing defenses rely on reactive blocklists or supervised classification models that focus on individual phishing instances, limiting their ability to identify structural reuse and detect coordinated phishing campaigns. To address this limitation, this study investigates whether HTML structure can serve as a robust fingerprint for identifying phishing template reuse. We model webpages as Document Object Model (DOM) trees and extract structural features, optionally enriched with HTML tag-based content information. These representations are then clustered using unsupervised learning methods to group structurally similar webpages. Three clustering algorithms are evaluated and compared, while also analyzing how the depth of the extracted DOM-tree affects cluster formation and overall clustering performance. Finally, cluster quality is also evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively, including a novel level-wise Jaccard Distance Score and manual inspection supported by visualization tools. Results demonstrate that structural representations of webpages can effectively reveal hidden similarities across phishing sites, enabling the detection of emerging and zero-day templates and supporting the analysis of coordinated phishing threats

</details>


### [356] [Demystifying Oversmoothing in Sheaf Neural Networks: An Index-Theoretic Criterion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16180)
*Junwen Dong,Yuhan Peng,Hao Li,Huitao Feng,Kelin Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new geometric approach to measure anti-oversmoothing capacity in Sheaf Neural Networks, replacing absolute harmonic dimension with a relative comparison criterion, and validates it with GyroSheaf experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analyses of Sheaf Neural Networks use absolute dimension of harmonic space (kerL) as an anti-oversmoothing indicator, but this can be misleading - some sheaf configurations inflate this dimension while having only constant harmonic sections that don't improve discriminative capacity.

Method: Introduced a relative, geometric approach to characterize anti-oversmoothing capacity precisely. Developed an index-theoretic comparison criterion under natural stalk transportation and global sheaf structure conditions. Created GyroSheaf with curved gyrovector-space stalks to extend the criterion to non-linear settings via local tangent-space linearization.

Result: Experiments across ten models confirm the theoretical criterion: sheaf models violating the criterion collapse despite having index jumps, while compliant models maintain depth-stable representations. The geometric approach successfully distinguishes genuine anti-oversmoothing capacity from trivial inflation.

Conclusion: The relative geometric approach provides a more reliable measure of anti-oversmoothing capacity in Sheaf Neural Networks than absolute harmonic dimension, with practical validation through GyroSheaf and comprehensive experiments showing criterion compliance correlates with stable deep representations.

Abstract: To combat oversmoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks, Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) were proposed as a generalization by equipping the graph with a sheaf structure and replacing the graph Laplacian with a sheaf Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$. Existing analyses connect sheaf diffusion to oversmoothing via the harmonic space ($\ker\mathcal{L}$), taking its absolute dimension as an indicator of anti-oversmoothing capacity. However, absolute dimension alone is not a reliable measure: certain sheaf configurations inflate $\dim \ker \mathcal{L}$ while their harmonic sections remain entirely constant, without enriching discriminative capacity. We instead introduce the first relative, geometric approach, yielding a precise characterisation of anti-oversmoothing capacity. Under natural conditions on stalk transportation and global sheaf structure, we establish an index-theoretic comparison criterion showing that one sheaf's harmonic space genuinely contains another's beyond trivial inflation. We illustrate this with a concrete instance and further introduce \textit{GyroSheaf}, a sheaf with curved gyrovector-space stalks, extending the criterion to the non-linear setting via local tangent-space linearization. Experiments across ten models confirm the theoretical criterion: sheaf models violating the criterion collapse despite possessing index jumps, while compliant models maintain depth-stable representations.

</details>


### [357] [Understanding and Stabilizing Deep Q-Learning via Controlled Bootstrapping and Regulated Value Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16182)
*Bozhou Chen,Yongyi Wang,Hanyu Liu,Xionghui Yang,Wenxin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systematic analysis of instability in deep Q-learning reveals three complementary sources of instability and proposes stabilization techniques leading to competitive performance on benchmark tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Q-learning has shown impressive results but suffers from notoriously unstable training. Existing research often looks at isolated factors like overestimation bias, but lacks a unified understanding of how different instability sources interact during recursive value estimation.

Method: Provides systematic analysis from three perspectives: operator-level bias in Bellman bootstrapping, estimator-level sensitivity of greedy action selection to regression noise, and parameter-dynamics imbalance under aggressive data reuse. Derives stabilization principles for controlled bootstrapping, ensemble quantile estimation, and spike-based parameter regulation.

Result: Identified a reward-triggered self-reinforcing trap and characteristic parameter spike dynamics. Experiments on Atari-100K and Procgen demonstrate competitive performance and improved training stability.

Conclusion: The paper presents a comprehensive framework for understanding DQL instability through multiple interacting factors and provides practical stabilization techniques that lead to better training stability while maintaining competitive performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Deep Q-learning (DQL) has achieved remarkable empirical success in reinforcement learning, yet its training process remains notoriously unstable. Existing studies often attribute instability to isolated factors such as overestimation bias or representation learning issues, lacking a unified understanding of how different sources of instability interact during recursive value estimation. In this work, we provide a systematic analysis of instability in deep Q-learning from three complementary perspectives: operator-level bias in Bellman bootstrapping, estimator-level sensitivity of greedy action selection to regression noise, and parameter-dynamics imbalance under aggressive data reuse. We identify a reward-triggered self-reinforcing trap and characteristic parameter spike dynamics, then derive stabilization principles for controlled bootstrapping, ensemble quantile estimation, and spike-based parameter regulation. Experiments on Atari-100K and Procgen demonstrate competitive performance and improved training stability.

</details>


### [358] [Multi-Granularity Sentiment Integration for LLM-Based Multimodal Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16201)
*Shanshan Lin,Yuesheng Wu,Chao Chen,Yizhe Yang,Zhihao Chen,Zexian Yang,Xiangwen Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MGSI is a multi-granularity sentiment integration framework for multimodal sentiment analysis that encodes audio/visual signals at different temporal scales and refines them through text-guided alignment and sentiment-aware enhancement before feeding to frozen LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based multimodal sentiment analysis methods struggle with effectively incorporating audio and visual signals because they compress these signals through shallow projection or coarse pooling before fusion, which weakens cross-modal alignment and erases fine-grained affective information.

Method: MGSI first encodes audio and visual streams at short-, medium-, and long-range temporal scales to preserve both local variations and global affective trends. It then refines non-text features through text-guided alignment, applies polarity- and intensity-aware enhancement to handle ambiguous samples, and compresses the multimodal representation into pseudo-tokens for efficient conditioning of a frozen LLM.

Result: Experiments on four public benchmarks show MGSI substantially outperforms frozen-LLM baselines and remains competitive with strong multimodal methods. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of multi-granularity temporal modeling, text-guided refinement, and adaptive sentiment calibration.

Conclusion: The MGSI framework successfully addresses the challenge of effectively incorporating audio and visual signals into LLM-based multimodal sentiment analysis by preserving temporal granularity and enhancing sentiment cues through text-guided refinement and sentiment-aware calibration.

Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict sentiment polarity and intensity from heterogeneous inputs such as text, audio, and vision. While large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic priors for MSA, effectively incorporating audio and visual signals effectively remains challenging. A key challenge is that audio and visual sentiment cues evolve over different temporal scales, yet many LLM-based methods compress these signals through shallow projection or coarse pooling before fusing them with text, which can weaken cross-modal alignment and erase fine-grained affective information. We propose MGSI, a multi-granularity sentiment integration framework for LLM-based MSA. MGSI first encodes audio and visual streams at short-, medium-, and long-range temporal scales, preserving both local variations and global affective trends. It then refines non-text features through text-guided alignment, and applies polarity- and intensity-aware enhancement to better handle ambiguous and near-neutral samples. The resulting multimodal representation is finally compressed into a small set of pseudo-tokens for efficient conditioning of a frozen LLM. Experiments on four public benchmarks show that MGSI substantially outperforms frozen-LLM baselines and remains competitive with strong multimodal methods. Further ablation and sensitivity analyses support the effectiveness of multi-granularity temporal modeling, text-guided refinement, and adaptive sentiment calibration.

</details>


### [359] [Conditional Evaluation of Language Models with Cheap Auxiliary Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16210)
*Zhi Zhang,Lingfeng Lyu,Yue Kang,Doudou Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LACE (Local Augmented Control-Variate Evaluation) is a semi-supervised estimator for conditional LLM evaluation that uses cheap auxiliary signals (like LLM-judge scores) combined with expensive gold labels to efficiently estimate where models succeed and fail across different performance profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard aggregate accuracy metrics hide important details about where models succeed and fail. While gold labels provide accurate conditional performance profiles, they're expensive to collect. Cheap auxiliary signals (LLM-judge scores, confidence scores, etc.) are available for all benchmark items but are often biased or miscalibrated. There's a need for an efficient method to estimate conditional performance profiles without requiring expensive gold labels for every item.

Method: LACE uses local centering: subtract the conditional mean of a cheap signal within the target profile region, making any linear augmentation have zero conditional mean (not changing the estimand). Uses local ridge control variate combining gold-label residual mean from labeled subset with cheap-signal mean from full item pool. The augmentation coefficient is used only for efficiency. The method is calibration-free and unbiased for grouped profiles.

Result: The paper proves calibration-free identification, unbiasedness for grouped profiles, local oracle optimality within centered linear augmentations, and first-order adaptivity to estimated coefficients. Shows efficiency gain governed by population local R², indicating how attainable efficiency from cheap signals varies across profile values. Also derives estimators for direct paired model gaps and deployment-weighted scores. Empirically evaluated on 8 benchmarks including MATH-500, ScienceQA, MMLU, etc.

Conclusion: LACE provides an efficient semi-supervised approach for conditional LLM evaluation that leverages cheap auxiliary signals without requiring full gold labels, offering calibration-free estimation with proven theoretical guarantees and demonstrated empirical effectiveness across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: Aggregate accuracy hides where models succeed and fail. Estimating conditional performance profiles from gold labels alone is expensive, while cheap auxiliary signals such as LLM-judge scores, pairwise comparisons, confidence scores, and judge-disagreement features can be collected for every benchmark item but are often biased or miscalibrated. We propose LACE (Local Augmented Control-Variate Evaluation), a semi-supervised estimator for conditional LLM evaluation. The key step is local centering: after subtracting the conditional mean of a cheap signal within the target profile region, any linear augmentation has zero conditional mean and therefore cannot change the estimand. The augmentation coefficient is used only for efficiency, and a local ridge control variate combines a gold-label residual mean from the labeled subset with a cheap-signal mean from the full item pool. We prove calibration-free identification, unbiasedness for grouped profiles, local oracle optimality within centered linear augmentations, and first-order adaptivity to the estimated coefficient. The resulting gain formula is governed by a population local $R^2$, which characterizes how the efficiency attainable from the cheap signals varies across profile values. We also derive corresponding estimators for direct paired model gaps and deployment-weighted scores. We empirically evaluate the primary performance-profile estimator on MATH-500, ScienceQA, MMLU, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, and ARC.

</details>


### [360] [Quantifying the Gap Between Laboratory Battery Test Patterns and Field Duty Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16212)
*Chunyang Zhao,Chresten Træholt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper quantifies the gap between laboratory battery tests and real-world EV operation by comparing six evidence sources using duty-structure metrics, showing significant differences in usage patterns and long-term aging outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Laboratory battery tests don't directly represent real-world electric vehicle duty profiles, creating a gap between controlled experiments and field performance data that needs quantification.

Method: Comparative analysis of six evidence sources using duty-structure metrics: usage frequency, intensity, C-rate, and Duty-Structure Index (DSI) based on normalized current dispersion and ramping.

Result: Significant differences found: DSI ranges from 0.630 (field trace) to 2.936 (Oxford lab); aging varies - 80% retention occurs at 351 cycles (NASA) vs 6292 checkpoints (Oxford); field operation shows median 137.2 km/day intensity.

Conclusion: Battery performance metrics are duty-pattern dependent; application-oriented studies should report explicit duty-profile descriptors alongside chemistry, capacity, and aging metrics for better comparability.

Abstract: Laboratory battery tests provide the main empirical basis for battery performance and degradation studies, but their operating patterns do not directly represent field duty profiles. This paper quantifies the gap by comparing six accessible evidence sources covering controlled cycling, drive-cycle testing, dynamic cycling, NMC811 laboratory ageing, a real electric-vehicle charging trace, and fleet-scale electric-vehicle state-of-health (SOH) data. The analysis combines usage frequency, usage intensity, usage C-rate, and a duty-structure index (DSI) based on normalized current dispersion and ramping. The representative single-segment DSI ranges from 0.630 for the field source trace and 0.699 for NASA to 2.936 for Oxford and 2.855 for Imperial, while usage C-rate ranges from 0.14-0.40 for Imperial, NASA, Stanford, and Hyundai to 2.00 for Oxford. Long-term ageing also differs: the 80 percent retention region occurs near 351 NASA cycles, 6292 Oxford checkpoints, and 1019 Stanford cycles. In chemistry-aligned NMC/NCM evidence, Imperial retains 0.813 under standard cycling and 0.865 under drive-cycle ageing, while the field source has median SOH 0.889 with visible dispersion. Field operation further shows a median use intensity of 137.2 km/day and 56.9 percent of charges ending at or above 95 percent SOC. These results show that battery performance metrics are conditional on the duty pattern that generated them; application-oriented studies should report explicit duty-profile descriptors together with chemistry, capacity, and ageing metrics.

</details>


### [361] [Beyond Peak Backlog: Conditional Energy and Temporal Geometry in Capacity-Constrained Delayed Bandit Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16216)
*Anling Xiang,Yuwen Yang,Yang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a scheduler-side conditional-energy interface for bandit convex optimization with limited feedback tracking capacity, achieving better delay complexity than existing approaches by separating rate adaptation from perturbation filtration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing one-point bandit convex optimization algorithms with limited feedback tracking capacity C pay √(Tσ_max) in delay complexity, which is worse than the √(d_tot) dependence achievable with unlimited tracking. There's a need to bridge this gap and understand how limited tracking capacity affects optimization performance.

Method: Introduces a scheduler-side conditional-energy interface that separates rate adaptation from one-point perturbation filtration. This handles dependent importance weights created by randomized admission of feedback. The approach works under semi-clairvoyant oracle and pathwise hard-capacity constraints, with requirements C ≥ ln T + 1.

Result: Achieves delay complexity scaling as O(√(E_C d_tot)) with only explicit restart factor E_C (removable with public constant-factor peak bound). For strongly convex problems, obtains temporal cost H_A(d) = Σ_t σ_t/(A+t). Shows timing matters under curvature - different delay vectors with identical aggregate statistics can have polynomially different minimax regret.

Conclusion: Limited feedback tracking capacity introduces new complexity considerations beyond aggregate delay statistics. The proposed conditional-energy interface improves delay complexity and reveals that timing structure (not just aggregate summaries) affects minimax regret under curvature constraints.

Abstract: What is the right delay complexity when a learner can track only $C$ pending feedback items and discarded feedback is permanently lost? Existing one-point bandit convex optimization guarantees in this model pay $\sqrt{Tσ_{\max}}$, where $σ_{\max}$ is the peak backlog, although unlimited tracking admits the sharper $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}$ dependence on total delay. We introduce a scheduler-side conditional-energy interface that separates rate adaptation from the one-point perturbation filtration and handles the dependent importance weights created by randomized admission. Under the same semi-clairvoyant oracle and pathwise hard-capacity contract, this yields an untuned learner whose delay term scales as $O(\sqrt{E_C d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$, with only an explicit restart factor $E_C$; a public constant-factor peak bound removes this factor while $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ remains unknown. Under strong convexity, the same interface yields the temporal cost $H_A(d)=\sum_t σ_t/(A+t)$. Two delay vectors with identical delay multisets, $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$, $σ_{\max}$, and capacity can nevertheless have polynomially different minimax regret, showing that timing matters under curvature even when aggregate delay summaries agree. Finally, a continuous hard family converts tracking capacity into a zeroth-order query budget and gives a complementary capacity-starvation lower endpoint. The upper bounds require $C\ge \ln T+1$ and do not constitute a complete capacity minimax characterization.

</details>


### [362] [A Privacy Study of Sparse Collaborative Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16236)
*Maximilian Andreas Hoefler,Karsten Mueller,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparsification in collaborative inference reduces communication cost significantly but provides much weaker privacy protection than expected, with the sparse activation positions alone enabling high-fidelity reconstructions and re-identification of individuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates privacy risks in collaborative inference where models are split between edge devices and servers. While sparsification of activations is commonly used to reduce communication costs and is thought to improve privacy, the authors question this assumption by examining whether sparse activations truly protect private input information.

Method: The researchers decompose sparse activations into two components: retained values and their positions. They then perform input reconstruction attacks from each component in isolation to assess privacy leakage. They test this approach across natural-image and face datasets, examining scenarios with both low transmission cost and low task utility.

Result: Sparsification reduces privacy leakage far less than it reduces transmission costs. The positions of sparse activations alone constitute a serious privacy risk, enabling high-fidelity reconstructions and re-identification of individuals. This leakage persists even when both transmission cost and task utility are low, showing that positional information is highly revealing.

Conclusion: The positions of sparse activations should be treated as sensitive transmitted data and carefully audited in collaborative inference systems. Current approaches that treat positions as side information for decoding underestimate the privacy risk, and new privacy protection mechanisms are needed specifically for positional information.

Abstract: Collaborative inference (CI) splits a model between an edge device and a server, whereby the client computes an intermediate activation, transmits it, and the server completes the computation. This raises two concerns, the communication cost of the transmission and the risk that it reveals private information about the input. Recent work reduces this cost by sparsifying activations and entropy-coding the result. Sparsity has also been argued to improve privacy, on the intuition that transmitting fewer values reveals less about the input. We test this claim by decomposing the sparse activation into the retained values and the set of positions they occupy, and by reconstructing inputs from each component in isolation. We find that sparsification reduces the leakage far less than it reduces the transmission cost, and that the remaining risk shifts to the positions, which prior analyses treat as side information for decoding. Across natural-image and face datasets, the positions alone constitute a serious privacy risk, enabling high-fidelity reconstructions and re-identification of individuals. The leakage from the positions persists even when both the transmission cost and the task utility are low. We conclude that the positions of sparse activations should be treated as sensitive transmitted data and audited carefully in the context of collaborative inference. Code is available at https://github.com/an7123/Privacy-Study-Sparse-CI.

</details>


### [363] [Optimizing Multi-Market Participation of Battery and Electrolyser Systems Based on Field Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16238)
*Chunyang Zhao,Stoyan Trenchev,Shi You,Chresten Træholt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study demonstrating the economic benefits of multi-market participation for battery storage and Power-to-X electrolyzers using real hardware performance data and market conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With increasing renewable energy share creating need for flexible resources, and expanding electricity markets creating revenue stacking opportunities, most studies neglect real hardware behavior like ramp limits, efficiency, and setpoint-tracking accuracy.

Method: Experimental and modeling results for a 55 kW/79 kWh BESS and electrolyzer (three 2.4 kW units), with key characteristics identified through measurements and embedded into a price-driven optimization framework for Danish electricity and ancillary service markets using real 2022-2025 market data.

Result: Optimized daily profits for multi-market participation: 1,749.27 DKK for BESS and 289.46 DKK for electrolyzer, demonstrating viable business cases.

Conclusion: The work highlights the importance of incorporating experimental performance data when evaluating participation across multiple markets and years, showing that real hardware behavior significantly impacts economic optimization.

Abstract: The increasing share of renewable energy in power systems creates a need for fast-response and flexible resources to maintain system stability. With the expansion of electricity markets and ancillary service products, opportunities arise to stack revenues across multiple services. Long-term Power-to-X (PTX) electrolysers and short-term battery energy storage systems (BESS) are prevalent flexible resources, yet most studies neglect real hardware behavior, such as ramp limits, efficiency, and setpoint-tracking accuracy. This work presents experimental and modeling results for a 55 kW/79 kWh BESS and an electrolyser comprising three 2.4 kW units. Key characteristics are identified through measurements and embedded into a price-driven optimization framework for participation in the Danish electricity and ancillary service markets, utilizing real market data from 2022 to 2025. The optimized daily profits for multi-market participation are 1,749.27 DKK and 289.46 DKK for the BESS and electrolyser, respectively. With the demonstrated business cases for BESS and PTX systems, this work highlights the importance of incorporating experimental performance when evaluating participation across multiple markets and years.

</details>


### [364] [The Trade-off Between Covariate Dependence and Latent Structure in Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16245)
*Małgorzata Łazęcka,Ewa Szczurek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified supervised framework for disentangled representation learning that shows an inherent trade-off between latent independence and one-to-one latent-covariate alignment, with applications for post-hoc realignment of pretrained models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unsupervised disentanglement approaches fail to guarantee semantic alignment with covariates, while supervised approaches struggle with correlated covariates and can't simultaneously achieve both latent independence and one-to-one latent-covariate alignment.

Method: Introduces a unified supervised framework coupling latent dimension-covariate dependence with constraints on latent structure, proving inherent trade-offs between independence and alignment. Provides closed-form transformations for post-hoc realignment of pretrained models and integrates them into informed factor analysis (iFA).

Result: Shows ordered disentanglement regimes by alignment strength, enables post-hoc realignment of CLIP, DINOv2, and ViT representations, and demonstrates controllability of structured latent representations on simulated and real multi-omics data.

Conclusion: The framework enables both post-hoc alignment of existing models and iFA integration for controllable disentangled representations, addressing limitations of current approaches through explicit handling of the independence-alignment trade-off.

Abstract: Disentangled representation learning seeks latent representations whose indicidual dimensions each align with a distinct covariate. Unsupervised approaches typically target latent dimension independence, yet this gives no guarantee that the resulting dimensions align with semantically meaningful covariates. Supervised approaches structure the latent space using observed covariates, but under correlated covariates they cannot simultaneously control one-to-one latent-covariate alignment and latent independence. We introduce a unified, supervised framework that couples latent dimension-covariate dependence with constraints on the latent structure. Within this framework, we show an inherent trade-off, where enforcing latent independence or exclusive one-to-one latent-covariate dependence comes at a provable cost in latent-covariate alignment. We prove that the resulting disentanglement regimes are ordered by the strength of that alignment. Each regime admits a closed-form transformation of the latent space. We apply these transformations post-hoc to realign the representations of pretrained models such as CLIP, DINOv2, and ViT, and we fold them into the inference of informed factor analysis (iFA), a probabilistic model with covariate-informed factors. On simulated and real multi-omics data, we show that both post-hoc alignment and iFA enable controllability of structured latent representations.

</details>


### [365] [SAUL: Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16249)
*Jaewan Choi,Junyoung Yang,Sangdon Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAUL is a new machine unlearning method for LLMs that uses sharpness-aware augmented Lagrangian optimization with explicit forgetting constraints to achieve better trade-offs between erasing target knowledge and preserving general utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine unlearning in LLMs faces a critical trade-off between erasing target knowledge (forgetting) and preserving general utility (retaining). Existing methods typically specify forgetting implicitly through optimization objectives, which may not provide precise control over the forgetting level.

Method: SAUL formulates unlearning as a constrained minimization problem with explicit forgetting constraints. It uses an augmented Lagrangian controller that adaptively adjusts forget-side pressure based on constraint violation. Features sharpness-aware updates on both retain and forget objectives, and a dual-optimizer design maintaining role-separated states for stable dynamics.

Result: SAUL demonstrates favorable forgetting-utility trade-offs over representative sharpness- and perturbation-based baselines on TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE benchmarks. The augmented-Lagrangian controller alone, when applied as a drop-in modifier to existing methods, improves post-forgetting utility.

Conclusion: SAUL provides an effective framework for machine unlearning in LLMs with explicit forgetting control, achieving better trade-offs between knowledge erasure and utility preservation than prior methods. The augmented-Lagrangian approach offers practical value for improving existing unlearning techniques.

Abstract: Machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs) faces a critical trade-off between erasing target knowledge and preserving general utility.
