We propose SAUL (Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning), which formulates unlearning as a constrained minimization problem following the principle of "forget enough, but no more than necessary." At its core, SAUL formulates forgetting as an explicit constraint with a prescribed satisfaction criterion, whereas prior unlearning methods typically specify the desired level of forgetting implicitly through optimization objectives. An augmented Lagrangian controller adaptively adjusts forget-side pressure according to constraint violation and can eventually deactivate the forget-side update as the prescribed criterion remains satisfied. Sharpness-aware updates on both retain and forget objectives, together with a dual-optimizer design that maintains role-separated states, further stabilize the resulting unlearning dynamics. We evaluate SAUL on the TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE benchmarks, demonstrating favorable forgetting-utility trade-offs over representative sharpness- and perturbation-based baselines under benchmark-specific forgetting criteria. Beyond the complete SAUL framework, we further show on TOFU that applying the augmented-Lagrangian controller as a drop-in modifier to representative baselines improves their post-forgetting utility, demonstrating the practical value of explicit forgetting control.

</details>


### [366] [Efficient Coreset Selection via K-Nearest Neighbor Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16270)
*Yingfan Liu,Leiyu Zhang,Jiadong Xie,Mingzhe Wang,Jeffrey Xu Yu,Jiangtao Cui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KNNG-CS is an efficient coreset selection method that uses K-nearest neighbor graphs to select representative data points with linear storage, achieving comparable accuracy to existing methods while being significantly faster and more memory-efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing gradient-approximation coreset methods like CRAIG and cluster-based variants suffer from high computational and memory costs due to their reliance on dense pairwise distances or large item-cluster bound matrices, especially on large datasets.

Method: The paper proposes KNNG-CS, which constructs a K-nearest neighbor graph to capture local neighborhood structures, estimates the importance of each data item based on this graph, and greedily selects representative nodes without maintaining quadratic distance matrices. The method requires only linear storage proportional to the number of edges in the graph.

Result: Experiments on four real-world datasets show that KNNG-CS achieves comparable accuracy to existing gradient-approximation coreset methods while reducing selection time by 2.3×-41.2× and peak memory usage to 0.3%-7.5% of the baselines.

Conclusion: KNNG-CS provides a lightweight and efficient coreset selection approach that maintains accuracy while dramatically reducing computational and memory overhead compared to existing methods, making it practical for large-scale datasets.

Abstract: Coreset selection reduces the cost of model training by replacing a large training set with a small representative subset. Existing gradient-approximation coreset methods such as CRAIG and cluster-based variants can preserve model accuracy. Still, their selection stages often rely on dense pairwise distances or large item-cluster bound matrices, leading to high time and memory costs on large datasets. This paper proposes KNNG-CS, a lightweight coreset selection method based on a $K$-nearest neighbor graph. KNNG-CS exploits local neighborhood structures to estimate the importance of each data item and greedily selects representative nodes without maintaining a quadratic distance matrix. The method requires only linear storage in the number of edges. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that KNNG-CS achieves accuracy comparable to representative gradient-approximation coreset methods, while reducing selection time by $2.3\times$-$41.2\times$ and peak memory to $0.3\%$-$7.5\%$ of the baselines.

</details>


### [367] [Foresight-England: Development of a National-Scale Generative AI Model of Electronic Health Records for Medical Event Prediction across the COVID-19 Pandemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16273)
*Simon Ellershaw,Christopher Tomlinson,Zeljko Kraljevic,Spiros Denaxas,Harry Hemingway,Cathie Sudlow,Angela M. Wood,Anoop D. Shah,Richard Dobson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Foresight-England is the first national-scale generative foundation model for EHRs, developed as a COVID-19 research pilot using NHS England data, with quantitative results currently unavailable due to paused data access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a national-scale generative foundation model for electronic health records to model both direct and indirect effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, creating a methodological template for population-scale EHR foundation models.

Method: A 243-million-parameter transformer decoder trained from scratch on de-identified EHRs of 61 million individuals, integrating primary/secondary care, death registrations, and COVID-19 data. Uses autoregressive modeling to predict next medical events with zero-shot inference capabilities and a tokenization scheme preserving clinical granularity of ICD-10, OPCS-4, and SNOMED CT codes.

Result: Quantitative results for COVID-19 hospitalisation and mortality prediction (including subgroup analyses by demographics and vaccination status) are currently unavailable due to NHS England pausing data access for the project, as detailed in the Project Status section.

Conclusion: The paper presents Foresight-England as a methodological template and case study in building population-scale EHR foundation models, highlighting the challenges of such large-scale projects in healthcare, though specific quantitative findings cannot be shared due to paused data access.

Abstract: Foresight-England (Foresight-E) is the first national-scale generative foundation model of electronic health records (EHRs), developed as a research pilot strictly for COVID-19 research. We evaluated its ability to model the direct and indirect effects of the pandemic. Trained from scratch entirely within the NHS England Secure Data Environment, Foresight-E is a 243-million-parameter transformer decoder. It was trained and evaluated on de-identified, longitudinal EHRs of approximately 61 million individuals, integrating primary/secondary care, death registrations, and COVID-19 data. Training and validation used a 90% subset (54.9 million) spanning November 2018 to December 2022; the remaining 10% (6.1 million) was held out for evaluation. Foresight-E models patient timelines autoregressively, predicting the next medical event given their prior history. At inference, it operates zero-shot, predicting any concept in its ~40,000-code vocabulary without task-specific training. Our tokenisation scheme retains the clinical granularity of ICD-10, OPCS-4, and SNOMED CT codes, jointly representing absolute and relative timing. We designed an evaluation framework for 30-day COVID-19 hospitalisation and mortality, including subgroup analyses by demographic factors and vaccination status. To assess generalisation to unseen future data and the pandemic's indirect effects, we tested the model on medical events from 2023 (beyond its training period), benchmarking against logistic regression and XGBoost. As detailed in the Project Status section, NHS England has paused access to data for the Foresight-E project, meaning quantitative results are currently unavailable. Instead, we share our strategy for tokenisation, architecture, training, inference, and evaluation as a methodological template and case study in the challenges of building population-scale EHR foundation models.

</details>


### [368] [SCALE: State-Calibrated Latent Embeddings for JEPA Planning in the Right Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16287)
*Jiaming Hu,Yan Zheng,Tian Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCALE adds lightweight regularization to improve planning in world models by aligning latent space geometry with task-relevant state distances, enhancing how state information influences planner decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current joint-embedding predictive world models (like DINO-WM and LeWM) have complementary strengths but differ in how task-relevant state information shapes latent geometry. DINO-WM's leading principal components retain more state information, making state more influential in planning decisions. The paper aims to give end-to-end learned representations (LeWM) the favorable geometric properties of pretrained ones.

Method: Proposes SCALE (State-CAlibrated Latent Embeddings) - a lightweight training-time regularizer that correlates sampled pairwise latent distances with distances in a standardized task-relevant state space. This aligns latent geometry without replacing LeWM's learned encoder, improving how task-relevant state information shapes the representation consumed by planners.

Result: Across five tasks, three planning solvers, and five compute budgets, SCALE consistently improves every task-solver average over baseline LeWM. It achieves this with minimal overhead (single lightweight regularizer, no planning-time cost), outperforming latent-to-state regression controls that matched decodability but lacked geometric alignment.

Conclusion: Planning performance depends not just on whether task-relevant information is present in embeddings, but crucially on whether that information shapes the latent geometry consumed by planners. SCALE demonstrates that aligning latent distances with state distances is essential for effective planning in world models.

Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive world models plan by scoring predicted terminal embeddings against a goal embedding using a cost defined on the representation itself. Two prominent strategies for obtaining non-collapsed representations are to inherit a pretrained feature space, as in DINO-WM, and to learn an embedding end to end with anti-collapse regularization, as in LeWorldModel (LeWM) with SIGReg. These strategies show complementary strengths across tasks. Although task-relevant state is decodable from the full embeddings of both models, DINO-WM's leading principal components usually retain substantially more state information than LeWM's. Because Euclidean planning costs are dominated by high-variance directions, this difference affects how strongly state can influence candidate selection. We propose SCALE (State-CAlibrated Latent Embeddings) to give the end-to-end LeWM representation the favorable geometric property observed in DINO-WM. SCALE induces this property by correlating sampled pairwise latent distances with distances in a standardized task-relevant state space, without replacing LeWM's learned encoder. Across five tasks, three planning solvers, and five compute budgets, SCALE improves every task--solver average over LeWM. A latent-to-state regression control matches or exceeds SCALE's full-embedding decodability yet leaves latent--state distance alignment essentially unchanged and yields less consistent planning gains. SCALE adds a single lightweight training-time regularizer and no planning-time overhead. These results show that planning depends not only on whether task-relevant information is present, but also on whether it shapes the geometry consumed by the planner.

</details>


### [369] [Advancing Open and Reproducible Relational Learning: RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel and RPI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16319)
*Adrian Hayler,Klemens Flöge,Alan Arazi,Rishabh Ranjan,Jure Leskovec,Felix Birkel,Brendan Roof,Anurag Garg,Kristina Collins,Lydia Sidhoum,Jonas Kübler,Siyuan Guo,Oscar Key,Jan Hendrik Metzen,Rylee Grace,David Salinas,Arthur Cahu,Simon Bing,Benjamin Jäger,Tuana Çelik,Mihir Manium,Vitor Monteiro,Jake Robertson,Jerry Chen,Eliott Kalfon,Tomás Pereda,Lilly Wehrhahn,Dominik Safaric,Tobias Schroeder,Georg Grab,Diana Kriuchkova,Clara Cornu,Philipp Singer,Nick Erickson,Vahid Balazadeh,Marie Salmon,Simone Alessi,Kürşat Kaya,Philipp Jund,Léo Grinsztajn,Yann LeCun,Bernhard Schölkopf,Madelon Hulsebos,Lennart Purucker,Sauraj Gambhir,Frank Hutter,Noah Hollmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Prior Labs' alpha release of three open-source software tools for relational learning: RelArena-α (a unified benchmarking framework), TabPFN-Rel (a relational model that currently ranks first), and RPI (a relational predictive interface for easier adoption).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The relational learning community lacks reliable, reproducible ways to compare different methods on emerging datasets and tasks. There's a need for standardized evaluation protocols and tools to accelerate research towards meaningful real-world impact.

Method: The authors developed three open-source tools: 1) RelArena-α - a unified framework for running and comparing baselines on RelBench v1 with standardized data loading, evaluation protocols, and tuning regimes, inspired by established tabular benchmarks. 2) TabPFN-Rel - a purpose-built relational harness for TabPFN-3 that improves upon RDBLearn. 3) RPI - a model-agnostic interface for defining problems on new databases and applying models from RelArena-α.

Result: TabPFN-Rel is currently ranked first among models on RelArena-α, serving as a strong baseline. The results add evidence that flattening relational databases into single tables remains competitive with specialized relational architectures on real-world tasks.

Conclusion: This alpha release represents an initial commitment to open science and collaboration with the community. The tools aim to catalyze progress in relational learning by providing standardized evaluation frameworks and practical interfaces for both researchers and early-adopting practitioners.

Abstract: This first release of Prior Labs in relational learning shows our continued commitment to open science. We open-source three pieces of software that we expect to accelerate research in the field towards meaningful real-world impact. We aim to steer further development based on feedback from, and in collaboration with, the community. Given the early stage of development, our $α$-release targets researchers and early-adopting practitioners. Over the past years, a variety of datasets and tasks for relational learning have emerged, but the community has not converged on a reliable, reproducible way to compare different methods on these tasks. Our $α$-release, RelArena-$α$, provides a unified framework for running and comparing baselines on RelBench v1 by standardizing data loading, evaluation protocols, tuning regimes, and support for systems with custom tuning, inspired by established tabular benchmarks such as TabArena. We plan to work with the research community to further develop RelArena-$α$ into a catalyst for progress in the relational learning community. We release the initial version of TabPFN-Rel, a purpose-built relational harness for TabPFN-3. Currently ranked first among models on RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel makes key improvements upon RDBLearn. Beyond its ranking, TabPFN-Rel serves as a strong baseline, adding to the growing evidence that flattening a relational database into a single table remains competitive with specialized relational architectures on real-world tasks.
  To facilitate adoption of relational learning methods in research and industry, we release an initial $α$-version of our Relational Predictive Interface, RPI, an open-source, model-agnostic interface that enables early adopters to easily define problems on new databases and apply any model implemented in RelArena-$α$, including TabPFN-Rel, to these problems.

</details>


### [370] [Transfer Learning of Keystroke Dynamics for Cross-Device User Authentication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16334)
*Nuwan Kaluarachchi,Sevvandi Kandanaarachchi,Kristen Moore,Arathi Arakala,Conrad Sanderson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Transfer learning approach for cross-device keystroke authentication using limited training data and extended feature sets achieves state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Keystroke dynamics work well for single-device authentication but face challenges in cross-device scenarios due to distribution drifts caused by different form factors (phone vs tablet), requiring adaptation of learned patterns.

Method: Uses inductive transfer learning to adapt keystroke dynamics from one device to another, combines adapted data with limited training data from the secondary device, employs extended keystroke feature sets for better discrimination, and trains a robust binary classifier.

Result: Achieves equal error rate of 14.2% on BBMAS dataset for cross-device scenario, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The proposed cross-device authentication system using transfer learning effectively addresses distribution drift issues, demonstrating practical feasibility for real-world applications requiring multi-device behavioral biometric authentication.

Abstract: Keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) can be used as a behavioural biometric modality for user authentication, with applications such as fraud prevention. While the modality has been shown to work well for single device authentication, its application to cross-device scenarios is more challenging. Dynamics learned on one device (eg., phone) may not be directly applicable to authentication on a secondary device with a different form factor (eg., tablet) due to changes in typing patterns that can lead to distribution drifts. To address this, we propose a cross-device user authentication system based on inductive transfer learning, where keystroke dynamics learned on one device are adapted to a secondary device. The adapted data is then combined with necessarily limited training data for the secondary device, which is used to robustly train a binary classifier. Furthermore, an extended set of keystroke features is used to better capture discriminative dynamics. Experiments on the BBMAS dataset show that proposed system achieves an equal error rate of 14.2% for the cross-device scenario, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [371] [Task-Anchored Representation Shaping for Pre-Trained Model-Based Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16345)
*Zhiming Xu,Huiyu Yi,Zhen-Hao Xie,Baile Xu,Furao Shen,Jian Zhao,Suorong Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAILS is a lightweight post-PTM module that resolves cross-task ambiguity in continual learning by using fixed task anchors to compose relevant evidence across tasks and directly correct feature representations before prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While pre-trained models provide strong foundations for continual learning, adapting well to individual tasks doesn't guarantee reliable inference over all learned tasks due to cross-task ambiguity. Task boundaries are often artificial and semantically entangled, making inputs from unknown tasks ambiguous even with strong PTM features.

Method: TAILS (Task-Anchored Inference Latent Shaping) is a lightweight post-PTM module that uses fixed task anchors as persistent references. It interprets each sample's feature representation relative to these anchors, composes relevant evidence across tasks into latent recall, and directly corrects the feature representation before prediction without changing the original PTM, method-specific modules, or classifier.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple PTM-based continual learning paradigms show that TAILS improves both classification and task-inference performance with modest parameter overhead and negligible inference cost.

Conclusion: TAILS effectively resolves cross-task ambiguity at the representation level while being lightweight and compatible with diverse continual learning approaches, demonstrating that addressing representation-level ambiguity is key to reliable continual inference.

Abstract: Pre-trained models (PTMs) provide a strong foundation for continual learning by offering stable representations that facilitate lightweight adaptation to new tasks. However, adapting well to each task does not ensure reliable inference over all learned tasks. Since task boundaries are often artificial and semantically entangled, an input from an unknown task can remain ambiguous even with strong PTM features, making cross-task prediction a key bottleneck. We propose Task-Anchored Inference Latent Shaping (TAILS), a lightweight post-PTM module that can be integrated into diverse continual learners and optimized through a decoupled step. TAILS uses fixed task anchors as persistent references to accumulated knowledge. It interprets each sample's feature representation relative to these references, then composes relevant evidence across tasks into latent recall. Rather than selecting a task-specific path or adjusting classifier outputs, TAILS uses latent recall to directly correct the feature representation before prediction. It therefore resolves cross-task ambiguity at the representation level, while leaving the original PTM, method-specific modules, and classifier unchanged. Extensive experiments across multiple PTM-based continual learning paradigms show that TAILS can improve classification and task-inference performance with modest parameter overhead and negligible inference cost.

</details>


### [372] [OceanDepths: A Global Dataset of Paired Subsurface and Surface Ocean Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16373)
*Simon Donike,Ruben Cartuyvels,Antonino Ian Ferola,Elisa Carli,Diego Fernandez Prieto,Marie-Helene Rio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OceanDepths is a first-of-its-kind AI-ready dataset pairing satellite surface data (SST, SSS, SSH) with co-located subsurface temperature/salinity profiles at 0.1°×0.1° resolution globally (2000-2024), providing a challenging testbed for AI methods due to extreme subsurface sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The world's oceans are critically underobserved compared to land or atmosphere. No standardized, high-resolution dataset couples satellite surface fields to co-located in situ depth profiles in AI-ready format for comprehensive ocean understanding.

Method: Created OceanDepths dataset by pairing satellite-derived L4 products (SST, SSS, SSH) with EN4 subsurface temperature/salinity profiles, complemented by GLORYS12 ocean reanalysis data. Provides 0.1°×0.1° spatial resolution, weekly temporal resolution (2000-2024), with 9.5M paired profiles interpolated to 50 standardized depth levels globally.

Result: Produced first open, global, regridded AI-ready dataset with 4D multivariate structure covering surface and subsurface ocean properties. Dataset includes configurable system for spatial patching and demonstrates subsurface state reconstruction with baseline models. Available on Hugging Face.

Conclusion: OceanDepths addresses critical gap in ocean observation by providing standardized, high-resolution, AI-ready dataset that can support development of observation-based forecast methods and serve as challenging testbed for novel AI approaches due to extreme sparsity of subsurface observations (~0.01% per depth level).

Abstract: Despite comprising over 70\% of its surface, the world's oceans are critically underobserved compared to the land surface or the atmosphere.Understanding the global ocean requires jointly observing its surface and subsurface structure, yet no standardized, high-resolution dataset couples satellite surface fields to co-located \emph{in situ} depth profiles in an AI-ready format.Existing resources either consist of model-reconstructed gridded products rather than observations, cover only a single variable or basin, or operate at resolutions too coarse for mesoscale dynamics.We introduce \textsc{OceanDepths}, the first open, global, regridded AI-ready dataset that pairs satellite-derived sea surface temperature (SST), sea surface salinity (SSS), and sea surface height (SSH) L4 products with co-located EN4 subsurface temperature and salinity profiles, complemented by matched GLORYS12 ocean reanalysis data to support comparisons or multi-stage learning.The dataset spans 2000--2024 at \SI{0.1}{\degree}$\times$\SI{0.1}{\degree} spatial resolution and at weekly temporal resolution, covering the entire globe's sea surface and with over 9.5 million paired profiles interpolated to 50 standardized depth levels.We provide a configurable system to split the globe in equally sized spatial patches.The 4D multivariate structure, high resolution, long temporal extent, and extreme sparsity of subsurface observations (${\sim}$0.01\% per depth level) make \textsc{OceanDepths}a challenging testbed for novel AI methods.We demonstrate subsurface state reconstruction as an example task with simple baseline models, but also envision \textsc{OceanDepths}to support the development of observation-based forecast methods and other related tasks.\added{Available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ESA-philab/OceanDepths.}

</details>


### [373] [Coverage-Maximizing Multinomial Subset Routing under Operational Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16375)
*Quan Zhou,Yiyan Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MSR is a new online routing framework using multinomial policies to sample experts, focusing on best-expert rewards rather than additive rewards, with OMD-Approachability algorithm achieving optimal regret and constraint violation rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current routing methods assume additive rewards from deterministic expert subsets, but many real-world applications (like routing across specialized models) only reward the best-performing expert in the selected subset, creating a gap in existing combinatorial bandit and subset-selection frameworks.

Method: Multinomial Subset Routing (MSR) maintains a multinomial distribution over K experts, samples M experts i.i.d. each round, and uses only distinct experts. The OMD-Approachability algorithm combines online mirror descent with Blackwell's Approachability to handle bandit feedback where only the winner's reward is observed, while satisfying long-term operational constraints.

Result: Theoretical analysis proves OMD-Approachability achieves O(1/√T) regret for both reward maximization and constraint violation, which is optimal. Empirical validation on a real-world crowdsourcing dataset demonstrates practical effectiveness.

Conclusion: MSR provides a novel routing framework that better captures real-world scenarios where only the best expert matters, with provable optimal performance under operational constraints using the OMD-Approachability algorithm.

Abstract: We introduce Multinomial Subset Routing (MSR), a new online routing framework over $K$ experts in which the learner keeps a multinomial routing policy instead of a deterministic subset of experts. At each round, the learner samples $M$ experts i.i.d. from the multinomial policy, and the resulting set of distinct sampled experts forms the routed subset.
  The reward depends only on the best-performing expert(s) in the routed subset. This reward structure arises naturally in routing across specialized models but is not captured by standard combinatorial bandits or subset-selection methods, which optimize deterministic subsets and typically assume additive rewards. We require the selection to satisfy several long-term, two-sided operational constraints under bandit feedback, observing only the winner's reward each round. We propose OMD-Approachability, combining online mirror descent with Blackwell's Approachability, and prove it achieves $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ regret in both reward and constraint violation. We ground the framework in practical application domains and validate it empirically on a real-world crowdsourcing dataset.

</details>


### [374] [FETERS: Few-Shot Early Time-Series Classification via Effective Ratio Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16385)
*Chen-An Tai,Yujia Wu,Vincent S. Tseng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FETERS is a few-shot early time-series classification framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance without needing to train a separate stopping module, using class-wise leave-one-out evaluation and combining Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing early time-series classification methods assume access to sufficient labeled training data, which is unrealistic in real-world applications with limited annotation. Under few-shot settings, learning both a sample-level stopping module and effective classification features becomes challenging.

Method: FETERS avoids training an additional stopping module by selecting a dataset-level stopping ratio through class-wise leave-one-out evaluation on the support set. It uses a penalty-based reward function to manage the accuracy-earliness trade-off. For classification, it combines Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations.

Result: Extensive experiments on 69 public datasets across 14 domains show FETERS achieves state-of-the-art performance in 5-shot setting with the highest average harmonic mean, best HM on 38 datasets, and outperforms current SOTA on 44 datasets. It also remains competitive in full-shot settings.

Conclusion: FETERS effectively addresses the few-shot early time-series classification problem by eliminating the need for training a separate stopping module while achieving strong performance across various domains through its novel combination of evaluation strategy and feature representation.

Abstract: Early time-series classification (ETSC) aims to make accurate predictions from partially observed time series as early as possible. Although various stopping mechanisms and feature learning strategies have been developed for ETSC, most existing methods assume access to sufficient labeled training data, which may be unrealistic in applications with limited annotation. Under limited supervision, learning an additional sample-level stopping module and extracting effective classification features can both become challenging. In this paper, we propose FETERS, a few-shot ETSC framework that selects a dataset-level stopping ratio through class-wise leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation on the support set and uses a penalty-based reward function to manage the accuracy-earliness trade-off, thereby avoiding the need to train an additional stopping module. FETERS further combines Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations for classification. Extensive experiments on 69 public datasets spanning 14 domains show that FETERS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in the 5-shot setting, with the highest average harmonic mean (HM) and the best HM on 38 datasets, while outperforming the current SOTA method on 44 datasets. FETERS also remains competitive in the full-shot setting, demonstrating its effectiveness in managing the accuracy-earliness trade-off.

</details>


### [375] [SoftModel: A Neural Model That Grows Its Own Topology -- Governed Structural Growth for Continual In-Service Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16409)
*Zhoumin Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A system for lifelong learning where model structure is never frozen, using governance to control structural changes (width, hierarchy, composition) based on actual performance needs rather than predefined topologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current neural systems freeze twice: after training ends and by having fixed topologies. This limits lifelong learning in non-stationary environments. The paper proposes total plasticity as an axiom - nothing in the model should ever be frozen, enabling continual, in-service learning on changing data streams.

Method: Developed a growable soft model with an algebra of structural operators (width, hierarchy, composition, input interfaces, grown cycles, attention heads) that are exact, budgeted, and audited. Changes are governed by a held-out reality gate that treats parametric and structural changes uniformly. The system is operated end-to-end by a production LLM.

Result: Shows that governed growth preserves learning ability across long task sequences in standard continual-learning benchmarks. The marginal value of new capacity was unobservable before adoption, so growth governance works ex-post. The system enables stability through audit properties rather than immobility.

Conclusion: Total plasticity enables lifelong learning where structure follows demand, removing the silent capacity ceiling of fixed topologies. Stability becomes an audit property rather than requiring freezing. The governance approach extends to evaluative signals and provides a complete map of successes and failures through pre-registered experiments.

Abstract: Today, a neural system is almost always used in two phases -- trained, then deployed -- and in that regime it freezes twice: training ends, and the topology itself was never a degree of freedom. We take the opposite premise as an axiom -- total plasticity: no part of a model, including its structure, is ever frozen -- and derive the governance a lifelong learner then requires. The design's target regime is continual, in-service learning: a long-lived model on a non-stationary stream, whose stability comes from governance rather than immobility and whose capacity follows demand. The result is a growable soft model: an algebra of structural operators (width, hierarchy, composition, input interface, grown cycles, attention heads), each exact at application, budgeted, and audited, with adoption decided solely by a held-out reality gate that treats parametric and structural change uniformly. A complete from-scratch system realizes the whole account; its factory surface is operated end-to-end by a production LLM. Two conclusions follow from the axiom by construction: stability under lifelong change becomes an audit property of the lifecycle, and structure that follows demand removes the silent cap a fixed topology places on later capability where the capacity floor binds. A third is measured: in the worlds where this was measured, the marginal value of new capacity was unobservable before adoption, so workable growth governance took its ex-post form. The same governance extends to evaluative signals, and the core method is evaluated on standard continual-learning benchmarks, where governed growth preserves the ability to keep learning along long task sequences. A pre-registered experimental program adjudicates the mechanism and value claims on the tested problems and reports its failures at full prominence; the map -- positive and negative -- is the contribution.

</details>


### [376] [TRACE-CASH: Trial-History-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Configuration Exploration in Time-Series CASH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16410)
*Yu-Han Huang,Yujia Wu,Vincent S. Tseng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACECASH is a novel hybrid sequential optimizer that combines actor-critic methods with fixed rules for time-series forecasting model selection and hyperparameter optimization, outperforming various alternative approaches across multiple evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a lack of controlled comparisons for heterogeneous search methods in time-series combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimization (TS-CASH), which is complicated by temporal choices, chronological validation, and costly evaluations. Existing methods haven't been systematically compared under a shared TS-CASH evaluation protocol.

Method: TRACECASH is a task-local hybrid sequential optimizer that combines grouped actor-critic candidate generation with fixed rules for model coverage, validation-guided exploitation, and exploration after stalled progress. It uses a model actor to propose initial forecasting models, three model-conditioned actors for temporal, architectural, and training actions, and a model-specific decoder to construct the final configuration.

Result: TRACECASH achieved the lowest mean rank on both MASE and WQL metrics compared to six alternative methods (random, Bayesian, evolutionary, multi-objective, and language-model-assisted search) across 41 dataset-frequency task variants. It also had the lowest window-averaged test-MASE rank in predefined full and late windows.

Conclusion: The complete TRACECASH procedure is competitive among the evaluated methods for time-series forecasting model selection and hyperparameter optimization, demonstrating effectiveness in the complex TS-CASH problem domain.

Abstract: Combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimization (CASH) searches a conditional space in which the selected model determines which hyperparameters are active. In time-series forecasting, temporal choices, chronological validation, and costly evaluations further complicate this search. Controlled comparisons of heterogeneous search methods under a shared time-series CASH (TS-CASH) evaluation protocol remain limited. Within this setting, we study TRACECASH, a task-local hybrid sequential optimizer combining grouped actor-critic candidate generation with fixed rules for model coverage, validation-guided exploitation, and exploration after stalled progress. A model actor proposes an initial forecasting model; three model-conditioned actors generate temporal, architectural, and training actions; and a modelspecific decoder constructs the configuration ultimately evaluated. We compare TRACE-CASH with six alternatives spanning random, Bayesian, evolutionary, multi-objective, and language-model-assisted search across 41 dataset-frequency task variants. TRACE-CASH has the lowest mean rank on both MASE and WQL. Descriptively, it also has the lowest window-averaged test-MASE rank in the predefined full and late windows. These results support the complete TRACECASH procedure as competitive among the evaluated methods.

</details>


### [377] [Evolving Executable Pipeline Programs for AutoML with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16416)
*Sofoklis Kitharidis,Cor J. Veenman,Jan N. van Rijn,Thomas Bäck,Niki van Stein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LACE is an AutoML framework that searches over complete executable Python pipeline programs using evolutionary algorithms and LLMs as variation operators, outperforming traditional AutoML systems while providing fully inspectable and editable pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional AutoML systems are limited to searching within predefined spaces of components and hyperparameters, cannot generate novel pipeline structures, and produce black-box models that practitioners cannot easily inspect or modify directly.

Method: LACE uses an evolutionary loop that maintains a population of scikit-learn-compatible Python classes, with a large language model (GPT-5.4-mini) acting as the variation operator to generate new pipeline programs. It searches over complete executable pipeline programs rather than predefined components.

Result: On 68 OpenML classification tasks, LACE significantly outperformed auto-sklearn, H2O, and XGBoost baselines, with no significant difference against AutoGluon (the strongest search-based system). While newer tabular foundation models achieve higher accuracy on supported tasks, LACE provides complete coverage and editable pipelines.

Conclusion: LACE's main contribution is not raw accuracy but a code-based search space that offers complete coverage, produces pipelines practitioners can reuse directly, and allows extension through prompt editing rather than framework modification, bridging the gap between automated ML and human interpretability.

Abstract: Automated machine learning (AutoML) systems search for pipelines within a space of preprocessing operators, learners, and hyper-parameters specified in advance: they can select and tune known components, but cannot produce structure outside that space. We present LACE, an AutoML framework that instead searches over complete executable pipeline programs: an evolutionary loop maintains a population of scikit-learn-compatible Python classes, and a large language model acts as the variation operator. To our knowledge, LACE is the first to formulate general tabular pipeline AutoML this way, evaluated on standardized OpenML tasks under a leakage-controlled protocol that withholds dataset identity from the generator. Because every candidate is ordinary Python, the returned pipeline and the search that produced it can be inspected and edited directly, rather than only through a framework's model objects. On 68 OpenML classification tasks, LACE with GPT-5.4-mini significantly outperforms auto-sklearn, H2O, and a fixed XGBoost baseline, with no detectable difference against AutoGluon, the strongest search-based system evaluated, while covering the full benchmark. Newer tabular foundation models are more accurate on the subset of tasks they support, but apply a fixed pretrained predictor rather than returning an editable task-specific program. LACE's contribution is therefore not raw accuracy but a search space defined by code: complete coverage, pipelines practitioners can reuse directly, and a component set extended by editing the prompt rather than the framework.

</details>


### [378] [PertMind: Eliciting Emergent Biological Reasoning in LLM via Reinforcement Learning on Cellular Perturbation Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16419)
*Zhenchao Tang,Xiaogang Xu,Tianxu Lv,Jiahui Guan,Jiale Zhou,Haohuai He,Zhi Song,Hanbo Huang,Jiehui Huang,Jiafei Wu,Zhe Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PertMind uses cellular perturbation atlases as reinforcement learning environments with experimental gene responses as rewards, enabling biological reasoning without manually curated biological reasoning traces. It improves perturbation-response prediction across diverse biological tasks while retaining general language capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current large language models can describe biological mechanisms, but scalable post-training still requires costly, manually curated biological reasoning traces. The authors seek to overcome this limitation by leveraging experimental data directly as training signals.

Method: Introduced PertMind, which combines trusted-trajectory supervised initialization with multi-level reinforcement signals (gene, pathway, and format-level). Uses cellular perturbation atlases as reinforcement learning environments where measured gene responses serve as computable rewards for biological reasoning.

Result: PertMind improved response inference in unseen cellular contexts while retaining general language capabilities. Transferred without task-specific post-training to multiple biological tasks: reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation. Generated biological profiles supporting competitive representations across multiscale downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Experimental reinforcement learning can concentrate reusable biological strategies already accessible to pretrained models. Perturbation-derived reinforcement learning offers a scalable route for transforming expanding experimental atlases into training environments for general-purpose biological reasoning, eliminating the need for costly manual curation of biological reasoning traces.

Abstract: Large language models can describe mechanisms, yet scalable post-training still depends on costly, manually curated biological reasoning traces. Here we show that cellular perturbation atlases can instead become reinforcement-learning environments, where measured gene responses provide computable rewards for biological reasoning. We introduce PertMind, which combines trusted-trajectory supervised initialization with gene-, pathway-, and format-level reinforcement signals. Trained only on forward perturbation-response prediction, PertMind improved response inference in unseen cellular contexts while retaining general language capabilities. It also transferred without task-specific post-training to reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation. PertMind further generated biological profiles that supported competitive gene, cell, and donor representations across multiscale downstream tasks. These results support the hypothesis that reinforcement on experimental endpoints can concentrate reusable biological strategies already accessible to pretrained models. More broadly, perturbation-derived reinforcement learning offers a scalable route for transforming expanding experimental atlases into training environments for general-purpose biological reasoning.

</details>


### [379] [Localized TabICLv2: Scaling Tabular In-Context Learning through k-NN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16429)
*Beimnet Bekele Guta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Localized TabICLv2 reduces inference costs by retrieving only k nearest training neighbors for each test point instead of using full training context, achieving significant speedups with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-context tabular ICL suffers from attention cost that grows with training-context size, limiting its ability to handle large datasets efficiently.

Method: Retrieves only k nearest training neighbours for each test point, measured by similarity in the model's Stage 2 row-representation space. No architectural changes needed, accuracy retention improved through additional Stage 2 and Stage 3 fine-tuning.

Result: On TabArena classification tasks: fine-tuned localized model retains 98.64% of Full TabICLv2 accuracy, achieves median 2.18× speedup in batch inference, and ~249× median speedup in single-query serving setting.

Conclusion: Localized TabICLv2 provides an efficient method to reduce inference costs while maintaining high accuracy through neighbor retrieval and targeted fine-tuning, making tabular ICL more practical for large datasets.

Abstract: Foundational models for tabular data have made significant progress in recent years, with TabICLv2 reporting state-of-the-art performance on several tabular classification tasks. However, full-context tabular ICL still suffers from attention cost that grows with the training-context size, which limits its ability to handle large datasets efficiently. Localized TabICLv2 introduces a method that reduces the inference cost of TabICLv2 by retrieving only the k nearest training neighbours for each test point, measured by similarity in the model's Stage 2 row-representation space, rather than using the full training context. This requires no architectural changes, and we show that accuracy retention can be improved through additional Stage 2 and Stage 3 fine-tuning. On TabArena classification tasks, the fine-tuned localized model retains 98.64% of Full TabICLv2 accuracy and it achieves a median 2.18$\times$ speedup in batch inference, and reaches approximately 249$\times$ median speedup in the single-query serving setting.

</details>


### [380] [Reference-free logged energy-oracle recovery for neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems: conforming Riesz reconstruction and archive-level selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16473)
*Karim Bounja,Lahcen Laayouni,Boujemaa Achchab,Abdeljalil Sakat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a reference-free selection method for neural PDE solutions using a computable Riesz monitor that provides energy-error bounds without needing exact solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural PDE training produces multiple checkpoints, but selecting the best one is problematic because exact energy errors are inaccessible (no exact solution), and loss-based selection doesn't necessarily recover the optimal solution. There's a need for a practical way to select the best neural approximation from training archives without reference solutions.

Method: Introduces a selection rule based on minimizing a computable conforming Riesz monitor for symmetric coercive variational problems. Uses exact residual-energy identity and conforming projection to create a monitor that serves as an unconditional lower bound converging monotonically to energy errors. Under saturation conditions, hierarchical enrichment provides computable upper estimates, creating lower-upper brackets. Proves uniform recovery for finite archives and addresses order-sensitivity issues in archive selection.

Result: The method achieves uniform recovery, convergence to logged-oracle error, and under saturation conditions provides near-oracle bounds with certification of unique selection. Demonstrates energy-scale calibration, oracle-level selection, and modest post-processing costs on diffusion and elasticity problems including non-manufactured perforated plates.

Conclusion: The proposed criterion successfully replaces inaccessible exact-error minimization with computable, training-independent post-training selection on the intrinsic energy-error scale. It requires only computed candidates and the variational problem, providing practical oracle-level selection for neural PDE approximations without needing exact solutions.

Abstract: Neural PDE training yields a finite checkpoint archive, yet its logged energy errors are inaccessible without the exact solution, while loss-based selection does not necessarily recover the logged energy oracle. For admissible neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems, we introduce a reference-free selection rule based on minimizing a computable conforming Riesz monitor. The exact residual-energy identity and conforming projection make the monitor an unconditional lower bound converging monotonically to each logged energy error under nested conforming refinement; under saturation, hierarchical enrichment yields a computable upper estimate and hence a lower-upper bracket. A key finding is that archive selection is order-sensitive: unresolved checkpoint-dependent components can reverse the oracle-non-oracle ranking at finite resolution, so checkpointwise recovery alone is insufficient. For finite archives, we prove uniform recovery, yielding convergence to the logged-oracle error and, without saturation, logged-oracle selection at sufficiently fine auxiliary resolution. Under saturation, the bracket gives a computable near-oracle bound and certifies unique logged-oracle selection upon interval separation. We also bound logging-resolution loss and certify oracle inclusion over prescribed comparison trajectories. The resulting criterion replaces inaccessible exact-error minimization by computable, training-independent post-training selection on the intrinsic energy-error scale, requiring only the computed candidates and the variational problem. Experiments on diffusion and elasticity, including a non-manufactured perforated plate, demonstrate energy-scale calibration, oracle-level selection, and modest post-processing cost.

</details>


### [381] [Pallas: A Proactive KV Cache Migration Framework for LLM Inference in AI-RAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16477)
*Tianhang Ding,Jianchun Liu,Hongli Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pallas is a proactive KV-cache migration framework for AI-RAN that prepares inference state at predicted target base stations before handover, reducing service interruption time and inter-token latency during LLM serving in mobile networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In AI-RAN systems, cellular handover separates mobile users from their LLM inference state (KV cache) when moving between base stations. Existing approaches either keep inference at the source (increasing latency) or recover state at target (causing service interruption), both with significant performance penalties.

Method: Pallas proactively migrates KV-cache by predicting handover targets and preparing inference state in parallel with ongoing inference. It partitions token sequences into historical prefix and evolving suffix, with target reconstructing prefix through local prefill while source streams KV blocks for suffix. An online scheduler selects prefetching window based on mobility predictions and runtime telemetry.

Result: Across three LLMs and 100-500 Mbps inter-base station links, the vLLM-based prototype reduces average service interruption time by factors of 2.28-89.68 compared to target-side recovery approaches, and lowers average inter-token latency by 16.0%-50.0% compared to source-side forwarding.

Conclusion: Pallas effectively addresses the handover problem in AI-RAN by proactively preparing inference state at predicted targets, significantly improving both service continuity and latency performance for LLM serving in mobile networks.

Abstract: AI-RAN brings large language model (LLM) serving close to mobile users, but cellular handover can separate an active request from its inference state: the user attaches to a target base station (gNB) while the large and growing key-value (KV) cache remains at the source. Retaining inference at the source preserves service continuity but persistently increases inter-token latency (ITL), whereas recovering the state at the target restores serving locality but requires KV-cache transfer, recomputation, or a combination of both only after handover, directly prolonging service interruption time (SIT).
  This work presents Pallas, a \textit{proactive} KV-cache migration framework that prepares the inference state at the predicted target before handover, in parallel with ongoing source-side inference and token delivery. At the preparation trigger, Pallas partitions the token sequence into a stable historical prefix and an evolving suffix. The target reconstructs the prefix through local prefill, while the source streams the KV blocks generated for the suffix. At handover, the target assembles both portions into an up-to-date KV cache and resumes decoding locally, leaving only unfinished preparation to contribute to SIT. An online scheduler selects the \textit{prefetching window}, which determines how early preparation begins before handover, based on mobility predictions and runtime telemetry. Across three LLMs and $100$--$500~\mathrm{Mbps}$ inter-gNB links, our vLLM-based prototype reduces average SIT by factors of $2.28$--$89.68$ over target-side recovery approaches and lowers average ITL by $16.0\%$--$50.0\%$ compared with source-side forwarding.

</details>


### [382] [Graph Machine Learning: An Opportunity for Power Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16494)
*Martin Sadric,Sebastian Pütz,Christian Nauck,Veit Hagenmeyer,Frank Hellmann,Dirk Witthaut,Benjamin Schäfer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Survey of nearly 800 papers on graph machine learning applications in power systems, identifying opportunities for GML to address operational challenges while highlighting gaps in benchmarks and reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Power systems face increasing complexity from renewable integration, decentralization, and real-time demands. Traditional model-based methods are too slow, while machine learning offers faster alternatives. Graph machine learning provides natural framework for incorporating grid topology as inductive bias.

Method: Comprehensive survey and analysis of nearly 800 papers at intersection of GML and power systems, covering applications in forecasting, state estimation, optimization, control, fault diagnosis, and cybersecurity.

Result: Power systems provide rich benchmark setting for GML with hard physical constraints, multi-scale dynamics, safety requirements, and scarce data. GML offers scalable, topology-aware approximations with good generalization and computational efficiency. Identifies limited real-world deployment, need for interpretable models, and scarcity of standardized benchmarks and open datasets.

Conclusion: Calls for community to prioritize benchmark studies and release open datasets/models to improve reproducibility and scientific credibility. Provides structured requirements catalog for ML-ready power grid benchmarks to guide future dataset development.

Abstract: Modern power systems face growing operational complexity driven by the integration of renewable energy sources, decentralization, and the need for real-time decision-making across a wide range of timescales. Addressing these challenges traditionally relies on model-based methods that, while accurate, can be too slow for operational demands. Machine learning (ML) has therefore emerged as a faster, data-driven alternative. As grid topology plays a central role in power system operation, graph machine learning (GML) methods offer a natural framework for incorporating topological dependencies as an inductive bias. We survey nearly 800 papers at the intersection of GML and power systems, covering forecasting, state estimation, optimization, control, fault diagnosis, and cybersecurity. Power systems constitute an unusually rich benchmark setting for GML, as they combine hard physical constraints, multi-scale dynamics, safety-critical requirements, and scarce labeled data within a single, well-defined domain. Conversely, power systems can benefit from utilizing GML to complement classical solvers, as GML provide scalable, topology-aware approximations with promising generalization and computational efficiency. We identify open challenges, including limited real-world deployment and the need for interpretable models in safety-critical settings. Despite the rapidly growing number of publications, standardized benchmarks and open datasets remain scarce, leaving many results difficult to reproduce and undermining the long-term scientific credibility of the field. We further derive a structured requirements catalog for ML-ready power grid benchmarks, intended to guide future dataset development and improve reproducibility across studies. We call on the community to prioritize dedicated benchmark studies and the release of open datasets and models.

</details>


### [383] [When Tool-Backed Skill Retrieval Fails: Source-Style Collapse in Executable Capability Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16502)
*Yiqi Liu,Joseph James,Yang Wang,Chenghao Xiao,Chenghua Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ToolScout: A source-aware routing method that prevents source-style collapse in tool retrieval for large-scale agents by using TF-IDF fingerprints as routing guards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale agents rely on retrieval to access external capabilities, but retrieval layers can silently fail even with fixed capability corpora due to "source-style collapse" - where retrievers fine-tuned on one source fail on another source in the same benchmark.

Method: Proposes ToolScout, a source-aware routing method that uses TF-IDF fingerprints as routing guards to identify source styles where fine-tuned retrievers are likely to fail. Demonstrates this approach on mixed query streams and verifies the method works across different tool representations.

Result: TF-IDF-based routing dramatically improves coverage from 22.3% to 86.1% on mixed 4,996-query streams. Across five collapsed sources, 20 matched examples raise coverage-weighted global top-1 proxy from 1.3% to 53.9%. The failure and routing behaviors persist across different tool representations.

Conclusion: Source-style collapse is a significant problem in tool retrieval for agents, and TF-IDF fingerprints provide an effective, cheap signal for detecting mismatch and enabling source-aware routing through ToolScout, which substantially improves retrieval coverage and performance.

Abstract: Large-scale agents increasingly rely on retrieval to access external capabilities. We study this retrieval gate in structured tools and APIs, a measurable class of tool-backed executable skills that must be surfaced before an agent can plan, incorporate, or act. In this setting the retrieval layer can silently fail even when the capability corpus is fixed: on ToolRet, a retriever fine-tuned on one source-specific slice collapses on another source-specific slice of the same benchmark, with FT-1100 despite its higher lexical overlap with the gold tools. We call this failure mode source-style collapse. Query-side TF-IDF fingerprints flag source styles on which the fine-tuned retriever is likely to fail better than semantic or length-based proxies, giving a cheap signal for mismatch over a fixed tool corpus. We propose ToolScout, a source-aware routing method that uses this signal as a routing guard: on the mixed 4,996-query stream, TF-IDF-based routing raises coverage from 22.3% to 86.1%, and across five collapsed sources 20 matched examples raise the coverage-weighted global top-1 proxy from 1.3% to 53.9%. The same failure and routing behaviors persist when tools are rerendered as executable skill cards, which rules out raw API-schema format as the sole cause.

</details>


### [384] [One Residual with Three Reuses: A Wristband Front End for Gesture Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16542)
*Sam Rifaki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A wrist-worn hand sensing system combining 60 GHz FMCW radar with IMU using shared residual generator achieves energy-efficient gesture detection and robust pose tracking under occlusion/drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous wrist-worn hand sensing for gesture interfaces and motor symptom monitoring needs always-on operation within coin-cell power budget while maintaining robustness under occlusion and on-body sensor drift.

Method: Design study of wristband front-end with classifier wake-up gating, mmWave vs IMU routing, and innovation-based EKF measurement reweighting all sharing a single on-chip residual generator, implemented on edge MCU with minimal memory footprint.

Result: System achieves detection probability of 0.72/0.80 at 1% false-alarm rate across four public datasets, reduces classifier invocation energy by 47% at 90% gesture recall, and lowers pose tracking error by 4.6× under measurement bias drift compared to baseline.

Conclusion: The shared residual generator approach enables energy-efficient, robust wrist-worn hand sensing for continuous gesture detection and motor monitoring within power constraints, with hardware implementation deferred to follow-on work.

Abstract: Continuous wrist-worn hand sensing for gesture interfaces and motor symptom monitoring needs an always-on front end that fits inside a coin-cell power budget while pairing a micro-electro-mechanical-systems (MEMS) inertial measurement unit (IMU) with a 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar to stay robust under occlusion and on-body drift. We present a design study of such a wristband front end in which classifier wake-up gating, mmWave versus IMU routing, and innovation-based EKF measurement reweighting share a single on-chip residual generator. The shared generator occupies 14.4 KB of program memory and 278 B of state and runs at 110K multiply-accumulates (MACs) per frame on an Ambiq Apollo4 Blue Plus class edge microcontroller unit (MCU). Across four public sensor data corpora (IPN Hand, SHREC 2021, MiliPoint 60 GHz FMCW radar, EAT-Radar) the front end reaches detection probability $P_D = 0.72/0.80$ at a 1% false-alarm rate, sustains a 47% classifier invocation energy reduction at 90% gesture detection recall, and lowers pose tracking root-mean-square error by $4.6\times$ under measurement bias drift relative to an adaptive Kalman with $R$-inflation baseline. Measured silicon power and on-body capture are deferred to follow-on hardware; the contribution here is a design study.

</details>


### [385] [Learning Generalizable Reconstruction of High-Dimensional Neural Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16569)
*Anima Kujur,Zahra Monfared*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PCA-DMD is a scalable operator-theoretic framework for reconstructing long-duration neural recordings by learning linear Koopman evolution in PCA latent space, achieving high accuracy and zero-shot cross-subject generalization without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate reconstruction of long-duration local field potential (LFP) recordings is challenging due to their high-resolution, multichannel, transient nature and variability across subjects, requiring methods that can handle these complexities effectively.

Method: PCA-DMD segments LFP recordings into overlapping windows, projects them into compact PCA space, learns linear Koopman evolution in the latent space using Dynamic Mode Decomposition, and reconstructs continuous signals through inverse projection and overlap-add aggregation.

Result: PCA-DMD outperformed Classical DMD, SpDMD, MrDMD, and HODMD on hippocampal recordings (KLD=0.0761, HD=0.0847). It achieved high zero-shot cross-subject generalization (correlations 0.9504-0.9800) without fine-tuning, maintained stable reconstruction across 400,000-900,000 samples, and validated on independent Neuropixels data (mean correlation 0.7427).

Conclusion: PCA-DMD provides an interpretable, generalizable, and computationally scalable framework for reconstructing high-dimensional neural dynamics, with Koopman spectral analyses revealing dominant eigenvalues near the unit circle for stable dynamics representation.

Abstract: Accurate reconstruction of long-duration neural recordings is challenging because local field potentials (LFPs) are high-resolution, multichannel, transient, and variable across subjects. We present PCA-DMD, a scalable operator-theoretic framework that segments LFP recordings into overlapping windows, projects them into a compact PCA space, learns linear Koopman evolution in the latent space, and reconstructs continuous signals through inverse projection and overlap-add aggregation. On 200,000-sample hippocampal recordings, PCA-DMD outperformed Classical DMD, SpDMD, MrDMD, and HODMD, achieving KLD=0.0761 and HD=0.0847. In all-pair cross-subject zero-shot generalization at 300,000 samples, correlations were 0.9504-0.9800, with HD=0.0010-0.0072 and KLD=0.0005-0.0022, without target-subject fine-tuning. Out-of-sample temporal prediction showed close one-step agreement on temporally held-out LFP segments across the unseen interval and multiple channels. Scalability analysis from 400,000 to 900,000 samples showed stable zero-shot reconstruction, with mean correlation remaining about 0.965-0.968 while computational cost increased predictably. External validation on an independent 93-channel Allen Neuropixels recording yielded mean and median channel-wise correlations of 0.7427 and 0.7990, respectively. Koopman spectral and mode analyses revealed dominant eigenvalues concentrated near the unit circle. PCA-DMD therefore provides an interpretable, generalizable, and computationally scalable framework for reconstructing high-dimensional neural dynamics.

</details>


### [386] [Variational Outlier-Robust Gaussian Process Regression with Generative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16606)
*Arslan Majal,Aamir Hussain Chughtai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Robust Gaussian process regression model that handles outliers through observation-specific contamination modeling and variational learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gaussian process regression is sensitive to outliers due to its conventional Gaussian observation likelihood, which can lead to inaccurate model learning and predictions when data contains outliers.

Method: Introduces a generative GPR model that captures observation-specific contamination and adaptively mitigates outlier influence. Uses variational generalized expectation-maximization to learn latent variables and GPR model parameters.

Result: The method remains competitive with and often outperforms robust GPR baselines in prediction accuracy across synthetic and real datasets under various contamination settings. Maintains cubic computational scaling comparable to standard GPR methods.

Conclusion: The proposed robust GPR model effectively handles outliers while maintaining competitive performance and computational efficiency compared to existing robust GPR methods.

Abstract: Outliers can substantially distort Gaussian process regression (GPR) due to its conventional Gaussian observation likelihood, leading to inaccurate model learning and prediction. To address this limitation, this article introduces a generative GPR model that captures observation-specific contamination and adaptively mitigates the influence of outliers. Subsequently, a variational generalized expectation-maximization procedure is used to learn the latent variables and GPR model parameters. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets under different contamination settings demonstrate that the proposed method remains competitive with-and in several cases outperforms-robust GPR baselines in prediction accuracy. Moreover, the proposed method shares the cubic computational scaling of the compared GPR methods.

</details>


### [387] [Hoeffding adaptive splitting trees for data stream classification with concept drift and ensemble learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16659)
*Daniel Nowak Assis,Jean Paul Barddal,Fabrício Enembreck*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees (HAST) that combine periodic splitting (for ensemble diversity) with adaptive splitting (for concept drift adaptation), achieving state-of-the-art performance in data stream classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Hoeffding Trees in ensembles lack adaptability, while adaptive-splitting trees as base learners often fail to create sufficient diversity within ensembles. There's a need for base learners that can both adapt to concept drift and promote ensemble diversity.

Method: Proposed two novel decision tree models called Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees (HAST) that combine periodic splitting strategy (from Hoeffding Trees) with adaptive splitting mechanisms using change detection algorithms to identify performance decay and determine split points.

Result: HAST models enhance ensemble performance and achieve state-of-the-art results across comprehensive evaluation including benchmark comparisons, computational cost analysis, and concept drift adaptation.

Conclusion: Combining periodic and adaptive splitting strategies in decision tree base learners addresses the diversity limitation of purely adaptive trees while maintaining adaptability, resulting in superior ensemble performance for data stream classification.

Abstract: Ensembles of decision trees are well-established methods for data stream classification. In ensemble learning, Hoeffding Trees are widely adopted as base learners, performing periodic split attempts according to the Hoeffding bound. Recent studies, however, indicate that this standard splitting mechanism lacks adaptability, while adaptive trees that trigger splits in response to performance degradation have achieved superior results. In this paper, we identify limitations in the use of adaptive-splitting decision trees as ensemble base learners, showing that change detectors often fail to promote sufficient diversity within ensembles. To address this issue, we propose two novel decision tree models, termed Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees. These models combine the periodic splitting strategy of Hoeffding Trees, which fosters ensemble diversity, with adaptive splitting mechanisms that employ change detection algorithms to identify performance decay and determine split points. Experimental results demonstrate that Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees enhance ensemble performance and achieve state-of-the-art results across a comprehensive evaluation, including benchmark comparisons, computational cost analysis, and concept drift adaptation.

</details>


### [388] [UniTAC: Universal Task-Aware Compression via Weighted Distortion Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16696)
*Homa Esfahanizadeh,Matin Mortaheb,Jinfeng Du,Harish Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniTAC is a single learned image codec that adapts from universal to task-specialized operation at runtime without retraining, using per-component importance vectors as side information to steer reconstruction fidelity to the active task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical AI systems like autonomous vehicles and robots need to exchange high-dimensional sensory data under tight bandwidth, latency, and energy constraints. Task-specific codecs are brittle when the downstream task evolves, and retraining a new codec per task is infeasible in the field.

Method: UniTAC abstracts the task as a per-component importance vector (derived from gradient attribution of downstream models) transmitted as low-overhead side information. Trained once over a broad family of such vectors against weighted-reconstruction distortion, it keeps a fixed backbone and single human-viewable reconstruction whose fidelity is steered by swapping the injected importance vector. The authors analyze weighted rate-distortion problems, characterize task-consistent distortion measures, and design a Vision Transformer codec with token-level conditioning.

Result: On a localized task at 0.034 bits per pixel, a single UniTAC model achieves 91.4% accuracy, only 1.9% below task-based codec (93.3%) and significantly above universal codecs (76.9%). The approach enables task-adaptive compression without retraining.

Conclusion: UniTAC successfully bridges the gap between universal and task-specialized image codecs, enabling runtime task adaptation without model retraining by using task importance vectors as conditioning information. This provides a practical solution for physical AI systems that need to adapt compression to evolving downstream tasks under resource constraints.

Abstract: Physical AI systems such as autonomous vehicles and robots rely on timely exchange of high-dimensional sensory signals under tight bandwidth, latency, and energy budgets. Because the task driving downstream decisions evolves over time, a task-specific codec is brittle and retraining one per task is infeasible in the field. We propose UniTAC, a single learned image codec spanning universal (task-agnostic) to task-specialized operation, re-targeted at runtime without retraining. The task is abstracted as a per-component importance vector, derived, e.g., from gradient attribution of any downstream model, and transmitted as low-overhead side information that conditions both encoder and decoder. Trained once over a broad, randomized family of such vectors against weighted-reconstruction distortion, UniTAC keeps a fixed backbone and a single human-viewable reconstruction whose fidelity is steered to the active task by swapping the injected vector. We analyze the underlying weighted rate-distortion problem, characterizing when a diagonal weighted distortion is task-consistent and how weights relate to task sensitivity. Guided by this, we design a Vision Transformer (ViT) codec whose token-level conditioning natively realizes this weight-driven code. On a localized task at 0.034 bpp, a single UniTAC model reaches 91.4% accuracy, only 1.9% below a task-based codec (93.3%) and above universal codecs (76.9%).

</details>


### [389] [Learning to Unlearn: Machine Unlearning via Learning the Unlearning Behaviors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16700)
*Hang Zhang,Kaifeng Zhang,Yixiao Ma,Weijie Xu,Ye Zhu,Kai Ming Ting*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Learning-to-UnLearn (L2UL) introduces a learning-based, model-agnostic approach for machine unlearning that learns efficient unlearning behaviors from data distributions, achieving accuracy comparable to retraining with better computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods suffer from high computational costs when dealing with massive training data, as complex unlearning functions become bottlenecks even for smaller models. There's a need for more efficient unlearning approaches that can handle data-intensive scenarios while maintaining privacy compliance.

Method: The paper proposes Learning-to-UnLearn (L2UL), the first learning-based model-agnostic approach inspired by Learning to Optimize. Instead of manually designing complex unlearning functions, L2UL learns unlearning behaviors from a distribution perspective to acquire simple and efficient unlearning functions via learning.

Result: Experimental results show L2UL achieves accuracy comparable to retraining while exhibiting impressive efficiency, particularly in data-intensive scenarios. The method also demonstrates good performance and scalability on larger models like ResNet.

Conclusion: L2UL provides an effective learning-based alternative to traditional machine unlearning methods, offering comparable accuracy to retraining with significantly better computational efficiency, making it suitable for practical applications with large datasets.

Abstract: Various machine unlearning techniques have been developed in response to privacy legislation requirements, enabling individuals to exercise their legal right to have their data $D_f$ removed from a machine learning model. This process is typically accomplished via the use of an unlearning function denoted as $U$. Existing methods focus on designing an intricate $U$ to unlearn $D_f \subset D$ from a previous model $A(D)$, so that the unlearned model performs as closely as possible to the retrained model $A(D \setminus D_f)$. However, these methods often suffer from high computational costs when dealing with massive training data, as the complex structures of $U$ become a bottleneck even for models with fewer parameters.
  Inspired by Learning to Optimize, we introduce the first learning-based model-agnostic approach, Learning-to-UnLearn (L2UL). Our core insight is to shift from manually designing $U$ to learning the unlearning behaviors from a distribution perspective, thereby acquiring a simple and efficient $U$ via learning. Our experimental results demonstrate that the accuracy achieved by L2UL is comparable to that of retraining while exhibiting impressive efficiency, particularly in data-intensive scenarios. Furthermore, we validate the performance and scalability of our method on larger models ResNet.

</details>


### [390] [The Ethical Decision Head: Operationalizing Normative Ethics in Autonomous Vehicles via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16710)
*Thomas Mbrice,Ammar Ali,Sami Mian,Khai Hern Low,Eric Chen,Arshia Aghajani,Wolf Schäfer,Amin Shirangi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reinforcement learning framework (Ethical Decision Head) learns moral driving behavior from human preferences, revealing humans reward self-sacrifice over pure casualty minimization, exposing a gap between philosophical ethics and practical human judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous vehicles reach higher autonomy levels (Level 4/5), they need to handle safety-critical decisions with moral implications. Current decision systems lack ethical reasoning capabilities aligned with human values in collision scenarios.

Method: Developed Ethical Decision Head (EDH), a deep RL framework encoding ethical reasoning as differentiable reward signals. Used Proximal Policy Optimization with Bradley-Terry reward model trained on 200 collision-imminent scenarios with pairwise human preference annotations.
